content.tagline: Mountains at the heart of Asia
content.overview:
High in the middle of Asia, Afghanistan is a landlocked country of snowy mountains, dusty plains and green river valleys. It borders Pakistan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and, along a thin finger of land called the Wakhan Corridor, China. At roughly 652,000 km² it is slightly smaller than Texas, and about 40 million people live there. The capital, Kabul, sits in a bowl of mountains nearly 1,800 meters above sea level.

For thousands of years, Afghanistan was a crossroads where traders, armies and ideas passed between Persia, India and Central Asia along the Silk Road. That history left behind a mix of peoples, including Pashtuns, Tajiks, Hazaras and Uzbeks, who speak Dari, Pashto, Turkmen and other languages.

Most Afghans live in villages and farm wheat, fruit and nuts, though Kabul and other cities have grown quickly. Decades of war have made life hard, and since 2021 the country has been ruled by the Taliban movement.
content.landAndNature:
The Hindu Kush mountains run like a spine across the country, with peaks above 7,000 meters in the far northeast. Rivers such as the Kabul, Helmand and Amu Darya flow out of the snowfields to water valleys where farmers grow pomegranates, grapes, apricots and almonds. In the southwest lie the sandy Registan Desert and salt flats, while the north opens into rolling grassland.

Winters are bitterly cold and summers hot and dry. Snow leopards, Marco Polo sheep with huge curling horns, ibex and wolves live in the high mountains. Band-e-Amir, a chain of six deep-blue lakes held back by natural dams of mineral rock, became the country's first national park in 2009.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Dari (a form of Persian) and Pashto are the main languages, and nearly everyone is Muslim. Hospitality is a serious matter: guests are offered green tea, nuts and dried fruit the moment they arrive. Flat naan bread comes with almost every meal, and the national dish, Kabuli pulao, is rice cooked with carrots, raisins and lamb.

Afghans have flown kites for centuries, and kite fighting, where flyers try to cut each other's strings, is a beloved pastime. The traditional sport buzkashi is played on horseback, with riders wrestling for a goat carcass. Poetry is treasured; the famous poet Rumi was born near Balkh in the 1200s. Nowruz, the spring new year, is celebrated with music, picnics and the attan, a whirling circle dance.
content.history:
People have lived here for tens of thousands of years, and the region of Bactria was rich long before Alexander the Great marched through around 330 BC. Buddhism flourished later; giant Buddha statues were carved into a cliff at Bamiyan in the 500s. Islam arrived in the 600s and 700s.

The modern state began in 1747 when Ahmad Shah Durrani united the tribes. In the 1800s Britain fought three wars trying to control Afghanistan but never fully succeeded. The country was a monarchy until 1973. In 1979 the Soviet Union invaded, starting a ten-year war, followed by civil war and Taliban rule from 1996. After the attacks of September 11, 2001, a US-led coalition removed the Taliban and a republic was set up. The Taliban returned to power in 2021 when foreign troops left.
funFacts: Lapis lazuli, the deep-blue stone used in ancient Egyptian jewelry, has been mined in Afghanistan's Badakhshan province for more than 6,000 years.
The two giant Buddhas of Bamiyan, about 55 and 38 meters tall, stood for 1,400 years before the Taliban destroyed them in 2001.
Afghanistan is famous for pomegranates; the fruit from Kandahar is considered among the sweetest in the world.
The Afghan hound, a dog with long silky hair, was bred to hunt in cold mountain country.
In buzkashi, the national sport, horseback riders battle to carry a goat carcass across a goal line.
The Wakhan Corridor is so narrow that in places the country is only about 15 kilometers wide.

content.tagline: Home of the giant sable antelope
content.overview:
Angola stretches along the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa, covering about 1.25 million square kilometers, nearly twice the size of Texas. Its capital, Luanda, is a bustling port city of high-rise towers and crowded neighborhoods that is one of the largest cities in Africa. Around 36 million people live in Angola, making it the most populous Portuguese-speaking country on the continent. A small separate piece of the country, Cabinda, lies to the north, cut off from the rest by a strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Angola is rich in oil and diamonds, and the money they bring has built gleaming office blocks in Luanda, although many Angolans still live in poverty in the countryside and in city outskirts. The country is a republic with an elected president and parliament. After decades of war that ended in 2002, Angolans have been rebuilding roads, railways, and schools, and a young population, more than half under 20, is shaping a fast-changing nation known for its music and dance.
content.landAndNature: From a narrow, dry coastal plain the land climbs steeply to a vast central highland, the planalto, where most people farm. Mount Moco, the highest point, reaches about 2,600 meters. Great rivers begin here: the Cuanza flows to the Atlantic, the Cubango wanders southeast to feed Botswana's Okavango Delta, and the mighty Congo River forms part of the northern border. In the far south the Namib Desert crosses in from Namibia, home to the welwitschia, a plant with two leathery leaves that can live for more than a thousand years. The Kalandula Falls on the Lucala River plunge over 100 meters in a wide curtain. Angola's national symbol is the giant sable antelope, with curved horns over 1.5 meters long, which was feared extinct until it was rediscovered in 2004.
content.peopleAndCulture: The largest groups are the Ovimbundu, Ambundu, and Bakongo, and languages such as Umbundu, Kimbundu, and Kikongo are spoken alongside official Portuguese. Most Angolans are Christian. A typical meal centers on funge, a smooth porridge of cassava or corn, served with muamba de galinha, chicken simmered in palm oil with okra. Angola's musical influence reaches far beyond its borders: semba, an older dance style, is an ancestor of Brazil's samba, and kizomba, a smooth partner dance from the 1980s, is now taught in dance schools worldwide. Basketball is a national strength, with the men's team winning the African championship 11 times, and the soccer team is nicknamed the Palancas Negras, the black sables.
content.history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled here over a thousand years ago and built kingdoms such as Kongo and Ndongo, whose rulers held the title ngola, the source of the country's name. Portuguese ships arrived in 1483, and Luanda was founded in 1576. For about 300 years Angola was one of the main sources of enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic, especially to Brazil. Queen Nzinga of Ndongo fought the Portuguese for decades in the 1600s. A war of independence began in 1961, and Portugal withdrew in 1975. Almost immediately a civil war broke out between rival movements backed by Cold War powers; it lasted 27 years, killed hundreds of thousands, and left the land littered with mines. Peace came in 2002, followed by an oil boom.
funFacts: Angola's flag shows half a cogwheel, a machete, and a star, symbols chosen when the country became independent in 1975.
The kizomba dance craze that fills clubs from Lisbon to Los Angeles began in the neighborhoods of Luanda.
The giant sable antelope survived the civil war hidden in a remote forest and was confirmed alive by camera traps in 2004.
The welwitschia of Angola's Namib Desert grows only two leaves in its entire life, which can last over a thousand years.
Kalandula Falls is about 400 meters wide, making it one of the largest waterfalls in Africa by volume.

content.tagline: Land of the eagles
content.overview:
On the western edge of the Balkan Peninsula, Albania faces Italy across the Adriatic and Ionian Seas. It is a small country, about the size of the US state of Maryland, but it packs in snowy mountains, wild rivers, olive groves, and a long coastline of turquoise bays known as the Albanian Riviera. The capital, Tirana, is famous for apartment blocks painted in bold oranges, purples, and greens, an idea launched by a mayor who was also a painter.

About 2.8 million people live in Albania, and millions more Albanians live in neighboring Kosovo, North Macedonia, Italy, and beyond. The language, Albanian, forms its own separate branch of the Indo-European family, related to no other living tongue. For most of the 20th century the country was cut off from the world under a strict communist government, but since the early 1990s it has become a parliamentary republic, joined NATO, and applied to join the European Union. Tourism is growing fast as visitors discover its beaches and mountain villages.
content.landAndNature: Roughly seven-tenths of Albania is mountainous. In the far north rise the Albanian Alps, nicknamed the Accursed Mountains for their jagged, hard-to-cross peaks, where shepherds still move flocks to high pastures each summer. The Vjosa River flows for about 270 kilometers without a single dam, which earned it protection in 2023 as Europe's first wild-river national park. Lake Ohrid, shared with North Macedonia, is more than a million years old and home to fish found nowhere else. The coast has a warm Mediterranean climate, while inland winters bring deep snow. Brown bears, wolves, and the extremely rare Balkan lynx survive in the forests, and Dalmatian pelicans nest in the Karavasta Lagoon.
content.peopleAndCulture: Albanians speak two main dialects, Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south. Most people are Muslim, with large Orthodox and Catholic Christian communities, and the country is known for religious tolerance. Hospitality is a point of honor: an old code called besa means keeping a promise and protecting guests at any cost. Meals often begin with byrek, a flaky pastry filled with cheese or spinach, and might include tavë kosi, lamb baked with yogurt. In the south, groups sing iso-polyphony, a layered style of harmony recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is the favorite sport, and strong coffee served slowly in cafés is a daily ritual. Mother Teresa, the famous nun, was ethnically Albanian.
content.history: The Illyrians lived here more than 2,000 years ago, followed by Roman and Byzantine rule. In the 1400s the national hero Gjergj Kastrioti, known as Skanderbeg, held off the Ottoman Empire for 25 years, but Albania eventually spent more than four centuries under Ottoman control. Independence was declared in 1912. After World War II, communist leader Enver Hoxha ruled from 1944 until his death in 1985. He banned religion, sealed the borders, and had roughly 170,000 concrete bunkers built in case of invasion. Communism collapsed in 1991, and hard years of poverty and emigration followed. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and has been a candidate to join the European Union since 2014.
funFacts: Albanians call their country Shqipëri, often translated as Land of the Eagles, which explains the black double-headed eagle on the red flag.
Some of the country's 170,000 Cold War bunkers have been turned into museums, cafés, and even a hostel.
In Albania, a sideways shake of the head traditionally means yes, and a nod means no, the opposite of most of Europe.
Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes on Earth and holds about 200 species that live nowhere else.
The ancient city of Butrint has ruins from Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Venetian times layered on one small peninsula.

content.tagline: A mountain microstate with two princes
content.overview:
Tucked high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, Andorra is one of the smallest countries in the world. At 468 square kilometers it would fit inside New York City with room to spare. The capital, Andorra la Vella, sits about 1,000 meters above sea level, making it the highest capital city in Europe. Around 80,000 people live here, and most of them are not Andorran citizens but residents from Spain, Portugal, and France who came for work.

Andorra has an unusual government. It is a co-principality, meaning it has two heads of state at once: the President of France and the Catholic Bishop of Urgell in Spain. In practice a parliament called the General Council makes the laws. The official language is Catalan, the only country where that is true. Andorra earns its living from visitors, about eight million a year, who come to ski in winter, hike in summer, and shop in its tax-free stores. It uses the euro but is not a member of the European Union.
content.landAndNature: Every part of Andorra is mountainous. Three steep valleys, carved by the Valira rivers, meet at the capital, and the peaks around them top 2,900 meters at Coma Pedrosa, the highest point. Winters bring heavy snow that feeds the Grandvalira and Pal-Arinsal ski areas, while summers are mild and sunny. Dozens of small glacial lakes, called estanys, sit in high rocky basins above forests of pine and fir. Chamois, a nimble mountain goat-antelope, leap across cliffs, marmots whistle from the meadows, and golden eagles and huge bearded vultures circle overhead. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, a quiet glacial valley with no road at all, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
content.peopleAndCulture: Catalan is the official language, but Spanish, Portuguese, and French are heard everywhere, and many children grow up speaking three or four languages. Traditional dishes reflect hard mountain winters: trinxat is a hearty mash of potato, cabbage, and bacon, and escudella is a thick stew of meat, beans, and pasta served at winter festivals. On the night of the summer solstice, young people carry blazing torches down the mountainsides in the falles, a fire festival recognized by UNESCO. Tiny Romanesque stone churches with slender bell towers, some nearly a thousand years old, dot the villages. Skiing is the national sport, and Andorra sends a small team to every Olympic Games.
content.history: Legend says the emperor Charlemagne granted Andorra its first charter in the 800s, and the national anthem still praises him. Real records begin in 1278, when a dispute between a French count and the Bishop of Urgell was settled by agreeing to share power over the valleys. That arrangement, with the count's rights passing over time to the French head of state, has lasted more than 700 years, making Andorra one of the oldest continuous states in Europe. For centuries its people farmed, raised sheep, and grew tobacco in isolation. Andorra stayed neutral in both world wars. In 1993 it adopted its first written constitution, giving real power to an elected parliament, and joined the United Nations the same year.
funFacts: Andorra has no airport and no army; France and Spain are responsible for its defense.
The country has one of the longest life expectancies in the world, often placed in the top five.
Andorra la Vella, at over 1,000 meters, is the highest capital city in Europe.
With about eight million visitors a year, tourists outnumber residents roughly a hundred to one.
Andorra's tax-free shops make it a giant open-air mall, and its main avenue is lined with electronics and perfume stores.

content.tagline: Seven emirates of desert and skyline
content.overview:
The United Arab Emirates sits on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, with long coasts on the Persian Gulf and a short one on the Gulf of Oman, bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman. It covers about 83,600 km², a little smaller than Austria, and most of it is desert.

Roughly 10 million people live in the UAE, but only around one in ten is an Emirati citizen; the rest come from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Egypt and dozens of other countries to work. Arabic is the official language and English is used almost everywhere. Abu Dhabi is the capital and largest emirate; Dubai is the best-known city.

The country is a federation of seven emirates, each with its own ruler, joined under a president. Oil made it wealthy from the 1960s, and it has since built airlines, ports, finance and tourism, along with some of the tallest buildings in the world.
content.landAndNature: Sand dunes cover most of the interior, part of the great Rub al Khali, reaching south toward the Liwa oasis where date palms grow in long green strips. The Hajar Mountains rise in the east near Fujairah, bare and jagged, cut by wadis that flood after rare rains. Summers are extremely hot and humid along the coast, often above 45°C, and the country relies on desalinated seawater. Mangroves fringe parts of the coast and shelter flamingos and young fish, and the waters hold dugongs, second in number only to Australia's. The Arabian oryx, once hunted to extinction in the wild, was bred in captivity and returned to reserves here, and the sand gazelle and Arabian leopard survive in small numbers.
content.peopleAndCulture: Emirati culture keeps desert and sea traditions alive: falconry, which has UNESCO heritage status, camel racing with robot jockeys, and the ayyala dance, performed with rows of men swinging thin canes. Pearling was the old livelihood before oil, and dhow boats still sail the creeks. Coffee with cardamom, dates, machboos spiced rice and luqaimat, sweet fried dough balls in date syrup, are traditional foods, though restaurants serve dishes from all over the world. Most Emiratis are Muslim, and Ramadan reshapes the daily rhythm. Because the population is so international, dozens of languages are heard on a single street. Cricket, soccer and camel racing all draw crowds, and the country hosts Formula One and major tennis and golf tournaments.
content.history: Trading settlements and copper mines existed here 4,000 years ago, connected to Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. For centuries, coastal towns lived on pearl diving, fishing and trade with India and East Africa. Britain signed treaties with local rulers in the 1800s, giving the area the name Trucial States, and took charge of their foreign affairs. Japanese cultured pearls ruined the pearl trade in the 1930s, bringing hard years. Oil was discovered in Abu Dhabi in 1958. When Britain withdrew from the Gulf, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan led the union of six emirates on December 2, 1971, with Ras Al Khaimah joining in 1972. Oil income built schools, hospitals, roads and cities at remarkable speed, turning small coastal towns into global hubs within one lifetime.
funFacts: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the world's tallest building at 828 meters, with more than 160 floors.
Dubai International is one of the busiest airports in the world for international passengers.
The UAE sent a spacecraft, Hope, into orbit around Mars in 2021, the first Arab interplanetary mission.
Emirati falcons travel with their own passports and can sit in aircraft cabins on certain airlines.
The Liwa oasis grows millions of date palms, and one Emirati date festival awards prizes for the finest fruit.

content.tagline: From steaming jungle to icy Patagonia
content.overview:
Argentina stretches down the southeastern side of South America for more than 3,500 kilometers, from tropical waterfalls in the north to glaciers and windswept islands near Antarctica. It is the eighth-largest country in the world, about 2.78 million km², roughly four times the size of Texas, with about 46 million people. Its neighbors are Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay, and the Atlantic Ocean washes its long eastern coast.

Around a third of Argentines live in and around the capital, Buenos Aires, a huge city of grand avenues, cafes and tango halls on the Río de la Plata. Many families have Italian and Spanish roots, which shows in the food, the accents and the passion for soccer. Spanish is the national language, and Guaraní is also official in the northeastern province of Corrientes.

Argentina is a federal republic with an elected president. Farming and ranching on the vast grasslands called the Pampas have made it one of the world's great producers of beef, wheat and soybeans.
content.landAndNature:
The Andes form Argentina's western wall, crowned by Aconcagua, which at about 6,960 meters is the highest mountain outside Asia. East of the mountains lie the Pampas, flat, fertile grasslands that seem to run forever, and in the south the dry, windy plateau of Patagonia. In the far northeast, the Iguazú Falls thunder over 275 separate cascades on the border with Brazil.

Climate ranges from subtropical heat in the north to freezing cold in Tierra del Fuego, the island at the continent's tip. The Perito Moreno Glacier in Patagonia is famous for the towers of blue ice that crash into Lake Argentino. Wildlife includes guanacos (wild relatives of llamas), rheas, the Andean condor, Magellanic penguins, southern right whales and jaguars in the northern forests.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Argentines speak Spanish with a distinctive rhythm shaped by Italian immigrants, and "che" is a friendly way to get someone's attention. Life revolves around long meals: the asado, a slow barbecue of beef over wood coals, is a weekend ritual, along with empanadas, milanesas and dulce de leche, a caramel spread eaten on everything. Friends share mate, a bitter herbal tea sipped through a metal straw from a gourd.

Soccer is a national obsession, and Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi are treated as heroes after leading the team to World Cup wins in 1986 and 2022. Tango, born in the working-class ports of Buenos Aires in the late 1800s, is the country's signature music and dance. Gauchos, the horse-riding cowboys of the Pampas, remain a proud symbol of rural life.
content.history:
Indigenous peoples such as the Diaguita, Mapuche, Guaraní and Tehuelche lived across the land long before Spanish explorers arrived in the early 1500s. Buenos Aires was permanently founded in 1580, and the region became part of Spain's empire. On May 25, 1810, the people of Buenos Aires set up their own government, and independence was declared in 1816; General José de San Martín then led armies over the Andes to free Chile and Peru as well.

Between 1880 and 1930 millions of Europeans, especially Italians and Spaniards, arrived by ship, and Argentina became one of the richest countries on Earth. The 1900s brought political turmoil, including the popular leader Juan Perón and a military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 in which tens of thousands of people were kidnapped and killed. After a failed war with Britain over the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, democracy returned in 1983.
funFacts: The ballpoint pen was perfected and patented in Argentina in 1943 by László Bíró, a Hungarian immigrant; Argentines still call pens 'biromes.'
In 1892 Argentine police became the first in the world to solve a crime using fingerprints.
Argentinosaurus, one of the largest dinosaurs ever discovered, was found in Patagonia and may have weighed as much as ten elephants.
The country's name comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver, which early explorers hoped to find.
Ushuaia, on Tierra del Fuego, is often called the southernmost city in the world.
Buenos Aires has more bookshops per person than almost any other city on Earth.

content.tagline: An ancient land of stone and apricots
content.overview:
Armenia is a small, mountainous, landlocked country in the Caucasus, the rugged region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea where Europe and Asia meet. It borders Georgia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Türkiye. At about 29,700 km² it is roughly the size of Belgium or the US state of Maryland, and about 3 million people live there, with many more Armenians living abroad than at home.

The capital, Yerevan, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, founded as the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BC, decades before Rome. Its buildings are made of pink volcanic stone, and on clear days the snow-capped cone of Mount Ararat, which now lies across the border in Türkiye, fills the southern sky.

Armenia is a republic with an elected parliament and prime minister. Its people are proud of an alphabet, a church and a culture that have survived for more than 1,700 years despite conquests, exile and disaster.
content.landAndNature:
Almost all of Armenia sits above 1,000 meters, and its landscape is a tumble of volcanic plateaus, deep gorges and mountain ranges. Mount Aragats, an extinct volcano of about 4,090 meters, is the highest point. Lake Sevan, one of the largest high-altitude lakes in the world, covers about a twentieth of the country and is known as Armenia's "sea."

Summers are hot and dry, winters cold and snowy. Fields and orchards fill the Ararat Plain, where apricots, grapes and pomegranates ripen in the sun; the Latin name for the apricot, Prunus armeniaca, means "Armenian plum." Bezoar goats, brown bears, wolves and the rare Caucasian leopard live in the mountains, and the Armenian gull nests around Lake Sevan.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Armenian is a language with its own branch of the Indo-European family and its own 39-letter alphabet, created by the monk Mesrop Mashtots in the year 405. Most people belong to the Armenian Apostolic Church, and monasteries carved into cliffs, like Geghard and Tatev, are cherished places. Carved stone crosses called khachkars stand in churchyards all over the country.

Bread is central to every meal: thin lavash is baked against the walls of an underground clay oven, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Families share dolma, grilled khorovats meat and sweet dried fruit. The duduk, a wooden flute with a haunting sound, is the national instrument. Chess is a required school subject, and Armenia has produced several world-class grandmasters.
content.history:
The kingdom of Urartu ruled these highlands nearly 3,000 years ago, and Armenia's own kings followed. In 301, King Tiridates III made Christianity the state religion, the first country in the world to do so. For centuries afterward, Armenia was fought over by Persians, Romans, Arabs, Mongols, Ottomans and Russians, and Armenians spread out across the Middle East and Europe.

During World War I, in 1915, the Ottoman government deported and killed more than a million Armenians, a tragedy known as the Armenian Genocide. A short-lived independent republic in 1918 was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1920. Armenia declared independence again in 1991. Since then it has fought Azerbaijan over the region of Nagorno-Karabakh, which Azerbaijan took full control of in 2023, sending most of its Armenian population to Armenia.
funFacts: The world's oldest known leather shoe, about 5,500 years old, was found in Armenia's Areni cave, still laced up.
The same cave held the oldest known winery, where people were pressing grapes about 6,100 years ago.
Since 2011, chess has been a compulsory subject in Armenian primary schools.
The Wings of Tatev cable car, 5.7 kilometers long, set a world record for the longest nonstop reversible aerial tramway when it opened in 2010.
Yerevan is nicknamed the Pink City because its buildings are made of rose-colored volcanic tuff stone.
Roughly three times as many Armenians live outside Armenia as inside it.

content.tagline: A beach for every day of the year
content.overview:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small nation of two main islands in the eastern Caribbean, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Caribbean Sea. Antigua, the larger and busier island, is home to the capital, Saint John's, and nearly all of the country's roughly 100,000 people. Barbuda, about 40 kilometers to the north, is flat, quiet and ringed with pink-tinged sand. A third island, rocky Redonda, has no people at all. Together they cover just 442 km², smaller than many cities.

Islanders like to say Antigua has 365 beaches, one for every day of the year. Tourism is the biggest business, along with sailing, fishing and banking. Cruise ships dock in Saint John's beneath the white towers of the cathedral.

The country is an independent member of the Commonwealth. It has its own parliament and prime minister, while the British monarch remains head of state. English is the official language, and most people also speak a lively Antiguan Creole.
content.landAndNature:
Antigua is made mostly of limestone and old volcanic rock, with low rolling hills that rise to Boggy Peak, about 400 meters high. Because there are few rivers, the island can suffer droughts, and coral reefs sit close to shore in shallow, turquoise water. Barbuda is even lower and flatter, a coral island with a huge lagoon on its western side.

The climate is warm all year, with a rainy season from June to November that is also hurricane season; Hurricane Irma badly damaged Barbuda in 2017. Codrington Lagoon on Barbuda shelters one of the world's largest colonies of magnificent frigatebirds, whose males puff up bright red throat pouches. Hawksbill turtles nest on the beaches, and the rare Antiguan racer snake survives on tiny offshore islands.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Antiguans and Barbudans are descended from Africans brought to the islands to work on sugar plantations. English is the official language, and the local Creole is spoken at home and in songs. The national dish is fungee, a cornmeal and okra paste, served with pepperpot stew; ducana, a sweet potato dumpling, and saltfish are other favorites.

Cricket is close to a religion here. Antigua produced Sir Vivian Richards, one of the greatest batsmen ever, and the national stadium is named after him. Sailing is the other passion: Antigua Sailing Week draws yachts from around the world each spring. Carnival, held from late July into early August, celebrates the end of slavery with steel bands, calypso and soca music, and dancers in feathered costumes.
content.history:
The first people, ancestors of the Arawak and later the Kalinago, reached the islands more than 2,000 years ago, fishing and farming cassava. Christopher Columbus sailed past in 1493 and named Antigua after a church in Seville, Spain. English settlers arrived in 1632 and cut down the forests to plant sugarcane.

For two centuries, enslaved Africans did the brutal work of the plantations, and the harbor at English Harbour became a base for the British navy. Slavery was abolished in 1834, and formerly enslaved people built free villages across the island. Antigua remained a British colony until it gained full independence on November 1, 1981, with Barbuda as its partner. Since then the country has grown through tourism, and Nelson's Dockyard at English Harbour was named a World Heritage Site in 2016.
funFacts: Redonda, the country's uninhabited third island, was once mined for bird droppings, which were sold as fertilizer.
The magnificent frigatebird colony in Barbuda's Codrington Lagoon can hold several thousand birds at nesting time.
Antigua's highest hill was officially called Mount Obama from 2009 to 2016, then given back its old name, Boggy Peak.
The Antiguan racer was once called the world's rarest snake, with only about 50 left; conservation has raised the number to more than 1,000.
Barbuda's beaches look pink because they are mixed with crushed shells of tiny red sea creatures.
Nelson's Dockyard is the only working Georgian-era naval dockyard left in the world.

content.tagline: The island continent
content.overview:
Australia is the only country that covers an entire continent. It lies between the Indian and Pacific Oceans in the Southern Hemisphere, so its summer is December to February. At about 7.7 million km² it is nearly as big as the mainland United States, yet only about 26 million people live there. Most of them crowd into cities along the southeastern and eastern coasts, such as Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, while the vast, dry interior called the Outback is almost empty.

The capital is Canberra, a planned city built as a compromise when Sydney and Melbourne both wanted the job. Australia is a federation of six states and two territories, with an elected parliament and prime minister; the British monarch is head of state. English is the main language.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived here for at least 65,000 years, making theirs the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. Since 1788, immigrants from Britain, Ireland and later from all over the world have made Australia one of the most multicultural nations anywhere.
content.landAndNature:
Australia is the flattest and driest inhabited continent. Red deserts and scrubland fill the center, where the huge sandstone rock Uluru glows orange at sunset. Rainforests cling to the northeast coast, snow falls in the Australian Alps, and the fertile Murray-Darling river basin feeds farms in the southeast. Off Queensland stretches the Great Barrier Reef, the largest living structure on the planet, about 2,300 kilometers long.

Because the continent drifted alone for millions of years, its animals are unlike any others. Kangaroos, koalas and wombats carry their babies in pouches; the platypus and echidna are mammals that lay eggs. Australia also has the most venomous snakes in the world, saltwater crocodiles in the north, and eucalyptus forests that fill the air with a sharp, minty smell.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Australians are known for informal, friendly speech full of shortened words: breakfast is "brekkie," afternoon is "arvo," and almost everyone is "mate." About a quarter of the population was born overseas, so cities serve food from Greece, Vietnam, Lebanon, India and China alongside meat pies, barbecue and Vegemite spread on toast. Aboriginal art, with its dot paintings and Dreaming stories, is among the oldest art traditions in the world.

Sport is nearly a religion: cricket in summer, Australian rules football and rugby in winter, and swimming and surfing all year. The whole country stops for the Melbourne Cup horse race in November. Christmas often means a trip to the beach, and January 26 and Anzac Day (April 25) are major national days.
content.history:
Aboriginal peoples arrived at least 65,000 years ago, developing hundreds of languages and deep knowledge of the land. Torres Strait Islanders settled the northern islands. In 1770 British navigator James Cook charted the east coast, and in 1788 Britain founded a prison colony at Sydney Cove. Settlers spread across the continent, taking Indigenous land, and disease and violence killed a large share of the Aboriginal population.

Gold rushes in the 1850s drew hundreds of thousands of migrants. In 1901 the six colonies joined to form the Commonwealth of Australia. Australians fought in both world wars, and the 1915 Gallipoli campaign became a national legend. After 1945 millions of immigrants arrived from Europe and Asia. A 1967 vote gave the federal government power to make laws for Aboriginal people, and in 2008 the government formally apologized for past policies that removed Indigenous children from their families.
funFacts: Australia has more kangaroos than people, roughly two for every human.
The Dingo Fence, built to keep wild dogs away from sheep, runs about 5,600 kilometers, longer than the distance from New York to Los Angeles.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, the only animal known to do so.
In 1932 the army was sent to fight emus damaging wheat crops; the birds largely won the so-called Emu War.
The continent drifts north about 7 centimeters a year, so Australia's map coordinates have to be corrected from time to time.
Lake Hillier in Western Australia is bright bubblegum pink, probably because of salt-loving microbes.

content.tagline: Alps, waltzes, and grand old coffeehouses
content.overview:
Austria is a landlocked country in the heart of Central Europe, slightly smaller than the US state of Maine, where the Alps cover more than half the land. Its capital, Vienna, sits on the Danube River in the flat northeast and was for centuries the seat of one of Europe's most powerful royal families, the Habsburgs. Their palaces, opera houses, and grand cafés still give the city an imperial air. About 9 million people live in Austria, roughly a fifth of them in and around Vienna.

German is the official language, spoken in a distinctive Austrian accent and dialect. Austria is a federal republic of nine states with a parliament and a chancellor who leads the government. It has been officially neutral since 1955 and joined the European Union in 1995. Austrians are known for music, having produced Mozart, Haydn, Schubert, and the Strauss family of waltz composers, and for winter sports, with skiing close to a national religion. Villages of onion-domed churches and flower-decked wooden chalets fill the mountain valleys.
content.landAndNature: The Alps sweep across western and central Austria, topped by the Grossglockner at nearly 3,800 meters, with the Pasterze glacier at its foot. Hohe Tauern National Park, the largest in the Alps, shelters ibex, marmots, golden eagles, and bearded vultures that were brought back after disappearing. The Krimml Waterfalls tumble about 380 meters in three stages, among the tallest in Europe. In the north the Danube cuts through vineyards and forested hills, while the far east flattens into steppe around Lake Neusiedl, a shallow reed-fringed lake shared with Hungary and crowded with birds. Winters are snowy and cold in the mountains; summers are warm. Beneath the peaks near Werfen lies Eisriesenwelt, the largest ice cave in the world.
content.peopleAndCulture: Austrian life blends old and new. Vienna's coffeehouses, where a single cup buys hours at a marble table with newspapers, are on UNESCO's cultural heritage list. Favorite foods include Wiener schnitzel, a thin breaded veal or pork cutlet, apple strudel, fluffy shredded pancakes called Kaiserschmarrn, and the chocolate Sachertorte. Every New Year's Day the Vienna Philharmonic plays waltzes to a worldwide television audience, and the winter ball season fills palaces with dancers. Salzburg hosts a famous summer music festival and was the setting for the film The Sound of Music. Austrian skiers have won more Alpine World Cup races than any other nation, and children in mountain villages often ski before they can read. Traditional dirndl dresses and lederhosen appear at festivals.
content.history: Celts and then Romans settled the region, founding Vindobona, which became Vienna. From 1278 the Habsburg family ruled Austria for more than 600 years, expanding into an empire that stretched across Central Europe and twice fought off Ottoman armies at the gates of Vienna, in 1529 and 1683. The assassination of the Habsburg heir Franz Ferdinand in 1914 triggered World War I, and the empire collapsed in 1918. The small new republic was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938, and Austrian Jews suffered persecution and murder in the Holocaust. After World War II the country was occupied by the Allies until 1955, when it regained independence by promising permanent neutrality. Austria joined the European Union in 1995 and adopted the euro.
funFacts: The snow globe was invented in Vienna in 1900 by a man trying to make a brighter surgical lamp.
The Christmas carol Silent Night was first sung in 1818 in the small Austrian town of Oberndorf.
Vienna's Schönbrunn Zoo opened in 1752 and is the oldest zoo in the world still operating.
PEZ candy was created in Vienna in 1927 as a breath mint for adults; the name comes from Pfefferminz, German for peppermint.
The Eisriesenwelt ice cave stretches for about 42 kilometers, and its ice never fully melts.

content.tagline: The Land of Fire
content.overview:
Azerbaijan sits on the western shore of the Caspian Sea, the world's largest lake, where the Caucasus Mountains slope down to the water. It borders Russia, Georgia, Armenia and Iran, and a separate piece of the country, Nakhchivan, lies to the southwest, cut off from the rest by Armenian territory. The whole country covers about 86,600 km², slightly larger than Austria, with roughly 10 million people.

Natural gas seeps out of the ground here and sometimes burns for years, which is why Azerbaijan has been called the Land of Fire since ancient times. Oil made the capital, Baku, rich more than a century ago, and today its old walled city stands beside glass skyscrapers shaped like flames.

Most people are Azerbaijanis, who speak a Turkic language close to Turkish, and Russian is widely understood. The country is a republic with a strong presidency. Its economy depends heavily on selling oil and gas, and its people love tea, chess, carpets and music.
content.landAndNature:
Azerbaijan packs an unusual variety of climates into a small space, from the snowy Greater Caucasus in the north, where Bazardüzü rises above 4,400 meters, to humid, tea-growing lowlands near Lənkəran and dry semi-desert around Baku. The Kura and Aras rivers water a wide central plain of cotton fields and orchards.

Along the Caspian coast, mud volcanoes gurgle and burp gray sludge; the country has about 400 of them, more than anywhere else on Earth. Near Baku, the hillside of Yanar Dağ has burned nonstop for decades on escaping gas. The Caspian is home to sturgeon, the ancient fish whose eggs become caviar, and to a rare freshwater seal. In the mountains live brown bears, lynx, and the tough Karabakh horse, the national animal.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Azerbaijani, written in Latin letters, is the national language, and most people are Shia Muslims, though society is largely secular. Tea is served in pear-shaped glasses with jam or sugar cubes, and meals center on plov (saffron rice with meat and dried fruit), dolma and kebabs. Novruz, the spring new year, brings bonfires, painted eggs and trays of sweet pastries like pakhlava and shekerbura.

Azerbaijani carpets, woven in bold reds and blues, are so admired that UNESCO lists the craft as a cultural treasure. Mugham, a soulful improvised music, is performed with the tar and kamancha stringed instruments. Chess is hugely popular; the champion Garry Kasparov grew up in Baku. Since 2016 the streets of the capital have hosted a Formula 1 Grand Prix.
content.history:
Ancient peoples carved thousands of rock pictures at Gobustan, some more than 10,000 years old, and the region was later part of the kingdom of Caucasian Albania. Fire worship was strong in Persian times, and the Ateshgah fire temple near Baku still stands. Islam arrived in the 600s, followed by Turkic peoples who shaped the language.

Russia took the region from Persia in the early 1800s, and by 1900 Baku's oil fields produced about half the world's oil. In 1918 the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic became the first secular republic in the Muslim world and gave women the vote, but the Soviet army took over in 1920. Azerbaijan regained independence in 1991. It then fought Armenia over the mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh, losing control in the 1990s and winning it back in wars in 2020 and 2023.
funFacts: Baku lies about 28 meters below sea level, making it the lowest-lying national capital in the world.
Azerbaijan has around 400 mud volcanoes, roughly a third of all the mud volcanoes on Earth.
The world's first industrial oil well was drilled at Bibi-Heybat near Baku in 1846.
Yanar Dağ, the Burning Mountain, has flamed continuously since at least the 1950s, fed by natural gas leaking from the ground.
The Maiden Tower in Baku's old city is about 29 meters tall and around 900 years old, though nobody is sure what it was built for.
Azerbaijan claims nine of the world's eleven climate zones, from subtropical to alpine tundra.

content.tagline: Heart of Africa's drum tradition
content.overview:
Burundi is a small, hilly country in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, about the size of Maryland, pressed between Rwanda, Tanzania, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its southwestern edge dips into Lake Tanganyika, the second-deepest lake in the world. Burundi is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa: about 13 million people live here, and nearly every hillside is terraced with fields of beans, bananas, cassava, and coffee.

The political capital is Gitega, in the center of the country, while the much larger city of Bujumbura on the lakeshore remains the economic hub. Kirundi is spoken by almost everyone, and French is also official; Swahili is common in trade. Burundi is a republic with a president and parliament. It is one of the poorest countries in the world, and most families live by farming small plots. Yet it is famous for something joyful: its royal drummers, whose thunderous performances, with drums balanced on the players' heads, are known around the globe.
content.landAndNature: Burundi rises steeply from Lake Tanganyika, at about 770 meters, to a high central plateau and mountains that top 2,600 meters at Mount Heha. Because of the altitude, the climate is mild for a place so close to the equator, with two rainy seasons feeding rivers and the green hills that give the country its nickname, the land of a thousand hills, shared with Rwanda. One of the southernmost sources of the Nile is a spring near Rutovu. Lake Tanganyika holds hundreds of brightly colored cichlid fish found nowhere else, and hippos and crocodiles live along its shores. Kibira National Park, a mountain rainforest, shelters chimpanzees and colobus monkeys, while Rusizi park's marshes attract flamingos and other waterbirds.
content.peopleAndCulture: Burundians belong mainly to the Hutu and Tutsi groups, with a small Twa community, all sharing the Kirundi language and many customs. Most people are Christian. Daily meals are simple: beans, sweet potatoes, cassava, plantains, and a stiff porridge called ugali, with fish from the lake near the shore. Sharing a jug of banana or sorghum beer through long straws is a sign of friendship. The Royal Drummers of Burundi, recognized by UNESCO, perform with heavy drums carved from tree trunks; dancers leap while the karyenda drum, once a sacred symbol of the king, keeps the rhythm. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Burundian long-distance runners have competed strongly at the Olympics, winning gold in 1996.
content.history: The Kingdom of Burundi formed by the 1600s under a line of kings called mwami, ruling Hutu farmers, Tutsi cattle herders, and Twa hunters. Germany claimed the area in the 1890s, and after World War I Belgium ruled it together with Rwanda, favoring the Tutsi minority for positions of power and deepening divisions. Burundi became independent on July 1, 1962, at first as a kingdom, then as a republic in 1966. Decades of violence between Hutu and Tutsi followed, including mass killings in 1972 and a civil war from 1993 to 2005 in which about 300,000 people died. A peace agreement brought a power-sharing government. Political tensions rose again after 2015, and many Burundians fled abroad. In 2019 the capital was officially moved from Bujumbura to Gitega.
funFacts: Burundian drummers balance drums weighing dozens of kilograms on their heads while walking, dancing, and playing.
Lake Tanganyika is nearly 1,500 meters deep and holds about one-sixth of the world's fresh surface water.
A pyramid monument near Rutovu marks a spring that Burundians call the southernmost source of the Nile.
Burundi and Rwanda both use the nickname land of a thousand hills.
Vénuste Niyongabo won Burundi's first Olympic gold medal in the 5,000 meters at the 1996 Atlanta Games.

content.tagline: Chocolate, comics, and the capital of Europe
content.overview:
Belgium is a small, crowded country on the North Sea, about the size of Maryland, squeezed between France, the Netherlands, Germany, and Luxembourg. Nearly 12 million people live here, which makes it one of the most densely populated countries in Europe. It is really two main regions in one: Flanders in the north, where people speak Dutch, and Wallonia in the south, where they speak French. A small community in the east speaks German, so Belgium has three official languages. The capital, Brussels, is officially bilingual.

Brussels is also the home of the European Union's main institutions and the headquarters of NATO, which is why it is often called the capital of Europe. Belgium is a federal constitutional monarchy with a king and a parliament. Belgians are famous for chocolate, waffles, fries served with mayonnaise, hundreds of kinds of beer, and comic-strip heroes like Tintin and the Smurfs. The medieval cities of Bruges and Ghent, with their canals and stepped-gable houses, look much as they did 500 years ago.
content.landAndNature: Belgium slopes gently upward from the sea. Along its short 67-kilometer coast run wide sandy beaches and dunes, backed by flat polder farmland that was once drained from the sea. Central Belgium is a fertile plateau of farms and towns cut by the Scheldt and Meuse rivers. In the southeast rise the Ardennes, a rolling region of dense forests, rocky river gorges, and peat bogs; the highest point, the Signal de Botrange, is just 694 meters. Wild boar and red deer roam the Ardennes woods. The climate is mild and famously rainy. Each April the Hallerbos forest near Brussels turns into a carpet of purple-blue bluebells that draws visitors from around the world.
content.peopleAndCulture: Belgians take food seriously. Fries, which Belgians insist they invented, are sold in paper cones from street stands, moules-frites pairs them with mussels, and chocolate pralines were created in Brussels in 1912. Trappist monks brew some of the world's most respected beers, and Belgian beer culture is on UNESCO's heritage list. Comics are treated as an art form: Hergé created Tintin, Peyo drew the Smurfs, and Brussels is decorated with dozens of giant comic murals. At the Carnival of Binche, men in wax masks and ostrich-feather hats throw oranges to the crowd. The saxophone was invented by Belgian Adolphe Sax. Cycling legend Eddy Merckx and the national soccer team, the Red Devils, are sporting heroes, and painters Van Eyck, Rubens, and Magritte were all Belgian.
content.history: Julius Caesar wrote about the Belgae, Celtic tribes who lived here 2,000 years ago. In the Middle Ages, cloth-making towns like Bruges and Ghent were among the richest in Europe. The region then passed through Burgundian, Spanish, Austrian, French, and Dutch hands; Napoleon was finally defeated at Waterloo, just south of Brussels, in 1815. Belgium won independence from the Netherlands in 1830 and chose Leopold I as king. King Leopold II ran the Congo in Africa as his personal property from 1885 to 1908, a brutal period in which millions of Congolese died; Belgium then ruled it as a colony until 1960. Germany invaded neutral Belgium in both world wars, and the trenches of Flanders and the Battle of the Bulge in the Ardennes are remembered worldwide. Belgium helped found the European Union.
funFacts: Belgium's highway network is lit so brightly at night that astronauts can pick it out from space.
In 2010 and 2011 Belgium went 541 days without an elected government, a world record at the time.
The Atomium in Brussels, built for the 1958 World's Fair, is a 102-meter model of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.
The town of Spa gave the world the word spa; its mineral springs have drawn visitors since the 1300s.
Continental Europe's first passenger railway opened in Belgium in 1835, running between Brussels and Mechelen.

content.tagline: Birthplace of Vodun and warrior queens
content.overview:
Benin is a narrow country in West Africa, shaped a little like a raised torch, running north from a short Atlantic coast toward the Niger River. It is slightly smaller than Pennsylvania and shares borders with Togo, Nigeria, Burkina Faso, and Niger. About 14 million people live here. The official capital is Porto-Novo, but the government mostly works from Cotonou, the largest city and a busy port where swarms of yellow-shirted motorcycle-taxi drivers, called zemidjans, weave through traffic.

French is the official language, and dozens of local languages, including Fon, Yoruba, and Bariba, are spoken at home and in markets. Most people farm, growing cotton, cashews, corn, and yams, or trade across the Nigerian border. Benin is a presidential republic and has been one of West Africa's more stable democracies since a peaceful change of government in 1991. It is known as the birthplace of Vodun, a religion later carried to the Americas, and as the home of the powerful kingdom of Dahomey and its famous female warriors.
content.landAndNature: Behind the sandy coast lie lagoons and Lake Nokoué, where the village of Ganvié stands entirely on stilts over the water, with children paddling canoes to school. Inland the ground rises through farmland and patches of forest to a dry plateau. In the northwest the rugged Atakora hills reach about 650 meters. The far north belongs to the savanna: Pendjari and W national parks, part of the largest protected wilderness in West Africa, hold elephants, lions, cheetahs, hippos, and antelope among baobabs and tall grasses. Rain falls in two seasons in the south and one short season in the north, where the dusty harmattan wind blows from the Sahara in winter.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Fon are the largest people, followed by the Yoruba, Adja, Bariba, and Fulani, and the Somba of the northwest, who build clay fortress homes called tata somba with granaries on the roof. Vodun, a religion honoring spirits of nature and ancestors, has a national holiday on January 10 and lives side by side with Christianity and Islam. Meals are built around pâte, a firm corn dough, dipped into sauces of okra, tomato, or peanut, with fried plantains and grilled fish. Yoruba communities stage Gelede masquerades with tall carved masks. Singer Angélique Kidjo, a multiple Grammy winner, is Benin's most famous musician. Soccer is the favorite sport, and the national team is nicknamed the Squirrels.
content.history: Around 1600 the Fon founded the Kingdom of Dahomey, whose kings ruled from palaces at Abomey and kept an all-female army, the Agojie, feared across the region. The coastal town of Ouidah became one of the busiest slave-trading ports in Africa; more than a million captives passed through its Door of No Return to ships bound for Brazil, Haiti, and the United States. France conquered Dahomey in the 1890s after fierce resistance from King Béhanzin. Independence came on August 1, 1960. Coups followed, and from 1972 to 1990 a military-Marxist government ruled and renamed the country Benin after the nearby bight, or bay. A 1990 national conference launched a peaceful return to democracy that inspired other African nations. In 2021 France returned 26 royal treasures looted from Abomey.
funFacts: Ganvié, built on stilts in Lake Nokoué, is home to about 20,000 people and is sometimes called the Venice of Africa.
The Agojie women warriors of Dahomey inspired the 2022 movie The Woman King.
Benin is not the same as Benin City in Nigeria, which was the capital of a different ancient kingdom.
The name Porto-Novo means new port in Portuguese, a reminder of the traders who arrived in the 1500s.
The Royal Palaces of Abomey have walls decorated with colored clay reliefs telling the story of each king.

content.tagline: Land of upright people
content.overview:
Burkina Faso is a landlocked country in the heart of West Africa, roughly the size of Colorado, surrounded by six neighbors: Mali, Niger, Benin, Togo, Ghana, and Ivory Coast. Its name, chosen in 1984, combines words from two local languages and means land of upright, or honest, people. The capital, Ouagadougou, is a sprawling, low-rise city where bicycles and motorbikes outnumber cars and where Africa's largest film festival is held every two years.

About 23 million people live in Burkina Faso, and most of them farm small plots of millet, sorghum, corn, and cotton or raise cattle and goats. French is the official language, but Mooré, Dioula, and Fulfulde are heard far more often in markets and homes. Gold mining has become a major industry. The country has faced serious hardship: since 2015 armed groups have attacked villages in the north and east, forcing more than two million people from their homes, and the military took power in coups in 2022. Despite this, Burkinabè are known for warmth, music, and craftsmanship.
content.landAndNature: Most of Burkina Faso is a flat, gently rolling plateau of savanna dotted with baobab, shea, and acacia trees. The dry north edges into the Sahel, the semi-desert belt below the Sahara, where the harmattan wind coats everything in fine dust from November to February. The wetter southwest has sandstone cliffs, waterfalls at Banfora, and the strange rock formations of the Sindou Peaks. Three rivers give the country its old name, Upper Volta: the Black, White, and Red Volta, all flowing south into Ghana. Elephants, hippos, and antelope live in the Arly and W national parks in the southeast, and sacred crocodiles in the village pond at Bazoulé are fed by local people who consider them protectors.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Mossi are the largest people, and their traditional king, the Mogho Naaba, still holds a ceremony in Ouagadougou every Friday morning. Other groups include the Fulani herders, the Bobo, Gurunsi, and Lobi, whose painted mud houses and carved masks are admired worldwide. Most people are Muslim, with large Christian and traditional-religion communities living peacefully together. Tô, a thick millet or sorghum porridge, is eaten with peanut or okra sauce, and riz gras is a festive one-pot rice dish. Music built on the balafon, a wooden xylophone with gourd resonators, and the djembe drum fills celebrations. The FESPACO festival makes Ouagadougou the capital of African cinema, and soccer is the national passion; the team is called the Stallions.
content.history: Farming peoples settled the region thousands of years ago, and the ruins at Loropéni, stone walls over a thousand years old, show that trading towns once thrived on gold routes across the Sahara. From about the 1400s the Mossi built strong kingdoms with cavalry armies that resisted invaders for centuries. France conquered the area in the 1890s and made it the colony of Upper Volta. Independence came on August 5, 1960. A series of military coups followed. In 1983 a young officer named Thomas Sankara took power, renamed the country Burkina Faso, launched vaccination and tree-planting campaigns, and became a hero to many before he was assassinated in 1987. Blaise Compaoré then ruled for 27 years until protests forced him out in 2014. Since 2015 the country has struggled with violence from armed groups.
funFacts: Ouagadougou is often called the bicycle capital of Africa because so many residents cycle to work and school.
FESPACO, held in Ouagadougou since 1969, is the largest film festival on the African continent.
The ruins of Loropéni, with stone walls up to six meters high, are more than a thousand years old.
Villagers at Bazoulé sit on and feed the sacred crocodiles in their pond, which have never been known to attack them.
A person from Burkina Faso is called Burkinabè, a word that mixes three different languages.

content.tagline: Where great rivers meet the sea
content.overview:
Bangladesh is a low, green land built by rivers. The mighty Ganges (called the Padma here), the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) and the Meghna flow down from the Himalayas and spread into the largest river delta on Earth before reaching the Bay of Bengal. India wraps around the country on three sides, with a short border with Myanmar in the southeast.

Although it is only about 147,600 km², roughly the size of the US state of Iowa, Bangladesh is home to about 170 million people, making it one of the most crowded countries in the world. Nearly everyone speaks Bengali, also called Bangla, and most people are Muslim. The capital, Dhaka, is a city of some 20 million, famous for its swarms of colorful bicycle rickshaws.

Bangladesh is a parliamentary republic. Farming rice and jute remains important, but the country has become the world's second-largest maker of clothing, and its economy has grown fast in recent decades despite the constant challenge of floods and cyclones.
content.landAndNature:
Most of Bangladesh lies less than 10 meters above sea level, a vast floodplain of rice paddies crisscrossed by hundreds of rivers. Every summer the monsoon rains and melting Himalayan snow swell the rivers, and about a fifth of the country floods, leaving behind rich soil. Cyclones spinning up from the Bay of Bengal can drive seawater far inland. Only in the southeast, around Chittagong and the Hill Tracts, does the land rise into forested hills.

In the southwest, the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, spread across the delta into India. Bengal tigers prowl its muddy islands, sharing them with saltwater crocodiles, spotted deer and river dolphins. Cox's Bazar, on the southeast coast, has a sandy beach that stretches unbroken for about 120 kilometers.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Bengali is spoken by almost everyone, and Bangladeshis are so proud of it that students who died in 1952 protesting for the right to use their language are honored every February 21, now marked worldwide as International Mother Language Day. Rice and fish are eaten at nearly every meal; the silvery hilsa is the national fish, and mustard oil, chilies and lentils flavor the cooking. Sweets made from milk, such as mishti doi and roshogolla, end a meal.

Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year in April, fills the streets with processions, masks and music. Poetry and song are treasured; the poet Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthem. Cricket is the most popular sport, and kabaddi, a team tag-and-wrestling game, is the traditional national sport. Fine jamdani muslin weaving is a craft recognized by UNESCO.
content.history:
Bengal has been a rich land of farmers and traders for thousands of years, ruled by Buddhist and Hindu kingdoms such as the Pala dynasty and, from the 1200s, by Muslim sultans and later the Mughal emperors. Its fine cotton cloth was famous as far away as Rome. In 1757 the British East India Company defeated the ruler of Bengal at Plassey, and the region became the heart of British India for nearly two centuries, suffering terrible famines under colonial rule.

When India and Pakistan were divided in 1947, this mostly Muslim region became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by 1,600 kilometers of India. Bengalis grew angry at being treated as second-class, and after Pakistan's army launched a brutal crackdown in March 1971, a nine-month war of independence followed. With India's help, Bangladesh won its freedom on December 16, 1971, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
funFacts: Dhaka is called the rickshaw capital of the world, with hundreds of thousands of hand-painted cycle rickshaws on its streets.
Bangladesh is the world's second-largest exporter of clothing; a huge share of the T-shirts sold worldwide are sewn there.
The Sundarbans is the only mangrove forest on Earth where tigers live, and they are strong swimmers.
The national anthem was written by Rabindranath Tagore, who also wrote India's anthem; he is the only person to have written two.
Cox's Bazar beach runs about 120 kilometers, one of the longest natural sandy beaches in the world.
Bangladesh has about 700 rivers, and boats carry more passengers than trains in many regions.

content.tagline: Roses, rhythms, and the Black Sea
content.overview:
Bulgaria lies in southeastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, with the Danube River forming its northern border with Romania and the Black Sea washing its eastern shore. It is about the size of Tennessee. Two great mountain ranges cross the country, and between them stretch valleys of wheat, sunflowers, and roses. The capital, Sofia, sits at the foot of Vitosha Mountain, where city residents can be skiing half an hour after leaving downtown.

Around 6.5 million people live in Bulgaria, and the number has been falling as many young people move abroad for work. Bulgarian is the official language, written in the Cyrillic alphabet, which was developed by scholars in the medieval Bulgarian Empire and later spread to Russia and other Slavic lands. Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union and NATO. Its people are proud of ancient Thracian gold, Orthodox monasteries painted inside and out, and a yogurt so distinctive that a bacterium is named after the country.
content.landAndNature: The Balkan Mountains, called Stara Planina, run east to west across the middle of Bulgaria like a spine. To the south rise the Rila and Pirin ranges, where Musala, at 2,925 meters, is the highest peak in the whole Balkan Peninsula, and where glacial lakes lie in rocky bowls beneath ancient pine forests. Between the mountains, the Valley of the Roses fills with pink blossoms every May, harvested before dawn to make rose oil for perfumes. The Black Sea coast has long sandy beaches and warm summers, while the Danube plain has hot summers and cold, snowy winters. Brown bears, wolves, and chamois live in the mountains, and the Srebarna lake reserve on the Danube shelters rare Dalmatian pelicans.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Bulgarians are Orthodox Christians, with a sizable Turkish Muslim minority and Roma communities. Meals feature shopska salad of tomatoes, cucumbers, and crumbled white cheese, banitsa pastry filled with cheese and eggs, and yogurt in nearly everything, including the cold summer soup tarator. Bulgarian folk music is famous for women's choirs singing in tight, shimmering harmonies, and for dances in uneven rhythms that are tricky even for professional musicians. On March 1 people exchange martenitsa, red-and-white yarn charms worn until the first stork or blossom of spring. Kukeri dancers in shaggy costumes and bells chase away evil spirits in winter. Wrestling, weightlifting, and rhythmic gymnastics have brought many Olympic medals, and soccer is the most popular sport.
content.history: The Thracians, skilled horsemen and goldsmiths, lived here in ancient times before the Romans conquered the region. In 681 Bulgars from the east joined with local Slavs to found the First Bulgarian Empire, one of Europe's oldest states. Its scholars created the Cyrillic alphabet in the 800s and 900s. The Ottoman Empire conquered Bulgaria in 1396 and ruled for nearly 500 years; an uprising in 1876 and a war between Russia and the Ottomans led to independence in 1878. Bulgaria fought on the losing side in both world wars, though it refused to deport its Jewish citizens to Nazi camps. From 1946 to 1989 it was a communist state closely tied to the Soviet Union. Democracy returned in 1990, and Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.
funFacts: Bulgaria produces a large share of the world's rose oil; about 3,500 kilograms of petals go into one kilogram of oil.
The bacterium that turns milk into yogurt, Lactobacillus bulgaricus, is named after Bulgaria.
Bulgarians nod their heads to say no and shake them to say yes, confusing many visitors.
The Panagyurishte treasure, nine gold drinking vessels made by Thracians over 2,300 years ago, weighs more than six kilograms.
A recording of Bulgarian folk singing was carried into space in 1977 on the Voyager spacecraft's Golden Record.

content.tagline: Pearl of the Gulf
content.overview:
Bahrain is a small island country in the Persian Gulf, which Arab nations call the Arabian Gulf, tucked between Saudi Arabia and the Qatar peninsula. It is made up of one main island and about 30 smaller ones, covering roughly 765 km², about the size of New York City. A 25-kilometer causeway links it to Saudi Arabia by road.

Around 1.5 million people live in Bahrain, and more than half of them are workers from other countries, especially India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines. Most live in and around the capital, Manama, a modern city of glass towers, shopping malls and an old market called the souq. Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used in business.

Bahrain is a kingdom ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783, with a partly elected parliament. For thousands of years it grew rich from pearls fished from its shallow waters; today oil, banking and aluminum are the main industries, and it hosts the Middle East's first Formula 1 race.
content.landAndNature:
Bahrain is low, flat and dry. Its highest point, Jabal ad Dukhan or Mountain of Smoke, is only about 134 meters high. Most of the land is limestone desert, but freshwater springs once bubbled up from underground, even beneath the sea, which is why the name Bahrain means "two seas" in Arabic. Those springs watered date palm groves along the northern coast.

Summers are scorching and humid, often above 40 degrees Celsius, while winters are mild. Land has been reclaimed from the sea to build new neighborhoods. Offshore, the Hawar Islands are home to a huge colony of Socotra cormorants and to dugongs, gentle sea mammals that graze on seagrass. In the middle of the desert stands the Tree of Life, a lone mesquite tree about 400 years old with no obvious water source.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Bahrainis are Arabs, most of them Muslim, and Arabic is the language of daily life alongside English, Hindi, Urdu and Tagalog spoken by foreign workers. The national dish, machboos, is spiced rice with chicken, lamb or fish; sweet, gooey halwa flavored with saffron and rosewater is a favorite treat, and strong Arabic coffee is offered to every guest.

The pearl-diving past lives on in fidjeri songs, which crews of divers once sang on their boats. Falconry, camel racing and horse racing are traditional pastimes, while soccer is the most popular modern sport. The Bahrain Grand Prix has drawn Formula 1 fans since 2004. Ramadan is a time of evening feasts, and Eid holidays fill the streets with families and sweets.
content.history:
About 4,000 years ago Bahrain was the center of Dilmun, a trading civilization that linked Mesopotamia to the Indus Valley; tens of thousands of its burial mounds still dot the island. Persians, Greeks and Arab tribes ruled in turn, and Islam arrived in the 600s. Pearls from Bahrain were prized across the ancient world.

The Portuguese seized the island in 1521 and built a fort that still stands; Persian rulers followed, and in 1783 the Al Khalifa family took control. From 1861 Bahrain was a British protectorate, and in 1932 it became the first country on the Arab side of the Gulf to strike oil. Independence came in 1971. The ruler declared Bahrain a kingdom in 2002 and created an elected parliament. Large protests demanding more democracy in 2011 were put down with help from neighboring countries.
funFacts: The Bahrain Fort, or Qal'at al-Bahrain, sits on a mound built up from 4,000 years of layered settlements.
Bahrain was the first Gulf Arab state to find oil, in 1932, and it built the region's first oil refinery.
The King Fahd Causeway to Saudi Arabia is about 25 kilometers long and took four years to build.
The Tree of Life has survived roughly 400 years in bare desert, and scientists still debate where it gets its water.
Bahrain's Formula 1 race in 2004 was the first Grand Prix ever held in the Middle East.
The whole country is smaller than New York City, yet it has more than 30 islands.

content.tagline: Seven hundred islands in a turquoise sea
content.overview:
The Bahamas is a sprawling chain of about 700 islands and 2,400 tiny coral islets, called cays, scattered across the Atlantic Ocean southeast of Florida and north of Cuba. Only about 30 of the islands have people on them. The land adds up to roughly 13,900 km², a little smaller than the US state of Connecticut, but the islands spread across an area of sea the size of a large country.

About 400,000 Bahamians live here, and two-thirds of them are on New Providence Island, home to the capital, Nassau. Grand Bahama, the Abacos, Eleuthera, Andros and the Exumas are among the other well-known islands.

The shallow, sunlit sea gives the water a glowing blue-green color and supports fishing, boating and a huge tourism industry, along with international banking. The Bahamas is an independent country in the Commonwealth, with an elected parliament and prime minister; the British monarch is head of state. English is the official language.
content.landAndNature:
The islands are low and flat, built from coral limestone; the highest point, Mount Alvernia on Cat Island, is only about 63 meters tall. The name may come from the Spanish "baja mar," meaning shallow sea, and the surrounding banks are so shallow that the water appears almost white from the air. Pine forests cover the northern islands, and mangroves line quiet lagoons.

The climate is warm year-round, moderated by trade winds and the Gulf Stream, though hurricanes strike some years; Hurricane Dorian caused terrible damage in 2019. Andros has the world's third-largest barrier reef and hundreds of blue holes, deep underwater caves. Great Inagua hosts some 80,000 West Indian flamingos, the national bird. Bahamian rock iguanas, hutias and hawksbill turtles are among the native animals.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Bahamians are descendants of enslaved Africans, and their English is flavored with a warm island dialect. The sea shapes the menu: conch (pronounced "konk"), a large sea snail, is eaten raw in salad, fried as cracked conch or in fritters, alongside grouper, peas and rice, and johnnycake bread.

The country's great festival is Junkanoo, a parade of drums, cowbells, whistles and enormous crepe-paper costumes that fills the streets of Nassau in the early hours of December 26 and New Year's Day. Its roots reach back to celebrations by enslaved people who were given a few days off at Christmas. Sloop sailing races are the national sport, and Bahamian sprinters and swimmers have won Olympic gold medals. Rake-and-scrape music is played on goatskin drums and a carpenter's saw.
content.history:
The Lucayan people, relatives of the Taíno, settled the islands about a thousand years ago. On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas on a Bahamian island he called San Salvador. Within a few decades the Spanish had carried off the Lucayans as slaves, leaving the islands empty.

English settlers arrived in 1648, and in the early 1700s Nassau became a notorious pirate base used by Blackbeard and others until Britain restored order in 1718. After the American Revolution, loyalists moved in with enslaved Africans to grow cotton. Slavery was abolished in 1834. During US Prohibition and later with tourism, the islands prospered. The Bahamas became independent on July 10, 1973, and has been one of the most stable democracies in the region since.
funFacts: Dean's Blue Hole on Long Island plunges about 202 meters, one of the deepest known underwater sinkholes in the world.
On Big Major Cay in the Exumas, a colony of feral pigs swims out to greet arriving boats.
The Bahamas has no rivers at all; fresh water comes from rain trapped in the porous limestone.
Harbour Island is famous for a beach of pale pink sand colored by the shells of tiny marine animals.
The Andros Barrier Reef is the third-largest in the world, about 300 kilometers long.
Junkanoo costumes can weigh more than the dancers wearing them and take months to build from cardboard and crepe paper.

content.tagline: Where minarets and church towers share the skyline
content.overview:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a roughly heart-shaped country in the western Balkans, about the size of Costa Rica, wrapped by Croatia, Serbia, and Montenegro. Bosnia is the larger, mountainous northern part; Herzegovina is the sunnier southern region around the city of Mostar. The country touches the Adriatic Sea at just one spot, a 20-kilometer stretch of coast at the town of Neum. The capital, Sarajevo, lies in a long valley ringed by mountains that hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.

About 3.3 million people live here, belonging mainly to three groups: Bosniaks, who are mostly Muslim; Serbs, mostly Orthodox Christian; and Croats, mostly Catholic. Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are all official languages and are so close that everyone understands one another. Because of a peace agreement that ended a war in 1995, the country has an unusually complex government, with two self-governing regions and a three-person presidency that rotates the top job. Life today centers on family, slow coffee, and rebuilt old towns.
content.landAndNature: The Dinaric Alps cover most of the country, rising to Maglić at 2,386 meters on the border with Montenegro. In Sutjeska National Park, the Perućica forest is one of the last primeval forests in Europe, where beech and fir trees have never been logged. Rivers are a special glory: the Neretva runs a startling emerald green through Herzegovina, the Una spills over wide travertine waterfalls, and the Drina slices through deep canyons. Karst limestone hides caves like Vjetrenica, home to blind cave creatures. Brown bears, wolves, and chamois live in the highlands, and Hutovo Blato wetlands shelter thousands of migrating birds. Inland winters are snowy; Herzegovina has hot, dry Mediterranean summers.
content.peopleAndCulture: Sarajevo is nicknamed the Jerusalem of Europe because a mosque, a Catholic cathedral, an Orthodox church, and a synagogue stand within a few minutes' walk of each other. Coffee is brewed thick in a long-handled copper pot called a džezva and sipped slowly with a sugar cube. The most loved food is ćevapi, small grilled minced-meat sausages tucked into soft somun bread with raw onion, followed by flaky burek pies and syrupy baklava. Sevdalinka, a soulful traditional song style, is often called the Bosnian blues. Every summer, divers leap 24 meters from Mostar's Old Bridge in a contest held since the 1500s. Soccer and basketball are the top sports, and the writer Ivo Andrić won the Nobel Prize for his novel The Bridge on the Drina.
content.history: A medieval Kingdom of Bosnia flourished before the Ottoman Empire conquered it in 1463; over four centuries of Ottoman rule, many Bosnians became Muslim, and mosques, bridges, and bazaars were built. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878. On June 28, 1914, the heir to the Austrian throne was shot in Sarajevo, an event that set off World War I. Bosnia then became part of Yugoslavia. When Yugoslavia broke apart, Bosnia declared independence in 1992 and a terrible war followed among its peoples. About 100,000 people died, Sarajevo endured a siege of nearly four years, and in July 1995 around 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed at Srebrenica in what courts have ruled a genocide. The Dayton Agreement ended the fighting in late 1995, and the country became a candidate to join the European Union in 2022.
funFacts: Sarajevo tested one of Europe's first electric streetcar lines in 1885, before Vienna had one.
The Tunnel of Hope, dug under Sarajevo's airport during the siege, carried food, medicine, and people in and out of the city.
Mostar's Old Bridge was destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt stone by stone using original 16th-century methods, reopening in 2004.
Red resin fills some shell craters in Sarajevo's sidewalks; locals call these memorials Sarajevo roses.
Medieval tombstones called stećci, carved with dancers, hunters, and spirals, number about 60,000 across the region.

content.tagline: Forests, marshes, and ten thousand lakes
content.overview:
Belarus is a landlocked country in Eastern Europe, wedged between Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Russia, and Ukraine. At about 207,600 square kilometers it is close to the size of Kansas, and much like Kansas it is flat, but here the plains are covered by dense forests, slow rivers, and thousands of lakes rather than wheat.
