Around 9 million people live in Belarus, and about two million of them are in the capital, Minsk, a city of wide avenues and grand Soviet-era buildings rebuilt after World War II.

Belarusian and Russian are both official languages, and Russian is what most people use day to day. Belarus was part of the Soviet Union until 1991. It is a republic with a president who has held office since 1994; elections have been widely disputed, and huge protests followed the 2020 vote. The country keeps close ties with Russia. Belarusians are known for tractors and trucks built in Minsk, a growing software industry, and a deep love of potatoes, which appear in hundreds of dishes.
content.landAndNature: Glaciers flattened Belarus long ago, leaving gentle hills, sandy soils, and about 11,000 lakes. The highest point, Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, is only 345 meters. In the south spread the Pripyat Marshes, one of the largest wetlands in Europe, where rivers overflow each spring into a watery world of reeds, storks, and rare birds. Forests cover roughly 40 percent of the country. Belavezhskaya Pushcha, an ancient forest shared with Poland, protects the largest herd of European bison, the continent's heaviest land animal, along with wolves, lynx, and moose. Major rivers include the Dnieper and the Neman. The 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighboring Ukraine dropped much of its radioactive fallout on southern Belarus, and part of that region remains a closed reserve.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Belarusians are Orthodox Christians, with a Catholic minority in the west. Potatoes are the heart of the kitchen: draniki are crisp potato pancakes eaten with sour cream, and there are said to be hundreds of other potato recipes, along with borscht, mushroom soups, and kvass, a fizzy drink made from bread. Traditional shirts embroidered in red geometric patterns are worn at festivals like Kupalle, the midsummer night when people jump over bonfires and float flower wreaths on rivers. Straw weaving and the Slutsk sash, a richly patterned silk belt, are national crafts. Ice hockey and biathlon are the most followed sports. The painter Marc Chagall was born in Vitebsk, and writer Svetlana Alexievich won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2015.
content.history: Slavic tribes settled these forests over a thousand years ago and founded the Principality of Polotsk. In the 1200s and 1300s the Belarusian lands became the core of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, which later joined with Poland in a vast commonwealth. At the end of the 1700s the Russian Empire absorbed the region. After a brief independent republic in 1918, Belarus became a Soviet republic. World War II was catastrophic: roughly a quarter of the population died, Minsk was almost totally destroyed, and nearly all of the country's large Jewish community was murdered in the Holocaust. Belarus declared independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union broke apart. Alexander Lukashenko became president in 1994 and has stayed in power since, and the 2020 protests were met with mass arrests.
funFacts: The National Library of Belarus in Minsk is shaped like a giant glass diamond with 24 sides and lights up in colors at night.
Belarus, then a Soviet republic, was a founding member of the United Nations in 1945, even though it was not independent.
The country is sometimes called the lungs of Europe because of its huge forests and marshes.
Belarus tractors have been sold to more than 100 countries, and a model is even displayed in a Minsk museum.
The Mir and Nesvizh castles, both UNESCO World Heritage Sites, look like fairy-tale fortresses with red brick towers.

content.tagline: Reefs, rainforest and ancient Maya cities
content.overview:
On the Caribbean coast of Central America, wedged between Mexico and Guatemala, Belize is a small country where English is the official language, a legacy of its years as the colony of British Honduras. It covers about 23,000 km², roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, and has only about 400,000 people, making it one of the least crowded countries in the Americas.

The capital is Belmopan, a small planned city built inland after Hurricane Hattie flattened much of coastal Belize City in 1961. Belize City remains the largest town and main port. Along the coast runs the Belize Barrier Reef, the second-longest coral reef in the world, dotted with hundreds of sandy islands called cayes.

Belizeans come from many roots: Maya, Kriol, Mestizo, Garifuna, Mennonite, East Indian and Chinese, and many people switch easily between English, Kriol and Spanish. Belize is an independent member of the Commonwealth with an elected parliament; the British monarch is head of state. Guatemala has long claimed part of its territory, a dispute the two countries have asked international judges to settle.
content.landAndNature:
The north of Belize is flat and swampy, threaded with lagoons and rivers, while the south rises into the Maya Mountains, where Doyle's Delight reaches about 1,124 meters. More than half the country is still covered by forest. The climate is hot and humid, with a rainy season from June to November and a risk of hurricanes.

Offshore, the reef shelters sea turtles, manatees, nurse sharks and rays, and the Great Blue Hole, a perfectly round sinkhole more than 120 meters deep, is a magnet for divers. Inland, the Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary was the world's first reserve created to protect jaguars. Black howler monkeys, which Belizeans call baboons, roar through the treetops, and the keel-billed toucan, the national bird, flashes its rainbow beak. Baird's tapir is the national animal.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Kriol, an English-based language with African and Spanish influences, is the everyday speech of most Belizeans, alongside English in schools and Spanish in many towns. The Garifuna people, descended from Africans and Caribbean islanders, keep their own language, drumming and punta dance; their arrival in 1832 is celebrated every November 19 on Garifuna Settlement Day.

Rice and beans cooked in coconut milk with stewed chicken is the national favorite, along with fry jacks (puffy fried dough) for breakfast and hudut, a Garifuna fish and plantain stew. Soccer, basketball and cycling are popular, and the Cross Country Cycling Classic each Easter crosses the whole country. The September Celebrations mix the anniversary of the 1798 Battle of St. George's Caye with Independence Day parades and carnival.
content.history:
Belize lay at the heart of the Maya world. Cities such as Caracol, Lamanai and Xunantunich flourished between about 250 and 900 AD, with pyramids taller than any modern building in the country. When Spanish explorers arrived in the 1500s the great cities were long abandoned, though Maya villages remained.

English loggers, known as Baymen, settled the coast in the 1600s to cut logwood and mahogany, bringing enslaved Africans to do the work. In 1798 they defeated a Spanish fleet at St. George's Caye. Britain declared the territory the colony of British Honduras in 1862. Slavery had ended in the 1830s, and later Garifuna, Mestizo and Mennonite communities arrived. The colony was renamed Belize in 1973 and became independent on September 21, 1981.
funFacts: The Great Blue Hole is so large and round that it can be seen clearly from space.
Belize is the only country in Central America where English is the official language.
The Maya city of Caracol was once bigger than modern Belize City and had a temple 43 meters high.
Belize's flag is one of the only national flags to show human figures, two woodcutters.
Baird's tapir, the national animal, can weigh 300 kilograms and is nicknamed the mountain cow.
The Cockscomb Basin, set aside in 1986, was the first jaguar reserve anywhere in the world.

content.tagline: Rooftop of South America
content.overview:
Bolivia sits in the heart of South America, a landlocked country of high plateaus, snowy peaks and steamy lowlands. It borders Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina, Chile and Peru, and at about 1.1 million km² it is roughly the size of Texas and California combined. Around 12 million people live there.

The country has two capitals. Sucre, the constitutional capital, is a quiet city of white colonial buildings where the supreme court sits. La Paz, at about 3,600 meters above sea level, is where the president and congress work, making it the highest seat of government in the world. Visitors arriving by plane often feel breathless in the thin air.

Bolivia calls itself a Plurinational State because it recognizes 36 Indigenous peoples and languages alongside Spanish, including Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní. Most Bolivians have Indigenous roots, and traditional clothing, music and festivals are part of daily life. The country is a republic with an elected president, and mining, natural gas and farming support the economy.
content.landAndNature:
Two great chains of the Andes cross western Bolivia, cradling the Altiplano, a windswept plateau nearly 4,000 meters high. Here lies Lake Titicaca, shared with Peru, the highest large lake in the world that boats can navigate, and the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat on Earth, roughly 10,000 km² of blinding white crust that turns into a giant mirror when rain covers it.

East of the mountains the land drops through cloud forests called the Yungas into the hot Amazon basin and the dry Chaco. Madidi National Park, stretching from glaciers to jungle, may hold more species than any other protected area on the planet. Andean condors, vicuñas, pink river dolphins, jaguars and giant anteaters all live in Bolivia, and flamingos feed in red and green mineral lakes high in the southwest.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Spanish is the common language, but Quechua and Aymara are spoken by millions, especially in the highlands. Aymara women known as cholitas wear bowler hats, layered skirts and bright shawls; some are famous as wrestlers who perform in La Paz. Music played on panpipes, the charango (a small guitar) and drums accompanies dances at every fiesta.

Potatoes were first farmed near Lake Titicaca thousands of years ago, and Bolivians grow hundreds of varieties, along with quinoa, corn and llama meat. Salteñas, juicy baked pastries filled with meat and vegetables, are a mid-morning favorite. The Oruro Carnival, with its devil-masked Diablada dancers, is recognized by UNESCO as a treasure of world culture. Soccer is the top sport, and La Paz's high-altitude stadium leaves visiting teams gasping.
content.history:
The Tiwanaku civilization built stone temples near Lake Titicaca more than a thousand years ago, and in the 1400s the region became part of the Inca Empire. Spanish conquerors arrived in the 1530s and discovered a mountain of silver at Potosí. For centuries, Indigenous people and enslaved Africans were forced to work its mines, and the silver made Spain rich while millions of workers died.

Independence came in 1825 after long wars, and the new country was named after the liberator Simón Bolívar. Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884) and lost more land to Paraguay in the Chaco War of the 1930s. A 1952 revolution gave land to Indigenous farmers and the vote to everyone. In 2006 Evo Morales became the country's first Indigenous president, and a 2009 constitution created the Plurinational State.
funFacts: The Salar de Uyuni is so flat that satellites use it to calibrate their altitude instruments.
La Paz has the largest urban cable-car network in the world, with gondolas serving as public buses.
Bolivia still has a navy, even though it lost its coastline in 1884; it patrols Lake Titicaca and rivers.
The Yungas Road, dropping 3,500 meters in about 60 kilometers, was once nicknamed the world's most dangerous road.
Bolivia's Wiphala, a rainbow checkerboard flag of the Andean peoples, is an official national flag alongside the red, yellow and green one.
Some Andean women wrestlers, the Fighting Cholitas, compete in full traditional skirts and bowler hats.

content.tagline: Giant of the Amazon
content.overview:
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the fifth largest in the world, covering about 8.5 million km², nearly half the continent. It shares borders with every South American country except Chile and Ecuador, and its Atlantic coastline runs for more than 7,000 kilometers. Around 215 million people live there, more than in any other country in the Southern Hemisphere.

Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas, a result of its history as a Portuguese colony. Its people are a rich blend of Indigenous, African, European, Middle Eastern and Japanese heritage, and most live in big coastal cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Salvador. The capital, Brasília, was built from scratch in the late 1950s in the empty center of the country and laid out in the shape of an airplane.

Brazil is a federal republic with an elected president and 26 states. It is a giant producer of coffee, soybeans, beef, iron ore and oil, and its soccer teams, music and Carnival are famous around the world.
content.landAndNature:
The Amazon rainforest covers about 60 percent of Brazil, the biggest rainforest on Earth, and the Amazon River pours more water into the sea than any other river. Farther south, the Pantanal is the world's largest wetland, where jaguars, capybaras, giant otters and caimans are easy to spot in the dry season. The Cerrado grasslands, the dry Northeast interior called the sertão, and the green Atlantic Forest along the coast each have their own plants and animals.

Brazil holds more species than any other country: pink river dolphins, toucans, sloths, howler monkeys, anacondas, piranhas and thousands of kinds of butterflies. Iguaçu Falls, on the Argentine border, sends about 275 waterfalls crashing into a jungle gorge. The climate is mostly tropical, with a cooler, frostier south.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Brazilian Portuguese has a musical sound and words borrowed from Indigenous Tupi and African languages. Rio's Carnival, the world's biggest party, fills the streets with samba schools, drums and towering floats in the days before Lent. Music styles born here include samba, bossa nova, forró and funk carioca, and capoeira blends martial art, dance and music.

Soccer is everywhere, from beach games to the national team, which has won the World Cup a record five times; Pelé is honored as the greatest player of all time. Favorite foods include feijoada, a black bean and pork stew; pão de queijo, chewy cheese bread; açaí berry bowls; and brigadeiros, chocolate fudge balls served at every birthday party. Religion is mostly Catholic, with strong Afro-Brazilian traditions such as Candomblé, especially in Bahia.
content.history:
Millions of Indigenous people lived across Brazil when the Portuguese navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500. Portugal set up sugar plantations and brought nearly five million enslaved Africans to work them, more than any other country in the Americas; slavery was not abolished until 1888, the last in the region to end it.

In 1808 the Portuguese royal family fled Napoleon and made Rio de Janeiro the capital of their empire. In 1822 Prince Pedro declared Brazil an independent empire with himself as emperor. Brazil became a republic in 1889 and grew rich on coffee. The 1900s brought waves of immigrants, the building of Brasília, and a military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985 that jailed and tortured opponents. Democracy returned in 1985, and a new constitution was adopted in 1988.
funFacts: The Amazon River carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that flows into the world's oceans.
Brasília was built in just 41 months, and its plan, seen from above, looks like an airplane or a bird.
Brazil is named after brazilwood, a tree whose red sap was used to dye cloth in Europe.
Brazil has the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centered in São Paulo.
Ilha da Queimada Grande, off the coast, has so many venomous golden lancehead snakes that visiting is banned.
The Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio stands 30 meters tall and is struck by lightning several times a year.

content.tagline: Coral island of the eastern Caribbean
content.overview:
Barbados is the easternmost island of the Caribbean, standing alone in the Atlantic Ocean about 160 kilometers east of the main island chain. It is small, just 430 km², about 34 kilometers long and 23 wide, so a drive around the whole island takes only a few hours. Around 280,000 people live here, most of them along the sheltered western and southern coasts, and the capital, Bridgetown, sits on the southwest shore.

Unlike its volcanic neighbors, Barbados was built by coral. Over millions of years, coral reefs grew on top of an underwater ridge and were slowly lifted out of the sea, leaving a gently rolling island of limestone edged with white beaches.

Barbadians, who call themselves Bajans, speak English and a lively dialect. Tourism, rum and finance are the main industries. The country gained independence from Britain in 1966, and in 2021 it became a republic with a Barbadian president as head of state.
content.landAndNature:
The island rises gently from the calm Caribbean coast in the west to a spine of hills in the center, topped by Mount Hillaby at about 340 meters, then drops to the wild Atlantic coast in the east, where big waves crash against rocky shores at Bathsheba. Rainwater seeps through the porous limestone and carves underground streams and caverns; Harrison's Cave, with its stalactites and pools, is the most famous.

The climate is warm and breezy year-round, with a wetter season from June to November. Sugarcane fields still cover much of the interior. Green monkeys, brought from West Africa centuries ago, roam the gullies, and hawksbill turtles nest on the beaches. Flying fish, which leap from the water and glide on their wing-like fins, are the island's symbol.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Bajans are descended from West Africans, with smaller communities of European, Indian and mixed heritage. English is the official language, but everyday talk is Bajan, a rhythmic Creole. The national dish is cou-cou, a cornmeal and okra mash, served with flying fish in spicy sauce; other favorites are macaroni pie, fish cakes and sweet bread flavored with coconut.

Cricket is the national passion, and Barbados produced Sir Garfield Sobers, considered one of the greatest all-round players ever. The biggest celebration is Crop Over, a summer festival that began as the end-of-harvest party on sugar plantations and now ends with Grand Kadooment, a parade of costumed bands. Calypso and soca music fill the air, and the superstar singer Rihanna, born in Barbados, was named a national hero in 2021.
content.history:
Amerindian peoples lived on Barbados for centuries, but the island was empty when English settlers landed in 1627. They planted tobacco and then sugarcane, and Barbados became one of the richest colonies in the world, its wealth built on the labor of tens of thousands of enslaved Africans. The island's parliament, founded in 1639, is one of the oldest in the Americas.

A major slave uprising led by an enslaved man named Bussa was crushed in 1816, but slavery was finally abolished in 1834. Barbados stayed a British colony for more than three centuries, earning the nickname Little England, until independence on November 30, 1966. Its people built a stable democracy with high levels of education. On the 55th anniversary of independence in 2021, Barbados removed the British monarch as head of state and became a republic.
funFacts: The grapefruit is believed to have first appeared in Barbados in the 1700s as an accidental cross between an orange and a pomelo.
George Washington visited Barbados in 1751, the only trip he ever made outside what became the United States.
Rum has been made in Barbados since the 1600s, and the island claims to be its birthplace.
Barbados is ringed by coral reefs and has no rivers, only underground streams flowing through limestone.
A retired Concorde supersonic jet is on display at the island's airport museum.
Flying fish can glide more than 50 meters above the waves, and they appear on Barbadian coins.

BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.officialName: Nation of Brunei, Abode of Peace

content.tagline: The Abode of Peace on Borneo
content.overview:
Brunei is a tiny, wealthy sultanate on the north coast of Borneo, the world's third-largest island. It is surrounded on its land side by the Malaysian state of Sarawak, which even splits it into two separate pieces. The whole country covers about 5,800 km², a little smaller than the US state of Delaware, and is home to around 450,000 people.

Its full name, Brunei Darussalam, means "Brunei, Abode of Peace." The capital, Bandar Seri Begawan, is famous for its golden-domed mosques and for Kampong Ayer, a village of tens of thousands of people living in wooden houses on stilts over the river, linked by boardwalks and water taxis.

Brunei is one of the few remaining absolute monarchies; the Sultan is head of state, head of government and religious leader. Oil and natural gas, discovered in 1929, made the country rich, so citizens pay no income tax and receive free schooling and health care. Malay is the official language, English is widely spoken, and Islam is the state religion.
content.landAndNature:
Brunei is flat along the coast and hilly inland, with the highest point, Bukit Pagon, at about 1,850 meters in the remote Temburong district. The climate is equatorial: hot, humid and rainy all year, with more than 2,500 millimeters of rain annually. Mangroves line the river mouths and the wide, shallow Brunei Bay.

Because oil paid the bills, Brunei never cut down most of its forest, and roughly 70 percent of the country is still covered by pristine rainforest. Ulu Temburong National Park, reachable only by longboat, has a canopy walkway 50 meters above the ground. Proboscis monkeys with their long, floppy noses live in the mangroves, and hornbills, gibbons, clouded leopards, flying squirrels and thousands of insect species fill the jungle. Sea turtles nest on the beaches.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Bruneians are Malay Muslims, with Chinese and Indigenous communities such as the Iban and Dusun. Malay is the national language, but many people also speak English and Chinese dialects. Daily life follows a rhythm of prayer times, and during Ramadan families gather for evening feasts.

The national dish is ambuyat, a sticky, glue-like paste made from sago palm starch, twirled around bamboo chopsticks and dipped in a sour fruit sauce. Nasi katok, rice with fried chicken and chili paste, is a favorite cheap meal. Popular sports include soccer, badminton, silat (a Malay martial art) and sepak takraw, a game like volleyball played with the feet. The Sultan's birthday in July brings parades and celebrations, and the royal family is treated with deep respect.
content.history:
Brunei's history stretches back more than a thousand years as a trading port for camphor, spices and gold. In the 1400s and 1500s the Bruneian Empire ruled much of Borneo and parts of the Philippines, and its sultans converted to Islam. Survivors of Magellan's round-the-world voyage visited in 1521 and described a splendid court.

Over the following centuries the empire shrank as European powers and local rivals took territory, including land given up to the British adventurer James Brooke in Sarawak. Brunei became a British protectorate in 1888. Oil was found at Seria in 1929, transforming the economy. Japan occupied the country during World War II. Brunei chose not to join Malaysia in 1963 and became fully independent from Britain on January 1, 1984, under Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, who had ruled since 1967.
funFacts: Kampong Ayer, the water village in the capital, has been home to people for more than a thousand years and has its own schools, mosques and fire station.
The Sultan's palace, Istana Nurul Iman, has about 1,788 rooms and is said to be the largest residential palace in the world.
Brunei's sultan has one of the longest reigns of any living monarch, having taken the throne in 1967.
Bruneians pay no personal income tax, and the government covers school and medical costs.
Roughly 70 percent of Brunei is still original rainforest, one of the highest shares of any country.
The two parts of Brunei are separated by Malaysian land and linked by a 30-kilometer bridge opened in 2020.

content.tagline: Land of the Thunder Dragon
content.overview:
Bhutan is a small kingdom folded into the eastern Himalayas, squeezed between two giants, China to the north and India to the south. It has no coastline and no flat land to speak of; even the lowest valleys sit hundreds of meters above the sea. At about 38,400 km² it is a little smaller than Switzerland, and fewer than 800,000 people live there.

The Bhutanese call their country Druk Yul, the Land of the Thunder Dragon, and a white dragon coils across the national flag. The capital, Thimphu, is one of the few capitals in the world without a single traffic light; a police officer in white gloves directs cars at the main crossroads. Dzongkha is the national language, and Buddhism shapes nearly every part of life.

Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Instead of measuring success only by money, the government aims for Gross National Happiness, weighing health, culture and the environment. Farming, hydroelectric power sold to India, and carefully limited tourism support the economy.
content.landAndNature:
From subtropical jungles along the Indian border, the land climbs through pine and rhododendron forests to glaciers and peaks above 7,000 meters. Gangkhar Puensum, about 7,570 meters, is considered the highest mountain in the world that no one has climbed, because Bhutan forbids climbing its sacred summits. Rivers rush south through deep valleys, powering the country's dams.

The constitution requires that at least 60 percent of Bhutan stay forested, and more than 70 percent is. Those forests soak up more carbon dioxide than the country produces. Bengal tigers have been photographed above 4,000 meters, sharing the mountains with snow leopards, red pandas and the takin, a shaggy national animal that looks like a cross between a goat and a cow. Black-necked cranes fly in from Tibet each winter to the Phobjikha Valley.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Dzongkha is the national language, but about 20 other languages are spoken in the valleys, and English is used in schools. Most people are Buddhists, and prayer flags flutter from bridges and ridgelines. Men wear the gho, a knee-length robe, and women the kira, a long woven dress, to school, work and festivals.

The favorite dish is ema datshi, chilies cooked in melted cheese and eaten with red rice; Bhutanese treat chilies as a vegetable, not a spice. Archery is the national sport, played with loud teasing, singing and dancing between shots. Tshechu festivals fill fortress courtyards with masked dancers acting out Buddhist stories. Bhutan allowed television and the internet only in 1999, and it protects its culture carefully while young people also enjoy K-pop and soccer.
content.history:
People have farmed Bhutan's valleys for thousands of years, and Buddhism arrived from Tibet in the 600s and 700s, brought by teachers such as Guru Rinpoche, who is said to have flown to a cliff at Paro on the back of a tigress; the Tiger's Nest monastery clings there today. In the 1600s a Tibetan lama, Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, united the valleys and built the huge fortress-monasteries called dzongs that still serve as government offices.

Bhutan was never colonized, though it fought and then made treaties with British India. In 1907 Ugyen Wangchuck became the first hereditary king, founding the dynasty that still reigns. Later kings opened roads, schools and hospitals from the 1960s. The fourth king gave up much of his power, and in 2008 Bhutan held its first democratic elections and adopted a constitution.
funFacts: Bhutan is one of the few carbon-negative countries in the world; its forests absorb more carbon dioxide than its people produce.
Thimphu is one of the very few national capitals with no traffic lights; drivers follow the hand signals of police officers.
Climbing mountains above 6,000 meters is banned in Bhutan out of respect for the spirits believed to live there.
Bhutan banned plastic bags in 1999 and in 2004 became the first country to outlaw the sale of tobacco.
Many older Bhutanese celebrate their birthday on January 1, because exact birth dates were not recorded when they were born.
Bhutanese archers use bamboo bows and shoot at targets about 145 meters away, nearly twice the Olympic distance.

content.tagline: Elephants, diamonds, and a river that vanishes
content.overview:
Botswana is a landlocked country in southern Africa, about the size of France, yet home to only around 2.6 million people, making it one of the least crowded nations on Earth. The Kalahari Desert's red and gray sands cover roughly 70 percent of the land. The capital, Gaborone, sits near the South African border in the southeast, where most people live. English is the official language, and Setswana is the national language spoken in nearly every home.

When Botswana became independent in 1966 it was one of the poorest countries in the world, with only a few kilometers of paved road. A year later diamonds were discovered, and careful management of that wealth built schools, clinics, and highways. Botswana has held peaceful elections ever since and is often called one of Africa's most stable democracies; it is a republic with a president elected by parliament. Wildlife tourism is the other pillar of the economy, drawing visitors to see the Okavango Delta and the largest elephant population anywhere.
content.landAndNature: Most of Botswana is flat Kalahari scrubland where grasses, thorny acacias, and camelthorn trees survive on little rain. In the northwest the Okavango River flows in from Angola and, instead of reaching the sea, fans out across the sand into a huge maze of channels, lagoons, and islands: the Okavango Delta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site alive with hippos, crocodiles, and lechwe antelope splashing through the shallows. Northeast of it lie the Makgadikgadi Pans, blinding white salt flats left by an ancient lake, where flamingos breed after rains and zebras migrate in tens of thousands. Chobe National Park holds vast herds of elephants; the country has about 130,000, more than any other. Lions, wild dogs, cheetahs, and meerkats also thrive.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most citizens are Tswana, organized in traditional communities where a kgotla, an open-air meeting under a tree, lets everyone speak before decisions are made. The San, or Basarwa, are the region's oldest inhabitants and speak languages full of click sounds. The word pula means rain, so precious here that it became the name of the currency and a cheer shouted at celebrations. Seswaa, slow-cooked pounded beef served with a stiff sorghum porridge, is the national dish, and mopane worms are a crunchy snack. Soccer is the most popular sport, and the country's runners have won Olympic medals; Letsile Tebogo took gold in the 200 meters at the 2024 Paris Games. Choral singing and the segaba, a one-stringed fiddle, are traditional arts.
content.history: The San have lived in the Kalahari for tens of thousands of years, leaving thousands of rock paintings at the Tsodilo Hills. Tswana-speaking farmers and cattle herders arrived over the following centuries and formed several chiefdoms. In 1885 Britain declared the area the Bechuanaland Protectorate, and in 1895 three chiefs, Khama III, Sebele I, and Bathoen I, traveled to London and persuaded the British not to hand their land to a mining company. Independence came on September 30, 1966, under the first president, Seretse Khama. Diamonds found at Orapa in 1967 transformed the economy. Botswana was hit hard by the HIV epidemic and became a leader in providing free treatment. In 2024 voters elected a new party to power for the first time since independence, and the handover was peaceful.
funFacts: Botswana's roughly 130,000 elephants outnumber those of any other country on Earth.
The Makgadikgadi salt pans are so large and flat that they can be seen clearly from space.
The blue on Botswana's flag stands for rain and water, and its black and white stripes stand for racial harmony, like a zebra's coat.
The Okavango is one of the very few large rivers in the world that never reaches the ocean.
The Jwaneng mine in Botswana is often described as the richest diamond mine in the world by value.

content.tagline: Wild heart of the continent
content.overview:
The Central African Republic sits almost exactly in the middle of Africa, landlocked and far from any ocean. It is about the size of Texas but home to only around 5.5 million people, spread thinly across savanna and rainforest. The capital, Bangui, stands on the north bank of the Ubangi River, looking across the water to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Neighbors also include Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, Congo, and Cameroon.

French and Sango are the official languages. Sango, which began as a trade language on the rivers, is special because nearly everyone in the country speaks it, a rare thing in Africa. Most people farm cassava, peanuts, and millet or fish the rivers, and the country's forests and soils hold diamonds, gold, and valuable timber. The Central African Republic is a republic with an elected president, but decades of coups and a civil war that began in 2012 have made it one of the poorest and least stable countries in the world, with UN peacekeepers based there since 2014.
content.landAndNature: Most of the country is a rolling plateau of savanna grasslands 600 to 900 meters high, broken by scattered hills and, in the northeast, the Bongo massif. Rivers flow in two directions: northward toward Lake Chad and southward into the Ubangi and Congo systems, and their waterfalls, like Boali Falls near Bangui, drop over rocky ledges. In the southwest the dense Congo rainforest begins. Dzanga-Sangha reserve is famous for the Dzanga Bai, a forest clearing where dozens of elephants gather to dig for salty minerals, and for western lowland gorillas that can be visited on foot. Manovo-Gounda St Floris park in the north once had huge herds but has suffered from poaching. Rain falls heavily from May to October.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Central African Republic has more than 80 ethnic groups, including the Gbaya, Banda, Mandjia, Sara, and Mbaka, plus the Aka, forest peoples of the southwest whose intricate polyphonic singing, with many voices weaving separate melodies, is recognized by UNESCO. Most people are Christian, with a Muslim minority. Cassava is the staple, pounded into a dough called gozo and eaten with sauces of greens, peanuts, or smoked fish, and caterpillars are a seasonal treat. Music blends drums, the balafon xylophone, and the sanza thumb piano with modern Congolese rumba. Soccer and basketball are the favorite sports. Colorful wax-print clothing and beautifully braided hairstyles are part of everyday style in Bangui.
content.history: Farming and iron-working peoples lived here more than 2,000 years ago, and mysterious stone monuments near Bouar are among the oldest in Central Africa. From the 1600s to the 1800s slave raiders from the north and traders from the coast devastated the region. France claimed the territory in the 1880s and ruled it as Ubangi-Shari, forcing people to gather rubber and cotton. A beloved independence leader, Barthélemy Boganda, died in a plane crash in 1959, a year before independence on August 13, 1960. Military ruler Jean-Bédel Bokassa seized power in 1966 and even crowned himself emperor in 1977 before being overthrown. More coups followed. Fighting between armed groups since 2012 has displaced more than a million people, though elections and peace talks continue.
funFacts: Sango is one of the few African languages spoken by almost the entire population of its country.
At Dzanga Bai, up to a hundred forest elephants may gather at once to drink mineral-rich water.
In 1977 ruler Jean-Bédel Bokassa spent a fortune on a coronation ceremony modeled on Napoleon's.
The Aka people can imitate the calls of forest animals so precisely that hunters use the sounds to lure game.
Boali Falls, about 50 meters high and 250 meters wide, is a popular picnic spot an hour from Bangui.

content.tagline: The great northern land
content.overview:
Canada is the second-largest country on Earth, stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and north to the Arctic Ocean. It covers about 9.98 million km², yet only about 40 million people live there, most of them within 200 kilometers of the border with the United States, the longest border between two countries in the world. Huge parts of the north are forest, tundra and ice.

The capital, Ottawa, sits on the river between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Canada has two official languages, English and French; most people in Quebec speak French, a legacy of the colony of New France. Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver are the largest cities, and immigrants from every continent have made them among the most diverse in the world.

Canada is a federation of ten provinces and three territories, a parliamentary democracy with a prime minister; the British monarch is head of state. First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples were here long before Europeans, and their cultures and rights are an important part of national life.
content.landAndNature:
Canada's landscapes are enormous: the jagged Rocky Mountains in the west, the flat wheat prairies, the ancient rock and lakes of the Canadian Shield, the rolling farms and forests of the east, and the treeless Arctic tundra where the sun barely rises in winter. The country has more lakes than any other, including four of the five Great Lakes shared with the United States. Niagara Falls roars on the Ontario border, and the Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world, rising and falling about 16 meters.

Winters are long and snowy across most of the country. Moose, beavers, grizzly and black bears, wolves, caribou and bald eagles live in the vast forests, while polar bears gather near Churchill on Hudson Bay each autumn and belugas swim in Arctic waters.
content.peopleAndCulture:
About one in five Canadians was born in another country, and cities buzz with dozens of languages beyond English and French. Hockey is the national winter sport and a shared passion; kids learn to skate on frozen ponds and backyard rinks. Lacrosse, a game invented by Indigenous peoples, is the national summer sport, and basketball was invented by a Canadian, James Naismith.

Maple syrup is the country's sweetest export; Quebec makes about three-quarters of the world's supply, and families visit sugar shacks in early spring. Poutine, fries with cheese curds and gravy, is a beloved comfort food, along with butter tarts and Nanaimo bars. Indigenous art, from totem poles on the Pacific coast to Inuit stone carvings, is celebrated nationwide. Canada Day on July 1 brings fireworks across the country.
content.history:
Indigenous peoples have lived in Canada for more than 12,000 years, from the Haida of the Pacific coast to the Inuit of the Arctic. Vikings briefly settled Newfoundland around the year 1000. French explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in 1534, and Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in 1608, starting the fur-trading colony of New France. Britain conquered it in 1759–1763, and French speakers kept their language and laws.

On July 1, 1867, several colonies joined to form the Dominion of Canada, which grew westward with a railway completed in 1885. For over a century, the government forced Indigenous children into residential schools, a harm the country has formally apologized for. Canadians fought in both world wars, welcomed millions of immigrants, and gained full control of their constitution in 1982. Nunavut, an Inuit-governed territory, was created in 1999.
funFacts: Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined, by most counts more than two million.
Hawaiian pizza, topped with ham and pineapple, was invented in Ontario in 1962, not in Hawaii.
Letters addressed to Santa Claus, North Pole, postal code H0H 0H0, are answered by Canadian postal volunteers every year.
Insulin, the life-saving treatment for diabetes, was discovered in Toronto in 1921.
Mount Thor on Baffin Island has the greatest vertical cliff on Earth, a sheer drop of about 1,250 meters.
Canada's coastline is the longest of any country, more than 200,000 kilometers.

content.tagline: Alpine peaks, four languages, one country
content.overview:
Switzerland is a small, landlocked country wrapped around the middle of the Alps, hemmed in by France, Germany, Austria, Italy and Liechtenstein. It covers about 41,000 km², roughly twice the size of New Jersey, and mountains take up more than half of it. About 9 million people live there, most in the flatter belt between the Alps and the Jura hills where Zurich, Geneva, Basel and the capital, Bern, sit.

Switzerland has four national languages: Swiss German in the center and east, French in the west, Italian in the south, and Romansh, kept alive by a small community in the southeast. It is a federal republic of 26 cantons that run much of their own affairs, and Swiss voters decide national questions directly in referendums held several times a year. The country has stayed neutral in wars since 1815, which is why Geneva hosts the Red Cross and many United Nations agencies. Chocolate, cheese, watches and banking are its best-known industries.
content.landAndNature: The Alps curve across southern Switzerland with dozens of peaks above 4,000 meters, including the pyramid-shaped Matterhorn and Dufourspitze, the highest at 4,634 meters. Glaciers such as the Aletsch, the largest in the Alps, grind slowly down the valleys, though they are shrinking as the climate warms. Their meltwater feeds rivers that leave the country in every direction, including the Rhine and the Rhône, so Switzerland is often called Europe's water tower. Lakes Geneva, Constance and Lucerne fill deep basins carved by ice. Ibex, chamois, marmots and golden eagles live on the high slopes, and lynx and wolves have returned to the forests.
content.peopleAndCulture: Swiss life is shaped by mountains and by punctuality: trains run to the minute, and cable cars climb to villages with no roads at all. Cheese is serious business, from holey Emmental to Gruyère melted into fondue and scraped hot as raclette, and Swiss makers invented milk chocolate and the machine that grinds it smooth. Alphorns, yodeling and cattle parades down from summer pastures mark mountain traditions, while Fasnacht carnival fills Basel's streets with masks and drums for three days. Skiing, snowboarding, hiking and ice hockey fill the calendar, and citizens vote on national questions up to four times a year.
content.history: Celtic Helvetii tribes gave Switzerland the Latin name still stamped on its coins. In 1291 three forest communities swore an alliance in the mountains, a founding pact remembered every August 1, the national day. Swiss soldiers became Europe's most feared mercenaries before the country turned away from foreign wars. Reformation preachers such as Zwingli and Calvin split the cantons along religious lines in the 1500s. After a short civil war in 1847, Switzerland adopted a federal constitution in 1848 that still stands, among the oldest in the world. It stayed neutral through both world wars, hosted the founding of the Red Cross in 1863, and granted women the vote in national elections in 1971.
funFacts: Switzerland has four national languages, and Romansh is spoken by fewer than 50,000 people in one mountain region.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel, 57 kilometers long, is the world's longest railway tunnel, bored deep beneath the Alps.
Milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland in 1875, and conching, the process that makes chocolate smooth, followed soon after.
Swiss voters go to the polls several times a year to settle national questions themselves, more often than any other country.
Swiss coins carry the Latin word Helvetia, chosen so that no one of the country's four languages is favored.

content.tagline: A ribbon of land beside the Andes
content.overview:
Chile is one of the strangest-shaped countries in the world: a strip about 4,300 kilometers long but on average only 180 kilometers wide, squeezed between the Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean along the western edge of South America. If it were laid across the United States it would stretch from Alaska to Mexico. It covers about 756,000 km², slightly larger than Texas, and about 19 million people live there.

Because it is so long, Chile has almost every kind of landscape: the driest desert on Earth in the north, fertile vineyards and the capital, Santiago, in the middle, and forests, volcanoes, glaciers and fjords in the south. It also owns Easter Island, far out in the Pacific, and claims a slice of Antarctica.

Spanish is the language, and most Chileans live in cities, with about 7 million in the Santiago area. Chile is a republic with an elected president. Copper mining, fruit, fish and wine drive the economy, and the country is known for its poets, its earthquakes and its clear desert skies full of telescopes.
content.landAndNature:
The Atacama Desert in the north is so dry that some weather stations have never recorded rain, and its high, cloudless skies host some of the world's largest observatories. The Andes wall off the east; Ojos del Salado, about 6,890 meters, is the highest active volcano on Earth, and Chile has around 2,000 volcanoes in all. Because it sits where two plates of the Earth's crust collide, Chile suffers powerful earthquakes, including the strongest ever recorded, magnitude 9.5, near Valdivia in 1960.

Central Chile has a mild climate like California, while Patagonia in the far south is cold, windy and cut by fjords and glaciers, with the granite towers of Torres del Paine. Wildlife includes the Andean condor, puma, guanaco, huemul deer, Humboldt penguin and flamingos that feed on salt lakes high in the desert.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Chileans speak a fast Spanish full of local slang, often ending sentences with "po." Most people have mixed Spanish and Indigenous heritage, and the Mapuche are the largest Indigenous group. Two Chilean poets, Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda, won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and the country is proud of its writers and folk singers.

Food favorites include empanadas de pino stuffed with beef, onions, olives and egg; pastel de choclo, a corn and meat pie; the completo, a hot dog piled with avocado and tomato; and mote con huesillo, a sweet drink of wheat and dried peaches. Soccer is the top sport, while Chilean rodeo, in which two riders pin a calf against a padded wall, is the official national sport. The cueca, a handkerchief-waving courtship dance, is performed at Independence Day fiestas each September.
content.history:
The Chinchorro people of the northern coast made the world's oldest mummies about 7,000 years ago, long before Egypt. Later the Inca pushed south but were stopped by the fierce Mapuche, who also resisted Spanish conquerors for more than 300 years after Santiago was founded in 1541.

Chile declared independence in 1810 and won it in 1818 under Bernardo O'Higgins and José de San Martín. In the War of the Pacific (1879–1884) it took the mineral-rich north from Bolivia and Peru. In 1973 a military coup led by General Augusto Pinochet overthrew the elected government; his dictatorship killed or disappeared thousands of people before Chileans voted it out and democracy returned in 1990. In 2010 the world watched as 33 miners were rescued after 69 days trapped underground near Copiapó.
funFacts: Easter Island, 3,500 kilometers off the coast, has nearly 900 giant stone statues called moai, carved by the Rapa Nui people.
Parts of the Atacama Desert have gone centuries without measurable rain, and NASA tests Mars rovers there.
The 1960 Valdivia earthquake was the most powerful ever measured, and its tsunami reached Hawaii and Japan.
Chile produces more copper than any other country, roughly a quarter of the world's supply.
Chile stretches across 39 degrees of latitude, about the distance from Alaska to Mexico.
The Chinchorro mummies of northern Chile are the oldest deliberately preserved human bodies ever found.

content.tagline: Five thousand years of civilization
content.overview:
China is a vast country in East Asia, the third or fourth largest in the world by area at about 9.6 million km², and home to about 1.4 billion people, second only to India. It stretches from the Himalayas and the deserts of the far west to a long Pacific coastline, and it shares borders with 14 countries, more than any other nation except Russia.

The capital, Beijing, holds the Forbidden City, once home to emperors, while Shanghai is a giant port of skyscrapers. Most people speak Mandarin Chinese, the most spoken first language on Earth, though many regions have their own dialects; all are written with the same characters, a system thousands of years old.

China is governed by the Communist Party, which has held power since 1949, with the government based in Beijing. Since the late 1970s it has grown from a poor farming nation into the world's biggest manufacturer, building high-speed railways, huge cities and space rockets. The island of Taiwan governs itself, though China claims it as part of its territory.
content.landAndNature:
China's land tilts from the high Tibetan Plateau in the west, the "roof of the world" at more than 4,000 meters, down to fertile plains in the east. Mount Everest, on the border with Nepal, is the highest point on Earth. The Yangtze, Asia's longest river, and the Yellow River, cradle of Chinese civilization, both begin on the plateau and flow east to the sea. The Gobi and Taklamakan deserts fill the north and west, and in the south, limestone hills near Guilin rise like green teeth from the rivers.

Climates range from Siberian cold in the northeast to tropical heat on Hainan Island. Giant pandas munch bamboo in the mountain forests of Sichuan, and China also shelters golden snub-nosed monkeys, Siberian tigers, Chinese alligators and the Yangtze finless porpoise.
content.peopleAndCulture:
About nine in ten people belong to the Han Chinese group, while 55 recognized minorities, including Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongols and Zhuang, keep their own languages and traditions. Family is central to life, and the Lunar New Year, or Spring Festival, sends hundreds of millions of people home for dumplings, red envelopes of money and fireworks. Other holidays include the Mid-Autumn Festival with mooncakes and the Dragon Boat Festival with paddling races.

Chinese cooking varies by region, from Sichuan's fiery chilies to Cantonese dim sum, all eaten with chopsticks. Tea has been drunk here for thousands of years. Calligraphy, kung fu, opera and paper-cutting are treasured arts, and table tennis, badminton and basketball are the favorite sports. China's inventions include paper, printing, gunpowder, the compass, silk and porcelain.
content.history:
Farming villages along the Yellow River grew into China's first dynasties more than 3,500 years ago; the Shang wrote on oracle bones, the earliest Chinese writing. In 221 BC Qin Shi Huang united the warring states as the first emperor, began the Great Wall and was buried with an army of thousands of terracotta soldiers. Dynasties rose and fell for 2,000 years, including the Han, the glittering Tang, the Song, the Mongol Yuan, the Ming and the Qing.

In the 1800s Britain and other powers forced China into unequal trade treaties after the Opium Wars. The last emperor fell in 1911, and after Japanese invasion and civil war, Mao Zedong's Communists founded the People's Republic in 1949. Mao's policies caused a terrible famine and the chaotic Cultural Revolution. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping opened the economy, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty.
funFacts: China spans five geographical time zones but uses only one, so in the far west the sun can rise at 10 a.m.
All the sections of the Great Wall added together stretch more than 21,000 kilometers.
Toilet paper was first used in China more than 1,400 years ago, reserved at first for emperors.
China's high-speed rail network is the longest in the world, with more than 40,000 kilometers of track.
Fortune cookies were invented in the United States, not China, and are almost unknown there.
The Lunar New Year travel rush is the largest annual movement of people on Earth, with billions of trips.

content.tagline: Cocoa capital of the world
content.overview:
Ivory Coast, officially called Côte d'Ivoire, lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, bordered by Liberia, Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Ghana. It is about the size of New Mexico. The official capital is Yamoussoukro, a quiet planned city in the center of the country with one of the largest churches in the world, but the economic heart is Abidjan, a lagoon-side city of skyscrapers and bridges that is one of the biggest French-speaking cities anywhere.

Around 30 million people live in Ivory Coast, including millions of migrants from neighboring countries drawn by its farms and factories. French is the official language, and about 60 local languages, such as Baoulé, Dioula, and Bété, are spoken. The country grows more cocoa than any other nation on Earth, about 40 percent of the world's supply, along with coffee, cashews, and rubber. Ivory Coast is a presidential republic; it was long one of West Africa's most prosperous countries, suffered two civil wars in the 2000s, and has since rebuilt into one of Africa's fastest-growing economies.
content.landAndNature: The coast is lined with lagoons, sandbars, and beaches, backed by dense rainforest in the south where cocoa and rubber plantations have replaced much of the original forest. Taï National Park protects one of the last big blocks of West African rainforest, home to chimpanzees that crack nuts with stones, pygmy hippos, and forest elephants. The land rises gently to a savanna plateau in the north, and in the west the mountains around Man reach 1,752 meters at Mount Nimba on the Guinean border. Comoé National Park in the northeast is one of the largest protected savannas in West Africa. The Bandama and Sassandra rivers flow south to the sea. Rain is heavy in the south, and the north has a single wet season and a dusty dry season.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Akan peoples, including the Baoulé, live in the center and east, the Mandé in the northwest, the Gur in the north, and the Kru in the southwest. Islam and Christianity are both widespread. Attiéké, a couscous-like dish of grated cassava, is eaten with grilled fish and spicy sauce, and kedjenou is chicken slow-cooked in a sealed pot. Ivory Coast is the birthplace of coupé-décalé and zouglou dance music, and the reggae star Alpha Blondy came from here. Dance masks of the Baoulé, Dan, and Senufo peoples are prized by museums worldwide. Soccer is the great passion: the national team, the Elephants, won the Africa Cup of Nations three times, including as hosts in 2024, and produced stars such as Didier Drogba.
content.history: Kingdoms such as Kong and the Baoulé state of Queen Pokou flourished before Europeans arrived; the coast got its name from the ivory that traders sought in the 1400s and 1500s. France established control in the late 1800s and made Ivory Coast a colony in 1893, building plantations and the port of Abidjan. Félix Houphouët-Boigny led the country to independence on August 7, 1960 and ruled for 33 years, keeping close ties with France and turning cocoa and coffee into an economic miracle. After his death in 1993, disputes over who counted as truly Ivorian led to a coup in 1999 and civil wars in 2002 and 2010 to 2011, the latter after a disputed election. Peace returned, and Abidjan has boomed with new bridges, highways, and towers.
funFacts: Ivory Coast produces about 40 percent of the world's cocoa, so roughly two of every five chocolate bars start here.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is one of the largest churches on Earth, modeled on St. Peter's in Rome.
The country asked in 1986 that all languages call it Côte d'Ivoire, its French name, instead of translations.
Ivory Coast hosted and won the 2024 Africa Cup of Nations after nearly being eliminated in the group stage.
Pygmy hippos, which weigh about a tenth as much as regular hippos, live in the forests of Taï National Park.

content.tagline: Africa in miniature
content.overview:
Cameroon sits at the hinge of West and Central Africa, where the continent's coastline bends sharply south. It is a little larger than California and touches Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, and Equatorial Guinea. People call it Africa in miniature because almost every landscape on the continent appears here: beaches, rainforest, mountains, savanna, and near-desert. The capital, Yaoundé, spreads over seven hills inland, while Douala on the coast is the biggest city and main port.

About 28 million people live in Cameroon, speaking more than 250 languages. English and French are both official, a legacy of the country being split between British and French rule; most regions speak French, and two western regions speak English. Cameroon is a republic with a president who has held office since 1982. Farmers grow cocoa, coffee, bananas, and cotton, and oil is exported from the coast. The country is famous for soccer, for its music, and for the wildlife of its forests.
content.landAndNature: Mount Cameroon, an active volcano near the coast, rises 4,040 meters straight from the sea and is the highest peak in West and Central Africa; its slopes are among the rainiest places on Earth. Dense rainforest covers the south, home to forest elephants, lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, and the rare drill monkey. Dja Faunal Reserve is one of Africa's largest protected rainforests. Toward the north the forest gives way to grassy highlands and then to hot savanna, where Waza National Park has lions, giraffes, and elephants. The far north reaches Lake Chad and the edge of the Sahel. The Sanaga is the longest river. Lake Nyos in the northwest is a crater lake that released a deadly cloud of carbon dioxide in 1986.
content.peopleAndCulture: Cameroonians belong to many peoples, including the Bamiléké and Bamoun of the western highlands, the Fulani and Kanuri of the north, the Beti and Bassa of the south, and the Baka, forest dwellers famous for their hunting skill and complex singing. Christians live mostly in the south, Muslims in the north. Ndolé, a stew of bitter leaves, peanuts, and fish or shrimp, is the best-known dish, eaten with plantains or fufu. Makossa music from Douala and bikutsi from Yaoundé are danced across Africa. Soccer is a national obsession: the Indomitable Lions have won the Africa Cup of Nations five times and reached the World Cup quarterfinals in 1990, and Cameroon took Olympic gold in 2000.
content.history: Bantu-speaking farmers spread from this region across much of Africa thousands of years ago. The Sao culture built towns near Lake Chad, and later kingdoms such as Bamoun developed their own writing system. Portuguese sailors arriving in 1472 named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, river of shrimp, giving Cameroon its name. Germany made it a colony in 1884; after World War I it was divided between France and Britain. French Cameroon gained independence on January 1, 1960, and part of British Cameroon joined it in 1961, while the rest joined Nigeria. Ahmadou Ahidjo governed until 1982, when Paul Biya became president. Since 2017 conflict between the government and separatists in the English-speaking regions has displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
funFacts: Cameroon's name comes from the Portuguese word for shrimp, after sailors found the Wouri River teeming with them.
In 1990 Cameroon became the first African team to reach a World Cup quarterfinal, led by 38-year-old striker Roger Milla.
Debundscha, at the foot of Mount Cameroon, receives about 10 meters of rain a year, among the highest totals on Earth.
The Bamoun king Njoya invented an alphabet for his language around 1896 and later built a printing press for it.
Cameroon has more than 250 languages, one of the highest counts of any country in the world.

content.tagline: A river of rainforest at Africa's heart
content.overview:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo is the second-largest country in Africa and about one-quarter the size of the United States, so large that it spans two time zones. It lies in the center of the continent, mostly covered by the Congo rainforest, the second-largest tropical forest on Earth after the Amazon. The capital, Kinshasa, on the Congo River, is one of the biggest cities in Africa with over 15 million people. The country borders nine nations and has only a tiny sliver of Atlantic coast.

Around 100 million people live in the DR Congo, making it the most populous French-speaking country in the world. French is the official language, and Lingala, Kikongo, Swahili, and Tshiluba are national languages among more than 200 spoken. The country is a republic with an elected president. Beneath its soil lie some of the world's greatest reserves of copper, cobalt, diamonds, and gold, yet most people remain poor, and armed conflict has troubled the east for decades. Congolese music and dance, meanwhile, are loved across the whole continent.
content.landAndNature: The Congo River, second in the world by water volume, loops through the country in a giant arc, collecting hundreds of tributaries and crossing the equator twice. A vast basin of rainforest fills the center, with hardwood trees, orchids, and river villages reachable only by boat. To the east rise the mountains of the Albertine Rift, including the snowcapped Rwenzori and the Virunga volcanoes, where Nyiragongo holds one of the world's largest lava lakes. Virunga National Park, Africa's oldest, shelters mountain gorillas. The DR Congo is the only home of the bonobo, the okapi, a shy forest relative of the giraffe with zebra-striped legs, and the Congo peafowl. Elephants, chimpanzees, and hippos also live here, and Lake Tanganyika forms part of the eastern border.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Congolese belong to hundreds of ethnic groups, among them the Luba, Kongo, Mongo, and Mangbetu, and most are Christian. Cassava is the staple, cooked into fufu or leaves pounded into pondu, with grilled fish, chicken in peanut sauce, and plantains. Kinshasa is Africa's music capital: Congolese rumba and its faster child, soukous, with sparkling guitar lines, are danced from Dakar to Nairobi, and stars like Franco and Papa Wemba became legends. Sapeurs dress in flamboyant suits as a statement of pride. Soccer is the top sport, and Congolese-born players star in European leagues. Congolese painters and sculptors, from Mangbetu carvers to modern artists like Chéri Samba, are collected worldwide.
content.history: Bantu-speaking peoples built kingdoms such as Kongo, Luba, and Kuba in the centuries before Europeans arrived. In 1885 King Leopold II of Belgium took the entire Congo basin as his personal property and forced people to gather rubber and ivory under brutal conditions; millions died before Belgium took over as a colony in 1908. Independence came on June 30, 1960, but the first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, was murdered within months. Army officer Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in 1965, renamed the country Zaire, and ruled as a dictator until 1997. Wars from 1996 to 2003 drew in neighboring countries and cost millions of lives, and fighting by armed groups continues in the east. The first peaceful transfer of power through elections came in 2019.
funFacts: The Congo River is so deep, over 220 meters in places, that it is the deepest river in the world.
Bonobos, one of humans' closest relatives, live only in the forests south of the Congo River and nowhere else on Earth.
The okapi has zebra-striped legs, a giraffe's long tongue, and was unknown to science until 1901.
The country's cobalt mines supply most of the metal used in the batteries of phones and electric cars.
Kinshasa and Brazzaville, capitals of two different countries, face each other across the Congo River, close enough to see.

content.tagline: Gorilla forests on the great river's bank
content.overview:
The Republic of the Congo, often called Congo-Brazzaville to tell it apart from its much bigger neighbor, lies on the equator in Central Africa. It is a little smaller than Montana, with a short Atlantic coastline and long borders with Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The capital, Brazzaville, faces Kinshasa, capital of the DR Congo, directly across the Congo River, making them the two closest capital cities in the world after Rome and Vatican City.

Around 6 million people live here, and more than half of them are in Brazzaville or the port city of Pointe-Noire. French is the official language, and Lingala and Kikongo are widely spoken. Oil pumped from beneath the ocean provides most of the country's money, along with timber from its vast forests. The Republic of the Congo is a presidential republic, led for most of the time since 1979 by the same president. Rainforest covers about two-thirds of the land, sheltering some of the largest gorilla and elephant populations left in Africa.
content.landAndNature: A narrow coastal plain rises to the Mayombe hills, then dips into the fertile Niari valley before climbing to the Batéké Plateau, a high grassland of sandy soil and deep river gorges. North of it spreads the Congo Basin rainforest and one of the largest tropical swamp forests on Earth, where rivers wander through flooded woodland for hundreds of kilometers. Odzala-Kokoua National Park holds tens of thousands of western lowland gorillas along with forest elephants, chimpanzees, and bongo antelope, and Nouabalé-Ndoki park is so remote that its animals show little fear of humans. The Congo River, second only to the Amazon in water flow, forms much of the eastern border. Rain falls heavily most of the year, and the climate is hot and steamy.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Kongo people are the largest group, followed by the Teke, Mbochi, and Sangha, with forest peoples living in the north. Most Congolese are Christian. Cassava is the main food, eaten as chikwangue, a dense loaf wrapped in leaves, or as saka-saka, pounded cassava leaves cooked with palm oil and fish. Grilled fish and plantains are sold at roadside stands. Brazzaville shares with Kinshasa the birth of Congolese rumba, a swaying guitar music recognized by UNESCO, and its streets are famous for the sapeurs, men who dress in dazzling tailored suits and treat elegance as an art form. Soccer is the most popular sport, and the country's writers, such as Alain Mabanckou, have won major French literary prizes.
content.history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled the region long ago, and by the 1400s the Kingdom of Kongo and the Teke kingdom traded ivory and copper. Portuguese contact from 1482 led to centuries of slave trading from the coast. In 1880 the French-Italian explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Teke king, and France made the area a colony, later the capital of French Equatorial Africa; forced labor building a railway to the coast killed thousands. Brazzaville served as the capital of Free France during World War II. Independence came on August 15, 1960. A Marxist government ruled from 1969 to 1991. Denis Sassou Nguesso held power from 1979 to 1992, and after a civil war in 1997 he returned and has governed since.
funFacts: Brazzaville and Kinshasa are the only two national capitals in the world that face each other across a river.
The Congo River is so powerful that it pushes fresh water more than 100 kilometers out into the Atlantic Ocean.
Sapeurs of Brazzaville may save for months to buy a single designer suit, then parade it through the streets on weekends.
The country's swamp forests store enormous amounts of carbon in peat, in some places more than five meters deep.
During World War II, Brazzaville was for a time the capital of the Free French forces fighting Nazi Germany.

content.tagline: Two oceans and a thousand shades of green
content.overview:
Colombia sits at the top corner of South America, the only country on the continent with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. It borders Panama, Venezuela, Brazil, Peru and Ecuador and covers about 1.14 million km², nearly twice the size of Texas. Around 52 million people live there, most of them in the cool Andean highlands and along the Caribbean coast.

The capital, Bogotá, sprawls across a plateau 2,640 meters up in the mountains. Medellín, Cali and Cartagena, a walled colonial port on the Caribbean, are other major cities. Spanish is the national language, and Colombians are famous for their warmth, their music and their coffee.

Colombia is a republic with an elected president. It is the second most biodiverse country on Earth after Brazil, with more kinds of birds and orchids than any other nation. After decades of armed conflict between the government, guerrilla groups and drug cartels, a 2016 peace agreement brought new hope, and tourists now flock to its beaches, cities and jungles.
content.landAndNature:
The Andes split into three parallel ranges as they enter Colombia, creating deep valleys and high plateaus where most people live. East of the mountains lie the wide grasslands of the Llanos and then the Amazon rainforest, which covers about a third of the country. The Pacific coast is one of the rainiest places on Earth, and humpback whales come there each year to give birth.

Colombia has about 1,900 species of birds, more than any other country, from hummingbirds to the Andean condor, plus poison dart frogs, pink river dolphins, spectacled bears and jaguars. Wax palms, the tallest palm trees in the world at up to 60 meters, tower over the Cocora Valley. Caño Cristales, a river in the Serranía de la Macarena, blazes red, yellow and green for a few months each year because of an aquatic plant.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Colombians are a mix of Indigenous, Spanish and African heritage, and each region has its own flavor. Along the Caribbean coast, cumbia and vallenato accordion music set the rhythm; Cali calls itself the world capital of salsa dancing. The Barranquilla Carnival, one of the largest in the world, and Medellín's Festival of Flowers fill the streets with parades.

Arepas, grilled corn cakes, are eaten at every meal, along with ajiaco chicken soup in Bogotá and the enormous bandeja paisa platter of beans, rice, meat, plantain and avocado. Colombian coffee is prized around the world. Soccer is the national passion, and cycling is close behind, with Colombian riders winning major European races. The writer Gabriel García Márquez won the Nobel Prize in 1982 for novels full of magical realism, and singer Shakira is a global star.
content.history:
Ancient cultures such as the Tayrona, who built the stone terraces of the Lost City, and the Muisca, whose golden offerings in Lake Guatavita inspired the legend of El Dorado, thrived long before Europeans came. Spanish settlers founded Santa Marta in 1525 and Cartagena in 1533, which became a major port for gold and for enslaved Africans.

Independence fighters led by Simón Bolívar defeated the Spanish at the Battle of Boyacá in 1819, creating Gran Colombia, a union that included Venezuela and Ecuador until it broke apart in 1831. Panama separated in 1903. In the 1900s Colombia suffered civil violence, and from the 1960s a long war involving guerrilla groups, paramilitaries and drug cartels killed hundreds of thousands. A 2016 peace accord with the largest guerrilla group, the FARC, began a slow recovery.
funFacts: Colombia is named after Christopher Columbus, even though he never set foot on its land.
Most of the world's emeralds come from Colombian mines, and the finest are deep, glowing green.
Every Sunday, Bogotá closes more than 100 kilometers of streets to cars so people can bike and skate, a tradition since 1974.
Colombia grows and ships more cut flowers than any country except the Netherlands, mostly roses and carnations.
The national sport, tejo, involves throwing a metal disc at targets packed with small gunpowder charges that explode on impact.
Colombia is the only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.

content.tagline: The perfume islands of the Indian Ocean
content.overview:
The Comoros are a group of volcanic islands in the Indian Ocean, floating between the northern tip of Madagascar and the coast of Mozambique. The three main islands, Grande Comore, Anjouan, and Mohéli, together cover less area than Delaware. The capital, Moroni, sits on Grande Comore beneath the smoking bulk of Mount Karthala, one of the world's largest active volcanoes. A fourth island in the group, Mayotte, is governed by France, which the Comoros dispute.

About 850,000 people live on the islands, and they are crowded onto the coasts and lower slopes. Three languages are official: Comorian, which is close to Swahili; Arabic; and French. Almost everyone is Sunni Muslim, and the call to prayer echoes over whitewashed mosques and stone houses in old Arab-style towns. The Comoros is a federal republic where the presidency rotates among the islands. It is one of the poorer countries in the world, living from fishing, farming, and the export of vanilla, cloves, and ylang-ylang flowers for perfume.
content.landAndNature: Each island is a volcano of a different age. Grande Comore is the youngest and roughest, with black lava fields and Mount Karthala, whose 2,361-meter summit holds one of the largest craters on Earth, about three kilometers across; it erupted as recently as 2007. Anjouan is older and greener, with sharp ridges and rivers, while Mohéli, the smallest, has rolling hills and a marine park where humpback whales, dolphins, and green turtles gather. The climate is hot and humid with a rainy season from November to April. The islands are known for Livingstone's fruit bat, a giant with a 1.4-meter wingspan, and the surrounding deep waters are home to the coelacanth, an ancient fish once thought extinct for 65 million years.
content.peopleAndCulture: Comorians descend from African, Arab, Malagasy, and Persian settlers, and their culture blends all of these. Women wear colorful cloth wraps and sometimes paint their faces with a yellow sandalwood paste called msindzano to protect and beautify their skin. The grand marriage, a lavish multi-day wedding ceremony with feasts and dances, is the most important event in a person's life. Food centers on rice, cassava, and breadfruit with coconut milk, fish, and spices, and langouste, spiny lobster, in vanilla sauce is a specialty. Music mixes Swahili taarab, Arab rhythms, and African drumming. Soccer is the favorite sport, and the national team surprised everyone by reaching the knockout round of the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.
content.history: African and Austronesian settlers arrived by the 700s, followed by Arab and Persian traders who brought Islam and founded sultanates that traded spices and enslaved people across the Indian Ocean. Portuguese ships visited in the 1500s, but the islands stayed independent until France took control in the 1800s, making them a colony of plantations growing vanilla and perfume plants. In a 1974 vote, three islands chose independence, declared in 1975, while Mayotte voted to remain French. Since then the Comoros have suffered more than 20 coups and attempted coups, some led by hired mercenaries, and Anjouan tried to break away in 1997. A 2001 constitution gave each island more self-rule. The islands remain peaceful today, though politics are often disputed.
funFacts: The Comoros are among the world's top producers of ylang-ylang, a flower whose oil is used in many famous perfumes.
The coelacanth, a fish with limb-like fins thought extinct since the dinosaurs, was found alive in Comorian waters in 1938.
Mount Karthala's summit crater is about three kilometers wide, one of the largest of any active volcano.
Livingstone's fruit bats, found only on Anjouan and Mohéli, have wings that stretch nearly a meter and a half.
The Comoros are sometimes called the Perfume Islands because of the vanilla, clove, and ylang-ylang scents in the air.

content.tagline: Ten volcanic islands where music never stops
content.overview:
Cape Verde, officially Cabo Verde, is a chain of ten volcanic islands in the Atlantic Ocean about 570 kilometers off the coast of Senegal in West Africa. Together they are smaller than Rhode Island, and the islands are scattered so widely that ferries and small planes are the only way between them. The capital, Praia, is on Santiago, the largest island. Around 600,000 people live in Cape Verde, but more Cape Verdeans live abroad, especially in the United States and Portugal, than at home.

Portuguese is the official language, while Cape Verdean Creole, a blend of Portuguese and West African languages, is what everyone speaks every day. The islands were uninhabited until Portuguese settlers and enslaved Africans arrived in the 1400s, so today's culture is a mix of both worlds. Cape Verde is a stable multiparty republic and one of Africa's most peaceful democracies. Fishing, tourism on its white and black sand beaches, and money sent home by relatives abroad keep the economy going in a land with very little rain.
content.landAndNature: The islands are the tops of volcanoes rising from the ocean floor. Fogo island is a single giant cone whose peak, Pico do Fogo, stands 2,829 meters high and last erupted in 2014, burying two villages inside its crater. Santo Antão has knife-edge ridges and deep green valleys, while Sal and Boa Vista are flat and sandy, with dunes and turquoise water. Despite the name, which means green cape, the islands are dry, receiving only brief rains between August and October. Boa Vista's beaches are one of the world's most important nesting sites for loggerhead sea turtles. Humpback whales pass by in spring, and the tiny Raso lark, one of the rarest birds on Earth, lives on a single uninhabited island.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Cape Verdeans are of mixed African and Portuguese descent and are Catholic. Music is the soul of the islands. Morna, a slow, longing style sung with guitar and violin, was made world-famous by singer Cesária Évora and is recognized by UNESCO; faster styles such as coladeira, funaná, and batuque get everyone dancing. The national dish is cachupa, a slow-cooked stew of corn, beans, vegetables, and fish or meat, often fried up the next morning for breakfast. Carnival on São Vicente rivals Brazil's for color, and grogue, a sugarcane spirit, is made in small country distilleries. Soccer is the top sport; the national team is called the Blue Sharks, and the islands have produced strong basketball players too.
content.history: Portuguese sailors reached the empty islands around 1456 and settled Santiago a few years later. Ribeira Grande, now Cidade Velha, became the first European town in the tropics and a major stop in the Atlantic slave trade, where captives from Africa were held before being shipped to the Americas.
