Pirates, including Francis Drake, raided it repeatedly. Repeated droughts in the 1700s and 1800s caused terrible famines and pushed many Cape Verdeans to emigrate, often on American whaling ships. Under a long independence movement led by Amílcar Cabral, who was assassinated in 1973, Cape Verde became independent from Portugal on July 5, 1975. It held its first multiparty elections in 1991 and has changed governments peacefully ever since.
funFacts: More Cape Verdeans live outside the country than inside it, with large communities in Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
Cidade Velha was the first European colonial town in the tropics and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Pico do Fogo's 2014 eruption covered the village of Chã das Caldeiras in lava, but many residents rebuilt on top of it.
Sal island's salt pans in an old volcanic crater are so salty that swimmers float like corks.
Boa Vista hosts one of the three largest loggerhead turtle nesting populations in the world.

content.tagline: Pura vida in the rainforest
content.overview:
Costa Rica is a small country in Central America with a big reputation for nature. It lies between Nicaragua and Panama, with the Caribbean Sea on one side and the Pacific Ocean on the other. At about 51,000 km² it is slightly smaller than the US state of West Virginia, yet it holds roughly 5 percent of all the plant and animal species on Earth. About 5 million people live there, most of them in the cool Central Valley around the capital, San José.

Costa Ricans call themselves Ticos and greet each other with "pura vida," meaning "pure life," a phrase that sums up their relaxed, friendly outlook. The country is one of the oldest and most stable democracies in Latin America, and it abolished its army in 1948, spending the money on schools and hospitals instead.

Spanish is the language, and coffee, bananas, pineapples and computer parts are major exports. Above all, tourists come to zip-line through cloud forests, watch sea turtles hatch and spot sloths dozing in the trees.
content.landAndNature:
A chain of volcanoes runs down the middle of Costa Rica, including Arenal, a perfect cone that erupted regularly for decades, and Poás, whose crater holds a steaming acid lake. Mountains climb to about 3,800 meters at Cerro Chirripó, from which on a clear day both oceans can be seen. The Caribbean side is hot and wet; the Pacific northwest has a dry season.

About a quarter of the country is protected in parks and reserves. Monteverde's cloud forest drips with moss and orchids and hides the resplendent quetzal, a shimmering green bird sacred to ancient peoples. Sloths, howler monkeys, scarlet macaws, toucans, red-eyed tree frogs and jaguars all live here, and thousands of green sea turtles crawl onto Tortuguero beach each year to lay eggs. Nearly all the country's electricity comes from rivers, wind, sun and volcanic heat.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Ticos speak Spanish, and Caribbean coastal communities also speak an English-based Creole. Most people are Catholic, and family life is central. Breakfast usually means gallo pinto, rice and black beans fried together with onions and cilantro, while lunch is often a casado, a plate of rice, beans, salad, plantains and meat or fish.

Soccer is the national sport, and the whole country celebrated when the team reached the World Cup quarterfinals in 2014. Surfing draws crowds to both coasts. Brightly painted wooden ox carts, once used to haul coffee to the ports, are a national symbol and a UNESCO-recognized craft. Fiestas feature marimba music, bull-teasing events without harm to the bull, and fireworks. Costa Rica has one of the highest literacy rates in Latin America.
content.history:
Indigenous peoples such as the Chorotega and the Diquís, who carved hundreds of mysterious, perfectly round stone spheres, lived here for thousands of years. Christopher Columbus landed on the Caribbean coast in 1502 and the Spanish named the area Costa Rica, "rich coast," though it turned out to have little gold and became a poor, quiet farming colony.

Costa Rica became independent from Spain in 1821 along with the rest of Central America. Coffee farming brought wealth in the 1800s, and schools spread across the country. After a short civil war in 1948, the new government abolished the army, a decision written into the constitution. Since then Costa Rica has held peaceful elections for decades, and its president Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987 for helping to end wars in neighboring countries.
funFacts: Costa Rica has had no army since 1948, and December 1 is celebrated as Army Abolition Day.
The country covers only about 0.03 percent of the Earth's surface but holds around 5 percent of its species.
Ancient people carved more than 300 stone spheres, some over two meters wide and weighing 15 tons; no one knows exactly why.
Costa Rica is the world's largest exporter of pineapples.
On most days, about 99 percent of the country's electricity comes from renewable sources.
Costa Ricans often use "pura vida" to say hello, goodbye, thank you and everything is fine.

content.tagline: The Caribbean's largest island
content.overview:
Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, a long, crocodile-shaped country lying just 150 kilometers south of Florida. With about 110,000 km² of land, it is slightly smaller than the US state of Pennsylvania, and about 11 million people live there. The capital, Havana, is famous for its faded pastel mansions, seaside promenade and streets full of gleaming 1950s American cars kept running for decades.

Spanish is the language, and Cubans are known for music, dance and baseball. Since a revolution in 1959, Cuba has been a one-party socialist state led for many years by Fidel Castro. The government provides free schooling and health care, but shortages of goods are common, made worse by a trade embargo the United States has kept in place since the 1960s.

Sugar, tobacco and nickel have long been Cuba's main products, and tourists come for its beaches, colonial towns and rhythms. Most Cubans live in cities, and many have relatives who left for the United States and elsewhere.
content.landAndNature:
Cuba is mostly flat or gently rolling, with fertile plains that grow sugarcane and tobacco. Mountains rise in three places, highest in the Sierra Maestra of the southeast, where Pico Turquino reaches about 1,970 meters. In the west, the Viñales Valley is dotted with mogotes, steep, rounded limestone hills that look like giant green haystacks. Thousands of smaller islands and cays fringe the main island.

The climate is tropical, with a rainy season from May to October and hurricanes some years. Cuba is home to the bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world, about the size of a bumblebee. The Zapata Swamp shelters the rare Cuban crocodile, and painted snails called polymitas, striped in bright colors, live in the eastern forests. Coral reefs off the south coast are among the healthiest in the Caribbean.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Cubans are a mix of Spanish, African and other roots, and their culture is famous for blending them. Cuban son, rumba and salsa music, driven by drums, trumpets and claves, are danced everywhere from living rooms to city squares. Baseball is the national obsession, and Cuban boxers and athletes have won many Olympic medals. Dominoes played loudly on sidewalk tables is a favorite pastime.

Home cooking includes ropa vieja (shredded beef in tomato sauce), black beans and rice, fried plantains called tostones, and sweet guava paste with cheese. Coffee is strong and sugary. Religion mixes Catholicism with Santería, a faith with roots in West Africa. Cuba's national ballet and its film festival are well known, and the writer Ernest Hemingway lived near Havana for about 20 years.
content.history:
The Taíno people were farming and fishing in Cuba when Columbus arrived in 1492. Spain ruled the island for four centuries, bringing hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans to work on sugar plantations; slavery ended only in 1886. The poet José Martí inspired a war for independence, and after the Spanish-American War of 1898 Cuba became a republic in 1902, though the United States kept strong control over it.

In 1959 rebels led by Fidel Castro overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista. Castro's government took over businesses, allied with the Soviet Union and clashed with the United States, most dangerously in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, when the world came close to nuclear war. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Cuba faced severe hardship. Castro stepped down in 2008, and the Communist Party continues to govern.
funFacts: The bee hummingbird, found only in Cuba, weighs less than a penny and lays eggs the size of coffee beans.
Because new cars were hard to import for decades, tens of thousands of 1950s American cars still cruise Cuban streets.
Cuba has one of the highest numbers of doctors per person in the world and sends medical teams abroad.
Havana's Malecón seawall stretches about 8 kilometers and serves as the city's outdoor living room.
Cuba's national dance, the danzón, and its music styles helped create salsa in New York in the 1960s and 1970s.
The island is about 1,250 kilometers long but only around 100 kilometers wide on average.

content.tagline: Island of Aphrodite, divided by a line
content.overview:
Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, lying in its far eastern corner, closer to Turkey, Syria, and Lebanon than to mainland Europe. It is about the size of Connecticut. Golden beaches ring the coast, and two mountain ranges rise inland, with the capital, Nicosia, on the dusty plain between them. Ancient Greeks believed Aphrodite, the goddess of love, was born from the sea foam off its southwestern shore.

Around 1.3 million people live on the island. Greek and Turkish are the official languages, reflecting its two main communities. Since 1974 Cyprus has been divided: the Republic of Cyprus, which joined the European Union in 2004, governs the south, while the northern third is run by a Turkish Cypriot administration recognized only by Turkey. A United Nations buffer zone, the Green Line, runs between them and cuts right through Nicosia, making it the last divided capital in Europe. Tourism, shipping, and services drive the economy, and Cypriots enjoy one of the sunniest climates in Europe.
content.landAndNature: The Troodos Mountains fill the center and southwest of the island, topped by Mount Olympus at 1,952 meters, high enough for a short ski season in winter while people swim on the coast below. Their forests of black pine and golden oak hide tiny painted churches from the Middle Ages. Along the north coast runs the long, narrow Kyrenia range of jagged limestone. Between the ranges the Mesaoria plain grows wheat, olives, and carob. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild and wet. The Cyprus mouflon, a wild sheep with huge curled horns, lives only in the Paphos forest. Green and loggerhead turtles nest on beaches like Lara Bay, and salt lakes near Larnaca and Akrotiri fill each winter with thousands of pink flamingos.
content.peopleAndCulture: Greek Cypriots, mostly Orthodox Christian, make up the majority, and Turkish Cypriots, mostly Muslim, live largely in the north; both communities share a love of coffee, backgammon, and long family lunches. Halloumi, a squeaky white cheese that can be grilled without melting, is the island's most famous food, joined by souvlaki, sheftalia sausages, and meze, a parade of dozens of small dishes. Commandaria, a sweet wine, may be the oldest named wine still made, dating back at least 800 years. Easter is the biggest holiday in the south, with fireworks and roasted lamb, while Ramadan and Bayram are celebrated in the north. Soccer is the most popular sport, and Cypriot villages keep lace-making and pottery traditions alive.
content.history: People have lived on Cyprus for about 10,000 years, and the island's copper mines were so famous that its name and the word copper may share a root. Greeks settled around 1200 BC, followed by rule under Assyrians, Egyptians, Persians, Alexander the Great, Romans, Byzantines, Crusaders, Venetians, and, from 1571, the Ottoman Empire. Britain took control in 1878 and made it a colony. Cyprus became independent in 1960, but tension between Greek and Turkish Cypriots led to violence. In 1974 a coup backed by Greece's military government was followed by a Turkish invasion, and the island was split, with about 200,000 people displaced from their homes. Talks to reunite the island have continued for decades. The Republic of Cyprus joined the EU in 2004.
funFacts: Nicosia is the only capital city in Europe still divided by a barrier, with checkpoints in the middle of its old town.
A Cypriot village called Lefkara made lace so fine that, according to tradition, Leonardo da Vinci bought a piece for Milan's cathedral.
Cyprus has no natural lakes; its salt lakes fill only with winter rain and dry to white crusts in summer.
The Cyprus mouflon appears on the country's coins and was once hunted almost to extinction.
Cypriots consume more halloumi per person than anyone else, and the cheese has protected status in the European Union.

content.tagline: Castles, spires, and a hundred bridges
content.overview:
Czechia, also called the Czech Republic, is a landlocked country in the center of Europe, about the size of South Carolina, ringed by Germany, Poland, Slovakia, and Austria. Its capital, Prague, is one of the most visited cities in the world, a fairy tale of spires, a medieval astronomical clock, and a stone bridge lined with statues arching over the Vltava River. Around 10.9 million people live in the country, which is made up of three historic lands: Bohemia in the west, Moravia in the east, and a slice of Silesia in the north.

Czech is the official language, and Slovak, spoken in the neighboring country that was once joined with it, is understood by nearly everyone. Czechia is a parliamentary republic with a president and a prime minister, a member of the European Union since 2004 and of NATO since 1999. It is a highly industrial country, making cars, machines, and glass, and it has a long tradition of beer brewing, puppet theater, and classical music from composers like Dvořák and Smetana.
content.landAndNature: Czechia sits in a bowl. Bohemia is ringed by low mountain ranges, including the Krkonoše, or Giant Mountains, where Sněžka reaches 1,603 meters, and the forested Šumava along the Bavarian border, one of the largest wild areas in Central Europe. Inside the ring lie rolling hills, farmland, fishponds dug in the Middle Ages, and rivers such as the Vltava and Elbe. Moravia is gentler, with vineyards in the south and the karst caves of the Moravian Karst, including the Macocha Abyss, a sinkhole 138 meters deep. The Bohemian Switzerland park has sandstone towers and the largest natural rock arch in Europe. Lynx have returned to the Šumava, and storks nest on village chimneys. Winters are cold and snowy, summers warm.
content.peopleAndCulture: Czechs are known for dry humor and for drinking more beer per person than any other nation; Pilsner-style lager was invented in the city of Plzeň in 1842. Favorite foods include roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce, and sweet fruit dumplings. Puppet theater is a treasured art, and Czech cartoons such as the Little Mole are loved across Europe. Ice hockey rivals soccer as the national sport, and Czech players fill professional leagues worldwide. Writers Franz Kafka and Milan Kundera, composer Antonín Dvořák, and film director Miloš Forman all came from here. Easter brings decorated eggs, and Christmas Eve dinner is traditionally fried carp, sold live from tubs on the streets.
content.history: Slavic tribes settled Bohemia and Moravia by the 500s, and the Great Moravian Empire flourished in the 800s. The Kingdom of Bohemia became powerful in the Middle Ages, and under Emperor Charles IV in the 1300s Prague was the capital of the Holy Roman Empire and got Central Europe's first university. Religious reformer Jan Hus was burned at the stake in 1415, sparking wars. From 1526 the Habsburgs of Austria ruled for almost 400 years. Czechoslovakia was born in 1918 after World War I, but Nazi Germany dismantled it in 1938 and 1939. After the war a communist government took over; the Prague Spring reforms of 1968 were crushed by Soviet tanks. The peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communism, and in 1993 Czechia and Slovakia split into two friendly countries.
funFacts: Prague's astronomical clock has struck the hour with parading apostle figures since 1410, making it the oldest still working.
The word robot was invented by Czech writer Karel Čapek for a 1920 play about artificial workers.
Czechs drink more beer per person than any other country, roughly 130 liters a year on average.
Prague Castle is the largest ancient castle complex in the world, covering about 70,000 square meters.
Contact lenses as we know them were developed by Czech chemist Otto Wichterle, who built his first machine from a child's construction kit.

content.tagline: Castles, engineers, and a reunited nation
content.overview:
Germany sits at the center of Europe, sharing borders with nine countries, more than any other European nation. It is a little smaller than Montana, reaching from the North Sea and Baltic coasts in the north to the snowy Alps in the south. The capital, Berlin, is a lively city of museums, street art, and history, where a wall once divided East from West. Other great cities include Hamburg, with Europe's third-busiest port, Munich, home of the Oktoberfest, and Frankfurt, a banking hub of skyscrapers.

About 84 million people live in Germany, the most of any country in the European Union, and they speak German. Germany is a federal republic of 16 states with a parliament and a chancellor who runs the government. It has Europe's largest economy, built on engineering: cars, machines, chemicals, and precision instruments carry the label Made in Germany around the world. Germans are known for punctuality, recycling, forests full of hiking trails, hundreds of kinds of bread and sausage, and a history that has shaped the whole modern world.
content.landAndNature: Northern Germany is flat lowland of heath, lakes, and farmland, with sandy islands and mudflats along the coast where seals rest. The center rises into wooded uplands like the Harz Mountains and the Black Forest, whose dark firs inspired the Grimm brothers' fairy tales. In the far south the Bavarian Alps reach 2,962 meters at the Zugspitze. The Rhine River flows north past castles and vineyards through a gorge dotted with legends, and the Danube begins in the Black Forest on its way to the Black Sea. About a third of Germany is forest. Red deer, wild boar, and foxes are common, wolves have returned to the east, and lynx roam the Bavarian Forest. Lake Constance, shared with Switzerland and Austria, is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe.
content.peopleAndCulture: Germans bake more than 300 kinds of bread and make some 1,500 kinds of sausage, from Bavarian weisswurst to Berlin's currywurst, eaten with pretzels, sauerkraut, and potato salad. Munich's Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world, and Christmas markets fill town squares with lights, gingerbread, and carved wooden ornaments. Soccer is the national game; Germany has won the men's World Cup four times, and the Bundesliga draws huge crowds. Composers Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms, thinkers like Kant and Einstein, and writers Goethe and the Brothers Grimm were German. Children start school with a giant cone of sweets, the Schultüte. Germans love the outdoors, from hiking to spending Sunday afternoons over coffee and cake.
content.history: Germanic tribes stopped the Roman legions at the Rhine, and in 800 Charlemagne was crowned emperor of a realm that became the Holy Roman Empire, a patchwork of hundreds of small states. Johannes Gutenberg's printing press around 1450 and Martin Luther's Reformation in 1517 changed the world. Prussia's leader Otto von Bismarck unified Germany in 1871. Defeat in World War I brought hardship, and in 1933 Adolf Hitler and the Nazis seized power, started World War II, and murdered six million Jews and millions of others in the Holocaust. After 1945 Germany was split into democratic West Germany and communist East Germany, divided by the Berlin Wall from 1961. Peaceful protests brought the wall down in 1989, and the two Germanys reunited in 1990. Germany is a leading member of the European Union.
funFacts: Germany has more than 20,000 castles, and Neuschwanstein castle inspired the Sleeping Beauty castle at Disneyland.
The first printed books, automobile, jet engine, and MP3 format were all invented in Germany.
Germany has more than 1,500 kinds of sausage and over 300 kinds of bread, and the bread culture is on UNESCO's heritage list.
There is no general speed limit on many stretches of the German Autobahn highways.
The gummy bear was invented in Bonn in 1922 by Hans Riegel, whose company name came from his initials and his hometown.

content.tagline: Salt lakes and ships at Africa's gateway
content.overview:
Djibouti is a small, sun-baked country on the Horn of Africa, guarding the narrow strait where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden. It is about the size of New Jersey, wedged between Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia, with Yemen just across the water. Its location is its treasure: nearly all ships sailing between Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal pass by, and Djibouti's port also handles almost all the trade of its giant landlocked neighbor, Ethiopia.

About one million people live in Djibouti, and around two-thirds of them are in the capital, Djibouti City, which has the same name as the country. Arabic and French are official languages, and Somali and Afar are the languages of the two main peoples. Nearly everyone is Muslim. The country is a republic led by a president, and its stability in a troubled region has led France, the United States, China, Japan, and other nations to keep military bases there. The land is mostly desert, so most food is imported, and camels still cross the plains.
content.landAndNature: Djibouti sits where three pieces of the Earth's crust are pulling apart, and the results are dramatic. Lake Assal, a salt lake 155 meters below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth, ringed by a blinding white crust that people have mined for centuries. Lake Abbe, on the Ethiopian border, has a field of limestone chimneys up to 50 meters tall that steam in the dawn light. Volcanic plains of black rock stretch between them. The Goda Mountains in the north hold the small Day Forest, a surprising patch of juniper trees. The Gulf of Tadjoura draws whale sharks every winter, and the coral reefs are rich in fish. It is one of the hottest countries in the world, with summer highs above 45 degrees Celsius.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Somali, mainly of the Issa clan, and the Afar are the two main peoples, and both have traditions of nomadic herding, poetry, and long negotiations under acacia trees. Daily life includes chewing khat leaves in the afternoon, sipping spiced tea, and eating skoudehkaris, a rice dish with lamb and spices, or lahoh, spongy flatbread, often with French baguettes on the side. Women wear bright, flowing dresses; men often wear a wrapped skirt called a macawiis. Music is drum-based and lively, and traditional dances tell stories of clans and camels. Soccer is popular, and Djiboutian runners have competed in the Olympic marathon. Fishing dhows share the harbor with container ships and warships.
content.history: Afar and Somali herders have moved across this land for centuries, trading with Arabia and Ethiopia through small ports like Tadjoura and Zeila. France gained a foothold in 1862 and created the colony of French Somaliland, building Djibouti City and, in 1917, a railway to Addis Ababa that made it Ethiopia's link to the sea. In votes in 1958 and 1967 the territory chose to stay French, but independence finally came on June 27, 1977. Hassan Gouled Aptidon was the first president, ruling until 1999, when his nephew Ismaïl Omar Guelleh succeeded him. A civil war between the government and Afar rebels lasted from 1991 to 1994 and ended in a peace deal. A new electric railway to Ethiopia opened in 2018.
funFacts: Lake Assal is about ten times saltier than the ocean and lies 155 meters below sea level, the lowest point in Africa.
Djibouti hosts military bases from more foreign countries than any other nation, including the United States, France, China, and Japan.
The country's economy depends so heavily on its port that it handles roughly 95 percent of Ethiopia's foreign trade.
The limestone chimneys of Lake Abbe were used as an alien landscape in the 1968 film Planet of the Apes.
Whale sharks, the largest fish in the world, gather in the Gulf of Tadjoura each winter and can be snorkeled alongside.

content.tagline: The Nature Island of the Caribbean
content.overview:
Dominica is a rugged volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, lying between the French islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique. It is often confused with the much larger Dominican Republic, but the two are very different places. Dominica covers about 750 km², a little smaller than New York City, and only about 70,000 people live there, most of them along the coast around the capital, Roseau.

Islanders call it the Nature Island, and the name fits. Steep green mountains, some of them still-active volcanoes, rise straight from the sea, and rainforest covers most of the interior. Instead of white sand and big resorts, Dominica offers hot springs, waterfalls, hiking trails and whales offshore.

Dominica is also home to the Kalinago, the last remaining community of the Caribbean's original Indigenous people, who live on their own territory on the east coast. English is the official language, and many people also speak a French-based Creole. The country is an independent republic in the Commonwealth with an elected parliament and president.
content.landAndNature:
Dominica is one of the youngest and most mountainous islands in the Caribbean, with nine volcanoes packed into a small space; Morne Diablotins, the highest, reaches about 1,450 meters. Rain falls almost daily on the peaks, feeding so many streams that islanders say there is one river for each day of the year. In the Morne Trois Pitons National Park, a World Heritage Site, the Boiling Lake bubbles at close to 90 degrees Celsius, the second-largest hot lake in the world, and the Valley of Desolation hisses with steam vents.

Hurricanes are the great danger; Hurricane Maria in 2017 damaged nearly every building on the island. The forests shelter the sisserou parrot, a large purple-and-green bird found nowhere else and shown on the national flag. Sperm whales live in the deep waters offshore all year, and Champagne Reef fizzes with volcanic bubbles.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Dominicans are of African descent, with about 3,000 Kalinago people living in the Kalinago Territory, where they weave baskets and build traditional canoes. English is spoken in schools and government, while Kwéyòl, a Creole related to French, is heard in markets and songs. Creole Day in October celebrates the language with traditional dress in bright madras plaid.

Food centers on root vegetables, plantains, fresh fish and callaloo, a thick green soup, along with bakes, fried dough eaten for breakfast. The World Creole Music Festival each October fills Roseau with bouyon, zouk and reggae. Cricket is the favorite sport, and the Waitukubuli National Trail, about 185 kilometers long, lets hikers cross the whole island. Independence celebrations in November include a heritage day honoring the island's villages.
content.history:
The Kalinago, whom Europeans called Caribs, arrived from South America and named the island Waitukubuli, "tall is her body." Columbus sighted it on a Sunday in November 1493 and called it Dominica, Latin for Sunday. Its steep terrain and fierce defenders kept Europeans away longer than on other islands.

France and Britain fought over Dominica through the 1700s, and Britain won it for good in 1783. Enslaved Africans worked coffee and sugar plantations until slavery was abolished in 1834, and in 1838 Dominica became the only British Caribbean colony with a legislature controlled by Black members. The island joined the West Indies Federation in the 1950s and became independent on November 3, 1978. Hurricanes David in 1979 and Maria in 2017 caused huge damage, and the country now aims to become the world's first fully climate-resilient nation.
funFacts: The sisserou parrot on Dominica's flag makes it one of only a couple of national flags that use the color purple.
Dominica's Boiling Lake is about 60 meters across and so hot that its center is a constant rolling boil.
The Kalinago Territory in Dominica is the only remaining Indigenous community of its kind in the Caribbean.
Parts of the Pirates of the Caribbean films were shot in Dominica's rivers and forests.
The island has around 365 rivers, one for every day of the year, according to local tradition.
Sperm whales can be seen off Dominica in every month of the year, which is rare anywhere in the world.

content.tagline: Vikings, bicycles, and building blocks
content.overview:
Denmark is the smallest and southernmost of the Scandinavian countries, made up of the Jutland peninsula, which points north from Germany, and about 400 islands, of which around 70 are inhabited. The mainland part is about twice the size of Massachusetts. The capital, Copenhagen, spreads across two islands and is famous for its harbor, colorful waterfront houses, and streets where bicycles outnumber cars. The Kingdom of Denmark also includes two self-governing territories, Greenland and the Faroe Islands.

About 6 million people live in Denmark and speak Danish. It is a constitutional monarchy, with one of the oldest royal families in the world and a parliament that makes the laws. Danes pay high taxes and in return receive free schooling, university, and health care, and they regularly rank among the happiest people on Earth. The country produces wind turbines, medicines, and famous design, and it is home to LEGO bricks, fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen, and the cozy way of life Danes call hygge.
content.landAndNature: Denmark is flat and low; its highest natural point, Møllehøj, rises only 171 meters, and no place is far from the sea. The coastline stretches more than 7,000 kilometers if all the islands are counted, with sandy beaches on the west coast pounded by North Sea waves and gentler shores facing the Baltic. Farmland covers more than half the country, with fields of wheat, barley, and rapeseed and countless pig farms. At Skagen, the northern tip, two seas meet and their waves visibly collide. The chalk cliffs of Møns Klint gleam white above the sea, and the Wadden Sea mudflats host millions of migrating birds. Red deer roam the heaths of Jutland, and seals rest on sandbanks. The climate is mild, windy, and often cloudy.
content.peopleAndCulture: Danes value trust, equality, and hygge, the warm coziness of candles, good food, and friends on a dark winter evening. Nearly half of Copenhagen residents cycle to work or school along wide bike lanes. Open-faced sandwiches called smørrebrød, piled with herring, egg, or roast pork on dark rye bread, are a lunchtime classic, and flaky pastries known abroad as Danish are called wienerbrød at home. Handball and soccer are the top sports; Denmark won the 1992 European soccer championship as a last-minute replacement team. The author Hans Christian Andersen wrote The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, philosopher Søren Kierkegaard and physicist Niels Bohr were Danish, and Danish furniture and architecture set world styles in the 20th century.
content.history: Farmers settled Denmark after the last Ice Age, and around the year 800 the Vikings sailed from its shores to raid and trade across Europe, ruling parts of England for a time. King Harald Bluetooth united the country and brought Christianity around 965. In the Middle Ages Denmark ruled Norway and, for a while, Sweden, and it kept Norway until 1814. Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849. It lost territory to Prussia in 1864 but stayed neutral in World War I. Nazi Germany occupied Denmark from 1940 to 1945, and in 1943 Danes secretly ferried almost all of the country's Jews to safety in Sweden. Denmark joined NATO in 1949 and the European Union in 1973, though it kept its own currency.
funFacts: LEGO bricks were invented in the Danish town of Billund, and the name combines the Danish words for play well.
The Bluetooth wireless symbol is made from the runic initials of Viking king Harald Bluetooth.
Denmark's flag, a white cross on red, is considered the oldest national flag still in use, dating to the 1300s.
Copenhagen has more bicycles than people, and about 45 percent of residents commute by bike.
The Øresund Bridge and tunnel link Denmark to Sweden across 16 kilometers of sea, carrying cars and trains.

content.tagline: Where Europe's Americas began
content.overview:
The Dominican Republic occupies the eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola, the second-largest island in the Caribbean, which it shares with Haiti. At about 48,700 km² it is a little more than twice the size of the US state of New Jersey, and about 11 million people live there. Its capital, Santo Domingo, was founded in the 1490s and is the oldest continuously inhabited European city in the Americas, with the first cathedral, hospital and university of the New World.

Spanish is the national language, and Dominicans are known for their love of baseball, merengue music and dancing. Farming produces sugar, cocoa, coffee and tobacco, while tourism to beach resorts such as Punta Cana is the biggest business, drawing millions of visitors a year.

The country is a democratic republic with an elected president. It has both the highest mountain and the lowest point in the Caribbean, along with rainforests, deserts, mangroves and long white beaches lined with coconut palms.
content.landAndNature:
Four mountain ranges cross the country. The Cordillera Central holds Pico Duarte, about 3,100 meters high, the tallest peak in the Caribbean, where frost sometimes forms at dawn. In the dry southwest, Lake Enriquillo lies about 40 meters below sea level, the lowest point on any Caribbean island, and its salty water is home to American crocodiles and flamingos.

The climate is tropical, cooler in the mountains, with hurricanes possible from June to November. Rivers water fertile valleys of rice and sugarcane. The Bay of Samaná fills with thousands of humpback whales each winter, when they come from the North Atlantic to mate and give birth. The rhinoceros iguana, the Hispaniolan solenodon (a rare venomous mammal) and the palmchat, the national bird, are found on the island and nowhere else.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Dominicans are mostly of mixed African and Spanish heritage, and they speak a fast Caribbean Spanish. Baseball is the national passion; boys play with broomsticks and bottle caps, and the country has sent more players to America's Major League than any other nation outside the United States. Merengue, with its accordion, drum and metal scraper called a güira, is the national dance, and slower, romantic bachata was born in the countryside; UNESCO recognizes both.

The everyday lunch is "la bandera," the flag, made of white rice, red beans and stewed meat, and mangú, mashed plantains topped with onions, is a breakfast favorite. Carnival in February fills the streets with masked diablos cojuelos cracking whips. Family gatherings feature dominoes, loud music and sancocho, a rich seven-meat stew.
content.history:
The Taíno people lived in villages across Hispaniola when Columbus landed in 1492 and set up the first Spanish colony in the Americas. Within decades disease, war and forced labor had wiped out most of the Taíno, and enslaved Africans were brought in to replace them. Spain later neglected the colony while France built a rich sugar colony in the west, the future Haiti.

Haiti ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844, when Dominican rebels led by Juan Pablo Duarte declared independence on February 27. The young country went back under Spain from 1861 to 1865, was occupied by the United States from 1916 to 1924, and then suffered the brutal dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo from 1930 until his assassination in 1961. After a civil war in 1965, democracy slowly took root, and elections have been held regularly since the late 1970s.
funFacts: Larimar, a sky-blue stone, is found in only one mountainside on Earth, in the southwest of the Dominican Republic.
Dominican amber is famous for trapping ancient insects and even small lizards, some more than 20 million years old.
Santo Domingo's Alcázar de Colón was built for Christopher Columbus's son Diego, who governed the colony.
The Dominican flag is the only national flag in the world that features a Bible.
The Dominican Republic and Haiti are the only two countries that share one Caribbean island.
Merengue dancers say the shuffling step began with enslaved workers who danced while chained together.

content.tagline: From Mediterranean shores to Saharan dunes
content.overview:
Algeria is the largest country in Africa and the tenth largest in the world, covering about 2.4 million square kilometers, more than three times the size of Texas. Yet most of that land is the Sahara, and the great majority of its roughly 45 million people live in a narrow green strip along the Mediterranean coast. The capital, Algiers, climbs a hillside in tiers of white buildings, earning it the nickname Algiers the White.

Arabic is the official language, alongside Tamazight, the language of the Berber (Amazigh) peoples who lived here long before Arabic arrived. French, left behind from colonial times, is still widely used in business and schools. Algeria is a republic led by a president, and its economy depends heavily on oil and natural gas pumped from beneath the desert. Cities are modern and busy, while oasis towns in the south keep centuries-old rhythms shaped by date harvests and the heat.
content.landAndNature: Two mountain chains, the Tell Atlas and the Saharan Atlas, run parallel to the coast with a belt of high plateaus between them. South of the mountains the Sahara takes over for more than 80 percent of the country. It is not all sand: there are seas of dunes called ergs, gravel plains, and the rocky Hoggar Mountains, where Mount Tahat rises to about 2,900 meters. The Tassili n'Ajjer plateau is a maze of sandstone pillars and arches. Algeria's national animal is the fennec fox, whose enormous ears release heat and pick up the faint sounds of prey under the sand. Dorcas gazelles, Barbary macaques in the northern cedar forests, and a tiny population of Saharan cheetahs also survive here.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Algerians have both Arab and Berber ancestry, and Berber groups such as the Kabyle, Chaoui, and Tuareg keep their own languages and traditions. Nearly everyone is Muslim, and the weekend falls on Friday and Saturday. Couscous, steamed grains topped with vegetables and meat, is the national dish, joined by chorba soup, spicy merguez sausages, and honey-soaked makroud pastries. Sweet mint tea is offered to every guest. Raï, a lively pop music born in the port city of Oran, is famous across the Arab world and beyond. Soccer is a passion: the national team, the Desert Foxes, won the Africa Cup of Nations in 1990 and 2019. The writer Albert Camus, who won the Nobel Prize, was born in Algeria.
content.history: Berber kingdoms such as Numidia flourished here more than 2,000 years ago, trading and sometimes fighting with Carthage and Rome, whose ruins still stand at Timgad and Djemila. Arab armies brought Islam in the 7th century, and the Ottoman Empire later controlled the coast. France invaded in 1830 and ruled Algeria as part of France for 132 years, settling over a million Europeans on the best farmland. A brutal war of independence from 1954 to 1962 cost hundreds of thousands of lives before Algeria became free on July 5, 1962. One party governed for decades, and a civil war in the 1990s killed tens of thousands. Huge peaceful protests in 2019 led the long-serving president to resign.
funFacts: The rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer includes thousands of paintings, some up to 12,000 years old, showing giraffes and cattle in what is now desert.
Algeria is bigger than all of Western Europe's largest countries, France, Spain, Germany, and Italy, put together.
The Sahara's Grand Erg Oriental, a sea of dunes, is larger than the entire country of Ireland.
Ghardaïa, an oasis city in the M'zab valley, has kept the same pyramid-like layout for about a thousand years.
The Casbah of Algiers, a steep tangle of alleys and stairways from Ottoman times, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

content.tagline: Volcanoes, jungle and the Galápagos
content.overview:
Ecuador takes its name from the equator, the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth that passes just north of its capital, Quito. It sits on the northwest coast of South America between Colombia and Peru, and although it is one of the continent's smaller countries, about 277,000 km² or roughly the size of Colorado, it packs in four very different worlds: the Pacific coast, the Andes mountains, the Amazon rainforest and the Galápagos Islands, about 1,000 kilometers out to sea.

About 18 million people live in Ecuador. Quito, at about 2,850 meters, is the second-highest capital city in the world and has one of the best-preserved colonial old towns in the Americas. Guayaquil, on the coast, is the biggest city and main port.

Spanish is the main language, and Kichwa, the language of the Inca, is spoken by many Indigenous people in the highlands. Ecuador is a republic with an elected president, and it has used the US dollar as its money since 2000. Bananas, shrimp, oil, roses and cacao are its main exports.
content.landAndNature:
Two chains of the Andes run through Ecuador, forming an "Avenue of the Volcanoes." Cotopaxi, a snow-capped cone of about 5,900 meters, is one of the highest active volcanoes on Earth, and Chimborazo, about 6,260 meters, is the point on the planet farthest from the Earth's center because the globe bulges at the equator. East of the mountains, the Amazon lowlands steam with rain, home to jaguars, pink dolphins, anacondas and more kinds of birds than all of North America.

The Galápagos Islands, born from volcanoes, are famous for animals found nowhere else: giant tortoises that live more than 100 years, marine iguanas that swim in the sea, blue-footed boobies, and the only penguins that live north of the equator. Charles Darwin's visit in 1835 helped him develop the theory of evolution.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Ecuadorians are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous and Spanish heritage, and around a fifth are Indigenous, especially Kichwa-speaking peoples of the Andes and Shuar and Waorani communities of the Amazon. Highland markets like Otavalo overflow with woven ponchos, and women there wear embroidered blouses and layers of gold beads.

Food changes with altitude: ceviche of shrimp and encebollado fish soup on the coast; potato patties called llapingachos, roasted corn and hearty soups in the mountains. Soccer is the top sport, and ecuavoley, a three-a-side volleyball played with a heavy ball, is a homegrown favorite. The Inti Raymi sun festival in June and the New Year's Eve burning of "año viejo" effigies are lively traditions. The fine straw hats sold as Panama hats are woven in the Ecuadorian town of Montecristi.
content.history:
The Valdivia culture on Ecuador's coast made some of the oldest pottery in the Americas about 5,500 years ago. Highland kingdoms later fell to the Inca in the late 1400s, and the Inca emperor Atahualpa was born in the north. Spanish soldiers arrived in 1534 and founded Quito on the ruins of an Inca city.

Quito's citizens made one of the first calls for independence in Spanish America on August 10, 1809, and freedom was won at the Battle of Pichincha in 1822. Ecuador belonged to Gran Colombia until 1830, then became its own republic. The 1900s brought cocoa and banana booms, oil discoveries in the Amazon, border wars with Peru that ended with a 1998 treaty, and frequent changes of government. A 2008 constitution made Ecuador the first country to give legal rights to nature itself.
funFacts: Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo is the farthest point from the planet's center, farther than Everest.
Ecuador exports more bananas than any other country in the world.
Panama hats are not from Panama; they have been woven in Ecuador for centuries.
Quito and Kraków were the first two cities ever named UNESCO World Heritage Sites, in 1978.
Galápagos giant tortoises can weigh over 250 kilograms and live well past 100 years.
Ecuador has no currency of its own; it has used US dollars since 2000.

content.tagline: Gift of the Nile
content.overview:
Egypt sits in the northeastern corner of Africa, with its Sinai Peninsula reaching into Asia, so it is a bridge between two continents. The country is about one and a half times the size of Texas, but almost all of it is desert. Life clings to the Nile River, which runs the whole length of the country, and to its fan-shaped delta on the Mediterranean; around 95 percent of Egyptians live on about 5 percent of the land. The capital, Cairo, is a roaring metropolis of more than 20 million people, with the pyramids of Giza standing at its western edge.

Egypt has around 110 million people, the most of any Arab country. Arabic is the official language, and most Egyptians are Sunni Muslim, with a large Coptic Christian community whose church dates back nearly 2,000 years. Egypt is a republic with a president and a powerful military. Farming, tourism, the Suez Canal, and natural gas support the economy. Egyptians are proud of one of the oldest civilizations on Earth and of their modern role at the center of Arab music, film, and culture.
content.landAndNature: The Nile, the longest river in Africa, flows north through a green ribbon of fields just a few kilometers wide before spreading into the delta. West of it lies the Western Desert, part of the Sahara, with oases like Siwa, the strange chalk formations of the White Desert, and the Qattara Depression, 133 meters below sea level. East of the Nile the rocky Eastern Desert rises to hills along the Red Sea, whose coral reefs are among the most colorful in the world. The Sinai Peninsula has rugged red mountains; Mount Catherine, at 2,629 meters, is Egypt's highest point. Rain is rare almost everywhere. Camels, fennec foxes, and Egyptian cobras live in the deserts, and Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam has Nile crocodiles.
content.peopleAndCulture: Egyptians speak a lively dialect of Arabic understood across the Arab world thanks to Cairo's movies and pop songs. Family gatherings feature koshari, a street dish of rice, lentils, pasta, and crispy onions, ful medames, slow-cooked beans eaten at breakfast, and stuffed pigeon for celebrations. During Ramadan, streets glow with colorful lanterns called fanous, and families break their fast at sunset feasts. Soccer is a national obsession; the Pharaohs have won the Africa Cup of Nations a record seven times. Egypt also dominates world squash. Singer Umm Kulthum, whose concerts once stopped traffic, remains beloved, and Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Coptic Christians celebrate Christmas on January 7.
content.history: About 5,000 years ago King Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt, beginning a civilization of pharaohs that lasted nearly 3,000 years. Its people built the pyramids, carved hieroglyphs, mummified their dead, and invented papyrus paper and a 365-day calendar. Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BC, and after Cleopatra's death in 30 BC it became a Roman province. Arab armies brought Islam and the Arabic language in 641. The Ottoman Empire ruled from 1517, and Britain occupied the country from 1882. Egypt became a kingdom in 1922 and a republic in 1953 after officers led by Gamal Abdel Nasser overthrew the king. Nasser took control of the Suez Canal in 1956. A popular uprising in 2011 toppled longtime president Hosni Mubarak, and the military returned to power in 2013.
funFacts: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest structure made by humans for about 3,800 years.
Ancient Egyptians loved cats so much that they mummified them, and killing one could be punished by death.
Egypt has more than 100 pyramids, not just the three famous ones at Giza.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, saves ships about 7,000 kilometers compared with sailing around Africa.
The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, carried the same text in three scripts and unlocked the reading of hieroglyphs.

content.tagline: Art deco capital above the Red Sea
content.overview:
Eritrea stretches along the southwestern shore of the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa, about the size of Pennsylvania, with Sudan to the north, Ethiopia to the south, and Djibouti at its tip. Its name comes from the ancient Greek word for the Red Sea. The capital, Asmara, sits on a cool highland plateau at 2,300 meters and is famous for hundreds of art deco buildings from the 1930s, including a gas station shaped like an airplane, which earned it a place on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

Roughly 3.5 to 6 million people live in Eritrea; no census has been taken in decades, so estimates vary widely. Tigrinya, Arabic, and English are the working languages, and nine ethnic groups speak their own tongues. About half the population is Christian and half Muslim. Eritrea won independence from Ethiopia in 1993 after a 30-year war, and the same president has governed ever since without elections. Most people farm or herd, and many young Eritreans have left the country, partly because of a long national service requirement.
content.landAndNature: Eritrea climbs from one of the hottest coasts on Earth to cool green highlands in just 100 kilometers. The Danakil Depression in the south lies more than 100 meters below sea level and is a furnace of salt flats and volcanic vents. The central highlands, part of the Ethiopian plateau, have terraced fields and a mild climate, with Mount Soira reaching about 3,000 meters. To the west the land slopes down to the hot lowlands of the Gash and Barka rivers. Offshore, the Dahlak Archipelago has more than 100 islands with pristine coral reefs, dugongs, and dolphins. Elephants survive in the southwest near Gash-Setit, and the country is one of the last places where wild African asses roam.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Tigrinya are the largest group, followed by the Tigre, Saho, Afar, Bilen, Kunama, Nara, Rashaida, and Hedareb. Meals are shared from a single platter: injera, a spongy sourdough flatbread, is torn by hand and used to scoop up spicy stews called tsebhi. Coffee is roasted, ground, and served in a slow ceremony with popcorn. Italy's colonial years left a taste for pasta, espresso, and gelato, and Asmara's cafés serve cappuccino beside traditional coffee. Cycling is the national sport; Eritreans are the strongest cyclists in Africa and have raced in the Tour de France, and huge crowds line the roads for races. Orthodox Christian festivals like Timket and Muslim holidays are both national celebrations.
content.history: The region was part of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum, which traded across the Red Sea and adopted Christianity in the 300s; the port of Adulis was its gateway. Ottoman and Egyptian rulers later held the coast. Italy made Eritrea a colony in 1890, built Asmara's railway and modern buildings, and used it as a base to invade Ethiopia in 1935. Britain took over in 1941, and in 1952 Eritrea was joined to Ethiopia in a federation that Ethiopia soon dissolved. A war for independence began in 1961 and lasted 30 years until Eritrean fighters won in 1991, followed by an independence vote in 1993. A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed tens of thousands. A peace agreement was finally signed in 2018.
funFacts: Asmara's Fiat Tagliero building, finished in 1938, is a gas station designed to look like an airplane with 30-meter concrete wings.
A steam railway built by Italy still climbs from the coast to Asmara, rising 2,300 meters through 30 tunnels.
Eritrea has one of the strongest cycling traditions in Africa, and Daniel Teklehaimanot wore the King of the Mountains jersey at the 2015 Tour de France.
The name Eritrea comes from Erythra Thalassa, the ancient Greek name for the Red Sea.
The Dahlak Archipelago has more than 100 islands, but only a handful have any people living on them.

content.tagline: Flamenco, fiestas and Mediterranean sun
content.overview:
Spain fills most of the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, sharing it with Portugal and the tiny state of Andorra. Only about 14 kilometers of water separate its southern tip from Africa at the Strait of Gibraltar. Spain is roughly twice the size of Oregon and also governs the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean and the volcanic Canary Islands off the African coast. Madrid, the capital, sits almost exactly in the middle of the country on a high plateau.

About 48 million people live in Spain. Spanish, which Spaniards often call Castilian, is the national language, while Catalan, Galician and Basque are official in their own regions; Basque is related to no other known language. Spain is a constitutional monarchy, with a king as head of state and an elected parliament. It is the world's leading producer of olive oil, one of the most visited countries on Earth, and a place where life is built around late meals, long evenings and crowded public squares.
content.landAndNature: Spain is the second most mountainous country in Europe after Switzerland. The Pyrenees seal the border with France, the Picos de Europa rise above the green, rainy north, and the Sierra Nevada in the far south holds snow within sight of the Mediterranean. Between them spreads the Meseta, a wide plateau of wheat, vines and olive groves that bakes in summer and freezes in winter. The Canary Islands are volcanic, and Mount Teide on Tenerife is Spain's highest point at 3,715 meters. The marshes of Doñana shelter flamingos and the Iberian lynx, the world's rarest cat, brought back from the edge of extinction.
content.peopleAndCulture: Spanish life runs late: lunch near two, dinner after nine, and children playing in the plaza long after bedtime elsewhere. Tapas, small plates shared standing at a bar, turn eating into a social sport, and paella, jamón and tortilla de patatas are national staples. Every region guards its own festivals: the Fallas bonfires of Valencia, Seville's Easter processions and April fair, and the running of the bulls at San Fermín in Pamplona. Flamenco, with its guitar, handclaps and stamping heels, grew out of Andalusia's Roma communities. Soccer is close to a religion, and Spain won the World Cup in 2010.
content.history: Cave painters at Altamira left bison in red and black about 15,000 years ago. Phoenicians, Greeks, Carthaginians and then Romans settled the peninsula, followed by the Visigoths. In 711 Muslim armies crossed from North Africa and ruled much of Spain for centuries, making Córdoba one of the world's great cities of learning and leaving behind the Alhambra palace at Granada. Christian kingdoms gradually took the land back, finishing in 1492, the year Columbus sailed west for Spain. Silver from the Americas made Spain the strongest power in Europe before it slowly declined. A civil war from 1936 to 1939 brought General Franco to power as dictator until his death in 1975, after which Spain returned to democracy.
funFacts: Spain produces roughly half the world's olive oil, and some of its groves contain trees over a thousand years old.
The Sagrada Família church in Barcelona has been under construction since 1882 and is still unfinished.
Basque, spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France, is unrelated to any other known language on Earth.
La Tomatina in Buñol sends thousands of people hurling about 100 tons of ripe tomatoes at one another each August.
Spanish is the world's second most spoken native language, used by more than 400 million people as a first language.

content.tagline: Digital nation of forests and song
content.overview:
Estonia is the northernmost of the three Baltic states, facing Finland across the Gulf of Finland and Sweden across the Baltic Sea, with Latvia to the south and Russia to the east. It is about the size of New Hampshire and Vermont combined, and half of it is forest. The capital, Tallinn, has one of the best-preserved medieval old towns in Europe, a cluster of towers, guild halls, and cobbled lanes that looks like a storybook, right next to glass office buildings full of software start-ups.

Only about 1.3 million people live in Estonia, and they speak Estonian, a language related to Finnish rather than to the languages of its other neighbors. Estonia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and is a parliamentary republic, a member of the European Union and NATO, and a pioneer of digital government: citizens vote, sign documents, and start companies online, and nearly every school is connected. Estonians are known for quiet reserve, a deep love of nature, and mass choir festivals that gather tens of thousands of singers.
content.landAndNature: Estonia is flat and low, with its highest point, Suur Munamägi, just 318 meters above sea level. Forests of pine, spruce, and birch cover about half the land, and huge peat bogs, crossed by wooden boardwalks, cover much of the rest; Soomaa National Park floods so deeply each spring that locals call it the fifth season and travel by canoe. More than 2,000 islands lie off the coast, the largest being Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, with windmills, juniper heaths, and a meteorite crater at Kaali. Wolves, lynx, brown bears, and moose live in the forests, and flying squirrels glide between trees in the east. Lake Peipus, shared with Russia, is one of Europe's largest lakes. Winters are long, dark, and snowy, and the sea often freezes.
content.peopleAndCulture: Estonians treasure singing. Every five years the Song Celebration in Tallinn brings together up to 30,000 singers on one stage before crowds of 100,000, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Traditional foods include black rye bread, which is served with nearly every meal, sour cream, pickled herring, and blood sausage at Christmas, while kama, a roasted grain flour mixed with yogurt, is a favorite snack. Midsummer, called Jaanipäev, is celebrated with bonfires that burn all through the short night. Saunas are part of weekly life, and in winter people cut holes in the ice to swim. Cross-country skiing, basketball, and wrestling are popular, and Estonia is known for inventing the video-calling service Skype and for its love of wife-carrying and kiiking, swinging a full 360 degrees on a giant swing.
content.history: Finnic tribes have lived in Estonia for thousands of years, longer than almost any other people has stayed in one European homeland. German crusaders conquered the region in the 1200s, and for the next 700 years Estonians were ruled by Danes, Germans, Swedes, and, from 1710, the Russian Empire. A national awakening in the 1800s revived the language and started the song festivals in 1869. Estonia declared independence in 1918 and defended it in a war against Soviet Russia. In 1940 the Soviet Union seized the country, followed by Nazi occupation and then Soviet rule again, with mass deportations to Siberia. In 1989 two million people joined hands across the Baltic states in a peaceful protest called the Baltic Way, and Estonia regained independence in 1991. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004.
funFacts: Estonia was the first country in the world to allow voting over the internet in a national election, in 2005.
The Kaali crater on Saaremaa island was blasted out by a meteorite about 3,500 years ago and is now a round green pond.
Estonia has more than 2,000 islands, but people live on only about a dozen of them.
Tallinn's town hall pharmacy has been in business since at least 1422, making it one of the oldest in Europe.
Estonians have some of the world's largest per-person collections of folk songs, with more than 130,000 recorded.

content.tagline: Ancient highlands where coffee was born
content.overview:
Ethiopia rises from the Horn of Africa as a great mountain plateau, so high and cool that its capital, Addis Ababa, at 2,355 meters, is one of the highest capital cities in the world. The country is about twice the size of Texas and is landlocked, bordered by Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan, and Sudan. With about 125 million people, it is the second most populous country in Africa after Nigeria, and one of the fastest-growing economies on the continent.

Amharic is the official working language, written in its own curvy script called fidel, but more than 80 languages are spoken, including Oromo, Somali, and Tigrinya. Ethiopia is unusual in Africa because it was never colonized, apart from a five-year Italian occupation, and its Orthodox Christian church, ancient calendar, and traditions go back nearly 2,000 years. Today it is a federal republic divided into regions based on ethnic groups. Most Ethiopians farm, growing teff, coffee, and grains, and the country is the birthplace of coffee itself.
content.landAndNature: The Ethiopian Highlands, sometimes called the Roof of Africa, cover most of the country and are split by the Great Rift Valley, a giant crack in the Earth dotted with lakes. In the Simien Mountains, peaks over 4,500 meters drop in sheer cliffs, and gelada monkeys graze the grassy plateaus while walia ibex cling to the rocks. The Bale Mountains are home to the Ethiopian wolf, the rarest wild dog in the world. To the northeast the land plunges into the Danakil Depression, one of the hottest places on Earth, where the Erta Ale volcano keeps a permanent lava lake. The Blue Nile begins at Lake Tana and thunders over the Blue Nile Falls. Ethiopia has more unique species than almost any other African country, including the lammergeier vulture and the mountain nyala antelope.
content.peopleAndCulture: Ethiopians eat from a shared platter of injera, a spongy sourdough flatbread made from tiny teff grains, tearing pieces to scoop up spicy stews called wat; doro wat, chicken stew with a hard-boiled egg, is the festive favorite. Coffee is served in a ceremony where beans are roasted, ground, and brewed three times while incense burns. Ethiopia follows its own calendar, about seven years behind the Western one, with 13 months, and celebrates Timket, the Epiphany festival, with processions of priests under embroidered umbrellas. Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity and Islam are both centuries old here. The country is famous for distance runners such as Abebe Bikila, Haile Gebrselassie, and Tirunesh Dibaba, and its music uses a distinctive five-note scale.
content.history: Some of the oldest human ancestor fossils, including the 3.2-million-year-old Lucy, were found in Ethiopia. The Kingdom of Aksum, from about 100 to 900, was a trading power that raised giant stone obelisks and adopted Christianity around 330. In the 1100s and 1200s the churches of Lalibela were carved straight down into solid rock. Emperors ruled for centuries, and in 1896 Emperor Menelik II defeated an invading Italian army at Adwa, keeping Ethiopia independent when nearly all of Africa was colonized. Italy occupied the country from 1936 to 1941. Emperor Haile Selassie was overthrown in 1974 by a Marxist military junta, whose rule brought war and a terrible famine in 1984 and 1985. Rebels took power in 1991, and Eritrea split away in 1993. A civil war in the Tigray region from 2020 to 2022 killed many thousands.
funFacts: Legend says a goat herder named Kaldi discovered coffee in Ethiopia after noticing his goats dancing from eating red berries.
Ethiopia's calendar has 13 months, twelve of 30 days and one of five or six, and the year 2016 began in September 2023.
The churches of Lalibela were carved downward out of solid rock, so their roofs are level with the ground.
The fossil skeleton called Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974, belonged to a human ancestor who lived 3.2 million years ago.
Abebe Bikila won the 1960 Olympic marathon in Rome running barefoot, then won again in 1964 wearing shoes.

content.tagline: Land of a thousand lakes and saunas
content.overview:
Finland stretches from the Baltic Sea almost to the Arctic Ocean in the far north of Europe, squeezed between Sweden, Norway, and Russia. It is a little smaller than Montana but has about 188,000 lakes and roughly 180,000 islands, so from the air the country looks like a green cloth spattered with blue. Forests cover about three-quarters of the land. The capital, Helsinki, sits on a peninsula in the south, a city of harbors, granite, and clean modern design.

About 5.6 million Finns live here, mostly in the south. Finnish is the main language, a tongue related to Estonian and distantly to Hungarian, with long compound words and no articles; Swedish is the second official language, spoken along the coast, and the Sami people of Lapland speak their own languages. Finland is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union, and it joined NATO in 2023. Finns have topped world happiness rankings year after year, thanks to trust, excellent free schools, nature at everyone's doorstep, and about three million saunas.
content.landAndNature: Finland is mostly low and flat, shaped by glaciers that scraped the bedrock and left behind lakes, eskers, and boulders. The largest lake, Saimaa, is a labyrinth of islands and channels where the endangered Saimaa ringed seal lives, one of the rarest seals on Earth. In the north, Lapland rises into rounded fells; Halti, the highest point at 1,324 meters, sits on the Norwegian border. Above the Arctic Circle the sun never sets for weeks in summer and barely rises in midwinter, when the northern lights ripple across the sky. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, wolverines, and about 200,000 reindeer, herded by the Sami, live in the forests and tundra. The Baltic coast freezes in cold winters, and the Åland Islands form an archipelago of thousands of rocky isles.
content.peopleAndCulture: The sauna is the heart of Finnish life: families sweat together in wood-heated rooms, then plunge into a lake or roll in snow, and even apartment buildings and parliament have saunas. Foods include rye bread, salmon soup, Karelian pies filled with rice, reindeer stew in the north, and squeaky bread cheese with cloudberry jam. Midsummer bonfires blaze on lake shores, and at Christmas Finns claim Santa Claus lives on Korvatunturi fell in Lapland. Ice hockey is the national sport, and Finland has produced champion rally and Formula One drivers and ski jumpers. Composer Jean Sibelius, architect Alvar Aalto, and the Moomin books of Tove Jansson are national treasures. Finns are famously quiet and comfortable with silence, and coffee consumption is among the highest in the world.
content.history: Hunters reached Finland as the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago. From the 1100s Sweden gradually took control, bringing Christianity and Swedish law, and Finland stayed part of Sweden for about 600 years. In 1809 Russia won it in a war and ruled it as a grand duchy with some self-government, during which Finnish literature and national feeling grew, helped by the epic poem collection the Kalevala. Finland declared independence in 1917 as Russia collapsed into revolution, then suffered a short civil war. In the Winter War of 1939 and 1940 Finns fought off a far larger Soviet invasion but lost territory. After World War II Finland stayed neutral between East and West, built a strong welfare state, and joined the European Union in 1995. Russia's invasion of Ukraine led Finland to join NATO in 2023.
funFacts: Finland has about three million saunas for 5.6 million people, more than it has cars.
Finns hold the Wife Carrying World Championships every year, where the prize is the wife's weight in beer.
Finnish schools give almost no homework and start formal schooling at age seven, yet rank among the best in the world.
The country drinks more coffee per person than any other, about four cups a day on average.
Finland has more heavy metal bands per person than any other country, with more than 50 bands per 100,000 people.

content.tagline: Where the day begins
content.overview:
Fiji is a nation of more than 330 islands scattered across the South Pacific, about 2,000 kilometers north of New Zealand. Only around 110 of the islands are inhabited, and most people live on the two largest, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu. The land totals about 18,000 km², slightly smaller than the US state of New Jersey, and about 900,000 people call Fiji home. The capital, Suva, is a busy harbor city on Viti Levu.

Fijians greet everyone with a hearty "Bula!" Roughly six in ten people are Indigenous iTaukei Fijians, and about a third are Indo-Fijians, descendants of workers brought from India in the 1800s to cut sugarcane. That mix means Hindu temples stand near Methodist churches, and English, Fijian and Fiji Hindi are all official languages.

Fiji is a republic with an elected parliament. Tourism, sugar, fishing and bottled water support the economy, and the country is famous for rugby sevens, coral reefs and warm hospitality.
content.landAndNature:
Fiji's large islands are volcanic, with steep green mountains, rivers and waterfalls; Mount Tomanivi on Viti Levu rises to about 1,320 meters. The windward eastern sides are drenched in rain and covered in rainforest, while the western sides are drier and sunnier, which is where most resorts are. Hundreds of smaller coral islands and atolls ring turquoise lagoons.

Fiji calls itself the soft coral capital of the world, and reefs such as the Great Astrolabe Reef teem with fish, manta rays and sea turtles. On land there are no large native mammals, but the islands have the rare Fiji crested iguana, fruit bats, colorful parrots and the tagimoucia, a red-and-white flower that grows only on one mountain of Taveuni. The climate is warm and humid, with a cyclone season from November to April.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Village life among iTaukei Fijians centers on the chief, the church and the kava ceremony, in which a drink made from the ground root of the yaqona plant is shared from a wooden bowl. Indo-Fijians celebrate Diwali, the festival of lights, and their curries and roti sit alongside Fijian lovo feasts, in which meat and root vegetables are cooked in an underground oven of hot stones. Kokoda, raw fish marinated in lime and coconut cream, is a national favorite.

Rugby is Fiji's passion: the national sevens team won the country's first ever Olympic gold medal in 2016 and repeated the feat in 2021. The meke, a storytelling dance with chanting and clapping, is performed at celebrations, and on the island of Beqa the Sawau people walk barefoot across white-hot stones in a traditional firewalking ceremony.
content.history:
The first settlers, the Lapita people, reached Fiji about 3,000 years ago in ocean-going canoes, bringing pottery and farming. Over centuries their descendants built a society of chiefdoms, fortified villages and great double-hulled sailing canoes. Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sighted the islands in 1643, and later European traders and missionaries arrived.

In 1874 the leading chief, Cakobau, ceded Fiji to Britain. The colonial government brought more than 60,000 indentured workers from India between 1879 and 1916 to work on sugar plantations, creating the Indo-Fijian community. Fiji became independent on October 10, 1970. Tensions between the two main communities led to military coups in 1987, 2000 and 2006, and Fiji became a republic in 1987. Elections in 2014 restored democratic government.
funFacts: The 180th meridian passes through Fiji's island of Taveuni, so Fiji is one of the first countries to greet each new day.
Fiji's rugby sevens gold in 2016 was the nation's first Olympic medal of any kind.
Fijian firewalkers on Beqa island stride across stones heated in a fire for hours, a ceremony hundreds of years old.
The tagimoucia flower grows only on the slopes of one mountain on Taveuni and refuses to bloom anywhere else.
The Fiji banded iguana is emerald green with pale stripes, and scientists think its ancestors floated across the Pacific from the Americas on rafts of plants.
Cannibalism was practiced in old Fiji, and the wooden forks once used for it are now museum pieces.

content.tagline: Art, revolution, and a thousand cheeses
content.overview:
France is the largest country in Western Europe, a six-sided land the French call the Hexagon, about the size of Texas. It has coasts on the Atlantic Ocean, the English Channel, and the Mediterranean Sea, and borders with eight countries, including Spain across the Pyrenees and Italy and Switzerland across the Alps. The capital, Paris, on the Seine River, is one of the most visited cities on Earth, home to the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre museum, and Notre-Dame cathedral. France also includes overseas regions such as French Guiana in South America and islands in the Caribbean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific.

About 68 million people live in France and speak French, a language spoken by hundreds of millions more around the world. France is a republic with a directly elected president and a parliament, and it is a founding member of the European Union. It is the world's most popular tourist destination, a leader in fashion, food, film, aviation, and high-speed trains, and a country where the ideas of liberty, equality, and fraternity, born in its revolution, still shape daily life.
content.landAndNature: France has almost every kind of European landscape. The Alps rise in the southeast to Mont Blanc, at 4,808 meters the highest mountain in Western Europe, while the Pyrenees wall off Spain in the south. The Massif Central is a plateau of extinct volcanoes and deep gorges. Great rivers, the Loire, Seine, Rhône, and Garonne, cross plains of wheat, sunflowers, and vineyards. The coasts range from the white chalk cliffs of Normandy and the rocky coves of Brittany to the pine-backed dunes of the Atlantic, including the Dune of Pilat, Europe's tallest sand dune, and the sunny Riviera on the Mediterranean. In the marshy Camargue delta of the Rhône, wild white horses and pink flamingos share the lagoons. Wolves and brown bears have returned to the mountains, and ibex leap across alpine cliffs.
content.peopleAndCulture: French meals are an art: crusty baguettes, croissants, hundreds of cheeses, and dishes like boeuf bourguignon and ratatouille, eaten slowly at long tables. The lunch break is sacred, and the French meal is on UNESCO's heritage list. Paris fashion houses set global styles, and French painters such as Monet and Renoir invented Impressionism. Cinema was born here with the Lumière brothers, and the Cannes Film Festival remains the world's most glamorous. The Tour de France bicycle race is watched by millions each July, and France has won the soccer World Cup twice, in 1998 and 2018. Rugby, judo, and handball are also loved. Comic books, or bandes dessinées, like Asterix are taken seriously as literature. Bastille Day on July 14 brings parades and fireworks.
content.history: Prehistoric artists painted the caves of Lascaux about 17,000 years ago. Celtic Gauls were conquered by Julius Caesar in the 50s BC, and after Rome fell, the Franks under Charlemagne built a vast empire around 800. French kings ruled for a thousand years, building castles, cathedrals, and the palace of Versailles, and fighting England in the Hundred Years' War, when Joan of Arc became a hero. In 1789 the French Revolution overthrew the monarchy and declared the rights of man; Napoleon then conquered much of Europe before his defeat in 1815. France built a large colonial empire in Africa and Asia. It suffered terribly in World War I and was occupied by Nazi Germany from 1940 to 1944. After the war France helped create the European Union, and its colonies gained independence, often after painful wars.
funFacts: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be torn down after 20 years but was saved because it was useful as a radio antenna.
France has more time zones than any other country, twelve, because of its territories scattered around the globe.
The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world, and walking past every artwork would take months.
French law once required bakers to take vacations in shifts so Paris would never run out of bread.
The metric system, now used by nearly every country on Earth, was created during the French Revolution.

content.tagline: Four island states across the Pacific
content.overview:
The Federated States of Micronesia is a country of more than 600 islands spread across a stretch of the western Pacific about 2,700 kilometers wide, though all its land together comes to only about 702 km², a little smaller than New York City. It is organized into four states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, each with its own languages and traditions. The capital, Palikir, sits on the island of Pohnpei.

About 110,000 people live in Micronesia. English is the official language and serves as the common tongue between the states, while Chuukese, Pohnpeian, Yapese, Kosraean and several other languages are spoken at home. The country is a republic in free association with the United States, which handles defense and provides financial support, and Micronesians may live and work in the US. Fishing licenses, farming and aid support the economy, and rising seas and stronger typhoons threaten the lowest islands.
content.landAndNature: The islands come in two kinds: high volcanic islands such as Pohnpei and Kosrae, steep and green with rainforest and waterfalls, and low coral atolls barely above the waves. Pohnpei is one of the rainiest places on Earth, with some inland spots receiving more than 7,000 millimeters of rain a year. Mangroves fringe the shores, and the reefs are among the richest in the Pacific, with manta rays gathering at cleaning stations off Yap and sharks patrolling the drop-offs. Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of ships sunk during World War II, now coral gardens. Coconut crabs, the largest land crabs anywhere, climb the palms.
content.peopleAndCulture: Each state keeps its own customs. On Yap, huge stone discs called rai, some over three meters across, are still recognized as traditional money, and ownership passes by agreement without the stones ever being moved. On Pohnpei, ceremonies center on sakau, a drink pressed from a pepper plant root. Breadfruit, taro, yams, bananas, fish and coconut are staple foods, often baked in earth ovens. Sailing canoes and traditional navigation are being taught again to younger generations. Clan ties and respect for elders shape village life, most people are Christian, and baseball and basketball are played everywhere.
content.history: Voyagers settled these islands thousands of years ago, and on Pohnpei they built Nan Madol, a city of nearly a hundred artificial islets made from huge basalt logs stacked in the shallows between about 1200 and 1600, the only ancient city of its kind built on a coral reef.
