Spain claimed the islands, sold them to Germany in 1899, and Japan took them during World War I and later fortified them. Heavy fighting reached Chuuk in 1944. After the war the islands were administered by the United States under a United Nations trusteeship. The Federated States of Micronesia adopted a constitution in 1979 and became fully independent in 1986.
funFacts: On Yap, stone discs up to three meters wide still count as money, and owners change without the stones moving.
Nan Madol, built from stacked basalt logs on a reef, is the only ancient city of its kind in the Pacific.
Micronesia's islands are scattered over roughly three million square kilometers of ocean, though its land is tiny.
Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of ships sunk in 1944, now covered in coral and explored by divers.
Coconut crabs in Micronesia can weigh over four kilograms and crack open coconuts with their claws.

content.tagline: Where elephants and hippos walk the beach
content.overview:
Gabon straddles the equator on the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, bordered by Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, and the Republic of the Congo. It is about the size of Colorado, and rainforest covers close to 90 percent of it, one of the highest proportions of any country in the world. The capital, Libreville, is a seaside city of modern towers and palm-lined boulevards whose name means free town, given because it was founded for freed slaves.

Only about 2.4 million people live in Gabon, most of them in Libreville and the oil port of Port-Gentil, so vast stretches of the country are empty of people and full of animals. French is the official language, and Fang, Myene, and other Bantu languages are spoken at home. Oil, manganese, and timber have made Gabon one of the wealthier countries in Africa by average income, though many people remain poor. One family held the presidency for 56 years until the army removed the president in 2023. Gabon has set aside about a tenth of its land as national parks and is a world leader in protecting rainforest.
content.landAndNature: A narrow coastal plain of lagoons, mangroves, and empty beaches gives way to low mountains and plateaus covered in dense forest, drained by the mighty Ogooué River, which cuts the country in two and carries logs and canoes to the sea. Loango National Park is famous for elephants, buffalo, and hippos that wander onto the beach and even into the surf, while humpback whales breed offshore. Ivindo National Park hides the roaring Kongou Falls and a forest clearing, Langoué Bai, where gorillas and elephants gather. Gabon holds about half of Africa's forest elephants and tens of thousands of gorillas and chimpanzees, plus mandrills, the world's most colorful monkeys, which travel in troops of hundreds. Rain falls heavily most of the year, and the climate is hot and humid.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Fang are the largest people, along with the Myene, Punu, Nzebi, and Teke, and small communities of Baka forest dwellers. Most Gabonese are Christian, but the Bwiti tradition, with night-long ceremonies of harp music, dance, and a root called iboga, is followed by many and recognized as part of national culture. Meals feature cassava, plantains, and rice with fish, smoked meat, or nyembwe, chicken in a rich palm-nut sauce. Gabonese masks, especially the white-faced Punu masks, are among the most admired African art in the world's museums. Music mixes traditional harps and drums with modern styles, and soccer is the top sport; Gabon hosted the Africa Cup of Nations in 2012 and 2017. Libreville's markets overflow with fabrics, fruit, and seafood.
content.history: Bantu-speaking peoples moved into the forests over the past 2,000 years, and the Fang arrived from the north in the 1700s and 1800s. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in the 1470s, and for three centuries European ships traded for enslaved people, ivory, and hardwoods. France signed treaties with coastal chiefs in 1839, founded Libreville in 1849 for Africans freed from a captured slave ship, and made Gabon part of French Equatorial Africa. The explorer and doctor Albert Schweitzer built a famous hospital at Lambaréné in 1913. Gabon became independent on August 17, 1960. Omar Bongo took power in 1967 and ruled for 42 years, followed by his son Ali Bongo, until military officers seized power in August 2023, promising elections.
funFacts: At Loango National Park, elephants, buffalo, and hippos can be seen strolling along the beach beside the Atlantic surf.
Gabon is home to about 95,000 forest elephants, more than half of all that remain in Africa.
Libreville means free town in French; it was founded in 1849 for Africans freed from a slave ship.
Mandrills, with their blue and red faces, live in Gabon in troops that can number more than 800 animals.
Rainforest covers almost 90 percent of Gabon, and the country has pledged to keep it standing.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.officialName: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

content.tagline: Four nations on two main islands
content.overview:
The United Kingdom is made up of four nations: England, Scotland and Wales, which together form the island of Great Britain, and Northern Ireland, which shares a smaller island with the Republic of Ireland. Altogether it is about the size of Oregon, and nowhere in it lies more than about 120 kilometers from the sea. Around 68 million people live there, most of them in England.

London, the capital, sits on the River Thames and has been a major city for nearly 2,000 years. English is the main language, and Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and Irish are spoken and taught in parts of the country. The UK is a constitutional monarchy: a king or queen serves as head of state while an elected parliament at Westminster makes the laws, and Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have an assembly for local matters. The country joined the European Union in 1973 and left in 2020.
content.landAndNature: The UK's landscapes change quickly for so small a country. The Scottish Highlands hold the highest ground, topped by Ben Nevis at 1,345 meters, along with deep lochs including Loch Ness. The Lake District and the Pennine ridge run through northern England, Wales rises into the peaks of Eryri, and southern England rolls in chalk downs that end in the white cliffs of Dover. The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is a shore of about 40,000 six-sided basalt columns left by ancient lava. The Gulf Stream keeps winters mild and the weather famously changeable. Red deer, puffins, otters and red squirrels live here, and hedgerows shelter badgers and hedgehogs.
content.peopleAndCulture: Tea is a national habit, and roast dinners, fish and chips, curry and the full cooked breakfast all count as British food. Modern soccer was written down here, and the Premier League is watched worldwide; cricket, rugby, tennis at Wimbledon and the London Marathon fill the sporting year. The UK has shaped world culture out of all proportion to its size, from Shakespeare and Dickens to the Beatles and Harry Potter. Cities are strikingly diverse, and more than 300 languages are spoken in London alone. Older traditions run deep: bagpipes and Highland games in Scotland, Eisteddfod poetry festivals in Wales, and guardsmen in tall bearskin hats in London.
content.history: Stone Age builders raised Stonehenge about 4,500 years ago. Romans invaded in AD 43, followed by Anglo-Saxons and Vikings, and in 1066 the Normans conquered England. Magna Carta in 1215 limited the king's power, and parliament grew stronger after a civil war in the 1640s. England and Scotland united in 1707 and Ireland joined in 1801, though most of Ireland left in 1922. Britain built the largest empire in history, ruling roughly a quarter of the world, and British ships carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic before campaigners won abolition of the trade in 1807 and of slavery across most of the empire in 1833. Industry began here, and the empire ended after two world wars.
funFacts: The London Underground, opened in 1863, was the first underground railway anywhere in the world.
Each of the UK's four nations has its own flag, national soccer team and patron saint.
Scotland has around 790 islands, but fewer than a hundred of them have anyone living on them.
Big Ben is the name of the bell inside the tower beside parliament, not of the tower itself.
The industrial revolution began in Britain in the 1700s, powered by coal, iron and steam engines.
Britain's motorways and main roads still follow routes surveyed by Roman engineers nearly 2,000 years ago.

content.tagline: Birthplace of wine beneath the Caucasus
content.overview:
Georgia is a country on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, tucked beneath the towering Caucasus Mountains where Europe and Asia meet. It borders Russia, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Türkiye and is about 69,700 km², roughly the size of Ireland, with about 3.7 million people. It is not related to the US state of the same name; Georgians call their country Sakartvelo.

The capital, Tbilisi, was founded on hot sulfur springs about 1,500 years ago, and its name comes from the Georgian word for "warm." Old wooden balconies, a medieval fortress and modern glass buildings line the Kura River. Georgians speak a language unrelated to any other major language family, written in a curly alphabet of their own.

Georgia is a republic with an elected parliament. Two regions, Abkhazia and South Ossetia, broke away in the 1990s and are backed by Russia; Georgia and most of the world still consider them Georgian territory. The country is famous for feasting, wine, singing and mountain villages topped with stone towers.
content.landAndNature:
The Greater Caucasus forms Georgia's northern wall, with peaks such as Shkhara, about 5,190 meters, permanently capped in snow. In the high region of Svaneti, villages like Ushguli, one of the highest year-round settlements in Europe, are guarded by medieval stone towers. The Lesser Caucasus rises in the south, and between the two ranges lie fertile valleys of vineyards and orchards.

Along the Black Sea coast, the climate is humid and subtropical, with tea plantations and citrus groves around Batumi, while the east is drier. Georgia's limestone holds some of the deepest caves ever explored. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, chamois and the East Caucasian tur, a wild goat with sweeping horns, live in the mountains, and bearded vultures soar above the gorges.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Georgians are famous for the supra, a feast where a toastmaster called the tamada leads round after round of toasts to friendship, family and homeland. The table overflows with khachapuri, boat-shaped bread filled with molten cheese and egg; khinkali, twisted dumplings eaten by hand; and walnut sauces, herbs and pickles. Wine has been made here for about 8,000 years, fermented in huge clay jars called qvevri buried underground.

Most Georgians belong to the Georgian Orthodox Church, and ancient churches crown many hilltops. Polyphonic singing, in which several voices weave together without instruments, is so distinctive that UNESCO lists it as a cultural treasure. Wrestling, rugby and chess are popular, and the national ballet dancers leap and spin on the tips of their toes in soft boots.
content.history:
In Greek myth, Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis, in western Georgia, to steal the Golden Fleece, and real kingdoms of Colchis and Iberia thrived there in ancient times. Georgia adopted Christianity in the early 300s, one of the first countries to do so. Its Golden Age came in the 1100s and 1200s under King David the Builder and Queen Tamar, when Georgian culture and power reached their peak.

Mongol, Persian and Ottoman invasions followed, and in 1801 the Russian Empire began absorbing the Georgian kingdoms. A brief independence from 1918 to 1921 ended when the Soviet Red Army took control; the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin was born in the Georgian town of Gori. Georgia declared independence in 1991. Wars in Abkhazia and South Ossetia, the peaceful Rose Revolution of 2003 and a short war with Russia in 2008 have shaped its recent history.
funFacts: Fossils of early humans found at Dmanisi are about 1.8 million years old, the oldest ever discovered outside Africa.
Georgian is written in one of only about 14 alphabets in use in the world today, and it has no capital letters.
Archaeologists have found traces of wine in Georgian pottery from around 6000 BC, the oldest evidence of winemaking anywhere.
The world's deepest known caves, more than 2,200 meters deep, lie in the Arabika Massif of Abkhazia.
Tbilisi's name comes from "tbili," meaning warm, after the natural hot springs where the city was founded.
A traditional Georgian supra can include dozens of toasts, and the tamada must think of a new one every time.

content.tagline: Gold, cocoa, and the rhythm of highlife
content.overview:
Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, between Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, and Togo, and is about the size of Oregon. Its capital, Accra, is a fast-growing coastal city of markets, beaches, and tech start-ups, and it is one of the closest big cities in the world to the point where the equator meets the prime meridian. The country's name was borrowed from a medieval African empire, and its old colonial name, the Gold Coast, told of the metal that drew traders for centuries.

About 34 million people live in Ghana, and English is the official language, though most people speak Akan languages such as Twi, or Ewe, Ga, or Dagbani at home. Ghana was the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from European colonial rule, in 1957, and today it is one of the continent's most stable democracies, a republic that has handed power peacefully between parties several times. Ghana is the world's second-largest producer of cocoa, a major gold miner, and famous across Africa for its music, colorful kente cloth, and friendly spirit.
content.landAndNature: Ghana is mostly low plains and plateaus. The south has a coastline of sandy beaches, lagoons, and old forts, backed by tropical forests where cocoa trees grow in the shade. The Akwapim-Togo hills run along the eastern border, with Mount Afadja, at 885 meters, the highest point. In the center lies Lake Volta, created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965 and one of the largest human-made lakes in the world by surface area. The north is dry savanna with baobabs and shea trees, where Mole National Park shelters elephants, antelope, and baboons. Kakum National Park has a rope walkway strung high in the rainforest canopy. Rain is heaviest in the southwest, and the harmattan wind brings dust from the Sahara in winter.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Akan, including the Ashanti, are the largest group, with the Ewe, Ga-Adangbe, Mole-Dagbani, and many others. Most Ghanaians are Christian, with a large Muslim community in the north. Kente cloth, woven in bright strips by Ashanti and Ewe weavers, is worn at ceremonies, and Adinkra symbols stamped on fabric carry proverbs. Fufu, pounded cassava and plantain, is dipped in light soup or groundnut soup, and jollof rice sparks a friendly rivalry with Nigeria. Highlife music, born here in the early 1900s, and modern hiplife and Afrobeats fill the airwaves. Soccer is a passion; the Black Stars have won the Africa Cup of Nations four times. Funerals are huge celebrations of life, sometimes with custom-built coffins shaped like fish, cars, or airplanes.
content.history: Trading kingdoms rose here by the 1000s, and from about 1700 the Ashanti Empire, ruled from Kumasi and symbolized by a sacred Golden Stool, grew rich and powerful. Portuguese traders built Elmina Castle in 1482, the oldest European building in sub-Saharan Africa, and over the following centuries dozens of forts along the coast held enslaved Africans before shipment across the Atlantic. Britain fought several wars with the Ashanti and made the Gold Coast a colony in the 1800s. Led by Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana became independent on March 6, 1957, inspiring independence movements across Africa. Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966, and coups followed until 1992, when a new constitution brought lasting multiparty democracy. Ghana became an oil producer in 2010.
funFacts: Ghana's Lake Volta is one of the largest reservoirs in the world, covering about 8,500 square kilometers.
The Ashanti Golden Stool is believed to hold the soul of the nation and is never allowed to touch the ground.
Ghanaian craftsmen build fantasy coffins shaped like lions, sneakers, cocoa pods, and cameras to honor the dead.
Ghana is the second-largest cocoa producer in the world, growing much of the chocolate eaten in Europe.
Elmina Castle, built in 1482, is the oldest European building still standing south of the Sahara.

content.tagline: Water tower of West Africa
content.overview:
Guinea curves like a crescent along the Atlantic coast of West Africa, bordered by Guinea-Bissau, Senegal, Mali, Ivory Coast, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. It is about the size of Oregon. The capital, Conakry, spreads along a narrow peninsula and islands jutting into the sea, so the city is long and thin and always close to the water. Guinea is sometimes called Guinea-Conakry to avoid confusion with Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea.

About 14 million people live in Guinea, and French is the official language, though Fula, Malinke, and Susu are the languages of home and market. Nearly 90 percent of Guineans are Muslim. Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore used to make aluminum, along with iron, gold, and diamonds, yet most people remain poor and farm rice, cassava, and bananas. The country is a republic that has experienced several military takeovers, most recently in 2021. Its rivers feed much of West Africa, and its musicians and dancers have influenced the entire region.
content.landAndNature: Four regions make up Guinea. The coastal lowland is hot, humid, and laced with mangrove estuaries. Behind it rises the Fouta Djallon, a highland of sandstone plateaus, waterfalls, and deep valleys where cool air and heavy rain give birth to three of West Africa's great rivers, the Niger, Senegal, and Gambia, which is why Guinea is called the water tower of the region. Upper Guinea to the east is dry savanna along the upper Niger, and the forested Guinea Highlands in the southeast rise to Mount Nimba, 1,752 meters, whose slopes shelter chimpanzees that use stone tools and a rare toad that gives birth to live young. Hippos live in the rivers, and the coast is a stopover for millions of migrating birds.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Fula, or Peul, dominate the Fouta Djallon as cattle herders and traders, the Malinke live in the east, and the Susu along the coast; each has its own language, music, and dress. Meals are built on rice with sauces of peanut, palm oil, or leaf greens, and fish or meat, along with fried plantains and mangoes in season. Guinea's music is legendary: the balafon, the kora harp, and above all the djembe drum, whose players from Guinea taught the instrument to the world. Les Ballets Africains, the national dance company, has toured for decades, and singer Mory Kanté made international hits. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Guinean tailors are known across the region for embroidered robes called boubous.
content.history: The region was part of the great Mali Empire in the 1200s and 1300s, and in the 1700s Fula Muslim leaders founded a powerful state in the Fouta Djallon. Samori Touré built the Wassoulou Empire in the late 1800s and fought French troops for years before his capture in 1898. France ruled Guinea as a colony until 1958, when Guineans voted no in a referendum on staying with France, and became independent on October 2, 1958, the first French colony in Africa to do so. The first president, Ahmed Sékou Touré, ruled harshly until his death in 1984. Military leader Lansana Conté then governed until 2008. Guinea held its first truly democratic election in 2010, but the army seized power again in 2021.
funFacts: Three great rivers, the Niger, Senegal, and Gambia, all begin in Guinea's Fouta Djallon highlands.
Guinea holds roughly a quarter of the world's known bauxite, the ore used to make aluminum for cans and airplanes.
The Mount Nimba toad is one of the only toads in the world that gives birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.
Chimpanzees at Bossou in Guinea crack nuts with stone hammers and anvils, a skill studied by scientists for decades.
Conakry's main island, Tombo, is linked to the mainland by a causeway, and the city stretches 36 kilometers along a peninsula.

content.tagline: A river with a country wrapped around it
content.overview:
The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a thin strip of land following the Gambia River for about 450 kilometers inland from the Atlantic Ocean. Never more than 50 kilometers wide, it is surrounded on three sides by Senegal, like a finger poking into its neighbor. The whole country is smaller than Connecticut. The capital, Banjul, sits on an island at the river's mouth, though most people live in the nearby fast-growing coastal towns around Serekunda.

About 2.7 million people live in The Gambia, making it densely populated for Africa. English is the official language, and Mandinka, Wolof, and Fula are the most widely spoken at home. Most Gambians are Muslim. The country is a republic that returned to democracy in 2017 after 22 years under a strongman president. Farmers grow peanuts, rice, and millet along the river, fishermen bring in catches from the Atlantic, and tourists come to the beaches, especially from Europe in winter, for sun and birdwatching. Gambians call their country the Smiling Coast of Africa.
content.landAndNature: The Gambia River is everything here. It flows wide and salty between mangrove swamps near the coast, where oysters cling to roots, and becomes a fresh, winding ribbon between low sandstone banks upstream. The land on either side is flat savanna of grasses, baobabs, and palms, rarely rising more than 50 meters. Hippos and crocodiles live in the river's middle stretches, and chimpanzees rehabilitated on the Baboon Islands in the River Gambia National Park have formed thriving troops. The country is a birdwatcher's paradise, with more than 500 species recorded in a tiny area, from kingfishers and bee-eaters to fish eagles. The climate is hot, with a rainy season from June to October and dry, dusty months in between.
content.peopleAndCulture: Gambians belong mainly to the Mandinka, Fula, Wolof, Jola, and Serahule peoples, who live peacefully together and often speak several languages. Meals center on rice: benachin is a one-pot dish of rice, fish or meat, and vegetables, and domoda is a rich peanut stew. Attaya, strong green tea poured in three rounds, is shared for hours. Music comes from the kora, a 21-string harp made from a large gourd, played by griots, hereditary musicians who keep family histories in song. Wrestling matches with drumming and dancing draw big crowds, and soccer is the favorite sport. Gambian women make colorful tie-dyed cloth, and naming ceremonies and weddings are celebrated with feasts for the whole neighborhood.
content.history: Stone circles at Wassu and Kerbatch, some 1,200 years old, show that organized societies lived along the river long ago. The area later formed part of the Mali and Songhai empires and Mandinka kingdoms. Portuguese explorers arrived in the 1450s, and from the 1600s British and French traders competed here, shipping many thousands of enslaved people from posts such as James Island, now Kunta Kinteh Island, whose name honors the ancestor of the writer Alex Haley. Britain made the river a colony in 1888. The Gambia became independent on February 18, 1965, under Dawda Jawara, and was a democracy until Yahya Jammeh seized power in 1994 and ruled harshly for 22 years. He refused to accept an election defeat in 2016 but was forced out by neighboring countries in 2017.
funFacts: The Gambia is one of very few countries whose name officially includes The, a rule set when it became independent.
At its narrowest the country is only about 24 kilometers wide, and Senegal surrounds it on three sides.
Kunta Kinteh Island, a former slave-trading fort, is named after the ancestor in Alex Haley's book Roots.
More than 500 bird species have been recorded in The Gambia, an area smaller than Connecticut.
The Wassu stone circles are made of laterite pillars up to two meters tall, raised more than a thousand years ago.

content.tagline: Islands of rice, mangroves, and hippos
content.overview:
Guinea-Bissau is a small country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, wedged between Senegal and Guinea, about the size of Maryland and Delaware combined. Its coast is a maze of wide river estuaries, tidal creeks, and mangrove swamps, and offshore lie the Bijagós Islands, an archipelago of about 88 islands where only a couple dozen are inhabited. The capital, Bissau, is a low-rise port city on the Geba River estuary.

Around two million people live in Guinea-Bissau. Portuguese is the official language, but most people speak Upper Guinea Creole, a Portuguese-based creole known as Kriol, along with Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, and other languages. Roughly half of the people are Muslim, with large Christian and traditional-religion communities. It is one of the poorest countries in the world; farmers grow rice in the tidal flats and cashews, the main export, on the higher ground. The country is a republic, but coups and political disputes have troubled it since independence from Portugal in 1974.
content.landAndNature: Guinea-Bissau is flat and low, rising only to about 300 meters in the far east, and much of the coast floods at high tide. Rivers like the Geba, Corubal, and Cacheu spread into broad estuaries lined with mangrove forests that shelter fish, oysters, and manatees. The Bijagós Islands are a UNESCO biosphere reserve where saltwater hippos swim between islands and even wade in the ocean, and where green sea turtles lay eggs on Poilão island, one of the most important nesting beaches in the Atlantic. Inland savanna and woodland hold chimpanzees, monkeys, and antelope in the Cantanhez forests. Millions of migrating shorebirds arrive each winter from Europe. The climate is hot with a heavy rainy season from June to October.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Papel, and Manjaco are the largest peoples, and the Bijagó islanders keep distinct traditions, including a society where women have great authority and choose their husbands. Rice is the staple, grown in flooded paddies and served with fish, palm oil, or peanut sauce; cashew fruit is eaten fresh, and its nuts pay for school fees. Gumbe music blends Creole rhythms with guitars and drums, and Carnival in Bissau fills the streets with masks made of papier-mâché and dancers in raffia costumes. Wrestling and soccer are popular sports. Bijagó ceremonies feature carved masks of bulls, sharks, and sawfish, and village elders hold great respect. Many Bissau-Guineans have relatives in Portugal and Senegal.
content.history: The region was part of the Mali Empire's influence and the Kaabu kingdom of the Mandinka before Portuguese ships arrived in the 1440s. Portugal set up trading posts at Cacheu and Bissau that shipped enslaved people to the Americas, especially Cape Verde and Brazil, but controlled only the coast until the early 1900s. A guerrilla war for independence led by Amílcar Cabral began in 1963 and freed most of the countryside; Cabral was assassinated in 1973, and Portugal recognized independence in 1974. Guinea-Bissau's independence helped topple Portugal's dictatorship. Since then the country has suffered several coups, a civil war in 1998 and 1999, and the assassination of a president in 2009, and it has struggled with drug trafficking through its islands. Elections continue despite the turmoil.
funFacts: The hippos of the Bijagós Islands are among the only ones in the world that regularly swim in salt water and walk on ocean beaches.
Cashew nuts make up more than 90 percent of the country's exports, and the cashew harvest sets the rhythm of the year.
Guinea-Bissau's war of independence helped spark the 1974 revolution that ended dictatorship in Portugal.
Poilão island in the Bijagós is one of the most important green turtle nesting sites in the entire Atlantic Ocean.
In Bijagó culture, women traditionally choose their husbands and can also end a marriage by moving the man's belongings out.

content.tagline: Africa's only Spanish-speaking nation
content.overview:
Equatorial Guinea is one of the smallest countries on mainland Africa, about the size of Maryland, and it comes in two parts. Río Muni is a rectangle of rainforest on the coast of Central Africa between Cameroon and Gabon. The island of Bioko lies 40 kilometers off Cameroon's shore in the Gulf of Guinea, and it is there, not on the mainland, that the capital, Malabo, sits beneath a mist-wrapped volcano. Several smaller islands, including distant Annobón, complete the country.

About 1.7 million people live in Equatorial Guinea. Spanish is the main official language, a legacy of Spanish rule, making this the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa; French and Portuguese are also official, and Fang and Bubi are widely spoken at home. Oil discovered offshore in the 1990s made the country one of the richest in Africa by average income, and it built a brand-new planned city called Ciudad de la Paz in the forest. Yet the wealth is shared very unequally, and the same president has ruled since 1979, one of the longest reigns of any leader in the world.
content.landAndNature: Bioko island is a chain of volcanoes; Pico Basilé rises 3,011 meters directly above Malabo, and its southern slopes are among the wettest places in Africa, with more than 10 meters of rain a year. Those rainforests shelter seven kinds of monkeys, including the drill, and beaches where four species of sea turtle come ashore to nest. Río Muni on the mainland is low coastal plain climbing to forested hills, drained by rivers such as the Mbini. Monte Alén National Park protects lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, forest elephants, and the goliath frog, the largest frog in the world. Annobón, far to the southwest, is a tiny green volcanic island with a crater lake. The climate is hot and humid year-round.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Fang are the largest people on the mainland, while the Bubi are the original inhabitants of Bioko, and small communities of Fernandinos, descended from freed slaves, and Annobonese have their own Portuguese-based creole. Most people are Roman Catholic. Meals are built on cassava, plantains, and yams with fish or meat in peanut or palm-nut sauce, and pepper soup, a fiery broth with fish, is a favorite. Fang storytellers perform epic tales accompanied by the mvet, a harp-zither with a gourd resonator, and the balélé dance is performed on Bioko at Christmas. Soccer is the favorite sport; the country hosted the Africa Cup of Nations in 2012 and 2015, and the women's team has won the African championship twice.
content.history: Pygmy peoples and then Bubi and Fang settlers lived here before Portuguese sailors reached Bioko in 1472. Portugal traded the islands to Spain in 1778, and Spain slowly extended control to the mainland in the late 1800s, running cocoa plantations on Bioko with imported labor. Independence came on October 12, 1968, under Francisco Macías Nguema, whose rule became one of the most brutal in Africa; roughly a third of the population fled or died. His nephew Teodoro Obiang overthrew him in 1979 and has been president ever since. Oil production from 1996 brought sudden wealth, new highways, and towering government buildings, but human rights groups criticize the lack of political freedom and the poverty in which most citizens still live.
funFacts: Equatorial Guinea is the only country in Africa where Spanish is an official language.
Despite its name, the equator does not pass through Equatorial Guinea; the island of Annobón lies just south of it.
The goliath frog of Río Muni can weigh over three kilograms and grow longer than a house cat.
The capital, Malabo, is on an island, while a brand-new capital called Ciudad de la Paz is being built on the mainland.
The country's oil made its average income among the highest in Africa, but most of the money reaches only a few.

content.tagline: Cradle of democracy and the Olympics
content.overview:
Greece occupies the southern tip of the Balkan Peninsula, where the land shatters into thousands of islands scattered across the blue Aegean and Ionian Seas. It is about the size of Alabama, but no country in Europe has a longer coastline compared with its size. The capital, Athens, is one of the oldest cities in the world, its ancient Acropolis hill crowned by the Parthenon temple, standing above a sprawling modern city of about three million people.

Around 10.4 million people live in Greece and speak Greek, a language with its own alphabet that has been written for nearly 3,000 years. Most Greeks belong to the Orthodox Christian Church. Greece is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union, and it uses the euro. Shipping, tourism, olives, and farming drive the economy; Greek shipowners control one of the largest merchant fleets in the world. Ancient Greeks gave the world democracy, philosophy, theater, and the Olympic Games, and modern Greeks live among those ruins with a love of sunshine, sea, and long meals shared with family.
content.landAndNature: About 80 percent of Greece is mountains. The Pindus range forms the country's spine, and Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the gods, is the highest peak at 2,917 meters. The Vikos Gorge in the north is one of the deepest canyons in the world. Around 6,000 islands and islets, of which about 200 are inhabited, dot the seas: Crete is the largest, and the Cyclades are famous for whitewashed villages and blue-domed churches. Meteora's monasteries perch atop sandstone pillars hundreds of meters high. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild on the coast and snowy in the mountains. Loggerhead turtles nest on Zakynthos, rare monk seals hide in island caves, and wild goats called kri-kri live on Crete, while olive trees, some over a thousand years old, cover the hills.
content.peopleAndCulture: Greek life centers on family, food, and the outdoors. Meals feature olive oil, feta cheese, olives, grilled fish, souvlaki, moussaka, and honey-soaked baklava, often at tavernas late into the evening. Coffee is sipped slowly, and dancing in a line with arms on shoulders breaks out at weddings and festivals. Easter is the biggest holiday, with candlelit midnight services and roasted lamb. Greeks celebrate name days as much as birthdays. Soccer and basketball are the top sports; Greece won the European soccer championship in 2004 in a huge upset. Theater, born here 2,500 years ago, is still performed in ancient stone amphitheaters under the stars, and the bouzouki, a long-necked string instrument, gives Greek music its distinctive sound.
content.history: The Minoans of Crete built palaces by 2000 BC, followed by the Mycenaeans of Homer's epics. Around 500 BC, city-states like Athens and Sparta flourished; Athens created the world's first democracy, and thinkers such as Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle laid the foundations of Western philosophy and science. Alexander the Great spread Greek culture as far as India before Rome absorbed Greece in 146 BC. The Byzantine Empire, Greek-speaking and Christian, ruled from Constantinople for a thousand years until the Ottomans conquered it in 1453 and ruled Greece for nearly four centuries. Greeks won independence in a war beginning in 1821. Greece was occupied by Nazi Germany in World War II, suffered a civil war, and endured a military dictatorship from 1967 to 1974 before restoring democracy. It joined the European Union in 1981.
funFacts: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896, reviving a tradition that began in Olympia in 776 BC.
Greece has about 6,000 islands and islets, and about 200 of them have people living on them year-round.
The marathon race is named after the town of Marathon, from which a messenger supposedly ran to Athens in 490 BC.
Greeks are among the top consumers of olive oil in the world, using more than 12 liters per person each year.
Greece has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the Acropolis, Delphi, and the monasteries of Meteora.

content.tagline: The Spice Isle
content.overview:
Grenada is a small, hilly island at the southern end of the Caribbean's Windward Islands chain, about 160 kilometers north of Venezuela. The country includes two smaller islands to the north, Carriacou and Petite Martinique, and together they cover only about 344 km², roughly twice the size of Washington, D.C. Around 125,000 people live there, most of them on the main island.

The capital, St. George's, is often called the prettiest harbor town in the Caribbean, with pastel warehouses and red roofs curving around a horseshoe-shaped bay that fills an old volcanic crater. Nutmeg, mace, cinnamon, cloves and cocoa grow on the green hillsides, earning Grenada its nickname, the Spice Isle; a nutmeg even appears on the national flag.

English is the official language, and many people also speak a Creole. Grenada is an independent member of the Commonwealth with a parliament and prime minister, and the British monarch as head of state. Tourism, spices, chocolate and a medical school support the economy.
content.landAndNature:
Grenada was built by volcanoes, and its rugged center rises to Mount St. Catherine at about 840 meters. Rainforest cloaks the mountains, where Grand Etang, a lake in an extinct crater, is surrounded by trails, waterfalls and troops of mona monkeys brought from Africa centuries ago. Rivers tumble down to a coast of black and white sand beaches; Grand Anse, about 3 kilometers long, is the most famous.

The climate is warm year-round with a wet season from June to December. Hurricanes are rare this far south, but Ivan in 2004 damaged about 90 percent of the island's buildings. Just north of Grenada, an active underwater volcano called Kick 'em Jenny rumbles beneath the sea. Offshore reefs shelter turtles and rays, and the world's first underwater sculpture park sits in Molinere Bay.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Grenadians are descendants of Africans, with smaller East Indian and European communities, and English is spoken with a lilting island accent. The national dish is oil down, a one-pot stew of breadfruit, salted meat, callaloo greens and dumplings simmered in coconut milk until the oil rises to the top. Nutmeg flavors everything from ice cream to jam, and the island's dark chocolate is prized.

Spicemas, Grenada's carnival in August, features steel bands, calypso and soca music, and Jab Jab masqueraders covered in black oil and wearing horns. Cricket is the national sport, and sprinter Kirani James won Grenada's first Olympic medal, a gold, in 2012. On Carriacou, the Big Drum dance keeps African rhythms alive, and the annual regatta fills the harbor with handmade wooden boats.
content.history:
Kalinago and earlier Arawak peoples lived on Grenada when Columbus sailed past in 1498. The French seized the island in 1650 and drove the Kalinago to a last stand at a northern cliff now called Leapers' Hill. French planters brought enslaved Africans to grow sugar, and in 1763 Britain took the island. A major uprising led by Julien Fédon in 1795 nearly succeeded before it was crushed. Slavery ended in 1834, and nutmeg trees, introduced in the 1840s, became the new source of wealth.

Grenada gained independence from Britain on February 7, 1974. In 1979 a revolution led by Maurice Bishop set up a socialist government; when Bishop was killed by rivals in 1983, the United States and Caribbean nations invaded and restored elections. Grenada has been a stable democracy since, rebuilding after Hurricane Ivan in 2004.
funFacts: Grenada is one of only a handful of countries with a plant, the nutmeg, on its national flag.
The Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park, opened in 2006, was the first of its kind anywhere in the world.
Kick 'em Jenny, an active volcano just off the north coast, rises about 1,300 meters from the seafloor but stays underwater.
St. George's harbor sits inside the flooded crater of an ancient volcano.
Grenada is the world's second-largest producer of nutmeg, after Indonesia, despite being tiny.
Carriacou's name comes from a Kalinago word thought to mean "land of reefs."

content.tagline: Heart of the Maya world
content.overview:
Guatemala lies just south of Mexico in Central America, bordered by Belize, Honduras and El Salvador, with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. It covers about 109,000 km², roughly the size of the US state of Tennessee, and with about 18 million people it is the most populous country in Central America. Guatemala City, the capital, is the region's largest city.

Nearly half of Guatemalans are Maya, descendants of the civilization that built great stone cities in the jungle more than a thousand years ago. Spanish is the official language, but 22 Mayan languages such as K'iche', Q'eqchi' and Kaqchikel are spoken daily, along with Garifuna and Xinca. Women in highland villages wear hand-woven blouses called huipiles whose patterns reveal their hometown.

Guatemala is a republic with an elected president. Coffee, bananas, sugar and textiles are major products, and many Guatemalans work abroad and send money home. Volcanoes, colonial towns, colorful markets and the ruins of Tikal draw visitors from around the world.
content.landAndNature:
A ridge of about 37 volcanoes runs across southern Guatemala, several of them active. Fuego throws out ash and lava regularly, Pacaya lets hikers roast marshmallows over hot rocks, and Tajumulco, about 4,220 meters, is the highest peak in Central America. Lake Atitlán, ringed by three volcanoes and Maya villages, is often called the most beautiful lake in the world.

The north is the flat, forested Petén lowland, where the ruins of Tikal poke above the jungle canopy and spider monkeys, toucans and jaguars roam the Maya Biosphere Reserve. The Caribbean side is hot and humid; the highlands are cool and springlike, earning Guatemala the name Land of Eternal Spring. The resplendent quetzal, a brilliant green bird with tail feathers up to a meter long, is the national bird and gives its name to the currency.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Maya traditions are alive in Guatemala: the K'iche' epic Popol Vuh tells the story of creation, and the ancient Maya calendar is still used by spiritual leaders. The Sunday market at Chichicastenango overflows with woven textiles, masks and flowers. Ladinos, people of mixed heritage, and the Garifuna of the Caribbean coast add their own music and food.

Corn is sacred and central: tortillas come with every meal, along with black beans, tamales, and rich stews like pepián and kak'ik turkey soup. The Maya were the first people to make chocolate drinks from cacao. The marimba, a wooden xylophone, is the national instrument. During Holy Week, Antigua's streets are carpeted in colored sawdust designs, and on November 1 the towns of Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez fly enormous kites to honor the dead. Soccer is the favorite sport.
content.history:
The Maya civilization reached its height in Guatemala between about 250 and 900 AD, when cities such as Tikal, El Mirador and Quiriguá built towering pyramids, developed writing and tracked the planets with remarkable accuracy. Many cities were abandoned after 900, but Maya kingdoms in the highlands were still powerful when Spanish soldiers under Pedro de Alvarado invaded in 1524.

Guatemala became independent from Spain in 1821 and a separate republic in 1847. In the 1900s, coffee and banana companies, especially the US-owned United Fruit Company, held enormous power. A reform government was overthrown in a 1954 coup backed by the United States, leading to a civil war from 1960 to 1996 in which about 200,000 people, most of them Maya civilians, were killed. Peace accords in 1996 ended the fighting; four years earlier, the Maya activist Rigoberta Menchú had won the Nobel Peace Prize for defending Indigenous rights.
funFacts: Guatemala's currency, the quetzal, is named after a bird whose tail feathers the ancient Maya used as money.
Tikal's Temple IV, about 70 meters tall, appeared as a rebel base in the original Star Wars film in 1977.
The Maya used cacao beans as currency and drank chocolate spiced with chili, not sweetened with sugar.
Guatemala's name may come from a Nahuatl word meaning "place of many trees."
On the Day of the Dead, kite makers in Sumpango fly circular kites up to 20 meters across.
Antigua Guatemala was the colonial capital until earthquakes in 1773 destroyed much of it, prompting a move to the present capital.

content.tagline: Land of many waters
content.overview:
Guyana is the only country in South America where English is the official language. It sits on the continent's northeastern shoulder, facing the Atlantic Ocean, with Venezuela to the west, Brazil to the south and Suriname to the east. At about 215,000 km² it is roughly the size of the US state of Idaho, but only about 800,000 people live there, nearly all of them on a narrow coastal strip that lies below sea level and is protected by a long seawall.

The capital, Georgetown, is a city of wooden colonial buildings and canals, home to St. George's Cathedral, one of the tallest wooden churches in the world. Inland, the country is almost entirely rainforest, rivers and savanna, with few roads. The name Guyana comes from an Indigenous word meaning "land of many waters."

Guyanese people trace their roots to India, Africa, Indigenous nations, Europe and China. Guyana is a republic with an elected president. Sugar, rice, gold and bauxite were long its main products; huge oil discoveries offshore since 2015 have made it one of the fastest-growing economies on Earth.
content.landAndNature:
About 80 percent of Guyana is covered by rainforest, part of the vast Guiana Shield, one of the largest untouched wildernesses left in the tropics. Great rivers such as the Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice flow north to the coast, broken by rapids and falls. Kaieteur Falls on the Potaro River drops about 226 meters in a single plunge, roughly four times the height of Niagara, and a tiny golden frog lives its whole life inside the giant bromeliad plants around it.

In the southwest, the Rupununi savanna spreads out beneath the Kanuku Mountains. Guyana is home to giants: the jaguar, the giant anteater, the giant river otter, the harpy eagle, the arapaima, one of the largest freshwater fish, the black caiman, and the Victoria amazonica water lily, whose leaves can be two meters across.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Descendants of Indian indentured workers make up the largest group, followed by Afro-Guyanese, people of mixed heritage and nine Indigenous nations such as the Makushi and Wapishana. English is official, but most people speak Guyanese Creole day to day, and Hindu, Christian and Muslim holidays are all national celebrations: Diwali lamps, Christmas masquerades and Eid feasts.

The food reflects this mix. Pepperpot, a dark stew flavored with cassareep made from cassava, is an Indigenous dish eaten at Christmas; curry and roti, cook-up rice and Chinese-style fried rice are everyday favorites. Cricket is the national sport, and Guyana hosts matches for the West Indies team. Mashramani, on Republic Day in February, brings costume parades, calypso and steel bands to the streets of Georgetown.
content.history:
Arawak, Carib, Warao and other peoples lived along Guyana's rivers for thousands of years. Dutch traders settled in the early 1600s and built dikes and canals to farm the coast, bringing enslaved Africans to work sugar plantations. In 1763 an enslaved man named Cuffy led a major uprising in Berbice; he is now a national hero. Britain took over in 1814 and named the colony British Guiana.

After slavery ended in 1834, planters brought about 240,000 indentured workers from India between 1838 and 1917. Guyana became independent on May 26, 1966, and a republic in 1970. Politics has often divided along ethnic lines. Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, about two-thirds of Guyana's territory, a dispute now before the International Court of Justice. Since oil began flowing in 2019, the country has been changing rapidly.
funFacts: Kaieteur Falls is about 226 meters high, roughly four times the height of Niagara Falls, and sits deep in the rainforest.
Most of Guyana's coast lies below sea level, protected by a seawall first built by Dutch engineers.
The Victoria amazonica water lily, Guyana's national flower, has floating leaves strong enough to hold a small child.
Guyana is the only country in South America with English as its official language.
Guyana's national dish, pepperpot, is preserved by cassareep, a cassava sauce that keeps the stew edible for days without refrigeration.
Ninety percent of Guyanese live on a coastal strip that makes up only about 10 percent of the country.

HKG.name: Hong Kong
HKG.officialName: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China

content.tagline: Maya ruins and Caribbean reefs
content.overview:
Honduras sits in the middle of Central America, with a long Caribbean coastline to the north and a short stretch of Pacific shore on the Gulf of Fonseca to the south. It borders Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua and covers about 112,500 km², slightly larger than the US state of Tennessee. Around 10 million people live there, and the capital, Tegucigalpa, spreads across hills in the country's mountainous south.

Most Hondurans speak Spanish, while Garifuna, Miskito and English-speaking communities live along the Caribbean coast and on the Bay Islands. The ruins of Copán, a Maya city famous for its carved stone stairway, and the coral reefs around Roatán and Utila are the country's best-known treasures.

Honduras is a republic with an elected president. Coffee, bananas, palm oil and shrimp are big exports, and clothing factories employ many people. The country has struggled with poverty, hurricanes and crime, and many Hondurans have moved to the United States, sending money home that supports millions of families.
content.landAndNature:
Rugged mountains cover about three-quarters of Honduras, rising to Cerro Las Minas at about 2,870 meters. The Caribbean lowlands are hot and wet, dotted with banana plantations, while the vast, roadless rainforest of La Mosquitia in the east holds the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve and the ruins of a lost city found by explorers in 2015. Pine forests cover the cooler highlands.

Offshore, the Bay Islands sit on the Mesoamerican Reef, the second-largest coral reef system in the world; whale sharks gather off Utila, and Roatán's reefs are crowded with divers. Scarlet macaws, the national bird, flash red over Copán, and jaguars, tapirs, howler monkeys and manatees live in the wild east. Hurricanes are a constant threat; Hurricane Mitch in 1998 killed thousands and destroyed much of the country's roads and bridges.
content.peopleAndCulture:
About nine in ten Hondurans are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent, and Spanish is heard everywhere. The Lenca, Miskito and other Indigenous peoples keep their own traditions, and the Garifuna, descended from Africans and Caribbean islanders, are famous for punta drumming and dancing. Most people are Catholic or evangelical Christian.

The national snack is the baleada, a soft flour tortilla folded around beans, cheese and cream, sold at street stands everywhere. Tamales, fried fish with plantains, and coconut bread on the coast are other favorites. Soccer is the great passion, and the national team's matches bring the country to a standstill. La Ceiba's carnival in May is the biggest party of the year, and in Yoro people celebrate the Lluvia de Peces, when fish appear on the ground after heavy storms.
content.history:
The Maya city of Copán flourished between about 400 and 800 AD, ruled by a line of 16 kings who left behind exquisite stone portraits and the longest carved Maya text ever found. Christopher Columbus reached the mainland near Trujillo in 1502, and Spanish conquest followed; the Lenca chief Lempira led a fierce resistance in 1537 and the national currency is named after him.

Honduras became independent from Spain in 1821 and a separate republic in 1838. In the early 1900s US fruit companies came to dominate the economy, inspiring the term "banana republic." The country fought a short war with El Salvador in 1969. Military governments ruled for much of the century before elections resumed in 1982. Hurricane Mitch in 1998 and a coup in 2009 were major setbacks, and Honduras has worked since to strengthen its democracy.
funFacts: The name Honduras means "depths" in Spanish, said to come from Columbus's remark about the deep waters off the coast.
Copán's Hieroglyphic Stairway has about 2,000 carved glyphs, the longest known Maya inscription.
The term "banana republic" was coined in 1904 by the writer O. Henry in a story set in a fictional version of Honduras.
Whale sharks, the largest fish in the world, gather off the island of Utila almost year-round.
In the town of Yoro, small fish are found on the ground after storms in a yearly event locals call the Rain of Fish.
Honduras's national bird, the scarlet macaw, was revered by the ancient Maya at Copán, where it is still bred and released.

content.tagline: A thousand islands on a crescent coast
content.overview:
Croatia curves like a crescent moon around the northern Adriatic Sea and the western Balkans. Roughly the size of West Virginia, it has one of the most spectacular coastlines in Europe, with more than 1,200 islands, rocky coves, and walled medieval towns like Dubrovnik and Split. Inland, the capital, Zagreb, is a city of Austro-Hungarian avenues, red-tiled roofs, and busy cafés. Croatia borders Slovenia, Hungary, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro.

About 3.9 million people live here, and Croatian, written in the Latin alphabet, is the official language. Most Croats are Roman Catholic. Croatia became an independent country in 1991 as Yugoslavia broke apart, joined the European Union in 2013, and adopted the euro in 2023. It is a parliamentary republic. Tourism is the biggest industry, drawing millions of summer visitors to the beaches, and Croatians have punched far above their weight in sports, finishing second at the 2018 soccer World Cup with a population smaller than many cities.
content.landAndNature: Croatia has three very different regions. The long Dalmatian coast is a land of limestone, olive trees, lavender, and clear turquoise water, sheltered from the open sea by chains of islands such as Hvar, Brač, and Korčula. Behind the coast the Dinaric Alps rise steeply, with Dinara peak at 1,831 meters. Inland lie the flat, fertile plains of Slavonia along the Sava and Drava rivers. Plitvice Lakes National Park, a UNESCO site, features 16 lakes stepping down in terraces linked by waterfalls, colored startling shades of green and blue by minerals. Brown bears, wolves, and lynx live in the mountains, griffon vultures nest on Cres island, and Kopački Rit wetland teems with herons and storks. Summers are hot and dry on the coast, winters cold inland.
content.peopleAndCulture: Coastal life follows the sea: fishermen mend nets in harbors, and towns hold klapa singing sessions where groups of men harmonize without instruments, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Food changes with the region, from grilled fish, black cuttlefish risotto, and pašticada beef stew on the coast to spicy kulen sausage and paprika-rich fish stews in Slavonia. The necktie was invented here, evolving from scarves Croatian soldiers wore in the 1600s. Sports are a national pride: Croatia's soccer team, in its red-and-white checkerboard shirts, reached two World Cup finals, and the country excels at water polo, handball, tennis, and basketball. Dubrovnik's old city hosts a summer festival of theater, and the inventor Nikola Tesla was born in the Croatian village of Smiljan.
content.history: Illyrians and Greeks lived on the coast before Rome took over; the emperor Diocletian built a huge palace at Split around the year 300 that people still live inside today. Croats, a Slavic people, arrived in the 600s and formed a kingdom by 925. From 1102 Croatia was joined to Hungary, and later to the Habsburg Empire, while Venice ruled much of the coast and Dubrovnik stayed a proud independent republic for centuries. After World War I Croatia became part of Yugoslavia. During World War II a Nazi-backed regime committed atrocities. Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, and a war followed until 1995, destroying towns like Vukovar and killing thousands. The country joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013.
funFacts: The necktie descends from the cravat worn by Croatian soldiers in the 1600s; Croatia celebrates Cravat Day every October 18.
Croatia has more than 1,200 islands, islets, and rocks, but only about 50 of them are inhabited.
Diocletian's Palace in Split is a 1,700-year-old Roman palace that still contains homes, shops, and cafés.
Croatian inventor Nikola Tesla developed the alternating-current electricity system used in homes worldwide.
The Sea Organ in Zadar is a set of pipes under stone steps that plays musical notes as waves push air through them.

content.tagline: The first free Black republic
content.overview:
Haiti occupies the western third of the island of Hispaniola, which it shares with the Dominican Republic, in the Caribbean Sea. It covers about 27,750 km², slightly smaller than the US state of Maryland, and around 11.5 million people live there, making it one of the most crowded countries in the Americas. The capital, Port-au-Prince, sprawls around a wide bay on the southern coast.

Haiti made history in 1804 as the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people who overthrew their masters, and the second independent country in the Americas after the United States. Its name comes from the Taíno word Ayiti, "land of high mountains," and steep hills cover most of the country.

Nearly all Haitians speak Haitian Creole, or Kreyòl, and French is the second official language, used in government and schools. Haiti is a republic, though in recent decades it has faced dictatorship, coups, a devastating 2010 earthquake, hurricanes and gang violence, leaving it the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere. Haitians are known for their art, music and deep resilience.
content.landAndNature:
Mountains run across Haiti in several ranges, rising to Pic la Selle at about 2,680 meters in the southeast. Between them lie fertile valleys such as the Artibonite, where rice is grown, and the dry Central Plateau. The coast has coral reefs and small islands, including Île de la Gonâve in the great western bay.

The climate is tropical, cooler in the mountains, with a hurricane season from June to November. Over the centuries most of Haiti's forests were cut for farmland and charcoal, so heavy rains cause floods and landslides. Remaining wild places such as Pic Macaya National Park shelter rare frogs, orchids and the Hispaniolan solenodon, a shrew-like mammal with a venomous bite. Flamingos and crocodiles live in the salty Étang Saumâtre lake near the Dominican border.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Haitians are overwhelmingly of African descent, and their Creole language blends French words with African grammar. Faith is central: most people are Christian, and many also practice Vodou, a religion with West African roots that honors spirits through drumming, song and dance. Kompa music, with its rolling rhythm, and rara street bands with bamboo trumpets fill the streets, especially at Carnival, when Jacmel is famous for its papier-mâché masks.

Haitian painters are celebrated worldwide for bright, dreamlike scenes of village life, and buses called tap-taps are hand-painted like rolling artworks. Favorite foods include griot (crispy fried pork), rice and beans, fried plantains and spicy pikliz pickles. Every January 1, families eat soup joumou, a pumpkin soup once forbidden to enslaved people, to celebrate independence. Soccer is the national sport.
content.history:
The Taíno people lived on Hispaniola when Columbus arrived in 1492, and they were nearly wiped out within a century. France took the western part of the island in 1697 and made Saint-Domingue the richest colony in the world, producing sugar and coffee through the labor of about half a million enslaved Africans under brutal conditions.

In 1791 the enslaved people rose up, led by Toussaint Louverture and later Jean-Jacques Dessalines. They defeated French, Spanish and British armies, including troops sent by Napoleon, and declared independence on January 1, 1804. France later forced Haiti to pay a huge sum for its freedom, a debt that drained the country for over a century. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the Duvalier family ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986. A 2010 earthquake killed more than 200,000 people, and instability has continued since.
funFacts: Haiti's Citadelle Laferrière, built after independence to guard against a French return, is the largest fortress in the Americas.
Soup joumou, Haiti's independence soup, was added to UNESCO's list of the world's cultural heritage in 2021.
Haiti's flag was created in 1803 by tearing the white stripe out of the French tricolor and sewing the blue and red together.
Haiti was the first country in the Americas to permanently abolish slavery, in 1804.
Tap-tap buses get their name from the sound passengers make tapping the side to signal a stop.
Vodou has been an officially recognized religion in Haiti since 2003.

content.tagline: Thermal baths on the Danube
content.overview:
Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe, about the size of Indiana, spread across a wide, flat basin ringed by the Carpathian Mountains of its neighbors. The Danube River flows through the middle and splits the capital, Budapest, into hilly Buda on the west bank and flat, busy Pest on the east, joined by graceful bridges and watched over by a huge parliament building on the river. Budapest is famous for grand cafés, a century-old subway, and steaming thermal baths fed by more than a hundred hot springs.

About 9.6 million people live in Hungary. Their language, Hungarian, or Magyar, is unlike any of its neighbors' tongues; its closest relatives are Finnish and Estonian, and its ancestors came from the Ural Mountains more than a thousand years ago. Hungary is a parliamentary republic and has been a member of the European Union since 2004. Farms on the plains grow wheat, corn, sunflowers, and the paprika peppers that color Hungarian cooking, and factories build cars and electronics. Hungarians are proud inventors, from the ballpoint pen to the Rubik's Cube.
content.landAndNature: Most of Hungary is the Great Hungarian Plain, or Alföld, a flat expanse of farmland and grassland stretching east of the Danube; the Hortobágy, a vast steppe, is grazed by gray longhorn cattle and shaggy racka sheep with spiral horns, and herders there still ride horses in traditional style. The Danube and the Tisza are the great rivers. Low mountains rise in the north, with Kékes at 1,014 meters the highest point. Lake Balaton in the west is the largest lake in Central Europe, a shallow, warm summer playground for swimmers and sailors, and Lake Hévíz nearby is one of the world's largest natural thermal lakes. Caves honeycomb the Aggtelek karst. Great bustards, among the heaviest flying birds, stride across the plains, and storks nest on village poles.
content.peopleAndCulture: Hungarian food is hearty and red with paprika: goulash, a beef and vegetable soup, chicken paprikash with dumplings, stuffed cabbage, and lángos, fried dough topped with sour cream and cheese. Sweets include Dobos torte and chimney cakes roasted over coals. Most Hungarians are Christian, mainly Catholic or Reformed. Folk dance and the fiery music of Gypsy violin bands are national treasures, and composers Franz Liszt, Béla Bartók, and Zoltán Kodály drew on folk melodies. Soaking in thermal baths, some in ornate art nouveau buildings, is a weekly ritual, and chess games are played in the pools. Hungary has won more Olympic medals per person than almost any nation, especially in water polo, fencing, swimming, and canoeing.
content.history: Around 895 the Magyars, horse-riding warriors from the east, swept into the Carpathian Basin under their leader Árpád. King Stephen I made Hungary a Christian kingdom in the year 1000. The medieval kingdom was powerful until the Ottoman Turks won the Battle of Mohács in 1526 and occupied central Hungary for 150 years. The Habsburgs of Austria then ruled, and after a failed revolution in 1848 Hungary became an equal partner in Austria-Hungary in 1867. Defeat in World War I cost Hungary two-thirds of its territory. Hungary was allied with Nazi Germany in World War II, and about half a million Hungarian Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. Soviet forces installed a communist government, and an uprising in 1956 was crushed by Soviet tanks. Communism ended in 1989, and Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.
funFacts: The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by Hungarian architecture professor Ernő Rubik, who took a month to solve it himself.
Budapest has more thermal springs than any other capital city, with about 120 feeding its famous baths.
The ballpoint pen was patented by Hungarian journalist László Bíró in 1938, and pens are still called biros in many countries.
Hungarian has 14 vowels and words like megszentségteleníthetetlenségeskedéseitekért, 44 letters long.
Budapest's underground railway, opened in 1896, was the first electric subway on the European mainland.

content.tagline: Seventeen thousand islands on the equator
content.overview:
Indonesia is the largest island nation in the world, a chain of about 17,000 islands strung along the equator between the Indian and Pacific Oceans for more than 5,000 kilometers, about the width of the United States. Its land totals about 1.9 million km², and with roughly 275 million people it is the fourth most populous country on Earth and home to the largest Muslim population of any nation.

More than half of all Indonesians live on Java, the most crowded major island in the world, where the capital, Jakarta, sprawls with more than 10 million people; the government is building a new capital, Nusantara, on the island of Borneo. Sumatra, Sulawesi, Bali and the western half of New Guinea are among the other main islands.

Indonesian, or Bahasa Indonesia, is the shared national language, but people speak more than 700 local languages, from Javanese to Balinese. The national motto is "Unity in Diversity." Indonesia is a republic with an elected president, and it produces palm oil, coffee, rubber, nickel and natural gas.
content.landAndNature:
Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire and has about 130 active volcanoes, more than any other country. Tambora's eruption in 1815 was the largest in recorded history, and Krakatoa's 1883 blast was heard thousands of kilometers away. Earthquakes and tsunamis are constant dangers; a 2004 tsunami killed about 170,000 people in Aceh. The climate is hot, humid and rainy year-round.

The islands hold some of the richest wildlife anywhere. Komodo dragons, the world's largest lizards, hunt deer on a few eastern islands. Orangutans swing through the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo, which also shelter Sumatran tigers, rhinos and elephants. Birds of paradise dance in New Guinea, and the Rafflesia, the biggest flower on Earth, blooms in Sumatra. Indonesia's coral reefs are among the most diverse in the world.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Indonesia has hundreds of ethnic groups, the largest being the Javanese, and most people are Muslim, while Bali is mainly Hindu and parts of the east are Christian. Daily life mixes mosque calls, gamelan orchestras of bronze gongs, and wayang shadow-puppet plays that last all night. Batik, cloth patterned with wax and dye, is worn from schoolrooms to weddings.

Rice is the heart of every meal, in dishes like nasi goreng (fried rice), satay skewers with peanut sauce, spicy rendang beef and tempeh made from fermented soybeans. Badminton is the national sporting passion, and Indonesia has won Olympic gold in it many times; soccer and the martial art pencak silat are also popular. On Bali, the Nyepi new year is a day of complete silence when even the airport closes.
content.history:
Ancient humans lived here long ago; the tiny Homo floresiensis, nicknamed the hobbit, survived on Flores until about 50,000 years ago. Great trading kingdoms rose later, including Srivijaya on Sumatra and Majapahit on Java, and Buddhist and Hindu rulers built the temples of Borobudur and Prambanan. Islam spread through trade from the 1200s onward.

Europeans came for spices from the Moluccas, and the Dutch East India Company took control of the trade from 1602; the Netherlands ruled the islands as a colony for about 350 years. Japan occupied Indonesia during World War II, and on August 17, 1945, Sukarno proclaimed independence, which the Dutch recognized in 1949 after a war. Suharto ruled as an authoritarian president from 1967 until protests forced him out in 1998, and Indonesia has since become one of the world's largest democracies.
funFacts: Indonesia stretches across three time zones and more than 5,000 kilometers from west to east.
The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora cooled the whole planet and caused a "year without a summer" in Europe and North America.
The Komodo dragon can grow three meters long and has a venomous bite.
Borobudur, built in the 800s, is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, with more than 2,600 carved panels.
Indonesia has about 130 active volcanoes, more than any other country.
Ijen volcano on Java glows with blue flames at night as burning sulfur gas escapes from cracks.

content.tagline: A billion voices, a thousand traditions
content.overview:
India is home to more people than any other country, about 1.4 billion, roughly one in every six humans on Earth. It fills most of the South Asian subcontinent, a giant triangle of land that juts into the Indian Ocean, bordered by Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. At about 3.3 million km² it is the seventh-largest country, about one-third the size of the United States.

The capital, New Delhi, sits in the north; Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru are other giant cities. Hindi and English are used nationwide, and the constitution recognizes 22 languages, including Tamil, Bengali, Telugu and Marathi, each with tens of millions of speakers and often its own alphabet. Four major religions, Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, were born here, and India also has one of the world's largest Muslim populations.

India is the world's largest democracy, a federal republic of 28 states with an elected parliament and prime minister. It is a land of farmers and software engineers, ancient temples and space rockets, spicy street food and the world's biggest film industry.
content.landAndNature:
The Himalayas wall off northern India with the highest mountains on Earth, including Kangchenjunga, about 8,590 meters. Below them stretch the hot, crowded plains of the Ganges, a river sacred to Hindus. The Thar Desert bakes in the northwest, the Deccan Plateau fills the south, and rainforest drapes the Western Ghats along the coast. Each summer the monsoon sweeps in from the sea, delivering most of the year's rain in a few months.

India has more wild tigers than any other country, more than 3,000, along with Asian elephants, one-horned rhinos in Kaziranga, the last Asiatic lions in the Gir Forest, snow leopards, king cobras and the peacock, the national bird. In the Sundarbans, tigers swim between mangrove islands.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Indian life is a festival of color. Diwali fills homes with oil lamps and fireworks, Holi turns streets into clouds of colored powder, and Eid, Christmas and Sikh Vaisakhi are celebrated too. Food varies by region: wheat breads and rich curries in the north, rice, dosas and coconut in the south, and chai tea everywhere. More people are vegetarian in India than anywhere else.

Cricket is followed with wild devotion, and kabaddi, hockey and chess are also popular; chess itself began in India as chaturanga. Bollywood in Mumbai makes more films than any other place, full of song and dance. Yoga, classical dances like Bharatanatyam, sitar music and the ancient Sanskrit epics the Ramayana and Mahabharata remain part of daily culture. Indian mathematicians gave the world the decimal system and the concept of zero.
content.history:
The Indus Valley Civilization built planned brick cities with drains and baths about 4,500 years ago. Later came the Vedic age, the Buddha's teachings, and great empires: the Maurya under Ashoka, who spread Buddhism, and the Gupta, a golden age of science and art. From the 1500s the Mughal emperors ruled much of India and built the Taj Mahal.

British traders arrived in the 1600s, and by 1858 Britain ruled India directly. Mahatma Gandhi led a nonviolent struggle for freedom, and India became independent on August 15, 1947. The country was partitioned into India and Pakistan, uprooting about 15 million people and killing hundreds of thousands in violence; the region of Kashmir has been disputed between the two countries ever since. India adopted its constitution in 1950. It has since become a nuclear power, a technology hub and, in 2023, the first nation to land a spacecraft near the Moon's south pole.
funFacts: The Kumbh Mela pilgrimage draws tens of millions of people to the Ganges, the largest peaceful gathering of humans on Earth.
Indian Railways carries more than 20 million passengers a day and is one of the world's largest employers.
The game snakes and ladders began in India as a moral lesson about virtue and vice.
The word "shampoo" comes from the Hindi word champo, meaning to massage.
The Taj Mahal took about 20,000 workers and 22 years to complete, finished around 1653.
A floating post office operates on a houseboat on Dal Lake in Kashmir.

content.tagline: The Emerald Isle of storytellers
content.overview:
Ireland is a green island on the western edge of Europe, facing the Atlantic Ocean, with Great Britain across the Irish Sea to the east. The Republic of Ireland covers about five-sixths of the island, roughly the size of West Virginia; the northeastern corner, Northern Ireland, is part of the United Kingdom. The capital, Dublin, sits on the east coast at the mouth of the River Liffey, a city of Georgian brick houses, old pubs, and a university library holding a 1,200-year-old illustrated Bible, the Book of Kells.

About 5.3 million people live in the Republic. English is spoken by everyone, and Irish, a Celtic language, is the first official language, taught in every school and spoken daily in some western areas called the Gaeltacht. Ireland is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union. Once one of Europe's poorer countries, from which millions emigrated, it is now one of the richest, home to the European headquarters of many technology companies. Irish music, literature, and the celebration of St. Patrick's Day have spread around the world.
content.landAndNature: Ireland is shaped like a saucer: a central lowland of bogs, lakes, and pastures ringed by coastal hills and mountains. The highest peak, Carrauntoohil in County Kerry, reaches 1,038 meters. Mild, wet Atlantic weather keeps the grass so green that the island is called the Emerald Isle, and it almost never gets very hot or very cold. The west coast is wild and rugged: the Cliffs of Moher drop 214 meters into the ocean, and the Burren is a strange gray limestone landscape where Arctic and Mediterranean flowers grow side by side. The Giant's Causeway, in Northern Ireland, is famous for its hexagonal basalt columns. The River Shannon is the longest in the British Isles. Red deer roam Killarney, seals bask on rocks, and puffins nest on the Skellig islands.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Irish are famous for talk, music, and storytelling. Traditional sessions in pubs bring together fiddles, tin whistles, bodhrán drums, and uilleann pipes, and Irish dancing, with its fast footwork and still arms, is performed worldwide. Ireland has produced four Nobel Prize winners in literature, including W. B. Yeats and Samuel Beckett, along with James Joyce and Oscar Wilde. Gaelic games are unique to Ireland: hurling, played with wooden sticks and a small ball, is one of the fastest field sports on Earth, and Gaelic football fills stadiums every summer. Rugby and soccer are also loved. Foods include soda bread, Irish stew, and potatoes in many forms, and St. Patrick's Day on March 17 brings parades in every town.
content.history: Farmers built the great stone tomb of Newgrange around 3200 BC, older than the pyramids. Celtic culture arrived later, and in the 400s St. Patrick spread Christianity; Irish monks then produced beautiful manuscripts and carried learning across Europe during the Dark Ages. Vikings founded Dublin around 841, and Norman knights arrived in 1169, beginning 750 years of English involvement. English and Scottish settlers took land in the 1600s, and Catholics lost most of their rights. The Great Famine of 1845 to 1852, when the potato crop failed, killed about a million people and forced another million to emigrate. An uprising in 1916 and a war of independence led to the Irish Free State in 1922, with the north remaining British. Ireland became a republic in 1949 and joined the European Union in 1973.
funFacts: Halloween grew out of the ancient Irish festival of Samhain, when people believed spirits walked among the living.
Ireland has no native snakes, which legend credits to St. Patrick but scientists credit to the Ice Age and the surrounding sea.
The harp is Ireland's national symbol, and Ireland is the only country with a musical instrument as its official emblem.
About 70 million people around the world claim Irish ancestry, more than 13 times the population of Ireland itself.
Newgrange, a stone tomb built about 5,200 years ago, is lit by the rising sun only at the winter solstice.

content.tagline: Heir to ancient Persia
content.overview:
Iran, known for most of its history as Persia, is a large country in Southwest Asia stretching from the Caspian Sea in the north to the Persian Gulf in the south. It borders seven countries, including Iraq, Türkiye, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and covers about 1.65 million km², roughly the size of Alaska. Around 88 million people live there, most in cities such as the capital, Tehran, which sits beneath snow-capped mountains.

Persian, also called Farsi, is the national language, written in a form of the Arabic script, and many Iranians also speak Azerbaijani, Kurdish or other languages. Most people are Shia Muslims. Iran has been an Islamic Republic since a revolution in 1979; a Supreme Leader holds the highest authority, alongside an elected president and parliament.

Iranians are proud heirs of one of the world's oldest civilizations, famous for poetry, gardens, carpets and science. The country holds some of the largest oil and gas reserves on Earth, and its relations with Western countries have been tense for decades.
