content.landAndNature:
Iran is a high, dry land ringed by mountains. The Zagros range runs down the west, and the Alborz rises along the Caspian coast, crowned by Mount Damavand, a dormant volcano about 5,610 meters high, the tallest peak in the Middle East. In the interior lie two great deserts, the Dasht-e Kavir and the Dasht-e Lut, where satellites have measured some of the hottest ground temperatures ever recorded, above 70 degrees Celsius.

The Caspian shore, by contrast, is green and rainy, with rice paddies and tea gardens. Summers are scorching and winters can be snowy, especially in the northwest. Iran is the last home of the Asiatic cheetah, with only a few dozen left, and also shelters Persian leopards, wild sheep, brown bears and flamingos on its salt lakes.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Persian poetry runs deep in Iranian life; verses by Hafez, Rumi, Ferdowsi and Omar Khayyam are quoted at dinner tables, and families gather on the longest night of the year to read poems and eat pomegranates and watermelon. Nowruz, the new year on the first day of spring, is celebrated for two weeks with a table of symbolic objects, spring cleaning and visits to relatives.

Iranian food features saffron rice with a crispy golden bottom called tahdig, grilled kebabs, herb stews like ghormeh sabzi, and yogurt, fresh herbs and flatbread with every meal. Persian carpets, hand-knotted in intricate patterns, take months or years to make. Wrestling is the traditional national sport, soccer draws huge crowds, and Iran is a world power in weightlifting and volleyball.
content.history:
Around 550 BC Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, which became the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from Greece to India; its capital, Persepolis, still stands in ruins. Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC, but new Persian dynasties, the Parthians and Sasanians, ruled for centuries more. Arab armies brought Islam in the 600s, and Persian scholars such as Avicenna led the medieval world in medicine, astronomy and mathematics.

The Safavid dynasty made Shia Islam the state religion in the 1500s and built glorious Isfahan. In 1935 the country asked to be called Iran. In 1953 a coup backed by Britain and the United States strengthened the Shah, whose rule ended in the 1979 revolution led by Ayatollah Khomeini. A brutal war with Iraq followed from 1980 to 1988, and disputes over Iran's nuclear program have shaped its relations with the world since.
funFacts: Persian engineers built qanats, underground water tunnels, about 3,000 years ago, and many still carry water to desert towns.
Ancient Iranians built yakhchals, dome-shaped ice houses that kept ice frozen through desert summers without electricity.
Iran produces about 90 percent of the world's saffron, the most expensive spice, picked by hand from crocus flowers.
The Lut Desert holds the record for the hottest land surface ever measured from space, over 70 degrees Celsius.
Backgammon and polo were both played in ancient Persia, and polo may have been invented there.
Windcatchers, tall towers that pull cool breezes into houses, have kept Iranian homes cool for centuries.

content.tagline: Cradle of civilization
content.overview:
Iraq lies in the Middle East between two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, in a land the ancient Greeks called Mesopotamia, "between the rivers." It borders Türkiye, Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Syria, with a short coastline on the Persian Gulf. At about 438,000 km² it is roughly the size of California, and about 44 million people live there. The capital, Baghdad, straddles the Tigris in the center of the country.

Here, more than 5,000 years ago, people built the first cities, invented writing and the wheel, and wrote the first laws. Arabic is the main language, and Kurdish (Sorani) is official in the Kurdistan Region of the north, which governs itself with some independence; small communities still speak Aramaic, the language of Jesus. Most Iraqis are Muslims, split between the Shia majority and Sunni minority.

Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic. It has some of the world's largest oil reserves, and after decades of dictatorship, wars and terrorism, its people are rebuilding cities, markets and universities.
content.landAndNature:
The Tigris and Euphrates flow from the mountains of Türkiye across a broad, flat plain to the Persian Gulf, and almost all Iraqis live near them. In the south, the two rivers create vast marshes, reed-filled wetlands where Marsh Arabs have lived on floating islands in arched reed houses for thousands of years. The marshes were drained in the 1990s and partly restored, and are now a World Heritage Site.

West and south of the rivers, deserts stretch toward Syria and Saudi Arabia. In the northeast, the Zagros Mountains of Kurdistan rise above 3,600 meters, with snowy winters and green valleys. Summers on the plains are among the hottest on Earth, often above 45 degrees Celsius, and dust storms sweep across the land. Date palms, once numbering about 30 million, line the rivers.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Iraqis are mostly Arabs, with Kurds making up about a fifth of the population and smaller groups of Turkmen, Assyrians and Yazidis. Hospitality is a point of honor, and guests are served sweet tea in small glasses. The national dish is masgouf, a whole carp split open and slow-grilled beside a wood fire on the banks of the Tigris. Dates, flat bread, lamb kebabs and dolma are everyday foods.

Poetry and storytelling are treasured; Baghdad's Mutanabbi Street is lined with bookstalls and cafes. The maqam, a classical singing tradition, and the oud, a pear-shaped lute, are pillars of Iraqi music. Soccer is the great passion; when Iraq won the Asian Cup in 2007, people from every community celebrated together in the streets.
content.history:
About 5,500 years ago the Sumerians built Uruk and Ur, the world's first cities, and invented cuneiform writing on clay tablets. Later empires included Babylon, whose king Hammurabi issued one of the earliest law codes, and Assyria, with its winged-bull palaces at Nineveh. Alexander the Great died in Babylon in 323 BC. In 762 the Abbasid caliphs founded Baghdad, which became the largest and most learned city in the world, home to the House of Wisdom, until Mongol armies sacked it in 1258.

The Ottoman Empire ruled Iraq for four centuries until Britain took over after World War I. Iraq became a kingdom in 1932 and a republic in 1958. Saddam Hussein ruled as dictator from 1979 to 2003, leading wars against Iran and Kuwait and crushing opponents. A US-led invasion toppled him in 2003, followed by years of violence and the rise of the terrorist group ISIS, defeated in 2017.
funFacts: The Epic of Gilgamesh, written in Iraq more than 4,000 years ago, is the oldest known long story in the world.
Sumerians counted in units of 60, which is why an hour has 60 minutes and a circle has 360 degrees.
The citadel of Erbil in Kurdistan has been continuously lived in for about 6,000 years.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, were said to stand in Iraq, though no trace has been found.
Marsh Arabs build guest halls called mudhifs entirely from reeds, a design shown in Sumerian carvings 5,000 years old.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom in the 800s gathered scholars who translated and preserved Greek science and gave us the word algebra.

content.tagline: Land of fire and ice
content.overview:
Iceland is an island nation floating alone in the North Atlantic, just below the Arctic Circle, about halfway between Norway and Greenland. It is roughly the size of Kentucky, but it holds Europe's largest glaciers, more than 30 active volcano systems, hot springs, geysers, and waterfalls at nearly every turn. The capital, Reykjavik, on the southwest coast, is the northernmost capital city in the world and home to well over half of the country's people.

Only about 390,000 people live in Iceland, fewer than in many mid-sized cities, and they speak Icelandic, a language so little changed that schoolchildren can read the Viking sagas written 800 years ago. Iceland is a parliamentary republic, and its parliament, the Althing, founded in 930, is often called the oldest in the world. Almost all of the country's electricity and heating comes from clean geothermal and hydro power. Fishing built the economy, and tourism now brings in far more visitors each year than Iceland has residents, drawn by the northern lights, glaciers, and volcanic landscapes.
content.landAndNature: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of the Earth's plates pull apart, so the island is literally growing by about two centimeters a year and is riddled with volcanoes. Eruptions are frequent; one in 2010 grounded flights across Europe with ash, and new lava fields formed near Reykjavik in the 2020s. Vatnajökull is the largest glacier in Europe by volume, and ice caps cover about a tenth of the country. Geysers spout boiling water, and the original Geysir gave the word to the world. Waterfalls such as Gullfoss and Dettifoss thunder through canyons. There are no native reptiles, almost no trees, and only one native land mammal, the Arctic fox, but millions of puffins nest on the cliffs, whales feed offshore, and sturdy Icelandic horses graze the moss-covered lava.
content.peopleAndCulture: Icelanders have no family names in the usual sense; a child's last name is the father's or mother's first name plus son or dóttir, and everyone is listed by first name in the phone book. The country reads and writes more books per person than almost anywhere, and a flood of new titles appears each Christmas. Foods include lamb, fresh fish, skyr, a thick yogurt-like dairy dish, and hot dogs from a famous Reykjavik stand, while fermented shark is eaten mainly at midwinter feasts. Nearly every town has a geothermal swimming pool and hot tubs where neighbors chat. Soccer is loved, and Iceland's team reached the quarterfinals of Euro 2016. Strongman contests, chess, and handball are national passions, and singer Björk and the band Sigur Rós made Icelandic music famous.
content.history: Norse settlers, mostly from Norway, arrived around 870, led according to the sagas by Ingólfur Arnarson, who built a farm where Reykjavik now stands. In 930 chieftains founded the Althing, an assembly held each summer at Thingvellir, and in the year 1000 Iceland adopted Christianity by a vote there. Poets wrote the sagas, some of the greatest medieval literature, in the 1200s. Iceland came under Norwegian and then Danish rule from 1262, and centuries of cold, plague, and a catastrophic volcanic eruption in 1783 kept it poor. Independence movements grew in the 1800s, home rule came in 1904, and Iceland became a fully independent republic on June 17, 1944. Britain and the United States occupied the island during World War II. Iceland joined NATO in 1949 and weathered a severe banking crash in 2008.
funFacts: Iceland has no mosquitoes at all, one of the very few places on Earth where that is true.
About 90 percent of Icelandic homes are heated with hot water pumped straight from the ground.
Iceland's parliament, the Althing, was founded in 930 and is often called the oldest parliament in the world.
The country has no army, and its police officers usually do not carry guns.
Some Icelanders say they cannot rule out the existence of elves, and road projects have been rerouted around rocks said to be elf homes.

content.tagline: Ancient crossroads on the Mediterranean
content.overview:
Israel is a narrow country on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, bordered by Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt. It is about 20,800 km², a little smaller than the US state of New Jersey, yet it contains snowy mountains, fertile valleys, the Negev desert and the lowest place on Earth's land surface, the Dead Sea. About 9.5 million people live there.

Hebrew is the main language, revived from ancient texts to become a living tongue spoken by millions, and Arabic is spoken by Israel's Arab citizens, about a fifth of the population. Most Israelis are Jewish, with roots in Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Ethiopia. Israel considers Jerusalem its capital, though its status is disputed and most countries keep their embassies in Tel Aviv, the lively business and technology center on the coast.

Israel is a parliamentary democracy with an elected Knesset and prime minister. It is known for high-tech inventions, farms that bloom in the desert, and holy sites sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims. The neighboring West Bank and Gaza Strip are Palestinian territories whose future remains unresolved.
content.landAndNature:
Israel packs many landscapes into a small space. The Mediterranean coastal plain is warm and fertile. Inland, hills rise to Jerusalem and the Galilee, and Mount Hermon in the far north gets enough snow for skiing. The Jordan River flows south into the Sea of Galilee, the lowest freshwater lake in the world, and on into the Dead Sea, about 430 meters below sea level, so salty that swimmers float like corks and no fish can live in it.

The Negev desert covers more than half the country, with the giant Ramon Crater, a huge eroded valley. At the southern tip, Eilat's coral reefs on the Red Sea shimmer with tropical fish. Israel lies on a major bird migration route, and half a billion birds pass over each spring and autumn. The hoopoe, with its striped crest, is the national bird.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Israeli society is a blend of Jewish communities from dozens of countries plus Arab Muslims, Christians, Druze and Bedouin. The week pauses for Shabbat from Friday evening to Saturday night, when buses stop in many cities and families gather for dinner. On Yom Kippur, the holiest day, roads fall silent and children ride bikes down empty highways. Passover, Hanukkah and Purim, with its costumes, are widely celebrated, as are Ramadan and Christmas in Arab communities.

Food is Middle Eastern at heart: hummus, falafel in pita, shakshuka eggs in tomato sauce, and fresh salads at breakfast. Soccer and basketball are the favorite sports. Israel calls itself the Start-Up Nation for its many tech companies, and inventions developed here include drip irrigation and the cherry tomato variety sold around the world.
content.history:
Ancient Israelite kingdoms ruled these hills about 3,000 years ago, and Jerusalem's Temple became the center of Jewish worship. Rome destroyed the Second Temple in 70 AD and scattered the Jewish people, while the land passed through Byzantine, Arab, Crusader, Mamluk and Ottoman hands and its population became largely Arab. In the late 1800s Jews began returning under the Zionist movement, and Britain governed the area after World War I.

After the Holocaust killed six million Jews in Europe, the United Nations proposed dividing the land into Jewish and Arab states. Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, and war with neighboring Arab countries followed; hundreds of thousands of Palestinians became refugees. Israel captured the West Bank, Gaza and other lands in 1967, made peace with Egypt in 1979 and Jordan in 1994, and signed accords with the Palestinians in 1993, but conflict has continued, including a devastating war in Gaza from 2023.
funFacts: The Dead Sea shore is the lowest dry land on Earth, about 430 meters below sea level, and its water is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean.
Hebrew is the only ancient language ever revived to become the everyday speech of millions of native speakers.
About 500 million birds fly over Israel twice a year, making it one of the busiest migration corridors on the planet.
Drip irrigation, which waters plants drop by drop through thin tubes, was developed in Israel in the 1960s.
Masada, a mountaintop fortress by the Dead Sea, was the last stronghold of Jewish rebels against Rome in 73 AD.
Israel's national bird, the hoopoe, was chosen by a public vote in 2008 to mark the country's 60th birthday.

content.tagline: Boot-shaped home of Rome and the Renaissance
content.overview:
Italy is easy to spot on any map: a long boot kicking the island of Sicily across the Mediterranean Sea. The country is about the size of Arizona and stretches from the snowy Alps in the north down a spine of mountains to sun-baked southern shores. Its capital, Rome, was the center of an empire 2,000 years ago, and ancient ruins stand next to Renaissance palaces and modern scooters. Venice floats on canals, Florence is a museum of art, Milan is a fashion and business capital, and Naples sits beneath the volcano Vesuvius.

About 59 million people live in Italy and speak Italian, with many regional dialects and a few German- and French-speaking valleys in the north. Italy is a parliamentary republic and a founding member of the European Union. It has the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites of any country, and its food, from pizza and pasta to gelato and espresso, is eaten in every corner of the world. Two tiny independent states, Vatican City and San Marino, sit inside its borders.
content.landAndNature: The Alps form Italy's northern wall, with Monte Bianco, shared with France, the highest point at 4,808 meters, and the pale jagged Dolomites glowing pink at sunset. Below them the fertile Po Valley is Italy's farm belt and industrial heartland. The Apennine Mountains run the length of the peninsula. Italy is one of Europe's most volcanic countries: Mount Etna on Sicily is the tallest active volcano in Europe, Stromboli erupts almost constantly, and Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79. Lakes Como, Garda, and Maggiore lie at the foot of the Alps. The coasts range from the cliffs of Amalfi to the beaches of Sardinia. Wolves and brown bears live in the Apennines, Alpine ibex in the north, and olive groves and vineyards cover the hills.
content.peopleAndCulture: Italian life revolves around family and food. Each region has its own dishes: pizza from Naples, pesto from Genoa, risotto from Milan, and hundreds of pasta shapes, followed by gelato or a tiny cup of espresso. Most Italians are Roman Catholic, and the Pope lives in Rome. Italy invented opera, and composers such as Verdi and Puccini fill theaters worldwide; Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Botticelli created masterpieces of the Renaissance. Soccer is a national obsession, and Italy has won the World Cup four times. Ferrari and Vespa were born here, and Milan sets fashion trends. Every evening people stroll through town centers in the passeggiata, and festivals like Venice's Carnival and Siena's bareback horse race, the Palio, keep old traditions alive.
content.history: Legend says Rome was founded in 753 BC by Romulus. The Roman Republic and then the Roman Empire ruled the Mediterranean world for centuries, spreading roads, Latin, and law before the western empire fell in 476. Italy broke into rival city-states such as Venice, Florence, and Genoa, which grew rich on trade and, in the 1300s and 1400s, launched the Renaissance, a rebirth of art and science. Foreign powers, including Spain, France, and Austria, controlled much of the peninsula for centuries. Italy was finally united as one kingdom in 1861, led by figures like Garibaldi. Benito Mussolini ruled as a fascist dictator from 1922 and joined Hitler in World War II; Italy became a republic in 1946 and helped found the European Union.
funFacts: Italy has 60 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, more than any other country in the world.
About 3,000 euros in coins are tossed into Rome's Trevi Fountain every day and donated to charity.
The University of Bologna, founded in 1088, is the oldest university in continuous operation in the world.
Italians eat about 23 kilograms of pasta per person each year, more than anyone else on Earth.
Italy has three active volcanoes, Etna, Stromboli, and Vesuvius, and Vesuvius is the only one on the European mainland to have erupted in the last century.

content.tagline: Out of many, one people
content.overview:
Jamaica is the third-largest island in the Caribbean, lying south of Cuba and west of Haiti. It covers about 11,000 km², slightly smaller than the US state of Connecticut, and about 2.8 million people call it home. The capital, Kingston, sits on a wide natural harbor on the southeast coast beneath the Blue Mountains.

Few small countries have made such a big mark on the world. Reggae music, born in Kingston's neighborhoods, spread across the globe with Bob Marley, and Jamaican sprinters such as Usain Bolt have dominated Olympic tracks. Jamaican Patois, a lively Creole language, is spoken alongside English, the official language.

Most Jamaicans are descended from Africans brought to the island as slaves, joined by people of Indian, Chinese, European and Middle Eastern heritage, which explains the national motto, "Out of Many, One People." Jamaica is an independent member of the Commonwealth with a parliament and prime minister, and the British monarch as head of state. Tourism, bauxite mining, sugar and Blue Mountain coffee support the economy.
content.landAndNature:
Mountains fill the interior of Jamaica, climbing to Blue Mountain Peak at about 2,256 meters, where mist swirls around coffee farms that produce some of the world's most prized beans. In the west, Cockpit Country is a maze of steep limestone hills and hidden valleys riddled with caves. Rivers such as the Rio Grande and the Black River wind down to a coast of white beaches in the north and mangrove wetlands in the south.

The climate is tropical, cooler in the mountains, with hurricanes a risk from June to November. The red-billed streamertail hummingbird, called the doctor bird, is the national bird and found only on Jamaica. The island also has the Jamaican boa, crocodiles in the Black River, the giant swallowtail, one of the largest butterflies in the Americas, and colorful reef fish along the coast.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Jamaican Patois mixes English with West African words and rhythms, and sayings like "wah gwaan" (what's going on) are heard everywhere. Music is the heartbeat: ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall all began here, and Rastafari, a faith that grew up in Jamaica in the 1930s, gave reggae its dreadlocks and its message. Sound systems still shake neighborhood streets on weekend nights.

Jerk chicken and pork, rubbed with fiery spices and smoked over pimento wood, is the signature dish, along with ackee and saltfish, patties, festival dumplings and rice and peas. Cricket and soccer are loved, but track and field is the pride of the nation; kids race barefoot at school sports days, and the national high school championships fill a stadium. Carnival and the Independence Day celebrations in August bring parades and dancing.
content.history:
The Taíno people lived on the island they called Xaymaca, "land of wood and water," when Columbus arrived in 1494. Spain ruled until 1655, when England seized the island and turned it into one of the world's biggest sugar producers, worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Port Royal became a pirate haven until an earthquake sank much of it in 1692. Escaped slaves known as Maroons built free communities in the mountains and fought the British to a treaty in 1739.

A rebellion led by Sam Sharpe in 1831 helped push Britain to abolish slavery in 1834. Hard times followed for the freed people, and protests in the 1930s led to trade unions and political parties. Jamaica became independent on August 6, 1962. Since then its music and athletes have carried its culture around the world.
funFacts: Jamaica has won dozens of Olympic sprint medals, and Usain Bolt still holds the 100-meter and 200-meter world records.
Ian Fleming wrote all of his James Bond novels at his house, Goldeneye, on Jamaica's north coast.
Ackee, half of the national dish, is poisonous until it ripens and splits open naturally on the tree.
Jamaica's bobsled team competed at the 1988 Winter Olympics, inspiring the film Cool Runnings.
The doctor bird hummingbird lives only on Jamaica and has tail feathers longer than its body.
Jamaica built the first railway in the Caribbean in 1845, only two decades after the world's first passenger line.

content.tagline: Desert kingdom of Petra and the Dead Sea
content.overview:
Jordan sits in the Middle East at the edge of the Arabian Desert, a country about the size of Indiana, bordered by Syria, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Israel and the West Bank. Its only stretch of coast is a short strip on the Gulf of Aqaba at the Red Sea, roughly 26 kilometers long, where coral reefs grow close to the beach. Amman, the capital, climbs across a cluster of steep hills and ranks among the longest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

About 11 million people live in Jordan, most of them Arabs, along with large communities of Palestinian and Syrian refugees who arrived over decades of regional conflict. Arabic is the official language, and English is widely taught. Jordan is a constitutional monarchy led by a king of the Hashemite family. With little oil and very little fresh water, the country relies on services, trade and tourism, and the ancient city of Petra draws visitors from around the world.
content.landAndNature: A line of hills runs down western Jordan and drops steeply into the Jordan Rift Valley, part of the same crack in the Earth's crust that continues through East Africa. At its lowest lies the Dead Sea, about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest land surface on the planet; its water is so salty that swimmers float without effort and no fish can survive in it. East of the hills spreads desert, including Wadi Rum, a valley of red sand and towering sandstone cliffs often used to film scenes set on Mars. Jordan is one of the driest countries on Earth, and ibex, striped hyenas and migrating birds cross its reserves.
content.peopleAndCulture: Mansaf is the national dish and the centerpiece of celebrations: lamb cooked in a sauce of dried fermented yogurt, spread over rice and flatbread and eaten from one shared platter. Falafel, hummus and thick cardamom coffee fill ordinary days. Bedouin traditions of hospitality run deep, and offering food and shelter to a traveler is a point of honor; many Bedouin families now live in towns, while some still keep goat-hair tents in the desert. Embroidery, mosaic-making and silver jewelry are traditional crafts. Soccer and basketball are popular, and Jordanian taekwondo athletes have won Olympic medals.
content.history: At Ain Ghazal near Amman, archaeologists found human statues about 9,000 years old, among the oldest ever made. The Nabataeans, desert traders, carved the city of Petra from rose-colored cliffs more than 2,000 years ago and controlled the incense routes until Rome absorbed their kingdom. Byzantine churches with detailed floor mosaics followed, then Islamic rule from the 600s, crusader castles, and four centuries within the Ottoman Empire. After World War I Britain administered the area, and the Emirate of Transjordan gained full independence in 1946 as the Kingdom of Jordan. Jordan took part in the Arab-Israeli wars, governed the West Bank from 1950 until 1967, and signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994.
funFacts: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest dry land on Earth, about 430 meters below sea level.
Petra holds roughly 800 monuments carved straight into sandstone cliffs, including the famous facade called the Treasury.
The Dead Sea is so salty that people float on the surface and cannot easily sink beneath it.
The red desert of Wadi Rum has stood in for the surface of Mars in several films.
Jordan is one of the most water-scarce countries in the world, and many homes keep water in rooftop tanks.

content.tagline: Land of the Rising Sun
content.overview:
Japan is an island country off the east coast of Asia, a long curve of thousands of islands in the Pacific Ocean. Four main islands, Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu, hold most of its land and people, with the tropical Okinawa islands trailing far to the south. The country covers about 378,000 km², slightly smaller than California, and about 124 million people live there, packed onto the coastal plains because mountains cover about three-quarters of the land.

Tokyo, the capital, is the center of the largest metropolitan area on Earth, home to about 37 million people, yet its trains run on time to the second and its streets are famously clean. Japanese is the language, written with thousands of characters plus two phonetic alphabets. Japan is a constitutional monarchy: the emperor is a ceremonial head of state from the world's oldest royal family, while an elected parliament and prime minister govern.

Japan is known for blending ancient traditions such as tea ceremonies and temples with cutting-edge robots, bullet trains, video games and anime.
content.landAndNature:
Japan sits where four plates of the Earth's crust meet, so it has about 110 active volcanoes and thousands of earthquakes a year. Mount Fuji, a near-perfect snow-capped cone of about 3,776 meters, is the highest and most beloved peak. In 2011 a huge earthquake and tsunami struck the northeast coast, killing about 20,000 people. Hot springs called onsen bubble up everywhere, and even wild snow monkeys soak in them in winter.

Climate ranges from snowy Hokkaido, one of the snowiest places on Earth, to subtropical Okinawa. Spring brings the pink wave of cherry blossoms that sweeps north across the country, and autumn turns the maple forests red. Wildlife includes the Japanese macaque, sika deer, the huge Japanese giant salamander, red-crowned cranes and brown bears in Hokkaido.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Japanese culture prizes politeness, harmony and attention to detail. People bow in greeting, remove shoes indoors, and take care to keep public places spotless. Shinto shrines with red gates and Buddhist temples stand in every town, and matsuri festivals fill the streets with floats, drums and fireworks. Families gather in spring for hanami picnics under the cherry blossoms.

Food is an art: sushi, ramen, tempura, and bento lunch boxes arranged like pictures. Baseball is the most popular sport, and sumo wrestling, judo and karate are traditional ones. Japan invented manga comics, anime, karaoke, instant noodles and emoji, and its video games and robots are known worldwide. Children fold origami cranes, and traditional arts like calligraphy, flower arranging and the tea ceremony are still taught.
content.history:
The Jōmon people made some of the world's oldest pottery in Japan more than 14,000 years ago. Rice farming, writing and Buddhism arrived from China and Korea, and by the 700s emperors ruled from Nara and then Kyoto. From 1192 military lords called shoguns held real power, with samurai warriors serving them; Mongol invasions in the 1200s were defeated with help from typhoons. The Tokugawa shoguns closed Japan to most of the world for 250 years.

After American ships forced the country open in 1853, the Meiji Restoration of 1868 modernized Japan at astonishing speed. It built an empire, invaded China and attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor in 1941. World War II ended after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing well over 100,000 people. Japan adopted a peaceful constitution in 1947, rebuilt into the world's second-largest economy by the 1970s, and remains a leading technological nation.
funFacts: Japan has about 5 million vending machines, roughly one for every 25 people, selling everything from hot coffee to umbrellas.
The world's oldest company, Kongō Gumi, built temples in Japan continuously from 578 AD until 2006.
Shinkansen bullet trains have carried billions of passengers since 1964 without a single fatal accident caused by derailment or collision.
Japan's emperors trace their line back more than 1,500 years, the oldest continuous monarchy in the world.
Farmers in Japan grow square watermelons in glass boxes so they stack neatly in refrigerators.
A 2023 recount found Japan has 14,125 islands, more than double the number previously listed.

content.tagline: Endless steppe and a working spaceport
content.overview:
Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country and the ninth largest overall, bigger than all of Western Europe put together, yet only about 20 million people live there. It reaches from the Caspian Sea in the west to the mountains bordering China in the east, and from Siberia in the north to Central Asian deserts in the south. Astana, the capital, is a young, sharply modern city on the northern steppe with bitterly cold winters.

Kazakh and Russian are both official languages; Kazakh is a Turkic language, and the country is shifting its alphabet from Cyrillic to Latin letters. Kazakhstan is a republic. Oil, gas, uranium and metals make it the wealthiest country in Central Asia, and it mines more uranium than anywhere else on Earth. Almaty, the largest city, sits beneath snowy mountains in the southeast and served as the capital until 1997, when the government moved north.
content.landAndNature: Most of Kazakhstan is steppe, grassland so flat and open that the horizon can look like the sea, and it forms the largest dry steppe region in the world. The south holds desert and the shrunken Aral Sea, once the fourth largest lake on Earth until Soviet irrigation diverted the rivers feeding it, leaving rusting ships stranded on dry sand. Snow-capped Tian Shan peaks rise in the southeast, where Khan Tengri tops 6,995 meters. Saiga antelope, with bulging noses that filter dust and warm freezing air, migrate across the plains in enormous herds, and snow leopards hunt in the mountains, where wild apple trees still grow.
content.peopleAndCulture: Horses are central to Kazakh life: people ride them, race them, and drink kumis, fermented mare's milk that is sharp and slightly fizzy. Beshbarmak, meaning five fingers, is the national dish of boiled meat and wide noodles eaten by hand. Families still raise yurts, round felt tents, for weddings and summer camps. Kazakhs are known for hunting with golden eagles, riding out in winter with the huge birds on their arms to catch foxes and hares. The dombra, a two-stringed lute, accompanies long sung stories. Nauryz, the spring new year in March, brings feasting, games and horseback contests.
content.history: Nomadic horse peoples have crossed these grasslands for thousands of years, and researchers believe horses were first tamed in this region. Scythian burial mounds yielded a warrior's suit covered in thousands of gold pieces, known as the Golden Man. Silk Road caravans passed through southern cities such as Turkistan. Genghis Khan's armies swept in during the 1200s, and Kazakh khanates formed by the 1400s. The Russian Empire took control in the 1800s, and under Soviet rule in the 1930s forced collectivization caused a famine that killed a large share of the Kazakh population. The Soviets also tested nuclear weapons near Semipalatinsk. Kazakhstan became independent in 1991 and closed the test site.
funFacts: Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan launched the first satellite and the first human into space, and rockets still lift off there.
Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country in the world, bigger than all of Western Europe combined.
Kazakhstan mines more uranium than any other country, supplying much of the world's nuclear fuel.
Wild apples still grow in the mountains near Almaty, and scientists trace the cultivated apple back to them.
The Aral Sea shrank so far that fishing boats were left sitting on sand many kilometers from any water.

content.tagline: Safari plains and marathon champions
content.overview:
Kenya sits on the equator on the east coast of Africa, with the Indian Ocean on one side and Lake Victoria on the other. It is about the size of Texas and borders Ethiopia, Somalia, Tanzania, Uganda, and South Sudan. The capital, Nairobi, is a high-altitude city of glass towers, bustling markets, and a national park inside the city limits where giraffes graze with skyscrapers in the background. Mombasa on the coast is a historic port of Swahili culture and coral-stone old town.

About 55 million people live in Kenya, from more than 40 ethnic groups. English and Swahili are the official languages, and most Kenyans speak a third language at home. Kenya is a presidential republic and East Africa's economic hub, known for tea and coffee exports, flowers flown to Europe, and a mobile-phone money system that spread across the world. Tourists come for the great wildebeest migration and safaris among lions and elephants, and Kenyan runners dominate the world's marathons.
content.landAndNature: The Great Rift Valley slices through Kenya from north to south, a trench edged by cliffs and dotted with lakes; Lake Nakuru and Lake Bogoria glow pink with hundreds of thousands of flamingos. Mount Kenya, an extinct volcano with glaciers on the equator, is Africa's second-highest peak at 5,199 meters. The Maasai Mara grasslands in the southwest host the annual migration of more than a million wildebeest and zebras crossing from Tanzania, chased by lions and crocodiles. Amboseli's elephants walk beneath Kilimanjaro, just over the border. The north is hot desert around Lake Turkana, the world's largest desert lake. The coast has coral reefs, mangroves, and white beaches. Kenya's Big Five are lions, leopards, elephants, buffalo, and rhinos, and it is one of the best places on Earth to see them.
content.peopleAndCulture: Kenya's peoples include the Kikuyu, Luhya, Kalenjin, Luo, Kamba, Maasai, and Swahili, each with its own language and traditions; the Maasai are known for red shukas, beaded jewelry, and high jumping dances. Most Kenyans are Christian, with a Muslim community on the coast. Ugali, a stiff corn porridge, is eaten with sukuma wiki greens, beans, or nyama choma, roasted meat shared with friends, and chai tea is drunk all day. Kenya is the world's greatest running nation: Kalenjin athletes from the high Rift Valley have won countless Olympic and marathon titles, and Eliud Kipchoge ran the first marathon under two hours in 2019. Rugby sevens and soccer are also popular, and Nairobi's music mixes benga guitar with hip-hop.
content.history: Some of the oldest human fossils and stone tools have been found around Lake Turkana, earning Kenya the name cradle of humankind. Bantu and Nilotic peoples settled the interior over the past 2,000 years, while Arab and Persian traders built Swahili towns on the coast, such as Lamu, from the 700s. Portugal seized the coast in the 1500s, and Britain took control of the interior in the 1890s, building a railway to Uganda and settling white farmers in the highlands. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was harshly suppressed but hastened independence, which came on December 12, 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta. Daniel arap Moi ruled for 24 years, and multiparty democracy returned in 1992. A new constitution in 2010 spread power to counties.
funFacts: Nairobi is the only capital city in the world with a national park inside it, where lions and rhinos live 7 kilometers from downtown.
Kenyan runner Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours, in Vienna in 2019.
Kenya's mobile money system, launched in 2007, lets people pay for almost anything by phone and was copied worldwide.
Turkana Boy, a nearly complete 1.6-million-year-old skeleton, was found near Lake Turkana in 1984.
During the great migration, over a million wildebeest cross the Mara River, where crocodiles lie in wait.

content.tagline: Mountains, horses and high summer pastures
content.overview:
Kyrgyzstan is a small, mountainous country in Central Asia where mountains cover more than 90 percent of the land. Landlocked between Kazakhstan, China, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, it is about the size of South Dakota. The Tian Shan, whose name means heavenly mountains, fills most of the country with peaks, glaciers and high valleys. Bishkek, the capital, lies on a northern plain beneath a wall of snowy summits.

About 7 million people live in Kyrgyzstan. Kyrgyz, a Turkic language, is the state language, and Russian has official status and is widely used in the cities. Kyrgyzstan is a republic and has changed governments through popular protests several times since independence. Farming and herding support many families, and in summer whole households move up to the jailoo, high mountain pastures, living in yurts while their animals graze. Gold mining and money sent home by relatives working abroad are major sources of income.
content.landAndNature: Glaciers and snowfields blanket the high Tian Shan, where Jengish Chokusu reaches 7,439 meters on the border with China. Meltwater from these mountains feeds rivers that supply much of Central Asia. Lake Issyk-Kul, ringed by peaks at about 1,600 meters, is one of the largest and deepest mountain lakes in the world and never freezes, thanks to slightly salty water and great depth. The walnut forests near Arslanbob are the biggest natural walnut woods on the planet. Snow leopards, ibex, marmots and golden eagles live on the high slopes, and in spring the valleys turn red and purple with wild tulips and poppies.
content.peopleAndCulture: Kyrgyz culture grew out of a nomadic life on horseback, and horses still matter enormously. Kok-boru, a fierce team game played on horseback with a heavy goat carcass instead of a ball, is the national sport. Families drink kumis, fermented mare's milk, and eat beshbarmak, boiled meat served over wide noodles. Yurts, round felt tents, are raised for summer pastures and celebrations, and the pattern at the center of a yurt roof appears on the national flag. Shyrdak felt rugs are stitched in bold curling designs. The Manas, an oral epic longer than the Iliad and Odyssey together, is recited from memory by trained storytellers.
content.history: Nomadic peoples herded across these valleys for thousands of years, and Silk Road caravans crossed the high passes between China and the west. The Kyrgyz are thought to have moved south from the Yenisei region of Siberia over many centuries. Mongol armies arrived in the 1200s, and the Khanate of Kokand ruled parts of the land before the Russian Empire took control in the 1800s. Under Soviet rule from the 1920s, herders were forced onto collective farms, schools and hospitals were built, and Kyrgyz was written in Cyrillic letters. Kyrgyzstan became independent in 1991. Protests removed presidents in 2005, 2010 and 2020, and ethnic violence struck the south in 2010.
funFacts: Mountains cover more than 90 percent of Kyrgyzstan, and much of the country lies above 1,500 meters.
The Epic of Manas, recited from memory by specialists, is one of the longest poems ever composed.
The design in the middle of the Kyrgyz flag is the roof opening of a yurt, seen from inside looking up.
Lake Issyk-Kul never freezes despite its mountain setting, and its name means warm lake in Kyrgyz.
In kok-boru, the national sport, riders gallop while trying to heave a goat carcass into the opposing team's goal.

content.tagline: Kingdom of the Angkor temples
content.overview:
Cambodia lies in the heart of mainland Southeast Asia, bordered by Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, with a short coast on the Gulf of Thailand. It is about 181,000 km², roughly the size of the US state of Missouri, and home to about 17 million people. The capital, Phnom Penh, sits where the Mekong River meets the Tonlé Sap River.

Almost everyone speaks Khmer, a language with its own curvy alphabet, and most people are Buddhists. Cambodia's greatest treasure is Angkor, the ancient capital near Siem Reap, whose temples include Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world. The temple's five towers appear on the national flag, one of the few flags to show a building.

Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy with a king and an elected government, though one party has held power for decades. Most Cambodians farm rice or fish, and clothing factories and tourism have grown quickly. The country is still recovering from the 1970s, when the Khmer Rouge regime killed roughly a quarter of its people.
content.landAndNature:
Cambodia is a wide, low bowl of rice fields surrounded by hills: the Cardamom and Elephant Mountains to the southwest and the Dangrek range along the Thai border. The Mekong, one of the world's great rivers, flows through the country from north to south. Every monsoon season it swells so much that the Tonlé Sap River reverses direction and flows backward into the Tonlé Sap lake, which grows to about five times its dry-season size.

That flooding makes the lake one of the richest freshwater fisheries on Earth, with whole villages of floating houses moving with the water. The climate is hot year-round, wet from May to October. Rare Irrawaddy dolphins live in the Mekong, and the forests shelter Asian elephants, sun bears, gibbons and the giant ibis, the national bird.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Khmer people make up about 95 percent of the population, with Cham, Vietnamese and Chinese minorities. Buddhism shapes daily life; boys often spend time as monks, and saffron-robed monks collect food each morning. Cambodians greet each other with the sampeah, palms pressed together with a bow.

Fish is the key food, especially prahok, a strong fermented fish paste, and fish amok, a creamy coconut curry steamed in banana leaves. Breakfast is often noodle soup. The graceful Apsara dance, with slow hand movements copied from temple carvings, nearly died out in the 1970s and was revived. Kun Khmer kickboxing is the traditional sport, and soccer is popular. Khmer New Year in April means water fights and games, while the Water Festival in November brings colorful boat races to Phnom Penh.
content.history:
Early kingdoms called Funan and Chenla traded with India and China, bringing Hinduism and Buddhism to the region. In 802 Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire, which ruled much of Southeast Asia for 600 years from Angkor, a city of canals and temples that may have held nearly a million people, the largest in the world before modern times. Angkor Wat was built in the 1100s.

The empire faded after 1431, and Cambodia was squeezed by Thailand and Vietnam until France made it a protectorate in 1863. Independence came in 1953 under King Norodom Sihanouk. The Vietnam War spilled across the border, and in 1975 the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot seized power, emptying cities and forcing people into labor camps; about two million died from execution, starvation and disease. Vietnam ousted the regime in 1979, and United Nations-backed elections in 1993 restored the monarchy.
funFacts: Angkor Wat covers about 160 hectares and is the largest religious building on Earth, bigger than Vatican City.
Most Hindu temples face east, but Angkor Wat faces west, which some scholars think means it was built as a tomb.
Laser scans from aircraft revealed that medieval Angkor spread over an area the size of a modern city like Los Angeles.
The Tonlé Sap is the only major river in the world that reverses its flow every year.
Cambodians use two currencies every day: the riel for small purchases and US dollars for larger ones.
Kampot pepper, grown near the coast, is so prized that chefs around the world pay premium prices for it.

KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.officialName: Independent and Sovereign Republic of Kiribati

content.tagline: Scattered atolls across the date line
content.overview:
Kiribati is made up of 33 low coral islands scattered across a stretch of the Pacific Ocean larger than India, though the land itself adds up to only about 811 km², roughly the size of New York City. The country straddles both the equator and the international date line, so parts of Kiribati are among the first places on Earth to begin each new day. The capital, South Tarawa, is a crowded strip of land on an atoll in the west.

About 130,000 people live in Kiribati, nearly all of them I-Kiribati, a Micronesian people. Gilbertese and English are the official languages, and the country is a republic. Fishing licenses sold to foreign fleets, coconut products, and wages sent home by sailors working on cargo ships support the economy. Almost all of the land lies less than three meters above the sea, so rising sea levels and stronger storms are an immediate danger rather than a distant worry.
content.landAndNature: Kiribati's islands are atolls: rings of coral reef around shallow lagoons, built up over sunken volcanoes. Because the ground is coral sand, soil is thin and poor, and fresh water sits in a fragile lens beneath the surface that salt water can easily spoil. Coconut palms, pandanus and breadfruit are the main plants, and the ocean supplies most food, with reefs full of parrotfish, giant clams and reef sharks. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area, one of the largest marine reserves on Earth, guards some of the least disturbed coral in the Pacific. Kiritimati, also called Christmas Island, is the world's largest coral atoll and a nesting place for millions of seabirds.
content.peopleAndCulture: Life in Kiribati revolves around the sea and the extended family. Islanders once navigated open ocean by stars, swells and the flight of birds, and outrigger canoes are still built and raced. The maneaba, a large open meeting house with a steep thatched roof, stands at the center of every village, where elders discuss decisions and everyone gathers for feasts. Dancing is sharp and precise, with sudden birdlike movements of the arms and head, performed to sung chanting. Fish, coconut, breadfruit and taro make up daily meals. Christianity is widely practiced, and powerful church singing is a central part of island life.
content.history: Austronesian voyagers settled these atolls roughly 3,000 years ago, and later arrivals from Samoa, Tonga and Fiji added to the culture. European ships sighted the islands in the 1700s and 1800s, and whalers and traders followed. Britain declared a protectorate over the Gilbert and Ellice Islands in 1892 and mined the island of Banaba for phosphate until it was nearly stripped bare. In November 1943 the atoll of Tarawa was the site of one of the fiercest battles of the Pacific war. The Ellice Islands later separated to become Tuvalu, and Kiribati became independent on July 12, 1979. Rising seas have been the country's central concern ever since.
funFacts: Kiribati's islands are spread across an ocean area larger than India, but all its land would fit inside New York City.
In 1995 Kiribati shifted the international date line eastward so the whole country would share one calendar day.
Kiritimati, or Christmas Island, is the largest coral atoll in the world measured by land area.
Most of Kiribati lies under three meters above sea level, so rising seas threaten homes and drinking water alike.
The Phoenix Islands Protected Area is one of the largest marine reserves on Earth, and almost nobody lives inside it.

KNA.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KNA.officialName: Federation of Saint Christopher and Nevis

content.tagline: Two green volcanic islands, one nation
content.overview:
Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest country in the Americas by both land area and population, a pair of lush volcanic islands in the eastern Caribbean. Saint Kitts, the larger, is shaped like a paddle; Nevis, its round neighbor, lies about three kilometers away across a channel called The Narrows. Together they cover about 261 km², smaller than most cities.

Roughly 48,000 people live here, speaking English. Basseterre on Saint Kitts is the capital, a harbor town with a circular plaza modeled on London's Piccadilly Circus.

The country is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, and Nevis has its own assembly and considerable self-government. For 350 years the islands ran on sugar, until the last cane harvest in 2005; today tourism, offshore finance and a scenic railway built for sugar trains carry the economy. Both islands are green, steep and ringed by beaches of pale and black sand.
content.landAndNature: Each island is the top of a volcano. Mount Liamuiga on Saint Kitts rises to 1,156 meters and holds a crater lake in its rainforested summit; Nevis Peak, at about 985 meters, wears a permanent cap of cloud, which is how it got its name, from the Spanish for snows. Rainforest, elfin woodland and old sugar terraces cover the slopes, and the coasts alternate between golden sand in the south and dark volcanic sand in the north. Vervet monkeys, brought from Africa in the 1600s, now outnumber people and raid gardens. Hawksbill and leatherback turtles nest on the beaches, hummingbirds feed in gardens year-round, and the surrounding reefs shelter parrotfish, rays and the occasional migrating humpback whale.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Kittitians and Nevisians are descended from West Africans brought to the islands in slavery, and their culture blends African, British and Caribbean strands. Carnival, called Sugar Mas, runs from Christmas into early January with calypso competitions, steel pan, big drum music and masquerade troupes in tall feathered headdresses. Goat water, a rich stew of goat meat, breadfruit and dumplings spiced with cloves, is the national dish, served with johnnycakes. Cricket is the great sport, and the islands' players have represented the West Indies team for decades. Alexander Hamilton, a founding father of the United States, was born on Nevis in the 1750s, and his birthplace is now a museum.
content.history: The Kalinago people, and the Taíno before them, lived here when Christopher Columbus sailed past in 1493. English settlers arrived on Saint Kitts in 1624 and French settlers soon after, and the island became the first successful English colony in the Caribbean, earning it the nickname Mother Colony of the West Indies. Britain and France fought over it repeatedly until Britain gained full control in 1783. Plantation owners enslaved tens of thousands of Africans to cut sugar cane; slavery was abolished throughout the British Caribbean in 1834. The islands were governed with Anguilla until Anguilla broke away in 1967. Saint Kitts and Nevis became fully independent on September 19, 1983, the newest sovereign state in the Americas. Nevis narrowly voted against separating in a 1998 referendum.
funFacts: Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest country in the Western Hemisphere in both area and population.
Green vervet monkeys, brought from Africa centuries ago, are thought to outnumber the islands' human residents.
A narrow-gauge railway built to haul sugar cane now carries sightseers on a slow loop around Saint Kitts.
Brimstone Hill Fortress, a huge stone fort built by enslaved laborers, is nicknamed the Gibraltar of the West Indies.
Alexander Hamilton, whose face is on the US ten-dollar bill, was born on the island of Nevis.

content.tagline: Mountains, megacities, and global pop culture
content.overview:
South Korea occupies the southern half of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia, surrounded by sea on three sides and separated from North Korea by a fortified border in the north. It covers about 100,000 km², a little larger than Indiana, and mountains take up around 70 percent of that.

About 52 million people live in South Korea, speaking Korean and writing with hangul, an alphabet designed in the 1440s to be easy to learn. Seoul, the capital, sits on the Han River, and its metropolitan area holds roughly half the country's population, making it one of the largest urban regions on Earth.

South Korea is a democratic republic with an elected president. In a single lifetime it went from one of the world's poorest countries to a technology powerhouse making phones, ships, cars and semiconductors, while its music, films and television have found huge audiences worldwide.
content.landAndNature: Mountain ridges run down the east coast, dropping steeply to the sea, while the west and south flatten into rice plains and thousands of small islands. Jeju, a volcanic island in the south, has the country's highest peak, Hallasan at 1,947 meters, plus lava tube caves and stone walls built against the wind. The four seasons are distinct: cold, dry winters, a rainy season in summer called jangma, and autumn foliage that draws crowds to the mountains. Tidal flats along the west coast, where the tide can retreat kilometers, feed millions of migrating shorebirds. Asiatic black bears have been reintroduced to Jirisan, and the Demilitarized Zone, empty of people since 1953, shelters cranes and other rare wildlife.
content.peopleAndCulture: Korean meals arrive with banchan, many small side dishes, around rice and soup; kimchi, cabbage fermented with chili and garlic, is at almost every table, and families once buried jars of it to ferment through winter. Korean barbecue is grilled at the table, and bibimbap mixes rice with vegetables and egg. K-pop groups fill stadiums worldwide, and the film Parasite won the Academy Award for best picture in 2020, the first in a language other than English. Taekwondo, a Korean martial art, is an Olympic sport, and baseball and soccer draw big crowds. Competitive video gaming is a professional career with televised leagues. Chuseok, the autumn harvest festival, sends millions traveling home to honor ancestors.
content.history: Korean kingdoms, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, competed for the peninsula 1,500 years ago before Silla unified it. The Goryeo dynasty gave Korea its English name and printed books with movable metal type decades before Gutenberg. The Joseon dynasty ruled from 1392 to 1910; King Sejong's scholars created the hangul alphabet in 1443 so ordinary people could read. Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled harshly until 1945. At the end of World War II the peninsula was divided at the 38th parallel, Soviet forces in the north and American in the south, and two rival states formed in 1948. The Korean War of 1950–1953 killed millions and ended in an armistice, leaving the division in place. South Korea grew rapidly under military rulers, then became a full democracy after mass protests in 1987.
funFacts: The hangul alphabet was invented in the 1440s with letter shapes that copy the position of the mouth and tongue.
South Korea has some of the fastest internet in the world, and professional video gamers are treated as sports stars.
Koreans traditionally counted themselves a year old at birth, so many people had two different ages until the rules changed in 2023.
On Jeju island, haenyeo women have dived for shellfish without air tanks for centuries, some still working past age seventy.
Seoul's subway has hundreds of stations, mobile phone signal in every tunnel, and heated seats in winter.

content.tagline: Oil, desert and a famous seafront
content.overview:
Kuwait is a small country at the head of the Persian Gulf, tucked between Iraq and Saudi Arabia and roughly the size of New Jersey. Almost all of it is flat, gravelly desert, and it has no rivers or lakes at all; nearly every drop of drinking water comes from plants that take the salt out of seawater. Kuwait City, the capital, runs along a curving bay, marked by the three Kuwait Towers with their blue-tiled spheres.

About 4.3 million people live in Kuwait, but only around a third are Kuwaiti citizens; the rest are workers and their families from Egypt, India, Bangladesh, the Philippines and elsewhere. Arabic is the official language and English is widely used. Kuwait is a constitutional emirate, led by an emir alongside an elected national assembly that holds more power than most parliaments in the region. Enormous oil reserves make the country wealthy, and its summer heat is among the fiercest on Earth.
content.landAndNature: Kuwait is desert from end to end, with low ridges, shallow depressions and a coastline of mudflats and shallow bays along the Gulf. Summers are brutal: temperatures above 50 degrees Celsius have been recorded here, among the highest reliably measured anywhere, and shamal winds drive sand across the country. Rain falls only in winter, and after a wet season the desert can bloom briefly with wildflowers. Failaka Island lies offshore, and Bubiyan is a large, almost empty island of salt marsh. Flamingos, herons and crabs feed on the mudflats, while the Gulf holds dugongs, sea turtles and the pearl oysters that divers once hunted.
content.peopleAndCulture: Kuwaiti life mixes long-standing Gulf traditions with modern city living. The diwaniya, an evening gathering in a room set aside for guests, is where people meet to drink tea, talk politics and trade news, and it remains an important part of public life. Machboos, spiced rice with lamb or fish, is the national dish, and grilled fish from the Gulf is prized. Kuwaiti theater and television dramas are watched across the Arab world. Sea traditions survive in wooden dhow boats and pearl-diving songs. Soccer is followed closely, and in summer the air-conditioned malls serve as the country's town squares.
content.history: A small fishing and pearling settlement grew on this bay in the early 1700s, and the Al Sabah family has led it since 1752. Kuwaiti dhows traded along the Gulf and across to India, and pearl diving was the main livelihood until cheap cultured pearls from Japan ended the trade in the 1930s. Kuwait became a British protectorate in 1899 and gained full independence on June 19, 1961. Oil, first exported in 1946, transformed it within a single generation from a town of mud houses into a wealthy state. In August 1990 Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait; an international coalition drove the occupying forces out in February 1991, leaving hundreds of oil wells burning for months.
funFacts: Kuwait has no rivers or lakes, so most of its drinking water is made by removing salt from seawater.
Before oil, Kuwait's wealth came from pearl diving, with divers descending on a single held breath.
Temperatures in Kuwait have passed 50 degrees Celsius, among the hottest ever reliably recorded on the planet.
The Kuwait Towers, opened in 1979, hold water tanks inside the blue-tiled spheres above the seafront.
After oil wells were set alight in 1991, firefighting teams needed about eight months to put out the last of them.

content.tagline: Mountains, Mekong and golden temples
content.overview:
Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, a long strip of mountains and river valleys bordered by China, Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Myanmar. It is about the size of Utah, and forested hills cover most of it. The Mekong, one of the great rivers of Asia, runs down the western side and forms much of the border with Thailand, carrying boats, fish and the water that fills the rice fields.

About 7.5 million people live in Laos, making it one of the least crowded countries in Asia. Lao is the official language, and dozens of other languages are spoken by ethnic groups in the highlands. Laos is a one-party socialist republic. The capital, Vientiane, is a quiet riverside city of temples and French-era buildings, while Luang Prabang upriver is a World Heritage town where saffron-robed monks walk at dawn to collect food offerings. Most families farm, above all sticky rice.
content.landAndNature: Forested mountains cover most of Laos, rising to Phou Bia at about 2,820 meters, and the Annamite Range walls off Vietnam to the east. The Mekong and its tributaries carry fish, boats and seasonal floods; in the south at Si Phan Don, meaning four thousand islands, the river splits into a maze of channels and sandbanks where a few rare Irrawaddy dolphins survive. The Bolaven Plateau is cool and fertile, good for growing coffee. Monsoon rains fall from May to October. Laos's forests still hold clouded leopards, gibbons and Asian elephants, and the country was once known as the land of a million elephants.
content.peopleAndCulture: Sticky rice is eaten with the fingers at nearly every meal, rolled into a ball and dipped into laap, a minced meat salad with herbs and lime, or into spicy green papaya salad. Most Lao are Theravada Buddhists, and many young men spend a period as monks; in Luang Prabang, lines of monks collect rice each morning from residents kneeling by the road. The khene, a bamboo mouth organ, leads lam singing, in which performers trade sung verses back and forth. Boat races on the Mekong mark the end of Buddhist Lent, and the Rocket Festival sends homemade rockets skyward to ask for rain.
content.history: Farming villages and bronze-working cultures date back thousands of years here, and the Plain of Jars, thousands of giant stone jars scattered across hillsides, was made about 2,000 years ago for burial rites. In 1353 the kingdom of Lan Xang, the land of a million elephants, united the region and lasted until it broke apart in the 1700s. France colonized Laos in the 1890s. During the Vietnam War, American aircraft dropped an enormous quantity of bombs on Laos to cut supply routes, making it one of the most heavily bombed countries in history; unexploded bombs still injure people and make farmland dangerous. The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975, ending the monarchy.
funFacts: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, with no coastline at all.
The Plain of Jars holds thousands of stone jars, some more than two meters tall, carved about 2,000 years ago.
Unexploded bombs dropped during the Vietnam War still lie in Lao soil, and clearance teams work to remove them.
Lao families eat more sticky rice per person than anyone else in the world, shaping it into balls by hand.
The old kingdom of Lan Xang meant the land of a million elephants, a name still used for Laos today.

content.tagline: Cedars, mountains and Mediterranean cities
content.overview:
Lebanon is a small country on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, smaller than Connecticut, wedged between Syria and Israel. Two mountain ranges run its whole length parallel to the coast, with the fertile Bekaa Valley between them; from the higher slopes it is possible to ski in the morning and swim in the sea the same afternoon. Beirut, the capital, is a port city that has been destroyed and rebuilt many times over its long history.

About 5.5 million people live in Lebanon, along with many refugees from Syria and Palestinians whose families arrived decades ago. Arabic is the official language, French and English are widely spoken, and many Lebanese slide between all three in a single sentence. Lebanon is a republic whose top offices are shared among religious communities: the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim, and the speaker of parliament a Shia Muslim. Banking, farming and Lebanese families abroad shape the economy.
content.landAndNature: The Mount Lebanon range rises steeply from the coast to Qurnat as Sawda at about 3,088 meters and keeps its snow into spring, while the Anti-Lebanon range marks the Syrian border. Between them lies the Bekaa Valley, a fertile trough of vineyards, wheat and orchards. The cedar of Lebanon, a broad, flat-topped tree that can live more than a thousand years, appears on the national flag; ancient groves such as the Cedars of God survive in mountain pockets after centuries of logging. Jeita Grotto is a vast limestone cave with an underground river that visitors travel by boat. Wild boar, hyenas and migrating birds cross the highlands.
content.peopleAndCulture: Lebanese food travels the world: hummus, tabbouleh, kibbeh and grilled meats arrive as mezze, dozens of small dishes shared slowly around a table. Meals can stretch for hours, and hospitality is close to obligatory. Christians and Muslims of many denominations live side by side, so the calendar carries both Christmas and Ramadan. Fairuz, a singer beloved across the Arab world, plays in Beirut cafes most mornings. Poetry, publishing and journalism have long been Lebanese strengths, and the country has one of the highest literacy rates in the region. Basketball is enormously popular, alongside soccer and winter skiing.
content.history: The Phoenicians built Lebanon's coastal cities, including Byblos, Tyre and Sidon, more than 3,000 years ago, traded across the Mediterranean and spread an alphabet that became the ancestor of many written scripts used today. Romans raised the enormous temples at Baalbek. Later came Arab rule, crusader castles, and four centuries within the Ottoman Empire. France governed Lebanon after World War I, and independence came in 1943. A civil war among the country's communities, drawing in outside powers, lasted from 1975 to 1990 and left Beirut divided and scarred. In August 2020 a huge explosion of chemicals stored at Beirut's port killed more than 200 people and damaged much of the city.
funFacts: The Phoenician alphabet, developed in Lebanon's coastal cities, is an ancestor of the Greek, Latin and many other alphabets.
Byblos has been lived in for roughly 7,000 years and is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth.
The cedar of Lebanon on the national flag can live over a thousand years and spreads wide, flat branches.
On some spring days Lebanese people ski in the mountains in the morning and swim in the Mediterranean that afternoon.
Baalbek's Roman temple platform contains some of the largest cut stone blocks ever moved, each weighing hundreds of tons.

content.tagline: Africa's oldest republic, born of freedom
content.overview:
Liberia sits on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, between Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Ivory Coast, and is about the size of Tennessee. Its name means land of the free, because it was founded in the 1820s by freed African Americans, and its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe. The flag, with red and white stripes and a single white star on blue, looks like a cousin of the American flag, and the country is Africa's oldest republic.

About 5.5 million people live in Liberia. English is the official language, spoken in a lively Liberian form, and about 20 local languages, including Kpelle, Bassa, and Mano, are spoken across the countryside. Most people are Christian, with a Muslim minority. Liberia is a presidential republic that has held peaceful elections since two devastating civil wars ended in 2003. Rubber plantations, iron ore, and gold are the main exports, and Liberia's flag flies on thousands of ships worldwide because the country lets foreign shipowners register vessels there.
content.landAndNature: Liberia's coast is a line of sandy beaches, lagoons, and mangrove swamps pounded by Atlantic surf, backed by rolling hills and dense tropical rainforest. It holds a large share of the remaining Upper Guinea rainforest, one of the wettest and richest forests in Africa, with Sapo National Park at its heart. Forest elephants, chimpanzees, and the pygmy hippo, a shy nighttime animal about the size of a large pig, live there, along with rare zebra duikers and colorful hornbills. The land rises to the Nimba range in the north, where Mount Wuteve reaches about 1,440 meters. Rivers such as the St. Paul, St. John, and Cavalla flow to the sea. Liberia is one of the rainiest countries in Africa, with Monrovia getting about five meters of rain a year.
content.peopleAndCulture: Liberians belong to peoples such as the Kpelle, Bassa, Grebo, Gio, Mano, and Kru, plus the Americo-Liberians descended from the founders, and Liberian English blends all of these into a colorful spoken style. Rice is eaten at almost every meal, with palm butter, cassava leaf, or pepper soup, along with fufu and fried plantains. Secret societies called Poro and Sande have long taught young people traditions in the forest. Music mixes local rhythms with gospel and hipco, a Liberian hip-hop sung in local English. Soccer is the top sport, and George Weah, the only African player ever named world player of the year, went on to become president. Independence Day on July 26 is celebrated with parades and dancing.
content.history: Peoples such as the Kpelle and Kru lived here for centuries before the American Colonization Society began settling freed Black Americans on the coast in 1822. The settlers declared the independent Republic of Liberia on July 26, 1847, with a constitution modeled on the United States, but for over a century they ruled over the indigenous majority, who had few rights. A US rubber company set up huge plantations in 1926. A coup in 1980 led by Samuel Doe ended Americo-Liberian rule, and civil wars from 1989 to 2003 killed about 250,000 people and destroyed the country. Women's peace protests helped end the fighting. In 2005 Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected female president, and she later shared the Nobel Peace Prize. An Ebola outbreak in 2014 and 2015 killed thousands.
funFacts: Liberia's capital, Monrovia, is one of only two capitals in the world named after a US president; the other is Washington, D.C.
Liberia was the first African country to elect a woman president, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, in 2005.
The pygmy hippo lives almost only in Liberia's forests and is so shy it was unknown to Western science until the 1840s.
More ships are registered under Liberia's flag than almost any other country, even though few of them ever visit Liberia.
Liberia and Ethiopia were the only African nations that remained independent throughout the colonial era.

content.tagline: Roman ruins on the edge of the Sahara
content.overview:
Libya spreads across North Africa between Egypt and Tunisia, with a long Mediterranean coastline in the north and the Sahara Desert filling everything else. It is the fourth-largest country in Africa, about two and a half times the size of Texas, yet more than 90 percent of it is desert where almost no one lives. The capital, Tripoli, is a white city on the coast with an old walled medina, and nearly all Libyans live in a thin strip along the sea.

About 7 million people live in Libya, and Arabic is the official language; Berber (Amazigh) communities in the western mountains speak their own language, and nearly everyone is Sunni Muslim. Libya has some of the largest oil reserves in Africa, which once made it one of the continent's wealthiest countries per person. Since a 2011 uprising overthrew the dictator Muammar Gaddafi, however, rival governments and armed groups have fought for control, and daily life has often been disrupted. The country's spectacular Roman and Greek ruins and Saharan rock art remain among the finest anywhere.
content.landAndNature: Libya has three regions. Tripolitania in the northwest has coastal plains, olive groves, and the Nafusa Mountains, home to Berber villages and underground houses. Cyrenaica in the east rises into the green Jebel Akhdar hills, the wettest part of the country. Fezzan in the southwest is deep Sahara: the Ubari Sand Sea holds salt lakes fringed with palms between towering dunes, and the black volcanic Waw an Namus crater cradles three colored lakes. The Acacus Mountains hide rock paintings of giraffes and dancers thousands of years old. Rainfall is tiny; some desert areas may see no rain for a decade. Fennec foxes, jerboas, and desert monitors survive the heat, and the coast has some of the last untouched beaches in the Mediterranean, where loggerhead turtles nest.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Libyans are Arab or mixed Arab-Berber, with Amazigh, Tuareg, and Toubou minorities in the mountains and desert, and family and tribe remain important in daily life. Meals are shared from common dishes: bazin, a hard dough of barley flour served with lamb and tomato sauce, couscous, and shorba soup, followed by dates and sweet tea with mint, often poured with froth on top. Libyan tea ceremonies can last hours. Traditional clothing includes long white robes and embroidered vests for celebrations, and weddings run for days with music from the zokra bagpipe and drums. Soccer is the favorite sport, and the national team won the African Nations Championship in 2014. Ghadames, an ancient oasis town of covered whitewashed streets, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
content.history: Berbers lived here for thousands of years, and Phoenicians founded Tripoli while Greeks built Cyrene in the east around 630 BC. Rome ruled for centuries and left Leptis Magna, one of the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere, birthplace of the emperor Septimius Severus. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s, and the Ottoman Empire controlled the coast from 1551. Italy invaded in 1911 and ruled brutally as a colony until World War II. Libya became an independent kingdom in 1951, and oil was discovered in 1959. In 1969 a young officer, Muammar Gaddafi, seized power and ruled as a dictator for 42 years, until an uprising and NATO airstrikes toppled him in 2011. Since then Libya has been divided between competing governments, with periods of civil war and fragile ceasefires.
funFacts: Leptis Magna, near Tripoli, is so well preserved that its Roman theater, market, and harbor still stand largely intact.
The Ubari Sand Sea has lakes in the middle of the desert that are so salty swimmers float, and their shores are lined with palms.
Libya's Great Man-Made River is one of the largest irrigation projects ever built, pumping water from deep desert aquifers to the coast.
Under Gaddafi, Libya's flag was plain green, the only single-color national flag in the world, until it changed back in 2011.
Ghadames is called the pearl of the desert; its houses connect through covered alleys so people can walk the town in the shade.

content.tagline: Twin peaks rising from the sea
content.overview:
Saint Lucia is a teardrop-shaped volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, part of the chain of Lesser Antilles between Martinique to the north and Saint Vincent to the south. It is about 616 km², roughly three times the size of Washington, D.C., and almost entirely green and mountainous.

About 180,000 people live on the island. English is the official language, but most people also speak Kwéyòl, a French-based creole, at home. Castries, the capital, sits on a deep natural harbor on the northwest coast where cruise ships tie up beside the market.

Saint Lucia is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Bananas were once the main export and tourism now leads, drawn by the Pitons, two volcanic spires that rise straight out of the sea and appear on the national flag's home ground. For its size, Saint Lucia has produced a remarkable number of celebrated writers and thinkers.
content.landAndNature: The Pitons, Gros Piton and Petit Piton, are lava plugs that jut about 770 and 740 meters above the water near the town of Soufrière, and they are a World Heritage site. Nearby, the Sulphur Springs are billed as a drive-in volcano: a road runs into a collapsed crater where gray mud bubbles and steam hisses from vents. Rainforest covers the interior mountains, where the Saint Lucia parrot, a blue-faced green bird found nowhere else, was brought back from about 100 birds in the 1970s to over 1,000 today. Waterfalls drop into warm pools, mangroves line some bays, and reefs off the west coast draw divers. The island lies in the hurricane belt and has been battered more than once.
content.peopleAndCulture: Saint Lucian culture is a French-British-African mix, heard in Kwéyòl speech and tasted in green figs and saltfish, the national dish of boiled green bananas with salted cod. Jounen Kwéyòl each October celebrates creole language, food and dress across the villages. La Rose and La Marguerite are rival flower societies whose members parade in costume and sing on their own feast days, a tradition unique to the island. Saint Lucia Jazz draws musicians from around the world each May. Cricket is the main sport, and Darren Sammy captained the West Indies to two Twenty20 World Cups. The island has produced two Nobel laureates, the economist Arthur Lewis and the poet Derek Walcott, the highest number per person of any country.
