content.history: Kalinago people settled the island, calling it Iouanalao, after displacing earlier Arawak settlers. Europeans found it hard to hold: the island changed hands between Britain and France about fourteen times, earning it the nickname Helen of the West Indies after Helen of Troy. French planters established sugar estates worked by enslaved Africans, and Britain took final control in 1814. Slavery was abolished in 1834. Bananas replaced sugar as the great crop in the 1900s, and boatloads of green fruit shipped to Britain each week. Saint Lucia gained self-government in 1967 and became fully independent on February 22, 1979, remaining in the Commonwealth. Much of its economy has since shifted from farming to tourism, with hotels along the calm western coast.
funFacts: Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel Prize winners, more per person than any other country in the world.
The island changed hands between Britain and France about fourteen times, so both flags flew over it repeatedly.
A road leads right into the crater of Sulphur Springs, advertised as the world's only drive-in volcano.
The Saint Lucia parrot, found nowhere else, recovered from roughly 100 birds in the 1970s after strict protection.
Gros Piton and Petit Piton are hardened plugs of lava left behind after softer volcanic rock eroded away.

content.tagline: A castle, a prince, and the Rhine
content.overview:
Liechtenstein is one of the smallest countries on Earth, a sliver of Alpine valley and mountainside squeezed between Switzerland and Austria. At just 160 square kilometers it is smaller than Washington, D.C., and a fit walker can cross it in a day. The capital, Vaduz, is a small town on the Rhine River overlooked by a medieval castle where the prince and his family actually live. The country has no airport, no highway, and no army, yet it is one of the richest nations in the world per person.

About 40,000 people live in Liechtenstein, speaking German and an Alemannic dialect close to Swiss German. It is a constitutional monarchy where the prince holds real power, including the right to veto laws, alongside an elected parliament of 25 members. Liechtenstein has close ties with Switzerland, using the Swiss franc and sharing open borders. Its economy runs on banking and, surprisingly, industry: tiny Liechtenstein makes dental products, power tools, and machine parts sold worldwide, and it has more registered companies than citizens.
content.landAndNature: The Rhine River forms the entire western border, flowing through a flat valley floor where the villages and farms lie. From there the land climbs steeply into the Rätikon range of the Alps, with Grauspitz the highest point at 2,599 meters. The mountain villages of Malbun and Steg sit in a high side valley, where skiing draws visitors in winter and hikers in summer, and where the Sareis chairlift and the trail of the Fürstensteig cling to cliffs. About 40 percent of the country is forest. Chamois, ibex, marmots, and red deer live on the slopes, and golden eagles hunt overhead. Winters are cold and snowy in the mountains but mild in the valley thanks to the warm föhn wind that blows down from the Alps.
content.peopleAndCulture: Life in Liechtenstein is quiet, prosperous, and closely tied to its neighbors, with many people commuting in from Switzerland and Austria for work each day. Most citizens are Roman Catholic. Food is Alpine and hearty: käsknöpfle, small cheese dumplings with fried onions and applesauce, and ribel, a cornmeal dish once eaten by farmers, are national favorites. On National Day, August 15, the prince invites the entire population to a reception in the castle gardens, followed by fireworks over Vaduz. Skiing is the top sport, and the country has won all its Olympic medals in Alpine skiing, more per person than any nation. Liechtenstein is also famous among collectors for its beautiful postage stamps, which once brought in a large share of the national income.
content.history: Romans built a road through the Rhine valley, and Alemannic tribes settled here in the 400s. In the Middle Ages the lands of Vaduz and Schellenberg were small lordships within the Holy Roman Empire. In 1699 and 1712 the wealthy Liechtenstein family of Vienna bought them so they could have a seat in the imperial assembly, and in 1719 the emperor made them the Principality of Liechtenstein. For 200 years the princes barely visited. The country stayed neutral in both world wars and abolished its army in 1868. After World War I it turned from Austria toward Switzerland, adopting the Swiss franc in 1924. Prince Franz Josef II became the first prince to live in Vaduz Castle in 1938. Women gained the right to vote only in 1984, and Liechtenstein joined the United Nations in 1990.
funFacts: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are the world's only doubly landlocked countries, surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries.
The country's army was disbanded in 1868; legend says the last 80 soldiers came home from a war with 81 men, having made a friend.
Liechtenstein has won ten Olympic medals, all in Alpine skiing, more per person than any other country.
In 2011 Liechtenstein offered itself for rent to groups for about 70,000 dollars a night, complete with a symbolic key and custom street signs.
The prince invites every citizen to his castle garden for drinks each year on National Day, August 15.

LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.officialName: Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

content.tagline: Teardrop island of tea and elephants
content.overview:
Sri Lanka is a pear-shaped island in the Indian Ocean, just off the southeastern tip of India across a shallow strait dotted with sandbanks. It covers about 65,600 km², roughly the size of West Virginia, and packs beaches, rainforest, dry plains and misty mountains into a short drive.

About 22 million people live in Sri Lanka. Sinhala and Tamil are both official languages, and English is widely used. Colombo on the west coast is the commercial capital and largest city; the country's parliament sits in the nearby planned city of Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte.

Sri Lanka is a republic with an elected president and parliament. It is famous for Ceylon tea grown on cool highland slopes, for cinnamon and sapphires, for cricket, and for ancient Buddhist cities where enormous brick stupas and carved reservoirs have stood for 2,000 years.
content.landAndNature: A central massif of mountains rises to Pidurutalagala at 2,524 meters, catching two monsoons, one from the southwest between May and September and one from the northeast from December to February, which is why one side of the island can be soaking while the other is dry. Tea bushes cover the cool slopes, and rainforest survives in Sinharaja reserve, home to birds found nowhere else. The dry northern plains hold ancient irrigation tanks, giant reservoirs built by kings more than a thousand years ago and still watering fields. Sri Lanka has about 6,000 wild elephants, leopards in Yala park, sloth bears and the largest gatherings of wild Asian elephants anywhere. Blue whales, the biggest animals ever, feed off the southern coast.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Sri Lankans are Sinhalese and mainly Buddhist, with Tamil communities who are largely Hindu, plus Muslim and Christian populations, so temples, kovils, mosques and churches often stand within a few streets. Rice and curry means a plate of rice ringed by half a dozen dishes: dhal, coconut sambol pounded with chili, jackfruit, fish. Hoppers, bowl-shaped pancakes cooked in a small pan, are a breakfast favorite. Cricket is the national passion, and Sri Lanka won the World Cup in 1996. The Kandy Esala Perahera parades decorated elephants, dancers and drummers by torchlight for days each summer. Stilt fishermen on the south coast perch on poles planted in the surf.
content.history: Sinhalese settlers arrived from northern India around 500 BC, and Buddhism came in the 200s BC; the ancient capitals of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa built vast stupas, monasteries and reservoirs. Tamil kingdoms and invasions from southern India shaped the north. Portugal took coastal areas in the 1500s, the Dutch followed, and Britain seized the whole island by 1815, renaming it Ceylon and covering the highlands with tea after a disease destroyed the coffee crop. Independence came on February 4, 1948, and the country took the name Sri Lanka in 1972. From 1983 to 2009 a civil war was fought between the government and the Tamil Tigers, who sought a separate state in the north and east; tens of thousands died before the war ended. In 2004 the Indian Ocean tsunami killed more than 30,000 people here.
funFacts: Sri Lanka was the world's first country to elect a woman prime minister, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, in 1960.
Sigiriya is a palace and fortress built atop a 200-meter rock column, reached by stairs past 1,500-year-old wall paintings.
The country supplies most of the world's true cinnamon, peeled as thin bark and rolled into quills by hand.
Sri Lanka's flag includes a lion with a sword plus stripes representing its Tamil and Muslim communities.
Adam's Peak has a footprint-shaped mark at its summit revered by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians alike.

content.tagline: The kingdom in the sky
content.overview:
Lesotho is a small mountain kingdom completely surrounded by South Africa, one of only three countries in the world enclosed by a single neighbor. About the size of Maryland, it is the only nation on Earth that lies entirely above 1,000 meters, which is why it is called the Kingdom in the Sky. The capital, Maseru, sits on the western border along the Caledon River, and almost all the rest of the country is a tumble of high peaks, deep valleys, and grassy plateaus.

Around 2.3 million people live in Lesotho, and nearly all are Basotho, sharing one language, Sesotho, along with English as a second official tongue. Lesotho is a constitutional monarchy: the king is a symbol of the nation, while an elected parliament and prime minister run the government. It is a poor country where many people herd sheep and goats, grow corn, or work in South Africa's mines and factories. Lesotho sells water and electricity from its mountain dams to its giant neighbor, and its textile factories make jeans for American brands.
content.landAndNature: Lesotho's mountains are the Maloti and the Drakensberg, which rise to Thabana Ntlenyana at 3,482 meters, the highest point in southern Africa. Because of the altitude, winters are cold and snowy, unusual for Africa, and the country has a ski resort, Afriski. Rivers born here, including the Orange River, called the Senqu in Lesotho, cut spectacular gorges; Maletsunyane Falls drops 192 meters in a single plunge into a misty canyon. The Katse Dam, one of Africa's tallest, stores water sold to South Africa. The lowlands in the west are the only farmable strip. The rare bearded vulture nests on cliffs, and the spiral aloe, a plant whose leaves form a perfect spiral, grows only in these mountains. Dinosaur footprints are scattered in the sandstone.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Basotho are famous for their blankets: thick wool blankets in bold patterns are worn like cloaks by men and women against the mountain cold and given at weddings and coming-of-age ceremonies. The mokorotlo, a conical straw hat shaped like a mountain, is the national symbol and appears on the flag. Sure-footed Basotho ponies carry riders along mountain trails, and pony trekking is a national pastime. Most people are Christian. Meals center on papa, a stiff corn porridge, with moroho greens, beans, or meat, and sour porridge called motoho. Famo music, driven by the accordion, is played at gatherings, and lithoko praise poems honor chiefs and heroes. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Lesotho's long-distance runners compete internationally.
content.history: San hunter-gatherers painted rock shelters here thousands of years ago, and Sotho-speaking farmers arrived by the 1500s. In the early 1800s, as wars swept southern Africa, a chief named Moshoeshoe I gathered refugees onto the flat-topped mountain of Thaba Bosiu and united them into the Basotho nation, defeating attackers through clever diplomacy and defense. To protect his people from Boer settlers who took the fertile lowlands, Moshoeshoe asked Britain for protection in 1868, and Basutoland became a British protectorate. Independence came on October 4, 1966, as the Kingdom of Lesotho under King Moshoeshoe II. Decades of political disputes, a coup in 1986, and unrest in 1998 followed, but elections have continued, and the kingdom remains a distinct nation inside South Africa.
funFacts: Lesotho is the only country in the world whose entire territory lies more than 1,000 meters above sea level.
The Basotho blanket became a national dress after a British official gave one to King Moshoeshoe I in the 1860s.
Lesotho has one of the highest pubs in Africa, at the top of Sani Pass at 2,874 meters.
Fossilized footprints of dinosaurs are so common in Lesotho that some are used as landmarks by local herders.
The country is one of only three in the world enclosed entirely by a single neighbor, along with San Marino and Vatican City.

content.tagline: Basketball nation with a baroque heart
content.overview:
Lithuania is the largest and southernmost of the three Baltic states, lying on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea with Latvia to the north, Belarus to the east, and Poland and Russia's Kaliningrad region to the south. It is about the size of West Virginia, mostly flat, with forests, lakes, and farmland. The capital, Vilnius, has one of the largest and best-preserved baroque old towns in Europe, a maze of courtyards, church towers, and cobbled lanes.

Around 2.9 million people live in Lithuania and speak Lithuanian, one of the oldest living languages in Europe, so conservative that it still shares features with ancient Sanskrit. Most Lithuanians are Roman Catholic. The country is a parliamentary republic that regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1990, the first Soviet republic to do so, and it joined the European Union and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2015. Lithuania is a leader in lasers and technology, and its people are so devoted to basketball that it is called the country's second religion.
content.landAndNature: Lithuania is a land of glacial lowlands, with its highest point, Aukštojas Hill, at just 294 meters. About 3,000 lakes glitter in the east, and the Nemunas River winds across the country to a lagoon on the coast. The Curonian Spit, a 98-kilometer sandbar shared with Russia, has some of the highest drifting sand dunes in Europe, with pine forests on one side and the open Baltic on the other; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Forests cover about a third of the country and hold wolves, lynx, moose, and European bison in the Panevėžys region. White storks are so common that Lithuania has the highest density of nesting storks in Europe, and the stork is the national bird. Winters are cold and snowy, summers mild.
content.peopleAndCulture: Lithuanians treasure their ancient language, folk songs called sutartinės, sung in overlapping rounds, and the tradition of wooden cross-crafting, both recognized by UNESCO. Cepelinai, huge potato dumplings shaped like zeppelins and stuffed with meat, are the national dish, along with cold pink beet soup, dark rye bread, and šakotis, a spiky tree-shaped cake baked on a rotating spit. Midsummer, Joninės, is celebrated with wreaths and bonfires, and Užgavėnės, before Lent, features masked parades and burning a straw effigy of winter. Basketball is a national passion: Lithuania has won the European championship three times and Olympic bronze several times, and its players star in the NBA. The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai holds more than 100,000 crosses left by pilgrims.
content.history: Baltic tribes lived here for millennia, and in 1253 Mindaugas was crowned the first and only king of Lithuania. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania became one of the largest states in Europe in the 1400s, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, and joined with Poland in 1569 to form a commonwealth. Lithuania was the last pagan country in Europe, converting to Christianity in 1387. The Russian Empire absorbed it in 1795. Independence was declared in 1918, but the Soviet Union occupied Lithuania in 1940, followed by Nazi Germany, which murdered most of the country's large Jewish population, and then Soviet rule again, with mass deportations to Siberia. On March 11, 1990 Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence; Soviet troops killed 14 civilians in Vilnius in January 1991 before withdrawing.
funFacts: Lithuanian is considered the most conservative living Indo-European language, and linguists study it to understand ancient tongues.
The Hill of Crosses holds more than 100,000 crosses; Soviet authorities bulldozed it three times, and people rebuilt it each time.
Lithuania claims the geographic center of Europe, marked by a monument north of Vilnius, based on a 1989 French calculation.
Lithuania makes about a tenth of the world's scientific lasers, and they are used in labs on every continent.
The Vilnius neighborhood of Užupis declared itself an independent republic on April Fools' Day 1997, with its own constitution and army of about a dozen.

content.tagline: A grand duchy of castles and bankers
content.overview:
Luxembourg is a small landlocked country in Western Europe, tucked between Belgium, Germany, and France. It is about the size of Rhode Island, small enough to drive across in under an hour, yet it is one of the richest countries in the world per person. The capital, Luxembourg City, is perched dramatically on cliffs above two river gorges, with old fortress walls, bridges, and casemates, tunnels carved into the rock, giving it the nickname Gibraltar of the North.

About 670,000 people live in Luxembourg, and nearly half of them are foreign citizens, the highest share in the European Union; another 200,000 people commute in every day from neighboring countries to work. Luxembourgers speak three languages: Luxembourgish, a Germanic language, at home, plus French and German in school, government, and business. The country is a grand duchy, the world's only one, meaning its head of state is a grand duke, with an elected parliament running the government. Luxembourg is a founding member of the European Union and hosts several of its institutions, and its economy runs on banking, investment funds, steel, and satellites.
content.landAndNature: Luxembourg has two distinct halves. The north, called the Oesling, is part of the Ardennes plateau, a rugged region of forested hills, deep river valleys, and castle-topped villages, rising to about 560 meters at Kneiff, the highest point. The south, the Gutland or good land, is gentler and more fertile, with farms, orchards, and towns. Along the eastern border the Moselle River flows past steep vineyards that produce crisp white wines. The Mullerthal region, nicknamed Little Switzerland, is a maze of sandstone rock formations, narrow crevices, and mossy forest trails. Forests cover about a third of the country and hold red deer, wild boar, and wildcats, and the Our and Sûre rivers wind through quiet valleys. The climate is mild and fairly wet.
content.peopleAndCulture: Luxembourgers switch easily among Luxembourgish, French, German, and often English or Portuguese, since a large Portuguese community has lived here for decades. Most people are Roman Catholic. National dishes include judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, and gromperekichelcher, crispy potato fritters sold at fairs; the country is also proud of its Moselle wines and sparkling crémant. On the eve of National Day, June 23, the capital fills with fireworks and street parties. The Schueberfouer, a funfair founded in 1340, still takes over the city each summer, and the Echternach hopping procession, where thousands skip through the streets, is a UNESCO tradition. Cycling and soccer are popular, and Luxembourg has produced Tour de France winners.
content.history: Luxembourg began in 963 when Count Siegfried acquired a small castle on a rock called Lucilinburhuc, the little fortress. His descendants became dukes, and in the 1300s the House of Luxembourg produced four Holy Roman Emperors. The fortress city was so strong that Burgundians, Spanish, French, Austrians, and Prussians fought to hold it for 400 years. In 1815 Luxembourg became a grand duchy under the Dutch king, and it gained full independence in 1867 on condition that it tear down its fortress and stay neutral. Germany occupied it in both world wars, and the Battle of the Bulge raged across its north in 1944 and 1945. After the war Luxembourg helped found NATO, the European Union, and the Benelux customs union, and it became a center of European banking and institutions.
funFacts: Luxembourg was the first country in the world to make all public transportation free, in 2020.
Nearly half of Luxembourg's residents are foreign citizens, and more than 170 nationalities live in the country.
Luxembourg is the only grand duchy left in the world, ruled by a grand duke rather than a king or prince.
The capital's Bock casemates are 17 kilometers of tunnels carved into the cliffs, once holding soldiers, horses, and bakeries.
Luxembourg has the most Michelin-starred restaurants per person of any country in the world.

content.tagline: Art nouveau and amber on the Baltic
content.overview:
Latvia is the middle of the three Baltic states, lying between Estonia and Lithuania on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea, with Russia and Belarus to the east. It is about the size of West Virginia, flat and green, with about half of the land covered in forest. The capital, Riga, sits where the Daugava River meets the sea and is the largest city in the Baltic states. Its old town of church spires and its avenues of ornate art nouveau buildings, decorated with faces, flowers, and mythical beasts, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Around 1.9 million people live in Latvia, and the population has shrunk as many have moved to Western Europe for work. Latvian, one of only two surviving Baltic languages, is the official tongue, and Russian is spoken by a large minority. Latvia is a parliamentary republic that regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. Its people are known for choral singing, midsummer celebrations, and a deep bond with forests, rivers, and the sea.
content.landAndNature: Latvia is low and gently rolling, with the highest hill, Gaiziņkalns, reaching only 312 meters. Nearly 500 kilometers of coastline face the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Riga, with long white sand beaches backed by pine forests, and amber washes ashore after storms. The Daugava is the great river, and the Gauja winds through a valley of sandstone cliffs and caves in Gauja National Park. Thousands of lakes and vast bogs dot the east, and Kemeri National Park has raised bogs crossed by boardwalks. Forests of pine, spruce, and birch cover half the country and hide wolves, lynx, brown bears, and huge numbers of beavers, deer, and wild boar. White storks nest in almost every village, and the Ventas Rumba on the Venta River is the widest waterfall in Europe.
content.peopleAndCulture: Latvians celebrate the summer solstice, Jāņi, more than almost any other holiday: people wear oak-leaf and flower crowns, eat caraway cheese, sing, and stay up all night around bonfires. Every five years the Song and Dance Celebration gathers tens of thousands of singers and dancers in Riga. Traditional food includes gray peas with bacon, rye bread, smoked fish, and cold beet soup in summer. Most Latvians are Lutheran, Catholic, or Orthodox. Ice hockey is the national sport, and Latvia has won medals in basketball, bobsled, and luge; the country also produced the world's top 3x3 basketball team. Folk songs called dainas, more than a million lines of them, are a national treasure, and the Riga Central Market fills five old zeppelin hangars.
content.history: Baltic tribes such as the Latgalians, Livonians, and Curonians lived here for thousands of years before German crusaders conquered the region in the 1200s and founded Riga in 1201. German nobles and merchants ruled for centuries under Polish, Swedish, and, from the 1700s, Russian control. Latvian national feeling grew in the 1800s, and Latvia declared independence in 1918 as the Russian Empire collapsed. The Soviet Union occupied the country in 1940, followed by Nazi Germany, during which most of Latvia's Jews were murdered, and then Soviet rule again from 1944, with tens of thousands deported to Siberia. In 1989 Latvians joined the Baltic Way human chain, and independence was restored in 1991. Latvia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014.
funFacts: Riga has about 800 art nouveau buildings, more than any other city in the world.
Latvia's Ventas Rumba waterfall is only about two meters high but nearly 250 meters wide, the widest in Europe.
Riga's Christmas market claims the first decorated public Christmas tree, set up in 1510.
Latvians have collected more than 1.2 million folk song texts, so many that the collection is kept in a special cabinet.
About 200,000 Latvians, a tenth of the population, formed a human chain across the Baltics in 1989 to demand freedom.

MAC.name: Macau
MAC.officialName: Macao Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China

content.tagline: Where the Sahara meets the Atlantic
content.overview:
Morocco stands at Africa's northwest corner, close enough to Europe that on a clear day Spain is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar, just 14 kilometers of water. The country is a little larger than California, with coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, snow-capped mountains through the middle, and the Sahara Desert spreading across the south and east.

About 38 million people live in Morocco. Arabic and Berber, which its speakers call Tamazight, are the official languages, and French is widely used in business and schools. Rabat is the capital, Casablanca the biggest city and busiest port, while Marrakesh, Fez, and Meknes are old imperial cities of palaces, mosques, and walled medinas. Morocco is a kingdom, governed by a king together with an elected parliament.

Morocco also administers Western Sahara to the south, a disputed territory it largely controls and whose status the United Nations considers unresolved.
content.landAndNature: Three mountain ranges cross the country: the Rif above the Mediterranean, the Middle Atlas with its cedar forests, and the High Atlas, where Toubkal reaches 4,167 meters, the highest peak in North Africa and snowy enough for skiing. South and east of the Atlas the land dries into stony plains, palm-filled oases, and the dunes of Erg Chebbi, some more than 100 meters tall. Rivers such as the Draa run down from the mountains and vanish into sand. Barbary macaques, the only monkeys living wild north of the Sahara, swing through the cedars, while fennec foxes hunt in the desert. Off the Atlantic coast, cold currents feed huge shoals of sardines.
content.peopleAndCulture: Moroccans are mostly Arab and Amazigh (Berber), and many speak Darija, the Moroccan form of Arabic, at home; Amazigh has its own alphabet, Tifinagh, which appears on road signs. Nearly everyone is Muslim, and the call to prayer marks out the day. The food is famous: tagines slow-cooked in cone-lidded clay pots, couscous served on Fridays, harira soup, and sweet mint tea poured from high above the glass. Each evening storytellers, musicians, and food stalls take over the Jemaa el-Fna square in Marrakesh. Gnawa musicians play iron castanets and a three-stringed guembri at festivals in Essaouira. Soccer is the national sport, and in 2022 Morocco became the first African team to reach a World Cup semifinal.
content.history: Amazigh peoples have lived in North Africa for thousands of years. Phoenicians and then Romans built ports along the coast, and the Roman ruins of Volubilis still stand near Meknes. Arab armies brought Islam in the late 600s, and from Fez, founded around 789, a series of Moroccan dynasties ruled; the Almoravids and Almohads at their height governed an empire stretching into Spain. Morocco kept its independence while much of Africa fell to European powers, until France and Spain imposed protectorates in 1912. Nationalists and the sultan pressed for freedom, and independence came in 1956 under Mohammed V. The Alaouite dynasty, on the throne since the 1600s, still reigns, and a new constitution in 2011 shifted some powers to the elected parliament.
funFacts: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is recognized as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
The medina of Fez has thousands of narrow alleys and no cars; goods still move by donkey and handcart.
Goats really do climb argan trees in southwestern Morocco to reach the fruit, sometimes six or seven in a single tree.
The Noor solar complex near Ouarzazate uses curved mirrors spread over thousands of hectares to concentrate desert sunlight into power.
Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque stands partly over the Atlantic and has one of the tallest minarets on Earth, 210 meters high.

content.tagline: A city-state on Mediterranean cliffs
content.overview:
Monaco is the second-smallest country in the world, after Vatican City: about two square kilometers of steep hillside and harbor squeezed between France and the Mediterranean Sea. A steady walker can cross the whole country in under an hour. Because there is so little land, Monaco builds upward and outward, stacking apartment towers up the cliffs and laying whole neighborhoods on ground reclaimed from the sea.

About 39,000 people live in the principality, and French is the official language, though Italian, English, and the old Monégasque dialect are all heard on the streets. Monaco is a principality governed by a prince of the Grimaldi family together with an elected council, one of the last places in Europe where a royal family still runs the country day to day. Its capital is Monaco itself.

The country is known worldwide for the Monte Carlo casino, a harbor packed with yachts, and the Monaco Grand Prix, a Formula One race driven through ordinary city streets, past hotels and around a famous hairpin turn.
content.landAndNature: Monaco sits on a narrow shelf of the French Riviera, where the Maritime Alps drop almost straight into the sea. The Rock of Monaco, a limestone headland, juts into the water and carries the prince's palace and the old town on its flat top. Winters are mild and summers hot and dry, a Mediterranean climate with sunshine most days of the year. Almost no wild land remains, but the Exotic Garden clings to a cliff face with thousands of cacti and succulents above a cave of stalactites, and the country protects patches of sea where seahorses, groupers, and meadows of posidonia seagrass grow.
content.peopleAndCulture: Only about a quarter of residents hold Monégasque citizenship; the rest come from France, Italy, and more than a hundred other countries, so several languages mix in any cafe. The food is Riviera food: barbagiuan, a fried pastry stuffed with chard and cheese, socca pancakes made from chickpea flour, and seafood straight off the boats. The Oceanographic Museum, once directed by the explorer Jacques Cousteau, hangs above the waves with sharks and coral in its tanks. Monaco's biggest days are the Grand Prix in May, a winter circus festival that draws acrobats from everywhere, and the national holiday on November 19. The soccer club AS Monaco plays in the French league.
content.history: People sheltered in caves along this coast in prehistoric times, and Greek settlers founded a town here around 2,500 years ago; the Romans later called the harbor Portus Herculis Monoeci. In 1297 François Grimaldi seized the fortress on the Rock, by tradition disguised as a monk, and the Grimaldi family has held it almost ever since, making them one of Europe's longest-ruling dynasties. Monaco spent centuries under Spanish and then French protection, and in 1861 it won full independence while giving up most of its territory. The casino that opened soon after rescued the treasury. In 1956 Prince Rainier III married the American film star Grace Kelly, and Monaco joined the United Nations in 1993.
funFacts: Monaco is smaller than New York's Central Park, yet it is a fully independent country with its own small army of about 120 soldiers.
The Grand Prix runs on public roads: barriers go up for the race, and days later the same streets carry ordinary traffic again.
Monaco is the most densely populated country on Earth, with roughly 19,000 people living in each square kilometer.
About a fifth of Monaco's land has been reclaimed from the sea, and new districts are still being built on the water.
Monégasque citizens are barred from gambling in the Monte Carlo casino, a rule that dates back to the casino's earliest years.

content.tagline: Vineyards and underground wine cities
content.overview:
Moldova is a small landlocked country in Eastern Europe, wedged between Romania and Ukraine, about the size of Maryland. Its gently rolling hills are covered in vineyards, orchards, and sunflower fields, and wine is so central to life that the country has some of the largest wine cellars on Earth, whole underground cities of tunnels. The capital, Chișinău, is a leafy city of parks and Soviet-era apartment blocks in the center of the country.

About 2.5 million people live in Moldova, and the number has been falling as many work abroad. The official language is Romanian, which the constitution long called Moldovan; Russian, Ukrainian, and Gagauz are also widely spoken. Most people are Orthodox Christian. Moldova is a parliamentary republic and one of the poorest countries in Europe, and its eastern strip along the Dniester River, called Transnistria, has been run by a separatist government backed by Russia since a short war in 1992, though no country recognizes it. Moldova became a candidate to join the European Union in 2022.
content.landAndNature: Moldova lies between two rivers: the Prut on the western border with Romania and the Dniester in the east. Between them stretches a plateau of low hills, nowhere higher than 430 meters at Bălănești, cut by wooded valleys and dotted with villages. The soil is a rich black earth ideal for grapes, wheat, corn, and sunflowers, and forests of oak and beech cover about a tenth of the country, mainly in the central Codri hills. The Orheiul Vechi gorge holds cave monasteries carved into limestone cliffs above a looping river. In the south the land opens into dry steppe near the Black Sea, which Moldova touches only through a tiny stretch of Danube riverbank. Winters are cold, summers hot, and storks, deer, and wild boar are common sights.
content.peopleAndCulture: Moldovans share language and many traditions with Romanians but have their own flavor. Meals include mămăligă, a golden cornmeal porridge served with sheep cheese and sour cream, plăcinte pastries stuffed with cabbage, cheese, or pumpkin, sarmale cabbage rolls, and zeamă, a chicken noodle soup. Nearly every village family makes its own wine, and the National Wine Day in October draws crowds to Chișinău. Folk music with violins, accordions, and the pan flute called the nai accompanies fast circle dances such as the hora. Martisor, a red-and-white thread charm, is worn from March 1 to welcome spring. Soccer, wrestling, and weightlifting are popular, and the Gagauz people in the south keep a Turkic language and Orthodox faith.
content.history: The region was part of the medieval Principality of Moldavia, whose ruler Stephen the Great fought off Ottoman armies in the 1400s and built dozens of churches. In 1812 the Russian Empire took the eastern half, called Bessarabia, and after World War I it joined Romania. The Soviet Union seized it in 1940, made it the Moldavian Soviet Republic, and deported tens of thousands to Siberia; a famine in 1946 and 1947 killed many more. Moldova declared independence on August 27, 1991. Fighting broke out in 1992 when Transnistria, with Russian support, broke away, and that dispute remains frozen. Moldova has swung between pro-Russian and pro-European governments and, after Russia invaded neighboring Ukraine in 2022, moved firmly toward the European Union, which accepted it as a candidate that year.
funFacts: The Mileștii Mici winery holds the largest wine collection in the world, nearly two million bottles stored in 200 kilometers of tunnels.
Moldovans drink more alcohol per person than almost any nation, mostly homemade wine shared with guests.
Cricova's cellars are so vast that visitors tour them by car, and streets underground are named after grape varieties.
The Gagauz people of southern Moldova speak a Turkic language but are Orthodox Christians, a rare combination.
Moldova's flag is almost identical to Romania's, differing only by the coat of arms with an eagle in the center.

content.tagline: Island of lemurs and upside-down trees
content.overview:
Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world, floating in the Indian Ocean about 400 kilometers off the southeast coast of Africa. It is roughly the size of Texas, or a little bigger than France. Because it split from Africa and India tens of millions of years ago, its plants and animals evolved on their own, and about 90 percent of its wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth, including all of the world's lemurs. The capital, Antananarivo, sprawls over hills in the central highlands, with red-brick houses stacked up steep slopes.

Around 30 million people live in Madagascar. Malagasy, a language whose closest relatives are spoken in Borneo, is the national language, and French is also official, reflecting the island's settlement from Asia and its colonial past. Most people are farmers, growing rice in terraced paddies and raising humped zebu cattle, and the island produces most of the world's natural vanilla. Madagascar is a republic with a president, and it is one of the poorest countries in the world despite its natural riches. Deforestation threatens its unique forests.
content.landAndNature: A spine of highlands runs down the island's length, dropping steeply to a narrow, rainy east coast of rainforest and gently to a drier west and a desert-like south. The Tsingy de Bemaraha is a forest of razor-sharp limestone needles, and the Avenue of the Baobabs is lined with trees 30 meters tall, their fat trunks storing water; baobabs are called upside-down trees because their bare branches look like roots. Madagascar's 100-plus species of lemurs range from the mouse lemur, small enough to fit in a hand, to the dancing sifaka and the ghostly aye-aye. Chameleons here include the world's largest and smallest, and the fossa, a cat-like predator, hunts lemurs. Coral reefs ring much of the coast, and humpback whales breed off Île Sainte-Marie each winter.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Malagasy descend from Austronesian sailors who arrived from Indonesia and from African settlers, and 18 main groups, such as the Merina of the highlands and the Sakalava of the west, share one language. Rice is eaten three times a day, often with romazava, a meat and greens broth, or ravitoto, pork with pounded cassava leaves. Respect for ancestors is central: the Merina hold famadihana, a joyful ceremony in which family remains are rewrapped in fresh silk and danced with, and fady, or taboos, guide daily behavior. Music features the valiha, a bamboo tube zither, and salegy dance rhythms. Rugby is surprisingly popular alongside soccer, and the Malagasy love the strategy board game fanorona. Lamba cloth is worn in bright wraps.
content.history: Madagascar was one of the last large landmasses settled by humans; Austronesian seafarers arrived around 1,500 years ago in outrigger canoes, later joined by Africans and Arab traders. Kingdoms rose along the coast, and in the late 1700s King Andrianampoinimerina began uniting the island under the Merina kingdom, which built a European-style state with schools and a written language. France conquered Madagascar in 1895 and exiled the last queen, Ranavalona III. A rebellion in 1947 was crushed with tens of thousands of deaths. Independence came on June 26, 1960. Since then the island has gone through socialist rule, protests, and several political crises, including a 2009 coup, with elections returning in 2013. Vanilla, mining, and tourism sustain a struggling economy.
funFacts: About 90 percent of Madagascar's animals and plants live nowhere else on Earth, including more than 100 kinds of lemur.
Madagascar grows most of the world's natural vanilla, whose flowers must be pollinated by hand.
The Malagasy language is most closely related to a language spoken in Borneo, 7,000 kilometers across the Indian Ocean.
Brookesia nana, a chameleon from northern Madagascar, is about the size of a sunflower seed, the smallest known reptile.
Baobab trees can store thousands of liters of water in their trunks and live for more than a thousand years.

content.tagline: A thousand islands barely above the waves
content.overview:
The Maldives is a chain of about 1,200 coral islands strung across the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka, and only around 200 of them have people living on them. The land adds up to roughly 300 km², about twice the size of Washington, DC, scattered over some 90,000 km² of ocean. It is the flattest country in the world: the highest natural ground rises only about 2.4 meters above sea level.

Around 520,000 people live in the Maldives, nearly all of them Sunni Muslims. Maldivian, also called Dhivehi, is the national language and is written in a script that runs from right to left. The Maldives is a republic. Malé, the capital, is one of the most densely populated cities anywhere, a small island packed edge to edge with buildings. Tourism, with resorts built on their own islands, and tuna fishing support the economy. Because the land is so low, rising seas threaten the country directly.
content.landAndNature: The Maldives sits on the crest of an undersea mountain ridge, where coral has grown upward over millions of years into ring-shaped atolls; the English word atoll comes from Dhivehi. Each island is a low disc of white coral sand beside a lagoon of astonishing clarity. The reefs shelter more than a thousand fish species, along with manta rays, green turtles and whale sharks, the largest fish in the sea. At night some beaches glow blue where tiny plankton light up in the breaking waves. Warming ocean water has bleached long stretches of coral, and rising seas eat steadily at the islands' edges.
content.peopleAndCulture: Fish, especially skipjack tuna, is the heart of Maldivian cooking, smoked and dried into hard chips called Maldive fish and stirred into curries, or mixed with coconut, onion and chili into mas huni, eaten with flatbread for breakfast. Boduberu is the best-known music, a circle of drummers and singers building to a fast, pounding finish. The dhoni, a curved wooden boat, has carried Maldivians between islands for centuries. Most islands are small enough to cross on foot in minutes, and children grow up swimming before they can ride a bicycle. Soccer is the favorite sport.
content.history: Settlers, probably from southern India and Sri Lanka, arrived more than 2,500 years ago, and the islands became a Buddhist kingdom for many centuries. In 1153 the ruler converted to Islam and the country followed. Maldivian cowrie shells were used as money across Asia and Africa, making the islands valuable to traders. Portugal held Malé briefly in the 1500s, and from 1887 the Maldives was a British protectorate while keeping its own sultan. Independence came on July 26, 1965, and the country became a republic in 1968. The Indian Ocean tsunami flooded many islands in 2004. Since then the Maldives has spoken forcefully at world climate talks about rising seas.
funFacts: The Maldives is the flattest country in the world; its highest natural ground is only about 2.4 meters above the sea.
The English word atoll comes from Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives.
In 2009 the Maldivian cabinet held a meeting underwater in scuba gear to draw attention to rising sea levels.
Maldivian cowrie shells were once used as money in markets across Asia and Africa.
Only about 200 of the roughly 1,200 islands are inhabited, and many resorts occupy an entire island each.

content.tagline: Ancient pyramids, chilies and two coasts
content.overview:
Mexico stretches from the United States border south to Guatemala and Belize, a country about three times the size of Texas with long coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. It narrows in the south at the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, then hooks east into the flat limestone Yucatán Peninsula. Mexico City, the capital, sits in a high valley about 2,240 meters up and anchors one of the largest urban areas in the world.

About 130 million people live in Mexico, more than in any other Spanish-speaking country. Spanish is the national language, and some 70 Indigenous languages, including Nahuatl, Maya and Zapotec, are recognized and spoken by millions of people. Mexico is a federal republic of 31 states plus the capital. Mexican cooking, from tacos and tamales to slow-simmered mole, is listed by UNESCO as cultural heritage, and Mexican music, murals, films and writers are known around the world.
content.landAndNature: Two great mountain chains, the Sierra Madre Occidental and the Sierra Madre Oriental, run down either side of the country, with a high plateau between them and a belt of volcanoes crossing the middle; Pico de Orizaba reaches 5,636 meters, and Popocatépetl still puffs smoke near the capital. Northern deserts hold giant cardón cacti and roadrunners, while southern states are covered in rainforest with jaguars, howler monkeys and toucans. The Yucatán has no surface rivers at all, and rain drains into cenotes, deep water-filled sinkholes in the limestone. Each autumn millions of monarch butterflies arrive from Canada and cluster on fir trees in Michoacán.
content.peopleAndCulture: Corn is the foundation of Mexican cooking, ground into tortillas eaten at nearly every meal, and roughly 60 kinds of chili add heat and flavor to everything from fresh salsa to dark, chocolate-rich mole sauce. Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2 brings families to cemeteries with marigolds, sugar skulls and candles to remember relatives; it is a celebration rather than a day of mourning. Mariachi bands in silver-studded suits play at parties, and lucha libre wrestlers fight in bright masks. Soccer fills stadiums, and artists such as Frida Kahlo and the muralist Diego Rivera are known everywhere.
content.history: Great civilizations rose here thousands of years ago: the Olmec carved colossal stone heads, the Maya built stepped pyramids and tracked the stars with remarkable precision, and the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan on a lake island in 1325, growing it into one of the largest cities on Earth. Spanish forces under Hernán Cortés, joined by Indigenous allies and helped by diseases that killed enormous numbers of people, took the Aztec capital in 1521, and Spain ruled for three centuries. Mexico won independence in 1821, lost half its territory to the United States in a war ending in 1848, and passed through a revolution from 1910 to 1920 that reshaped land ownership and politics.
funFacts: Mexico City is sinking, dropping tens of centimeters a year in places because it was built on a drained lake bed.
Chocolate, chili, corn, tomatoes, avocados and vanilla were all first grown in Mexico before spreading worldwide.
Monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometers from Canada to a handful of Mexican forests where they gather each winter.
At Chichen Itza the main pyramid is built so that a shadow shaped like a snake slides down its steps at the equinox.
Mexico has more UNESCO World Heritage sites than any other country in the Americas.
The volcano rabbit, one of the smallest rabbits on Earth, lives only on volcano slopes near Mexico City.

content.tagline: Atolls, navigators and nuclear history
content.overview:
The Marshall Islands are 29 coral atolls and five single islands scattered across the central Pacific, with a total land area of only about 181 km², roughly the size of Washington, DC, spread over nearly two million square kilometers of ocean. The capital, Majuro, sits on an atoll so narrow that in places the road has the open ocean on one side and a calm lagoon on the other.

About 42,000 people live in the Marshall Islands. Marshallese and English are the official languages. The country is a republic in free association with the United States, an agreement that lets Marshallese live and work in the US while the US takes responsibility for defense; many Marshallese have moved to America. Coconut products, fishing licenses and a ship registry support the economy. With land averaging about two meters above sea level, rising seas and flooding are pressing everyday concerns.
content.landAndNature: The atolls are rings of coral reef and sandy islets enclosing lagoons, some of them enormous: Kwajalein's lagoon is among the largest in the world, over 2,000 km² of sheltered water. Soil is thin, so coconut palms, pandanus and breadfruit provide most crops and the sea provides most food. Reefs teem with reef sharks, giant clams and hundreds of coral species, and the lagoon at Bikini holds sunken warships now overgrown with coral. High tides increasingly wash across roads and into homes, and the salt spoils the freshwater lenses and taro pits that islanders have always depended on.
content.peopleAndCulture: Marshallese navigators were among the finest sailors in history, reading the way ocean swells bend around islands and teaching those patterns with stick charts, lattices of palm ribs and shells that mapped waves rather than coastlines. Outrigger canoes are still sailed and raced. Weavers turn pandanus leaves into fine mats, baskets and fans. Meals center on fish, breadfruit, coconut and rice, and community feasts often follow church services, since most Marshallese are Christian. A kemem, the party for a child's first birthday, is the biggest family celebration, with singing and enough food for a whole village. Basketball and volleyball are favorite sports.
content.history: Voyagers settled these atolls around 2,000 years ago and developed remarkable navigation skills. Spain claimed the islands, Germany bought them in 1885, and Japan took them during World War I. Fierce fighting between Japanese and American forces swept the atolls in 1944. From 1946 to 1958 the United States tested 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak, including the very large Castle Bravo test of 1954; communities were moved off their home islands, some people were exposed to fallout, and parts of those atolls remain unsafe to live on. The Marshall Islands became self-governing in 1979 and fully independent in 1986 under a compact with the United States.
funFacts: Marshallese navigators made stick charts from palm ribs and shells to teach how ocean swells bend around islands.
Kwajalein Atoll encloses one of the largest lagoons in the world, wider than the land area of many countries.
Sixty-seven nuclear weapons were tested at Bikini and Enewetak between 1946 and 1958, and some areas remain unsafe.
The two-piece swimsuit called the bikini was named after Bikini Atoll shortly after the first test there in 1946.
The country's land averages about two meters above the sea, so high tides can wash straight across the roads.

content.tagline: Mountain lakes at the Balkan crossroads
content.overview:
North Macedonia is a landlocked country in the heart of the Balkan Peninsula, about the size of Vermont and ringed by mountains, with Kosovo, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Albania as neighbors. Rivers cut down through the high country and gather in the Vardar, which flows south past the capital and on toward the Aegean Sea in Greece.

About 1.8 million people live here. Macedonian, a Slavic language written in Cyrillic, is the official language, and Albanian is co-official; roughly a quarter of the population is ethnic Albanian. Skopje, the capital, straddles the Vardar, where a stone Ottoman bridge links the old bazaar to a modern center crowded with statues. North Macedonia is a parliamentary republic and joined NATO in 2020.

The country changed its name from Macedonia to North Macedonia in 2019 under an agreement with Greece, which had objected that the old name overlapped with its own northern region of Macedonia.
content.landAndNature: Mountains fill most of the country: Golem Korab on the Albanian border rises to 2,764 meters, and dozens of peaks pass 2,000. Between them lie fertile basins where tobacco, peppers, and grapes ripen in hot, dry summers, while winter brings snow and skiing. Lake Ohrid, shared with Albania, is one of the oldest and deepest lakes in Europe, perhaps three million years old, and holds more than 200 species found nowhere else, including the Ohrid trout. Nearby Lake Prespa drains underground through limestone into Ohrid. Mavrovo National Park protects beech and pine forest where the rare Balkan lynx survives alongside bears, wolves, and chamois, and pelicans nest in the lake reeds.
content.peopleAndCulture: Macedonians and Albanians make up most of the population, with Turkish, Roma, Serb, and Vlach communities as well; Orthodox churches and mosques often stand within sight of each other. Meals are long and shared: ajvar, a red pepper relish made each autumn when families roast peppers by the sackful, tavche gravche, beans baked in a clay pot, flaky burek, and yogurt. Folk music uses the zurla, a piercing reed horn, and the tapan drum, and dancers link arms in a circle dance called the oro, often in uneven rhythms such as seven beats to a bar. Soccer and handball are the leading sports, and Skopje's bazaar has traded for some 600 years.
content.history: This land was part of ancient Paeonia, next to the kingdom of Macedon of Philip II and Alexander the Great, whose heartland lay in what is now northern Greece. Rome and then Byzantium ruled here, and in the 800s the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius spread Slavic writing from Ohrid, which became a center of learning. Ottoman rule lasted about five centuries, ending with the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. The territory joined Yugoslavia and became one of its six republics after World War II. It declared independence in 1991, the only republic to leave Yugoslavia without war, although a brief conflict with ethnic Albanian insurgents in 2001 ended in an agreement that expanded minority rights.
funFacts: Lake Ohrid is up to 288 meters deep and so ancient that scientists describe it as a museum of living fossils.
Kokino, a Bronze Age site of carved stone seats and markers, was used to track the rising sun about 3,800 years ago.
Mother Teresa, later a Nobel Peace Prize winner, was born in Skopje to an Albanian family in 1910.
The stone bridge over the Vardar in Skopje has carried people across the river for roughly 550 years.
North Macedonia and Greece ended a naming dispute of nearly thirty years in 2019, when the country added North to its name.

content.tagline: Timbuktu, mud mosques, and desert blues
content.overview:
Mali is a vast landlocked country in West Africa, about twice the size of Texas, stretching from the Sahara in the north to green savanna in the south. Seven countries surround it, including Algeria, Niger, and Senegal. The capital, Bamako, is a fast-growing city on the Niger River, which loops through the country like a lifeline, feeding farms, fish, and ancient trading towns such as Timbuktu, Djenné, and Gao.

Around 23 million people live in Mali, most of them in the south near the rivers. French is the official language, but Bambara is the most widely spoken, along with Fula, Songhai, Tamasheq, and others. Nearly all Malians are Muslim. Farmers grow cotton, millet, and rice, herders drive cattle across the Sahel, and gold mining makes Mali one of Africa's top producers. Mali is a republic, but since 2012 it has faced armed rebellions and attacks in the north and center and two military coups, and the army has run the government since 2021. Its music, from kora harps to electric desert blues, is loved around the world.
content.landAndNature: Northern Mali is Sahara, a land of sand seas, rocky plateaus, and the Adrar des Ifoghas mountains, where rain may not fall for years. The Sahel belt in the center is dry grassland with acacias and baobabs, home to camel and cattle herders. The Niger River spreads out into a huge inland delta near Mopti, flooding each year to create lakes and marshes where millions of birds gather and fishermen cast nets from slender pirogues. Farther south, wooded savanna gets enough rain for cotton and grain. The Bandiagara Escarpment is a 150-kilometer sandstone cliff where Dogon villages cling to the rock face. Hippos live in the Niger, and a small population of desert elephants near Gourma makes the longest elephant migration in Africa.
content.peopleAndCulture: Mali's peoples include the Bambara, Fula, Songhai, Soninke, Dogon, and Tuareg, each with rich traditions. Griots, hereditary singers and historians, keep centuries of history alive in song, accompanied by the kora, a 21-string harp, the ngoni lute, and the balafon. Malian musicians such as Ali Farka Touré, Salif Keita, and Oumou Sangaré are global stars, and Tuareg bands created a style called desert blues. Meals feature rice or millet with peanut or okra sauce, grilled fish from the Niger, and tô porridge. Dogon dancers perform on stilts in towering masks, and the Great Mosque of Djenné, the largest mud building in the world, is replastered by the whole town in a yearly festival. Soccer is the top sport, and Malian cloth called bogolan is dyed with fermented mud.
content.history: Mali is named for the Mali Empire, which from about 1235 to 1600 was one of the richest in the world, ruling the gold and salt trade across the Sahara. Its emperor Mansa Musa, who reigned in the early 1300s, is often called the wealthiest person who ever lived, and Timbuktu became a center of learning with universities and hundreds of thousands of manuscripts. The Songhai Empire followed until a Moroccan invasion in 1591. France conquered the region in the late 1800s and ruled it as French Sudan. Independence came on September 22, 1960 under Modibo Keïta. Military rule lasted until 1991, when protests brought democracy. In 2012 Tuareg rebels and armed Islamist groups seized the north, French forces intervened, and coups in 2020 and 2021 put the army in charge.
funFacts: Mansa Musa, emperor of Mali in the 1300s, gave away so much gold on a trip to Mecca that prices in Cairo dropped for years.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world, and the whole town replasters it every year in one day.
Timbuktu's private libraries hold hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on astronomy, math, and medicine, some over 700 years old.
Mali's desert elephants travel about 600 kilometers a year in a giant loop, the longest elephant migration in Africa.
Camel caravans still carry slabs of salt from the mines of Taoudenni across the Sahara to Timbuktu, a trade that is many centuries old.

content.tagline: Honey-colored fortress in the Mediterranean
content.overview:
Malta is a tiny island nation in the middle of the Mediterranean Sea, about 90 kilometers south of Sicily and 300 kilometers north of Libya. Its three inhabited islands, Malta, Gozo, and Comino, together cover just 316 square kilometers, smaller than many cities, yet more than 500,000 people live there, making Malta one of the most densely populated countries in the world. The capital, Valletta, is a fortified city of honey-colored limestone built by knights in the 1500s and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Maltese and English are the official languages. Maltese is unique: a language descended from Arabic, written in the Latin alphabet, and packed with Italian and English words, and it is the only Semitic language that is an official language of the European Union. Most Maltese are Roman Catholic, and the islands have more than 360 churches. Malta is a parliamentary republic that joined the EU in 2004 and uses the euro. Tourism, shipping, online gaming companies, and finance drive the economy, and the islands' harbors, beaches, and ancient temples draw millions of visitors.
content.landAndNature: Malta is a low, rocky plateau of limestone with no mountains, no rivers, and very few trees; the highest point, Ta' Dmejrek, is only 253 meters. The coast is dramatic, with sheer cliffs at Dingli, sea caves like the Blue Grotto, and sheltered bays with clear turquoise water perfect for snorkeling and diving among shipwrecks. Fields are divided by low rubble walls built over centuries, and prickly pear cactus and carob trees dot the countryside. Gozo is greener and quieter, and Comino has just a handful of residents and the famous Blue Lagoon. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild and rainy. Wildlife is small, from the Maltese wall lizard to migrating birds that rest on the islands in spring and fall, and the national plant is the Maltese rock-centaury.
content.peopleAndCulture: Maltese life revolves around village festas: each summer weekend a different town honors its patron saint with brass bands, streets draped in banners, and some of the noisiest fireworks in Europe. Food shows every influence that has touched the islands: pastizzi, flaky pastries filled with ricotta or peas, rabbit stew called fenek, ftira bread, and Sicilian-style sweets. Traditional wooden fishing boats called luzzu are painted in bright colors with eyes on the bow to ward off evil. Soccer is the favorite sport, and water polo is played in seaside pools all summer. Carnival in Valletta brings floats and costumes, and Good Friday processions are solemn and grand. Many Maltese speak three languages and switch between them mid-sentence.
content.history: Farmers built stone temples on Malta between 3600 and 2500 BC, including Ġgantija on Gozo, older than the pyramids and among the oldest free-standing buildings on Earth. Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, and Normans all ruled the islands; the Arabs left the language. In 1530 the Knights of St. John, a military religious order, took over and in 1565 withstood the Great Siege by a massive Ottoman army, then built Valletta. Napoleon seized Malta in 1798, and Britain took it in 1800. During World War II Malta was bombed relentlessly as a British base, and the whole population was awarded the George Cross for bravery. Malta became independent on September 21, 1964, a republic in 1974, and joined the European Union in 2004.
funFacts: Malta's Ġgantija temples were built around 3600 BC, more than a thousand years before Egypt's Great Pyramid.
The Maltese language is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and the only one official in the European Union.
Malta has about 365 churches, roughly one for every day of the year, on islands smaller than many cities.
The George Cross for bravery, awarded to all of Malta in 1942, appears on the country's flag.
Malta has no rivers or lakes, so much of its drinking water comes from plants that turn seawater fresh.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.officialName: Republic of the Union of Myanmar

content.tagline: Golden pagodas along the Irrawaddy
content.overview:
Myanmar stretches down the western edge of mainland Southeast Asia, from snowy Himalayan foothills to the warm Andaman Sea. It borders India, Bangladesh, China, Laos and Thailand, and at about 677,000 km² it is roughly the size of Texas. The Irrawaddy River runs the length of the country like a spine, carrying rice barges past villages, temples and teak forests.

About 54 million people live here. Burmese is the official language, written in a rounded alphabet of circles that scribes once traced on palm leaves so the strokes would not tear them. Naypyidaw, a planned city of enormous empty highways, became the capital in 2005, replacing Yangon, which is still the largest city and home to the gold-covered Shwedagon Pagoda.

Most people are Buddhist, and monks in dark red robes collect their food in bowls each morning. Myanmar is ruled by its military, which seized power in 2021 after a short period of elected government.
content.landAndNature: Northern Myanmar climbs into the eastern Himalayas, where Hkakabo Razi rises above 5,800 meters and is often called Southeast Asia's highest peak. South of the mountains lies the dry central plain around Bagan and Mandalay, then the wide delta where the Irrawaddy splits into dozens of channels before reaching the sea. The monsoon soaks the coast from May to October; the Rakhine hills can receive over five meters of rain a year. Teak trees, prized for shipbuilding, grow in forests still worked by trained elephants. Tigers, clouded leopards, hoolock gibbons and the rare Irrawaddy dolphin survive here, and fishermen on Inle Lake row standing up, wrapping one leg around the oar.
content.peopleAndCulture: Myanmar has more than 130 ethnic groups, including the Bamar majority and the Shan, Karen, Kachin, Chin, Rakhine and Mon peoples, each with its own language and dress. Many people wear a longyi, a tube of cloth knotted at the waist, and paint their cheeks with thanaka, a pale yellow paste ground from bark that cools the skin and blocks sun. Meals center on rice with curries, fermented tea-leaf salad called laphet thoke, and mohinga, a fish-and-noodle soup eaten for breakfast. Thingyan, the water festival in April, welcomes the new year with days of soaking strangers in the street. Chinlone, a graceful team game with a woven rattan ball, has no winners or losers.
content.history: Pyu city-states traded along the Irrawaddy 2,000 years ago. From 1044 the kings of Bagan built more than 10,000 brick temples on one plain, thousands of which still stand. Later Burmese kingdoms fought Siam and China until Britain conquered the country in three wars between 1824 and 1885, ruling it as part of British India. Japan occupied Burma during World War II. Independence came in 1948, led by Aung San, who was assassinated months before it arrived. The army took power in 1962 and held it for decades. Elections in 2015 brought a partly civilian government, but the military seized full control again in 2021, sparking widespread protest and armed conflict. Since 2017, violence in Rakhine State has driven more than 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee to Bangladesh.
funFacts: The plain of Bagan holds more than 2,000 surviving temples and pagodas, built in a burst of construction lasting about 250 years.
Myanmar sets its clocks 6 hours and 30 minutes ahead of London, one of only a few countries using a half-hour offset.
Most of the world's rubies, including the prized pigeon-blood red stones, come from the Mogok valley in Myanmar.
Fishermen on Inle Lake balance on one leg at the stern and row with the other, keeping both hands free for nets.
The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is covered in real gold plates and topped with thousands of diamonds.

content.tagline: Black mountains above a blue Adriatic
content.overview:
Montenegro is one of Europe's smallest countries, a piece of the Balkan coast about the size of Connecticut, wedged between Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Kosovo, and Albania. Its name means black mountain, and the land earns it: dark pine ridges and bare gray limestone rise within a few kilometers of the Adriatic Sea.

About 620,000 people live here, most speaking Montenegrin, a language closely related to Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian. Podgorica is the capital and largest city, while the old royal town of Cetinje, high in the hills, remains the ceremonial capital. Montenegro is a parliamentary republic, independent since a referendum in 2006.

In summer the walled seaside towns of Kotor and Budva fill with visitors who swim in water clear enough to see the seabed and take boats out to tiny island churches. Inland, shepherds still drive sheep up to mountain pastures when the snow melts, and villages cure ham and make cheese much as they always have.
content.landAndNature: The Bay of Kotor cuts deep inland between cliffs, a drowned river canyon so steep that visitors often mistake it for a fjord. Behind it the Dinaric Alps climb past 2,500 meters at Bobotov Kuk in Durmitor National Park, where glacial lakes sit ringed by pine forest and the Tara River has carved a canyon roughly 1,300 meters deep. Much of the rock is karst, limestone riddled with caves, sinkholes, and underground rivers. Lake Skadar, the largest lake in the Balkans, is a maze of water lilies and reeds where pelicans nest. Bears, wolves, lynx, and chamois live in the forests, and while the coast keeps dry Mediterranean summers, the mountains get deep snow.
content.peopleAndCulture: Montenegrins have a Balkan reputation for tall stature, pride, and unhurried hospitality; the local word inat, meaning stubbornness, is worn almost as a badge. Most people belong to Orthodox Christian churches, alongside Muslim and Catholic communities. Food changes with altitude: grilled meats, smoked ham called pršut, and sheep cheese in the highlands; fish, squid, and olive oil on the coast. Singers called guslars still perform epic poems to the scrape of the gusle, a one-stringed fiddle. Water polo is the national passion, and Montenegro's team wins European medals despite the country's tiny population, with basketball and soccer close behind. Summer brings brass bands, carnival parades, and a flower festival in Kotor.
content.history: Illyrian tribes lived here before Rome took the coast. In the Middle Ages the Slavic realm of Duklja, later called Zeta, grew up in these mountains, and after the Ottoman Empire swept across the Balkans, Montenegro's prince-bishops held out in the highlands around Cetinje for centuries. Its independence was recognized in 1878. In 1918 Montenegro joined the new kingdom that became Yugoslavia, and after World War II it was one of Yugoslavia's six republics under the communist leader Tito. When Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s, wars across the region killed tens of thousands of people; Montenegro remained joined to Serbia and was affected by the fighting and by international sanctions. It voted narrowly for independence in 2006 and joined NATO in 2017.
funFacts: Montenegro's name in Montenegrin, Crna Gora, translates literally as black mountain, a description of its dark forested slopes.
The Tara River canyon is the deepest in Europe, dropping about 1,300 meters below the plateau around it.
Our Lady of the Rocks, an island in the Bay of Kotor, was built up over centuries by sailors dropping stones into the sea.
Montenegro's water polo team, drawn from about 620,000 people, regularly beats countries fifty times larger.
Sveti Stefan, a stone fishing village on a rocky islet, is joined to the mainland only by a narrow sandbar.

content.tagline: Steppe, sky and galloping horses
content.overview:
Mongolia is a vast, high, dry country squeezed between Russia and China, about the size of Alaska, with fewer people for its size than almost anywhere on Earth. Only around 3.5 million people live in a land of some 1.56 million km², and roughly half of them are in the capital, Ulan Bator, also written Ulaanbaatar, which is the coldest capital city in the world.

Mongolian is the national language, written both in the Cyrillic alphabet and in a traditional upright script that runs from top to bottom. Mongolia is a republic with an elected president and parliament. Perhaps a quarter of the population still lives as herders, moving with sheep, goats, horses, cattle and camels between seasonal pastures and living in gers, round felt tents that can be taken down and packed onto a truck in about an hour. Mining copper, coal and gold is the biggest industry, and cashmere from Mongolian goats is exported worldwide.
content.landAndNature: Mongolia is high and dry, averaging about 1,580 meters above sea level and far from any ocean. The Gobi spreads across the south, a stony rather than sandy desert where dinosaur fossils lie so near the surface that whole nests of eggs have been uncovered. Grassy steppe covers the center, forest and taiga rise in the north near Siberia, and the Altai peaks in the west carry glaciers. Winters drop below minus 30 degrees Celsius, and a harsh winter called a dzud can kill millions of animals. Snow leopards, gray wolves, wild Bactrian camels and Przewalski's horse, the last truly wild horse, live here.
content.peopleAndCulture: Herding shapes daily life: families eat mutton, steamed dumplings called buuz, and dairy foods including dried curd and airag, fermented mare's milk. A guest in a ger is always offered food and a place to sit. The three games of the Naadam festival each July are wrestling, archery and horse racing, in which children ride for more than 20 kilometers across open country. Throat singers produce two notes at once, a deep drone with a whistling melody above it, and the morin khuur, a horsehead fiddle, is the national instrument. Some western Mongolian hunters still ride out with trained golden eagles.
content.history: Nomadic empires rose and fell on these grasslands for thousands of years. In 1206 Temujin united the tribes and took the title Genghis Khan, building the largest connected land empire in history, which under his grandson Kublai Khan reached from Korea to Hungary and ruled China. The empire eventually broke apart, and from the 1600s Mongolia came under Chinese Qing rule. Mongolia declared independence in 1911 and, with Soviet backing, became a communist state in 1924, closely tied to the Soviet Union for nearly seventy years; monasteries were destroyed and monks killed in the 1930s. Peaceful protests in 1990 brought democracy, and Mongolia has held free elections since.
funFacts: Mongolia has one of the lowest population densities on Earth, with roughly two people per square kilometer.
Ulan Bator is the coldest national capital in the world, with winter temperatures falling below minus 30 degrees Celsius.
The Gobi Desert has produced some of the richest dinosaur finds anywhere, including nests of fossilized eggs.
Genghis Khan's empire became the largest connected land empire in history, stretching from Korea to eastern Europe.
At the Naadam horse races the jockeys are children, and the horses gallop over 20 kilometers of open steppe.

MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
MNP.officialName: Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands

content.tagline: Coral coasts on the Indian Ocean
content.overview:
Mozambique stretches down the southeast coast of Africa, a long curve of land facing the Indian Ocean with roughly 2,500 kilometers of beaches, dunes, and coral reefs. It is about twice the size of California and shares borders with Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini, and South Africa. The Zambezi, one of Africa's greatest rivers, crosses the country and spreads into a wide delta before reaching the sea.

About 33 million people live in Mozambique. Portuguese is the official language, left behind by centuries of Portuguese rule, but most families speak an African language such as Makhuwa, Sena, or Changana at home. The capital, Maputo, sits in the far south and keeps wide avenues lined with jacaranda trees, Art Deco buildings, and a fish market where buyers pick their catch and have it grilled on the spot.

Mozambique is a republic with an elected president. Most people farm maize, cassava, and cashews, and fishers work the warm, shallow waters offshore.
content.landAndNature: Most of Mozambique is low, hot, and flat, a coastal plain that climbs to plateaus and highlands in the north and west, where Mount Binga reaches 2,436 meters on the Zimbabwean border. Rain comes with the summer monsoon between November and April, and tropical cyclones sometimes sweep in off the Indian Ocean. The Bazaruto and Quirimbas archipelagos shelter reefs and seagrass beds where dugongs graze, and whale sharks and manta rays gather off Tofo. Sea turtles nest on the beaches. Inland, Gorongosa National Park, emptied of animals during years of war, has been restocked and now holds elephants, lions, buffalo, and clouds of waterbirds. Baobabs with fat, barrel-like trunks stand in the dry woodlands.
content.peopleAndCulture: Mozambique's peoples include the Makhuwa, Tsonga, Sena, and Shona, along with Swahili communities on the coast; the north has been Muslim for centuries while the south is largely Christian. Cooking mixes African, Portuguese, Indian, and Arab ideas: grilled piri-piri chicken, prawns, coconut-milk stews called matapa made with cassava leaves and ground peanuts, and Portuguese-style bread rolls. Makonde carvers in the north shape dark ebony into sculptures known worldwide, and masked dancers perform at ceremonies. Marrabenta music, played on homemade guitars, grew up in the neighborhoods of Maputo, and the Chopi people's timbila orchestras of wooden xylophones are recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is everywhere, and Mozambique-born Eusébio became one of the great players of the 1960s.
content.history: Bantu-speaking farmers settled the region around 2,000 years ago, and by the 900s Swahili merchants on the coast were trading gold, ivory, and enslaved people with Arabia, India, and beyond; Sofala was a famous port. Vasco da Gama landed in 1498, and Portugal took the coast and then the interior, running plantations and forced-labor systems and taking part in the slave trade. A liberation movement, FRELIMO, fought a war from 1964 until independence on June 25, 1975. A civil war followed from 1977 to 1992 that killed about a million people and scattered landmines across the countryside. Peace brought elections and rebuilding, and the economy has grown quickly, though cyclones and poverty remain heavy burdens.
funFacts: Mozambique's flag is the only national flag in the world showing a modern rifle, set beside a hoe and an open book.
Maputo's railway station, finished in the early 1900s with a green dome and wrought iron, is often called one of the world's most beautiful.
Mozambique joined the Commonwealth in 1995, the first member that had never been part of the British Empire.
The Ilha de Moçambique, a coral island barely three kilometers long, served as the colony's capital for almost 400 years.
Cashew trees, brought from Brazil by Portuguese traders, became one of Mozambique's best-known crops.

content.tagline: Where the Sahara meets the Atlantic
content.overview:
Mauritania stretches across the western Sahara in northwest Africa, with the Atlantic Ocean on one side and Mali and Algeria on the other, and Senegal along its southern river border. It is about one and a half times the size of Texas, but three-quarters of it is desert, and the population is only about 5 million. The capital, Nouakchott, was a small fishing village when it was chosen as capital in 1958 and has since exploded into a sprawling city of more than a million people where sand drifts into the streets.

Arabic is the official language, and Hassaniya Arabic is the everyday speech of most Mauritanians, while Pulaar, Soninke, and Wolof are spoken by peoples in the south; French is widely used in business. Mauritania is an Islamic republic, and essentially all its people are Muslim.
