Fishing in some of the richest waters in the world, iron ore mining, and herding camels and goats support the economy, and gold and oil have been developed more recently. The country's society is divided between Arab-Berber Moors and Black African communities.
content.landAndNature: Most of Mauritania is flat Saharan plain of sand and gravel, broken by the sandstone plateaus of the Adrar and Tagant, where old caravan towns sit beside date-palm oases and the Richat Structure, a 40-kilometer ring of rock nicknamed the Eye of the Sahara, is visible from space. Only the Senegal River valley in the far south is green enough for farming. The Atlantic coast is where the desert simply ends in the sea: at Banc d'Arguin National Park, dunes meet shallow waters where more than two million migrating shorebirds gather each winter, one of the greatest bird spectacles on Earth. Dolphins there famously help local Imraguen fishermen drive fish into their nets. Sandstorms, blistering heat, and years without rain shape life in the interior.
content.peopleAndCulture: Mauritanians are Moors of Arab and Berber descent, both the lighter-skinned Bidhan and the Haratin, descendants of enslaved people, along with Fulani, Soninke, and Wolof peoples of the south. Nomadic traditions live on: families gather in tents on woven rugs to drink three rounds of sweet green tea, and camel racing and milk are prized. Meals feature thieboudienne, rice with fish and vegetables, méchoui, whole roasted lamb, and couscous. Women wear flowing colorful veils called melhfa, and men wear the wide blue or white daraa robe. Griots sing poetry to the tidinit lute and the ardin harp, and the ancient libraries of Chinguetti hold rare manuscripts. Soccer is the leading sport, and the national team reached its first Africa Cup of Nations in 2019.
content.history: Rock art shows that the Sahara here was once grassland grazed by cattle. Berber tribes controlled the caravan routes, and Chinguetti, founded in the 1200s, became a holy city where pilgrims gathered before crossing the desert to Mecca. The Almoravid movement that conquered Morocco and Spain in the 1000s began in this region. Arab tribes arrived in the 1400s and 1500s and mixed with the Berbers to form the Moors. France took control in the early 1900s. Independence came on November 28, 1960. Mauritania has had several military coups, a war over Western Sahara in the 1970s, and ethnic tensions in 1989. It was the last country in the world to abolish slavery, in 1981, and it made slavery a crime only in 2007, though the practice has not fully ended.
funFacts: The Richat Structure, a 40-kilometer bull's-eye of rock in the desert, is so distinctive that astronauts use it as a landmark.
An iron-ore train in Mauritania is one of the longest in the world, stretching about 2.5 kilometers, and people ride free on top of the ore.
Mauritania was the last country on Earth to abolish slavery, in 1981.
At Banc d'Arguin, wild dolphins help fishermen by herding mullet toward their nets, a partnership going back generations.
Chinguetti's libraries hold Islamic manuscripts up to 800 years old, kept by families in a town slowly being buried by sand.

content.tagline: Rainbow island of the dodo
content.overview:
Mauritius is a small island nation in the Indian Ocean, about 2,000 kilometers off the southeast coast of Africa and east of Madagascar. The main island, ringed by coral reefs and white beaches, is about the size of Rhode Island, and the country also includes Rodrigues and several tiny outer islands. The capital, Port Louis, is a busy harbor city with a colonial-era market, skyscrapers, and a racecourse that is one of the oldest in the world.

About 1.3 million people live in Mauritius, and they are a true mix: descendants of Indian laborers, African slaves, Chinese traders, and French and British settlers live side by side, and Hindu temples, mosques, churches, and pagodas stand within blocks of each other. English is the official language of parliament, French dominates the media, and Mauritian Creole is what everyone speaks at home. Mauritius is a stable parliamentary republic and one of Africa's wealthiest and best-governed countries, earning its living from tourism, sugar, textiles, and financial services.
content.landAndNature: Mauritius was born from a volcano that rose from the sea about eight million years ago and is now extinct; its jagged peaks, like Le Morne Brabant and the three-fingered Trois Mamelles, are its worn remains. A central plateau of sugarcane fields and tea gardens slopes down to a coast almost entirely enclosed by coral reef, creating calm turquoise lagoons. At Chamarel, the Seven Colored Earths are dunes of sand in stripes of red, brown, violet, and blue. Black River Gorges National Park protects the last native forest, home to the pink pigeon, the echo parakeet, and the Mauritius kestrel, all rescued from the brink of extinction. The dodo, a flightless bird found only here, was wiped out within a century of humans arriving. The climate is tropical, with cyclone season in summer.
content.peopleAndCulture: About two-thirds of Mauritians are of Indian origin, and Hinduism is the largest religion, followed by Christianity and Islam, so the calendar is packed with festivals: Diwali lights up homes, Cavadee sees devotees carry decorated arches, Chinese New Year brings dragon dances, and Christmas falls in summer. Food blends everything: dholl puri flatbreads stuffed with split peas, Creole rougaille tomato stew, Chinese fried noodles, and French pastries, often eaten at street stalls. Sega, a dance and music born among enslaved Africans, is performed to the beat of the ravanne drum with swaying hips and bare feet on the beach, and is recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is popular, and horse racing at Champ de Mars draws big crowds.
content.history: Arab and Malay sailors knew the island, but it was uninhabited when the Portuguese arrived in the early 1500s. The Dutch settled in 1638, named it after Prince Maurice of Nassau, cut down its ebony forests, and left in 1710; by then the dodo was extinct. France took over in 1715, brought enslaved Africans to grow sugar, and built Port Louis. Britain captured the island in 1810 and, after abolishing slavery in 1835, brought about half a million laborers from India to work the plantations, shaping the nation's makeup. Mauritius became independent on March 12, 1968, and a republic in 1992. It has been a peaceful democracy ever since. Mauritius still claims the Chagos Islands, which Britain separated before independence.
funFacts: The dodo, a flightless bird found only on Mauritius, went extinct less than a century after humans arrived, around 1680.
The Mauritius kestrel numbered only four birds in 1974 and was saved by breeding programs, becoming a conservation legend.
Mauritius issued some of the world's most valuable postage stamps in 1847; a single Post Office stamp has sold for millions.
The Champ de Mars racecourse in Port Louis, opened in 1812, is the oldest in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Seven Colored Earths at Chamarel never mix, even after heavy rain, because the sands settle back into separate stripes.

content.tagline: The warm heart of Africa
content.overview:
Malawi is a long, thin landlocked country in southeastern Africa, about the size of Pennsylvania, lying along the western shore of Lake Malawi, which fills about a fifth of its territory. It borders Tanzania, Mozambique, and Zambia. The capital, Lilongwe, is a spread-out city in the center, while Blantyre in the south is the commercial hub. Malawians call their country the Warm Heart of Africa for the friendliness of its people.

About 21 million people live in Malawi, making it one of the most densely populated countries in Africa, and most of them farm small plots of corn, tobacco, tea, and sugarcane. English and Chewa, also called Chichewa, are the official languages, and Tumbuka, Yao, and others are spoken in different regions. Most Malawians are Christian, with a Muslim minority along the lake. Malawi is a presidential republic that has held multiparty elections since 1994. It is one of the world's poorest countries, but it is known for peace, having never fought a war with a neighbor.
content.landAndNature: Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, is the star: about 580 kilometers long and up to 700 meters deep, it is the third-largest lake in Africa and holds more species of fish than any other lake on Earth, over 1,000 kinds, most of them colorful cichlids found nowhere else. Its clear waters and sandy beaches look like an ocean shore. The Great Rift Valley that cradles the lake is walled by highlands: the Nyika Plateau in the north is a rolling grassland of orchids, zebras, and roan antelope, and Mount Mulanje in the south rises to 3,002 meters, the highest peak in south-central Africa. Liwonde National Park along the Shire River has elephants, hippos, and reintroduced lions and rhinos, and fish eagles cry over the water. Baobabs dot the hot lakeshore.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Chewa are the largest group, along with the Lomwe, Yao, Ngoni, and Tumbuka. Nsima, a thick corn porridge, is eaten with relish of beans, greens, or chambo, a lake fish grilled or fried. Malawi's most famous tradition is Gule Wamkulu, the great dance of the Chewa, performed by masked dancers representing spirits and animals; it is recognized by UNESCO. Vimbuza healing dances of the Tumbuka are also on the list. Music mixes drums, the one-stringed banjo, and modern gospel and reggae, and Lake of Stars is a well-known music festival on the beach. Soccer is the favorite sport, and netball is popular with women; the national netball team, the Queens, ranks among the world's best. Many villages gather under trees for meetings and storytelling.
content.history: Bantu-speaking farmers settled around the lake by the 1000s and formed the Maravi kingdom, whose name became Malawi, meaning flames, perhaps from the lake glittering at sunrise. In the 1800s Yao and Swahili traders carried enslaved people from the region to the coast, and the Scottish missionary David Livingstone reached the lake in 1859 and campaigned against the slave trade. Britain made the area the protectorate of Nyasaland in 1891. John Chilembwe led an uprising in 1915. Independence came on July 6, 1964 under Hastings Kamuzu Banda, who ruled as president for life for 30 years, banning long hair and bell-bottom trousers. A referendum in 1993 brought multiparty democracy. In 2020 Malawi's courts overturned a flawed election and ordered a rerun, a first in Africa.
funFacts: Lake Malawi holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth, and most live nowhere else.
In 2020 Malawi became the first African country whose courts annulled a presidential election and ordered a new vote.
Under President Banda, men with long hair and women in trousers could be turned away at the border.
A Malawian teenager, William Kamkwamba, built a windmill from scrap to power his village, a story told in a book and film.
Mount Mulanje's Sapitwa peak, whose name means don't go there, is the highest point in south-central Africa.

content.tagline: Rainforest, towers and two land halves
content.overview:
Malaysia comes in two pieces separated by about 640 kilometers of the South China Sea. Peninsular Malaysia hangs south from mainland Asia below Thailand, ending just above Singapore, while East Malaysia occupies the northern third of Borneo, the world's third largest island, alongside Indonesia and Brunei. Together they are a little larger than New Mexico. Kuala Lumpur, the capital, is known for the twin Petronas Towers, once the tallest buildings in the world.

About 34 million people live in Malaysia, and the population is a genuine mixture of Malays and Indigenous groups together with large Chinese and Indian communities whose ancestors arrived generations ago. Malay is the national language and English is widely spoken, with Mandarin, Tamil and dozens of Indigenous languages heard every day. Malaysia is a constitutional monarchy with an unusual arrangement: nine hereditary state rulers take turns as king, each serving five years. Palm oil, electronics and natural rubber drive the economy.
content.landAndNature: Malaysia sits just above the equator, hot and humid all year, and its rainforests are among the oldest on Earth, far older than the Amazon. Mount Kinabalu in Borneo rises to 4,095 meters, the highest peak in Malaysia and a granite giant still slowly growing. Mangroves and coral reefs line the coasts, and the waters off Sipadan are famous among divers. Borneo's forests shelter orangutans, pygmy elephants and proboscis monkeys with long drooping noses, while the rafflesia, the largest single flower in the world, can reach a meter across and smells of rotting meat. The caves at Gunung Mulu include a chamber big enough to swallow dozens of airliners.
content.peopleAndCulture: Malaysian food is one of the country's great pleasures: nasi lemak, coconut rice with chili paste, is the unofficial national dish, and roti canai, laksa noodle soup, satay skewers and Chinese noodles are sold at open-air hawker stalls at all hours. Islam is the official religion, while Buddhist, Hindu, Christian and Indigenous communities keep their own festivals, so the calendar is unusually full: Hari Raya, Chinese New Year, Deepavali and Christmas are all marked, often with open houses where neighbors of any background are welcome. Badminton is a national obsession, and sepak takraw is played with a rattan ball and no hands.
content.history: Trading ports flourished along the Strait of Malacca for well over a thousand years, and the Malacca Sultanate became a great center of commerce in the 1400s, spreading Islam through the region. Portugal seized Malacca in 1511, the Dutch took it in 1641, and Britain gradually gained control of the peninsula and the Borneo territories, bringing Chinese and Indian laborers to work tin mines and rubber plantations. Japan occupied the region during World War II. Malaya became independent on August 31, 1957, and in 1963 joined with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia; Singapore left two years later. Malaysia has since grown into one of Southeast Asia's stronger economies.
funFacts: Nine of Malaysia's states have hereditary rulers who take turns serving five-year terms as the country's king.
The Petronas Twin Towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004 and are joined by a sky bridge.
Malaysia's rainforests are roughly 130 million years old, far older than the Amazon.
The rafflesia, found in Malaysian forests, produces the largest single flower on Earth and smells like rotting meat.
Sarawak Chamber at Gunung Mulu is among the largest cave chambers known, big enough to hold many jumbo jets.

content.tagline: Dunes, desert elephants, and endless sky
content.overview:
Namibia occupies Africa's southwest corner, where the Namib Desert, probably the oldest desert on Earth, runs the entire length of the Atlantic coast. The country is bigger than Texas but one of the emptiest places on the planet: only about 2.6 million people live there, roughly three for every square kilometer.

Windhoek, the capital, stands on a highland plateau in the middle of the country. English is the official language, while Afrikaans and German are still widely spoken from colonial days, and most families use a language such as Oshiwambo, Herero, Khoekhoe, Kwangali, Lozi, Ndonga, or Tswana at home. Namibia is a republic with an elected president, independent only since 1990, which makes it one of Africa's youngest nations.

Mining for diamonds and uranium, cattle and sheep ranching, fishing the cold Atlantic, and visitors drawn to the dunes and game parks keep the country running.
content.landAndNature: Two deserts bracket Namibia: the Namib along the coast, where the dunes of Sossusvlei rise more than 300 meters and glow orange at sunrise, and the Kalahari in the east. Between them lies a dry central plateau of thornbush and rocky hills. The cold Benguela Current keeps the coast foggy and almost rainless, and that fog is the only water for beetles that stand on their heads to let droplets run into their mouths. Etosha National Park surrounds a vast salt pan where elephants, black rhinos, lions, and springbok crowd the waterholes. Desert-adapted elephants and lions survive in the dry northwest, and Cape fur seals pack the beaches by the tens of thousands.
content.peopleAndCulture: The largest group is the Ovambo, alongside Herero, Damara, Nama, Kavango, Himba, San, and Afrikaner communities among many others. Herero women wear long Victorian-style dresses and horn-shaped headdresses, while Himba people in the northwest coat their skin and hair with a red mixture of ochre and butterfat. Most Namibians are Christian. Meals range from oshifima, a stiff millet porridge, to biltong, dried spiced meat, with German-influenced bakeries and sausages in Windhoek and Swakopmund. Soccer and rugby draw crowds, and the sprinter Frankie Fredericks won four Olympic silver medals in the 1990s. Independence Day on March 21 fills the streets with parades, and village conservancies manage wildlife and share the income from tourism.
content.history: San hunter-gatherers have lived in this land for tens of thousands of years, leaving rock engravings at Twyfelfontein; Bantu-speaking herders and farmers arrived later. Germany claimed the territory as German South West Africa in 1884. When the Herero and Nama peoples rose up against colonial land seizures in 1904, German forces drove them into the desert and into camps, killing the great majority of both peoples, a genocide that Germany formally acknowledged in 2021. After World War I South Africa took over and later imposed its apartheid racial laws. The SWAPO movement fought a long independence war from 1966, and Namibia finally became independent on March 21, 1990, with Sam Nujoma as its first president.
funFacts: Namibia was among the first countries in the world to write protection of the environment into its constitution.
The Skeleton Coast takes its name from the shipwrecks and whale bones left along its fog-bound beaches.
The Fish River Canyon is about 160 kilometers long and up to 550 meters deep, often called the second largest canyon on Earth.
The NamibRand Reserve has some of the darkest night skies anywhere and is protected as an international dark sky reserve.
In Deadvlei, camel thorn trees that died around 900 years ago still stand on a white clay pan, too dry to rot away.

content.tagline: Sahara sands and the great river
content.overview:
Niger is a landlocked country in West Africa, roughly twice the size of Texas and mostly Sahara Desert. Its name comes from the Niger River, which curves through the far southwestern corner and supplies the country's only major waterway, its capital, and much of its best farmland. Algeria and Libya lie to the north, with Chad, Nigeria, Benin, Burkina Faso, and Mali around the other sides.

About 26 million people live in Niger, nearly all of them in the greener southern strip near the Nigerian border. French is the official language, while Hausa, Zarma, Tamasheq, Fulfulde, and Kanuri are the languages of daily life. Niamey, the capital, stands on the banks of the Niger River.

Niger has one of the youngest populations on Earth, with about half its people under fifteen. Most families grow millet and sorghum or herd cattle, goats, and camels, and uranium is mined in the desert north. Niger is a republic, though the army seized power in a coup in 2023.
content.landAndNature: Most of Niger is desert. The Ténéré, a sea of sand and gravel in the east, is one of the emptiest places on the planet, and the dark volcanic Aïr Mountains rise from it, hiding pools and rock paintings made by herders back when the Sahara was green. Daytime temperatures often pass 40 degrees Celsius. In the south a belt of dry grassland called the Sahel gets a short rainy season, and the Niger River floods each year, watering rice fields where hippos wallow. The last wild giraffes in West Africa, a pale subspecies, wander among villages near Kouré, and W National Park shelters elephants, lions, and cheetahs.
content.peopleAndCulture: Niger's largest groups are the Hausa and Zarma farmers of the south, with Tuareg, Fulani, Kanuri, and Toubou herders across the north. Nearly everyone is Muslim. Millet is the staple, pounded into flour for thick porridge or dumplings and eaten with sauces of baobab leaf, okra, or peanut. Tuareg men wear the tagelmust, a long indigo head cloth, and travel by camel; the silver Agadez cross they make is worn all across West Africa. At the Cure Salée gathering, Wodaabe men dance the Gerewol for hours in bright makeup while women judge them. Traditional wrestling is the national sport, with a yearly championship that fills stadiums.
content.history: Rock art in the Sahara shows people herding cattle and hunting here thousands of years ago, when the desert was grassland. Later the region sat astride trans-Saharan caravan routes; Agadez grew into a major trading city, and parts of Niger came under the Songhai, Bornu, and Hausa states. France conquered the territory around 1900 and governed it as part of French West Africa. Niger became independent on August 3, 1960. Uranium discovered in the north brought income but also dependence on world prices, severe droughts struck in the 1970s and 1980s, and Tuareg rebellions broke out in the desert. Elected governments and military coups have alternated since, most recently in 2023.
funFacts: Niger and neighboring Nigeria are both named after the Niger River, which crosses only one corner of Niger itself.
The Tree of Ténéré was once the most isolated tree on Earth, with no other tree within about 400 kilometers.
Niger holds some of Africa's richest dinosaur beds; Nigersaurus, found here, had more than 500 teeth in a wide, straight-edged mouth.
The mud-brick minaret of the Agadez mosque, about 27 meters tall and studded with wooden beams, has been rebuilt for centuries.
Roughly 600 West African giraffes, the last wild ones anywhere, live unfenced among farms southeast of Niamey.

content.tagline: Africa's most populous nation
content.overview:
Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, home to more than 220 million people, about one in every six Africans. It faces the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, covers a little more land than Texas and Oklahoma together, and borders Benin, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon.

English is the official language, a shared tongue among speakers of more than 500 others; Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo are the largest. Abuja, a planned city built in the middle of the country, became the capital in 1991, while Lagos on the coast is the biggest city in Africa and the engine of its business. Nigeria is a federal republic of 36 states with an elected president.

Nigeria pumps more oil than any other African country, but abroad it is just as well known for what it makes: Nollywood, one of the busiest film industries in the world, and Afrobeats music that fills playlists from Lagos to London.
content.landAndNature: Nigeria changes as you travel north. The coast is a maze of lagoons, sandbars, and the Niger Delta, where the river splits into hundreds of creeks through the largest mangrove forest in Africa. Behind it lies rainforest, then wide savanna across the middle belt, and finally dry Sahel near the Sahara, where Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s. The Jos Plateau rises cool in the center, and Chappal Waddi near the Cameroon border, at about 2,400 meters, is the highest point. Forest elephants, chimpanzees, and rare Cross River gorillas survive in the southeastern hills, the stocky drill monkey lives only here and in Cameroon, and hippos and manatees swim the delta creeks.
content.peopleAndCulture: Nigeria has as many cultures as languages. Yoruba towns hold masquerade festivals with towering costumed figures, the Igbo celebrate the new yam harvest each August, and Hausa emirates parade horsemen in a durbar at the end of Ramadan. Roughly half the country is Muslim and half Christian. The food is bold and spicy: jollof rice, whose recipe Nigerians and Ghanaians argue over endlessly, egusi soup thickened with melon seeds, pounded yam, and suya, skewered beef rubbed with peanut and pepper. Fela Kuti invented Afrobeat in the 1970s, and Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart is read worldwide. Soccer is a national obsession, and the Super Eagles have won three Africa Cup of Nations titles.
content.history: The Nok people were smelting iron and sculpting life-size terracotta heads more than 2,000 years ago. Later came the kingdoms of Ife and Benin, whose brass and bronze casting astonished European visitors, the Igbo communities of the southeast, and the Hausa city-states and Sokoto Caliphate of the north. From the 1500s this coast became a center of the transatlantic slave trade, and more than a million people were shipped away from its ports. Britain seized Lagos in 1861 and by 1914 governed the whole territory. Nigeria became independent on October 1, 1960. The Biafran civil war from 1967 to 1970 cost around a million lives, mostly from hunger. Military rule ended in 1999, and elections have been held since.
funFacts: Nollywood releases well over a thousand films a year, making Nigeria one of the world's largest film producers by number of titles.
More than 500 languages are spoken in Nigeria, more than in almost any other country on Earth.
The Benin Bronzes, taken by British forces in 1897, sit in museums around the world, and some have now been returned to Nigeria.
The town of Igbo-Ora calls itself the twin capital of the world, because twins are born there at an unusually high rate.
Lagos began as a cluster of islands in a lagoon and now holds over 15 million people, growing by thousands every week.

content.tagline: Land of lakes and volcanoes
content.overview:
Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America by area, a bridge of land between Honduras and Costa Rica with the Caribbean Sea on one side and the Pacific Ocean on the other. It covers about 130,000 km², roughly the size of Greece, and a chain of volcanoes marches down its Pacific side.

About 7 million people live in Nicaragua, nearly all speaking Spanish, with English Creole and Indigenous languages such as Miskito spoken along the Caribbean coast. Managua, the capital, sits on the shore of Lake Managua and has been rebuilt after earthquakes more than once. The country is a republic whose government has been led by President Daniel Ortega since 2007; opposition parties and independent news outlets say they have been heavily restricted.

Coffee, beef, sugar and gold are the main exports. Nicaragua is famous for Lake Nicaragua, a freshwater sea big enough to hold islands with their own volcanoes, and for baseball, which here beats soccer.
content.landAndNature: A line of about twenty volcanoes, several of them active, runs parallel to the Pacific coast; Masaya lets visitors look down into a glowing lava lake, and Cerro Negro is young enough that people sled down its black ash slopes on boards. Lake Nicaragua, or Cocibolca, is the largest lake in Central America and holds Ometepe, an island formed by two volcanoes joined at the waist. Bull sharks swim up the San Juan River into the lake, one of the few freshwater populations in the world. The Caribbean side is a wide, wet lowland of rainforest, pine savanna and lagoons, including the Bosawás reserve, one of the biggest forests north of the Amazon. Howler monkeys, jaguars, sloths and hundreds of bird species live there.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Nicaraguans are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent, while the Caribbean coast is home to Miskito, Mayangna, Rama, Garifuna and Creole communities with their own languages and music. Gallo pinto, rice fried with red beans, is eaten at almost every meal, often with fried plantains, cheese and a corn drink. Nacatamales, big banana-leaf parcels of corn dough, meat and vegetables, are a Sunday tradition. Baseball is the national passion, and Dennis Martínez became the first Nicaraguan to pitch a perfect game in the major leagues. Rubén Darío, born here in 1867, changed Spanish poetry forever and is honored as the country's greatest writer. Patron saint festivals fill towns with masked dancers, fireworks and marimba bands.
content.history: Chorotega and Nicarao peoples farmed corn around the lakes long before Spanish ships arrived in 1522. Spain ruled for 300 years; Nicaragua became independent in 1821 and joined, then left, a short-lived Central American federation. In the 1800s the route across the country was a prized shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. United States Marines occupied Nicaragua for much of 1912–1933, and the guerrilla leader Augusto Sandino fought them until his murder in 1934. The Somoza family then ruled as dictators for more than 40 years. The Sandinista revolution overthrew them in 1979, and a war followed through the 1980s between the Sandinista government and US-backed Contra rebels, killing tens of thousands. Elections in 1990 brought peace. Protests in 2018 were met with force and hundreds died.
funFacts: Lake Nicaragua is home to bull sharks that swim in from the sea, leaping up the rapids of the San Juan River.
People sandboard down Cerro Negro volcano, one of the youngest volcanoes in the Americas, at speeds over 80 kilometers per hour.
Baseball, not soccer, is Nicaragua's national sport, brought by American sailors and teachers in the 1800s.
Deaf children in Managua invented an entirely new sign language in the 1980s, which linguists study as a language being born.
Ometepe island is shaped like a figure eight because two volcanoes grew together in the middle of a lake.

content.tagline: A country built below the sea
content.overview:
The Netherlands is a small, flat, crowded country on the North Sea coast of Western Europe, sharing borders with Germany and Belgium. About a quarter of its land lies below sea level, held back by dunes, dikes, and enormous storm barriers; much of that land was once seabed, pumped dry over centuries to make fields called polders. All together it is roughly twice the size of New Jersey.

About 18 million people live here and speak Dutch, and nearly everyone learns English at school as well. Amsterdam, laced with canals and tall narrow houses, is the capital, while the king, government, and parliament sit in The Hague, which also hosts international courts. The Netherlands is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament and was a founding member of the European Union.

Bicycles outnumber people, trains link compact cities, and fields and glass greenhouses make this small country one of the world's biggest exporters of food.
content.landAndNature: The Netherlands is famously level: its highest point, the Vaalserberg in the far southeast, reaches only 322 meters, and much of the country is a patchwork of drained polders divided by straight canals and ditches. The Rhine, Meuse, and Scheldt rivers meet here in a wide delta before spilling into the North Sea, and the Delta Works, a system of dams, sluices, and movable barriers, guards the southwest against storm surges. Along the north coast the Wadden Sea drains twice a day into vast mudflats where seals rest and millions of migrating birds feed. Spring brings tulip fields in stripes of color, and storks, spoonbills, and godwits nest in the wet meadows.
content.peopleAndCulture: Dutch life is organized around bicycles: there are more bikes than people, and children ride to school in all weather on separate red-paved paths. People have a reputation for being direct, punctual, and fond of gezelligheid, a hard-to-translate word for cozy togetherness. The food is plain and good: herring eaten with raw onion, stroopwafels, thin pancakes, cheeses such as Gouda and Edam, and salty licorice. Dutch painters changed art forever, from Rembrandt and Vermeer to Van Gogh. Soccer is the national game, and the Dutch style called Total Football reshaped the sport in the 1970s. Speed skating is huge, and when the canals freeze hard, whole towns take to the ice.
content.history: Germanic and Celtic tribes lived in this delta when Rome reached the Rhine. In the Middle Ages trading towns grew rich on shipping and wool, and in 1568 the Dutch provinces rebelled against Spanish rule, winning independence after eighty years of war. The 1600s were the Dutch Golden Age: Amsterdam became Europe's richest port and home to the world's first stock exchange, while the Dutch East and West India Companies built a trading empire from Indonesia to the Caribbean and New York, seizing colonies and trafficking hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Nazi Germany occupied the country from 1940 to 1945 and murdered about 100,000 Dutch Jews, among them Anne Frank. After the war the Netherlands helped found the European Union.
funFacts: Dutch people are the tallest in the world on average, with men close to 1.83 meters.
Schiphol Airport near Amsterdam sits about four meters below sea level, on the bed of a lake that was drained in the 1850s.
Kinderdijk has nineteen windmills from the 1700s that once pumped water out of the polders using wind power alone.
Nearly all Dutch children earn a swimming diploma, practicing in clothes and shoes, because water is never far away.
King's Day on April 27 turns the whole country orange, and children sell their old toys on the sidewalks.

content.tagline: Fjords, northern lights, and midnight sun
content.overview:
Norway runs up the western edge of Scandinavia in a long, narrow strip, its coastline so chewed by fjords and islands that, measured around every inlet, it stretches for tens of thousands of kilometers. The country is slightly larger than New Mexico, reaches far above the Arctic Circle, and shares land borders with Sweden, Finland, and Russia.

About 5.5 million people live in Norway, most of them in the south near Oslo, the capital at the head of a long fjord. Norwegian has two written forms, Bokmål and Nynorsk, and Sami languages are spoken by the Indigenous Sami people of the north. Norway is a constitutional monarchy with a king and an elected parliament called the Storting.

Oil and gas found under the North Sea in the 1960s made Norway wealthy, and the government saves much of that money in a fund meant for future generations. Almost all the country's electricity comes from water rushing down mountains through hydropower stations.
content.landAndNature: Glaciers of the last ice age gouged Norway's fjords, long sea inlets with cliffs dropping straight into deep water; Sognefjord reaches more than 200 kilometers inland. Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier on mainland Europe, and Galdhøpiggen, the highest peak, stands 2,469 meters tall. North of the Arctic Circle the sun never sets for weeks in summer and never rises for weeks in winter, when the aurora borealis ripples green across the sky. The Gulf Stream keeps the coast surprisingly mild and ice-free. Puffins, sea eagles, and millions of seabirds nest on cliff ledges, while reindeer, moose, arctic foxes, and lemmings live inland and musk oxen graze the Dovrefjell plateau.
content.peopleAndCulture: Norwegians spend time outdoors in every season, an idea they call friluftsliv, or open-air living, and children play outside in snow and rain from nursery age. Skiing began here, and Norway has won more Winter Olympic medals than any other country; cross-country skiing, biathlon, and ski jumping are followed the way soccer is elsewhere. The food leans on the sea: salmon, cod dried into stockfish, pickled herring, along with brown cheese, waffles, and open sandwiches. Constitution Day on May 17 fills the streets with children's parades and national costumes called bunads. The Sami herd reindeer and have their own parliament and flag.
content.history: Hunters followed the retreating ice into Norway roughly 11,000 years ago. From about 793, Norse seafarers known as the Vikings raided and traded across Europe, settled Iceland and Greenland, and reached North America around the year 1000, where Leif Erikson landed in a place he called Vinland. Harald Fairhair united much of Norway in the late 800s, and Christianity arrived soon after. Plague and politics left Norway under Danish rule for four centuries, then Swedish rule after 1814, the year it wrote its constitution. Full independence came peacefully in 1905. Nazi Germany occupied the country from 1940 to 1945, and resistance fighters sabotaged a plant making heavy water for German research. Oil found in 1969 transformed the economy.
funFacts: Measured around every fjord and island, Norway's coastline runs roughly 100,000 kilometers, more than twice the distance around the equator.
The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded each December in Oslo, the only Nobel prize not handed out in Sweden.
A king penguin at Edinburgh Zoo named Nils Olav is an honorary member of Norway's King's Guard and has been knighted.
In the town of Rjukan, giant mirrors on a mountainside bounce winter sunlight into the square, which otherwise sits in shadow for months.
Salmon sushi was largely a Norwegian idea, promoted in Japan during the 1980s to sell farmed Atlantic salmon.

content.tagline: Home of the highest mountains on Earth
content.overview:
Nepal is wedged between India and China along the spine of the Himalayas, a rectangle of land about the size of Arkansas that climbs from steamy lowland jungle to the summit of Mount Everest in less than 200 kilometers. Eight of the world's fourteen mountains above 8,000 meters stand wholly or partly inside its borders.

About 30 million people live in Nepal, speaking Nepali as the national language along with more than 100 others. Kathmandu, the capital, fills a green valley ringed by peaks, its old squares crowded with pagoda-roofed temples, brick palaces and shrines where pigeons, monks and motorbikes share the same courtyard.

Nepal was a kingdom for more than 200 years and became a federal republic in 2008. Most Nepalis are Hindu, with a large Buddhist minority; the Buddha was born at Lumbini in the southern plains. Farming terraces, tourism and the work of Nepalis abroad support much of the country.
content.landAndNature: Nepal has three stacked worlds. The Terai in the south is flat, hot and fertile, part of the Ganges plain. Above it rise the green middle hills, carved into stepped terraces where rice and millet grow. Higher still stand the Himalayas, including Everest at 8,849 meters, Kanchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Annapurna and Manaslu. Rivers born of glaciers cut gorges deeper than any in the world; the Kali Gandaki runs between two 8,000-meter giants. Chitwan and Bardiya national parks in the lowlands protect one-horned rhinos, Bengal tigers, gharial crocodiles and wild elephants. Snow leopards and red pandas live in the high forests, and the danphe, a rainbow-colored pheasant, is the national bird.
content.peopleAndCulture: Nepal is a mosaic of peoples: Newars in the Kathmandu Valley, Sherpas and Tamangs in the mountains, Magars, Gurungs, Tharus, Madhesis and many more. Dal bhat, lentil soup over rice with vegetable curry and pickles, is eaten twice a day by most families, and momo dumplings are the favorite snack. Festivals fill the calendar: Dashain, the longest, brings families home for two weeks, and Tihar honors crows, dogs and cows on separate days. The national sport is volleyball, though cricket and soccer draw big crowds. Sherpa climbers are the backbone of Everest expeditions, and Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit with Edmund Hillary in 1953. Nepal's flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
content.history: The Kathmandu Valley has been settled for more than 2,000 years, and Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini around the 500s BC. Newar kings built the valley's three rival royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, filling them with carved wooden temples. In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered the valley and united Nepal. British armies fought the Gorkhas to a standstill in 1814–1816 and afterward began recruiting Gurkha soldiers, who still serve in the British and Indian armies. Nepal was never colonized. The Rana family ruled as hereditary prime ministers from 1846 until 1951. A Maoist insurgency from 1996 to 2006 killed thousands, and in 2008 parliament abolished the monarchy. A huge earthquake in 2015 killed about 9,000 people and toppled historic temples.
funFacts: Nepal's flag is the world's only non-rectangular national flag, made of two stacked triangles bearing a moon and a sun.
Nepal keeps its clocks 5 hours and 45 minutes ahead of London, an offset shared with no other country.
Mount Everest grows a few millimeters taller each year as the Indian plate keeps pushing into Asia.
There is no New Year's Day in January here: the official Bikram Sambat calendar is about 57 years ahead and starts in April.
Kathmandu's Boudhanath is one of the largest stupas in the world, with painted eyes looking out in four directions.

content.tagline: The world's smallest island republic
content.overview:
Nauru is a single oval island in the Pacific Ocean, just south of the equator and about 300 kilometers from its nearest neighbor. At 21 km² it is the smallest republic on Earth and the third-smallest country of any kind, after Vatican City and Monaco. A person can drive all the way around it on the coast road in about half an hour.

Roughly 12,000 people live on Nauru, almost all of them in a narrow ring of villages between the beach and the cliffs. English and Nauruan are the official languages. Nauru has no official capital city in the usual sense; government offices sit in the district of Yaren, which is listed as the capital. The country is a republic with an elected parliament of 19 members.

For a few decades Nauru was extraordinarily rich from mining phosphate rock, then the money and much of the island's interior ran out.
content.landAndNature: A flat coastal strip of coconut palms and pandanus trees rings the island, rising to a limestone plateau Nauruans call Topside. That plateau was once thick with phosphate, a mineral made from ancient seabird droppings piled up over millions of years and prized as fertilizer. Mining stripped away the soil and left a moonscape of jagged coral pinnacles across about four-fifths of the interior. Buada Lagoon, a brackish pond ringed by trees, is the island's only sizable body of fresh-ish water. Offshore, coral reefs drop away steeply into deep ocean, and frigatebirds and noddies wheel above. Nauru gets steady sun, heavy tropical downpours, and droughts that can last months.
content.peopleAndCulture: Nauruans trace descent through twelve traditional clans, and the country's flag shows a twelve-pointed star for them. Families are close, feasts are large, and fish, coconut and rice are everyday foods, though imported canned and packaged food became common during the mining years. A striking old tradition is frigatebird catching: young birds are lured in, tamed and kept, then sometimes released to return home. Angam Day on October 26 marks the moment in 1932 when the Nauruan population recovered to 1,500 after disease and war had nearly wiped it out. Australian rules football and weightlifting are the favorite sports, and Nauru has won Commonwealth Games gold medals in weightlifting.
content.history: Micronesian and Polynesian voyagers settled Nauru at least 3,000 years ago. A British whaling captain sighted it in 1798 and named it Pleasant Island. Germany annexed Nauru in 1888, and phosphate was discovered in 1900. Australia, Britain and New Zealand mined it under a League of Nations mandate; Japan occupied the island during World War II and deported more than 1,200 Nauruans to Chuuk, where many died. Nauru became independent on January 31, 1968, bought out the mining company and, briefly, had one of the world's highest incomes per person. Bad investments and exhausted phosphate left the country nearly bankrupt by 2000. Since 2001 Nauru has earned much of its income by hosting an Australian offshore center for asylum seekers, an arrangement widely criticized by human rights groups.
funFacts: Nauru has no army, no rivers, and for many years no capital city in the ordinary sense.
The country once ran an airline with a single plane; when it needed repairs, the whole nation's air service stopped.
Nauru's phosphate began as seabird droppings, called guano, that built up on coral over millions of years.
The island's ring road is about 19 kilometers long, and driving it takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes.
Nauru was the smallest country ever to compete at the Olympic Games when it debuted in 1996.

content.tagline: Land of the long white cloud
content.overview:
New Zealand lies in the South Pacific about 2,000 kilometers southeast of Australia, far enough from anywhere that it was one of the last large landmasses humans reached. Two long islands, simply called the North Island and the South Island, plus hundreds of smaller ones, add up to roughly the area of the United Kingdom.

About 5 million people live here, and sheep outnumber them several times over. English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language are all official. Wellington, on a windy harbor at the bottom of the North Island, is the capital and the world's southernmost capital city; Auckland, further north, is the biggest city. New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, and it was the first country in the world where women won the right to vote, in 1893.

The country is known for mountains, glaciers, volcanoes, rugby, and a film industry that turned its valleys into Middle-earth.
content.landAndNature: Because New Zealand broke away from other lands about 80 million years ago, its wildlife evolved almost without mammals, so birds took over the jobs mammals usually do. The kiwi is a shaggy, nearly wingless night bird that lays an egg about a fifth of its own weight; the kea is a mountain parrot clever enough to pick apart backpacks. The Southern Alps run the length of the South Island, topped by Aoraki / Mount Cook at 3,724 meters, with glaciers that flow down into rainforest. The North Island has active volcanoes, boiling mud pools and geysers around Rotorua and Taupō, and the country sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, so earthquakes are common. Fiordland's flooded valleys, including Milford Sound, drop straight into deep black water.
content.peopleAndCulture: Māori, who arrived by ocean-going canoe from Polynesia, make up about one in six New Zealanders, and Māori words, place names and ceremonies are woven into daily life. The haka, a chanted posture dance, is performed at welcomes, funerals and before rugby matches by the All Blacks, the country's famous national team. Food cooked in a hāngī, an earth oven heated with hot stones, is a feast staple. New Zealanders call themselves Kiwis and are proud of inventing bungee jumping as a commercial sport and the electric fence, and of Edmund Hillary, the beekeeper who first climbed Everest with Tenzing Norgay. Pavlova, a crisp meringue cake piled with cream and kiwifruit, is claimed by both New Zealand and Australia.
content.history: Polynesian voyagers settled Aotearoa around 1250–1300, becoming the Māori and organizing into iwi, or tribes. Dutch navigator Abel Tasman sighted the coast in 1642, and James Cook mapped it in 1769. British settlers, whalers and missionaries followed. In 1840 more than 500 Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed the Treaty of Waitangi, but the English and Māori versions promised different things, and disputes over land led to wars in the 1860s and huge confiscations. New Zealand became self-governing and gave women the vote in 1893. Its soldiers suffered heavy losses at Gallipoli in 1915, remembered each Anzac Day. Since the 1970s the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated treaty breaches and arranged settlements, and the Māori language has been revived in schools and broadcasting.
funFacts: New Zealand has no native land snakes, and its only native land mammals are three species of bat.
The Lord of the Rings and Hobbit films were shot across the country, and the Hobbiton movie set is still open to visitors.
Wellington is the world's southernmost capital city and one of the windiest cities on Earth.
New Zealand was the first self-governing country to give women the vote, in 1893, decades before Britain or the United States.
The kakapo, a fat flightless parrot that climbs trees and cannot fly, numbers only a couple of hundred birds.

content.tagline: Frankincense, forts, and desert seas
content.overview:
Oman sits on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, with long coasts on the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and borders with the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Yemen. At about 310,000 km² it is roughly the size of Poland, and much of it is desert, gravel plain and bare mountain.

About 5 million people live in Oman, and Arabic is the official language, though English is widely used in business and schools. Muscat, the capital, is a low white city squeezed between dark mountains and the sea, guarded by Portuguese-built forts and famous for its grand mosque and opera house.

Oman is a monarchy ruled by a sultan, with an appointed council and a partly elected consultative assembly. Oil and gas pay for much of the country, but Oman is also known for dates, fish, copper and frankincense, the fragrant tree resin that made its southern coast rich thousands of years ago.
content.landAndNature: The Hajar Mountains curve along the north, rising to Jebel Shams at about 3,000 meters above a canyon so deep it is nicknamed Oman's Grand Canyon. Between the peaks, villages grow pomegranates and roses on terraces watered by falaj channels, ancient stone canals that carry mountain water for kilometers by gravity alone. Inland lies the Rub al Khali, the Empty Quarter, one of the largest sand deserts on Earth, and the Wahiba Sands, where dunes run in long orange ridges. The southern region of Dhofar catches the Indian Ocean monsoon each summer, turning its hills startlingly green. Wadis hold clear pools year-round, Arabian oryx roam protected reserves, and thousands of green turtles nest on the beach at Ras al Jinz.
content.peopleAndCulture: Omanis are known for quiet hospitality: guests are greeted with dates and cardamom coffee poured from a long-spouted pot called a dallah. Men often wear a white dishdasha robe and a kuma cap or a wrapped turban, and many carry a curved dagger, the khanjar, which appears on the national flag. Shuwa, meat spiced and wrapped in leaves then buried in a hot pit for a day or more, is the great feast dish. Camel racing and bullfighting without killing, where two bulls push head to head, are traditional entertainments, and soccer is the modern favorite. Omani sailors were legendary navigators, and their dhows carried goods to India, Africa and China.
content.history: Copper from Oman was traded to Mesopotamia more than 4,000 years ago, when the region may have been the land Sumerians called Magan. Frankincense from Dhofar traveled by camel caravan and ship to Egypt, Greece and Rome. Islam arrived in the 600s during the Prophet Muhammad's lifetime, and most Omanis follow the Ibadi branch. Portugal seized Muscat in 1507 and held it until Omani forces drove them out in 1650. Oman then built a maritime empire of its own, taking Zanzibar and stretches of the East African coast; for a time the sultan ruled from Zanzibar rather than Muscat. Britain gained strong influence in the 1800s. In 1970 Sultan Qaboos took power from his father and used oil income to build schools, hospitals and roads across a country that had almost none.
funFacts: Oman's falaj irrigation channels have carried mountain water to farms for about 2,000 years, and some are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
The Dhofar region turns green each summer when monsoon clouds sweep in, while the rest of Arabia bakes.
Frankincense trees grow wild in Oman, and their dried sap once traded for roughly its weight in gold.
Oman ruled the island of Zanzibar off Africa, and for part of the 1800s its sultan lived there instead of in Muscat.
Thousands of green sea turtles crawl ashore each year at Ras al Jinz, one of the largest nesting sites in the Indian Ocean.

content.tagline: Indus rivers beneath giant mountains
content.overview:
Pakistan stretches from the Arabian Sea north into some of the highest mountains on Earth, bordering India, China, Afghanistan and Iran. It covers about 880,000 km², roughly twice the size of California, and the Indus River runs almost its whole length, feeding one of the world's largest irrigation systems.

About 240 million people live in Pakistan, making it the fifth most populous country in the world. Urdu and English are the official languages, while Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Saraiki and Balochi are spoken at home by tens of millions. Islamabad, built in the 1960s below the Margalla Hills, is the capital; Karachi on the coast and Lahore in the east are far larger cities.

Pakistan is a federal parliamentary republic and the world's second most populous Muslim-majority country. It is known for cricket, for the ancient cities of the Indus Valley, and for the Karakoram peaks that draw climbers from everywhere.
content.landAndNature: Three great mountain ranges meet in northern Pakistan: the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush. K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world and among the deadliest to climb, stands in the Karakoram, along with glaciers such as the Baltoro that are among the longest outside the polar regions. South of the mountains spread the fertile plains of Punjab, watered by five rivers whose name means exactly that. The Thar Desert covers the southeast, and the dry Balochistan plateau the west. Snow leopards, markhor goats with corkscrew horns, and Himalayan brown bears live in the high country; the Indus River dolphin, nearly blind and found nowhere else, swims in the murky river below.
content.peopleAndCulture: Pakistani food is famous for its spice and variety: biryani rice, nihari stew simmered overnight, chapli kebabs, naan from clay ovens, and mangoes so good that summer is planned around them. Qawwali, a hypnotic devotional singing style built on hand claps and harmonium, was carried worldwide by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. Cricket is a national obsession, and Pakistan won the World Cup in 1992; squash players from one Pakistani family dominated the sport for decades. Truck art turns cargo trucks into rolling paintings covered in flowers, poetry and mirrors. Eid festivals bring feasts and new clothes, and Basant in Lahore once filled the sky with kites. Malala Yousafzai, shot for insisting girls attend school, became the youngest Nobel Peace Prize winner in 2014.
content.history: One of the world's first urban civilizations grew here: the Indus Valley cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had brick drains, public baths and planned streets around 2500 BC. Persians, Alexander the Great, the Maurya emperors and the Buddhist kingdom of Gandhara all left their mark. Islam arrived in Sindh in the 700s, and the Mughal emperors built Lahore's fort and mosques. Britain ruled the whole subcontinent from the 1800s. In 1947 British India was partitioned into India and Pakistan; about 15 million people fled across the new borders and hundreds of thousands were killed in the violence. East Pakistan broke away in 1971 to become Bangladesh. The mountainous region of Kashmir is claimed by both India and Pakistan and divided between them, and has been fought over since 1947.
funFacts: Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BC, had covered sewers and a great public bath long before ancient Rome existed.
The Karakoram Highway to China is one of the highest paved international roads in the world, crossing a pass near 4,700 meters.
Pakistan has five of the world's fourteen mountains above 8,000 meters, including K2.
Pakistani truck drivers spend a fortune decorating their vehicles with hand-painted flowers, portraits, poetry and jangling chains.
More than half of the world's hand-stitched soccer balls, including World Cup balls, are made in the city of Sialkot.

content.tagline: Where two oceans nearly meet
content.overview:
Panama is the narrow S-shaped country that joins Central and South America, touching Costa Rica in the west and Colombia in the east. At its slimmest the land between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean is only about 50 kilometers wide, and through that gap runs the Panama Canal, one of the great engineering works of the world.

About 4.4 million people live in Panama, speaking Spanish, with English and Indigenous languages such as Ngäbere and Guna also heard. Panama City, the capital, faces the Pacific with a skyline of glass towers rising beside a Spanish colonial old town.

Panama is a presidential republic. Because ships from everywhere pass through it, the country runs on trade, banking and shipping; more merchant ships fly Panama's flag than any other country's. Rainforest still covers much of the land, and the canal's watershed is protected because the canal needs the rain the forest helps hold.
content.landAndNature: Panama runs east to west rather than north to south, so from parts of the country the sun rises over the Pacific. A mountain spine divides the wet Caribbean side from the drier Pacific side, topped by Volcán Barú at 3,475 meters, from which both oceans can be seen on a clear day. The Darién, a roadless tangle of rainforest and swamp on the Colombian border, is the one gap in the highway that otherwise runs from Alaska to Argentina. Because Panama formed a land bridge about three million years ago, animals from two continents mixed here: jaguars, tapirs, sloths, capybaras and more than 1,000 bird species, including the huge harpy eagle, the national bird. Coral reefs and 1,500 islands line both coasts.
content.peopleAndCulture: Panama's people are a blend of Indigenous, Spanish, African and Caribbean heritage, with communities descended from West Indian workers who built the canal and railway. The Guna of the San Blas islands govern themselves and are known for molas, layered cloth panels stitched into bold patterns of birds, fish and geometric shapes. The pollera, an embroidered ruffled dress worn with gold jewelry and hair combs, appears at Carnival, the biggest party of the year. Sancocho, a chicken and root-vegetable soup seasoned with the herb culantro, is the comfort food. Baseball is the top sport, and Panama has sent many players to the major leagues; Roberto Durán became one of boxing's greatest champions. Salsa star Rubén Blades is from Panama City.
content.history: Indigenous peoples fished and farmed here for thousands of years. Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the isthmus in 1513 and became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas. Panama became Spain's treasure route: silver from Peru crossed by mule trail to be shipped to Spain, attracting pirates who burned Panama City in 1671. Panama joined Colombia after independence from Spain in 1821. France tried and failed to dig a canal in the 1880s, losing tens of thousands of workers to disease. In 1903 Panama separated from Colombia with United States backing, and the United States built the canal, opened in 1914, at the cost of about 5,600 more lives. A 1977 treaty handed the canal to Panama on December 31, 1999.
funFacts: A ship crossing the canal is lifted about 26 meters up into a lake by locks, then lowered back to the other ocean.
Because of Panama's curve, ships sailing from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travel southeast.
The Darién Gap is the only break in the Pan-American Highway, leaving about 100 kilometers with no road at all.
More ships are registered in Panama than in any other country, though most never come near it.
Panama's golden frog, a national symbol, waves its hands to signal to others over the roar of streams.

content.tagline: Inca stone, desert coast, Amazon green
content.overview:
Peru occupies the western side of South America, facing the Pacific Ocean and bordering Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Bolivia and Chile. At about 1.29 million km² it is the third-largest country in South America, roughly twice the size of Texas, and it packs three completely different worlds into one map: a bone-dry coastal desert, the high Andes, and the Amazon rainforest.

About 34 million people live in Peru. Spanish is the main language, and Quechua and Aymara, spoken in the highlands since before the Spanish arrived, are official too. Lima, the capital, is a huge coastal city where it almost never rains, home to nearly a third of all Peruvians.

Peru is a presidential republic. It is famous for Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel perched on a green ridge, for potatoes in thousands of varieties, and for a food scene that has made Lima one of the world's great eating cities.
content.landAndNature: The Andes run the length of Peru, with more than thirty peaks above 6,000 meters, including Huascarán at 6,768 meters. Between the ranges sit high plateaus and Lake Titicaca, the world's highest large navigable lake, shared with Bolivia. East of the mountains, rivers gather into the Amazon, and rainforest covers more than half the country. The coast is desert because the cold Humboldt Current chills the sea air; that same current makes Peru's waters some of the richest fishing grounds on the planet. Vicuñas, whose wool is the finest in the world, graze the altiplano, condors ride mountain updrafts, and the rainforest holds pink river dolphins, jaguars and giant otters.
content.peopleAndCulture: Peruvian food blends Indigenous ingredients with Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese cooking. Ceviche, raw fish cured in lime juice with chili and onion, is the national dish; lomo saltado is a stir-fry that came from Chinese immigrant kitchens. Farmers grow thousands of potato varieties and grains like quinoa at altitudes where little else survives. Andean music uses the panpipe and the small stringed charango, and weavers make textiles in patterns handed down for centuries. Festivals mix Catholic saints with older beliefs, as at Inti Raymi in Cusco, a re-enacted Inca sun festival each June. Soccer is the biggest sport, and paleta frontón and surfing are popular on the coast.
content.history: Peru holds some of the oldest cities in the Americas; Caral on the coast dates back about 5,000 years. The Moche, Nazca, Wari and Chimú cultures followed, leaving pyramids, gold work and the Nazca Lines. From the 1400s the Inca built the largest empire in the Americas, running from Ecuador to Chile, linked by 40,000 kilometers of stone roads and governed from Cusco without wheels, iron or writing as Europeans knew it. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and a small Spanish force captured the emperor Atahualpa, and within years the empire fell, with disease killing far more people than fighting did. Spain ruled for nearly 300 years, mining silver at Potosí with forced Indigenous labor. Peru declared independence in 1821. An internal conflict with the Shining Path guerrillas in the 1980s and 1990s killed tens of thousands.
funFacts: Peru grows more than 3,000 varieties of potato, in colors from purple to yellow and shapes from knobby to smooth.
The Nazca Lines are huge figures of a hummingbird, monkey and spider scratched into the desert, best seen from the air.
Inca builders fitted giant stones together so precisely that a knife blade cannot slip between them, without any mortar.
Machu Picchu was never found by the Spanish, and the outside world learned of it only in 1911.
The Inca recorded numbers and possibly words using quipus, bundles of knotted strings that scholars are still decoding.

content.tagline: Seven thousand islands in the Pacific
content.overview:
The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands in Southeast Asia, strung between the South China Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Only about 2,000 of the islands are inhabited, and the three biggest groups are Luzon in the north, the Visayas in the middle and Mindanao in the south. Together they cover about 342,000 km², a little larger than Italy.

About 115 million people live in the Philippines, speaking Filipino, which is based on Tagalog, and English, both official, plus more than 100 other languages including Cebuano and Ilocano. Manila, on Luzon, is the capital and the center of a metropolitan area of well over 13 million people.

The Philippines is a presidential republic and one of the two mainly Catholic countries in Asia. Millions of Filipinos work abroad as nurses, sailors and engineers, and the money they send home is a pillar of the economy.
content.landAndNature: The islands sit on the Ring of Fire, so volcanoes and earthquakes shape the land. Mayon volcano has an almost perfect cone; Taal is a volcano on an island in a lake on an island. Off the east coast lies the Philippine Trench, plunging more than 10,000 meters. The country lies in the path of about twenty typhoons a year, more than almost anywhere else. Rice terraces carved into the Cordillera mountains by the Ifugao 2,000 years ago climb like green staircases. The seas here hold more coral and fish species than anywhere else on Earth, part of the Coral Triangle. Tarsiers, palm-sized primates with enormous eyes, cling to branches in Bohol, and the Philippine eagle, one of the largest eagles alive, hunts in Mindanao's forests.
content.peopleAndCulture: Filipino life revolves around family, food and hospitality. Adobo, meat simmered in vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, is the best-known dish, alongside sinigang sour soup, lechon roast pig and halo-halo, a heaped dessert of shaved ice, sweet beans, fruit and ice cream. Jeepneys, brightly painted buses built from stretched jeep bodies, carry passengers along shared routes. Basketball is played on every village court, and boxer Manny Pacquiao became a national hero. Christmas celebrations start in September and run into January, the longest in the world, with star-shaped parol lanterns in every window. Karaoke is a beloved pastime, and the bamboo dance tinikling has dancers hopping between clapping poles.
content.history: People have lived in the islands for tens of thousands of years, trading with China and Southeast Asia and organized into small states called barangays; Islam spread in the south from the 1300s. Ferdinand Magellan reached the islands in 1521 and was killed by Lapu-Lapu's warriors on Mactan. Spain colonized the archipelago from 1565 and ruled for over 300 years, converting most people to Catholicism and naming the islands after King Philip II. A revolution began in 1896, and independence was declared in 1898, but the United States took control after the Spanish-American War, and a bitter Philippine-American War followed. Japan occupied the islands in World War II. Full independence came on July 4, 1946. Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law until the peaceful People Power revolution removed him in 1986.
funFacts: The Philippines has the world's longest Christmas season, with carols and decorations appearing as early as September.
Jeepneys began as surplus American army jeeps left after World War II, lengthened and decorated by local builders.
The Philippine tarsier weighs about as much as a deck of cards, and each of its eyes is bigger than its brain.
A whale shark, the world's largest fish, can be seen feeding off Philippine coasts, where it is called butanding.
The underground Puerto Princesa river flows for more than 8 kilometers through a cave straight into the sea.

content.tagline: Mushroom islands in turquoise water
content.overview:
Palau is a scatter of more than 300 islands in the western Pacific Ocean, at the far edge of Micronesia and about 900 kilometers east of the Philippines. Its total land area is only about 460 km², smaller than New York City, but its ocean territory is enormous, and most of that sea is now a protected sanctuary.

Roughly 18,000 people live in Palau, most of them on Koror island. English and Palauan are official languages, and some islands add their own. The capital, Ngerulmud, is a small hilltop complex of government buildings on the larger island of Babeldaob, making it one of the least populated capitals in the world.

Palau is a republic with an elected president, in free association with the United States. It is best known to divers as one of the finest places on Earth to see reefs, sharks and wrecks, and to scientists for protecting its waters early and firmly.
content.landAndNature: The Rock Islands are Palau's signature: hundreds of green limestone knobs, undercut by waves into mushroom shapes, floating in water so clear that boats seem to hover. Babeldaob, the largest island, has rivers, waterfalls and savanna as well as forest. Palau's reefs hold more than 1,300 kinds of fish and 500 kinds of coral, plus manta rays, sea turtles and the dugong. Jellyfish Lake, a saltwater lake cut off from the sea, is filled with millions of golden jellyfish that have lost most of their sting and migrate across the water each day following the sun. Saltwater crocodiles live in the mangroves, and the islands are hit by typhoons far less often than places further north.
content.peopleAndCulture: Palauan society traditionally traces family through the mother's line, and clan mothers choose and can remove chiefs. Villages centered on a bai, a tall meeting house with a steep thatched roof and painted storyboards along the beams telling legends; the same stories are now carved on wooden boards sold as art. Taro, tapioca, fish, fruit bats and reef fish feature in local meals. Visitors sign the Palau Pledge, stamped in their passports, promising to tread lightly on the islands. Canoe racing, baseball, which arrived with Japanese administration, and basketball are popular. The custom of bul, a chief's temporary ban on fishing a reef so it can recover, is an ancient form of conservation still respected today.
content.history: People reached Palau at least 3,000 years ago and built terraced hillsides and stone villages. Spain claimed the islands in the 1600s as part of its Pacific holdings, then sold them to Germany in 1899. Japan took them during World War I and ran them as part of its Pacific mandate, building towns, roads and phosphate mines. In 1944 the island of Peleliu saw one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war, and rusting tanks and plane wrecks remain. After the war Palau was administered by the United States under a United Nations trusteeship. Palauans wrote a constitution in 1979 that banned nuclear weapons from their territory, and after long negotiations Palau became independent on October 1, 1994, keeping close ties with the United States.
funFacts: Swimmers can float among millions of golden jellyfish in Palau's Jellyfish Lake, which have lost nearly all their sting.
Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary in 2009, banning shark fishing across its entire ocean territory.
Every visitor's passport is stamped with the Palau Pledge, an eco-promise written with the help of local schoolchildren.
Palau banned sunscreens containing chemicals harmful to coral reefs, one of the first countries to do so.
Ngerulmud, the capital, has only a few hundred residents and was built on a hill in the jungle in 2006.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.officialName: Independent State of Papua New Guinea

content.tagline: More languages than any other country
content.overview:
Papua New Guinea occupies the eastern half of New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, along with hundreds of smaller islands in the southwest Pacific. It shares a land border with Indonesia and lies just north of Australia across the Torres Strait. At about 463,000 km² it is a little larger than Sweden.

About 10 million people live here, and they speak more than 800 languages, more than any other country on Earth. Tok Pisin, a creole that grew out of English and local languages, is the everyday shared tongue, along with English and Hiri Motu. Port Moresby is the capital.

Papua New Guinea is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Most people live in villages and grow their own food on small gardens of sweet potato, taro and bananas. The country holds gold, copper and gas, and some of the least explored rainforest and coral reef left in the world.
content.landAndNature: A rugged mountain spine runs the length of the island, rising above 4,500 meters at Mount Wilhelm, high enough for frost and once for small glaciers. Below the peaks lie deep valleys hidden from the outside world until the 1930s, then swamps, mighty rivers like the Sepik and Fly, and mangrove coasts. The country sits on the Ring of Fire, with active volcanoes such as Tavurvur, which buried the town of Rabaul in ash in 1994. New Guinea's wildlife is astonishing: about 40 species of birds-of-paradise perform dances with shimmering plumes, tree kangaroos climb in the canopy, the world's largest butterfly, Queen Alexandra's birdwing, has a wingspan of about 25 centimeters, and cassowaries stalk the forest floor.
content.peopleAndCulture: With hundreds of distinct peoples, Papua New Guinea holds some of the greatest cultural variety on Earth. At sing-sings, villages gather to dance in feathered headdresses, shell ornaments and painted faces, each group showing its own designs. Sepik River carvers make masks and spirit houses famous in museums worldwide. Food is cooked in a mumu, a pit lined with hot stones, and staples include sweet potato, sago, fish and pig, with pigs also serving as wealth and bride-price. Rugby league is a national passion, and the Kumuls draw huge crowds. Shell money is still used in some ceremonies. Most people follow Christianity blended with older traditions, and many clans still make decisions through big-man leaders and consensus.
content.history: People have lived in New Guinea for about 50,000 years, and farmers in the Kuk swamp were growing crops around 9,000 years ago, making it one of the places where agriculture was independently invented. The rugged terrain kept communities separate, which is why so many languages developed. European powers divided the island in the late 1800s: the Netherlands took the west, Germany the northeast and Britain the southeast, with Australia taking over the British part and, after World War I, the German part. Fierce fighting took place here in World War II, including the Kokoda Track campaign. Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia on September 16, 1975. A civil war on Bougainville island over a copper mine lasted from 1988 to 1998, and Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence in 2019.
funFacts: Papua New Guinea has over 800 living languages, roughly one in every nine languages spoken on Earth.
The Huli wigmen of the highlands grow their own hair into ceremonial wigs decorated with feathers and flowers.
Farmers in the Kuk swamp were draining land and growing crops around 9,000 years ago, among the world's earliest farmers.
Male birds-of-paradise clear a stage on the forest floor and dance upside down to impress females.
Tok Pisin words are wonderfully descriptive: a beard is 'mausgras', mouth grass, and a piano 'bikpela bokis'.

content.tagline: Amber coasts, deep forests, rebuilt cities
content.overview:
Poland lies in the middle of Europe on a broad plain running from the Baltic Sea in the north to the Carpathian Mountains in the south, with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania, and Russia's Kaliningrad region around its edges. It is about the size of New Mexico.

About 38 million people live in Poland and speak Polish, a Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet and famous for its clusters of consonants. Warsaw, the capital, stands on the Vistula River; its old town was destroyed in World War II and rebuilt brick by brick from old paintings and photographs. Kraków, the former royal capital, kept its medieval squares intact. Poland is a parliamentary republic and joined the European Union in 2004.

The country builds everything from furniture and buses to video games, and its people are known for hearty food, mushroom hunting in autumn, and a deep attachment to their history.
content.landAndNature: Most of Poland is flat farmland and forest shaped by ice-age glaciers, which also scooped out the thousands of lakes in the Masurian district of the northeast. The Baltic coast has long sand beaches and shifting dunes that creep inland several meters a year in Słowiński National Park, and amber from ancient pine forests washes up on the shore. In the far south the Tatra Mountains, part of the Carpathians, rise to Rysy at 2,499 meters, with alpine meadows and highland shepherds. Białowieża Forest on the Belarusian border is one of the last great lowland forests of Europe, home to several hundred European bison, along with wolves, lynx, and white storks nesting on village rooftops.
content.peopleAndCulture: Polish meals begin with soup: sour rye żurek, beet barszcz, or chilled chłodnik. Pierogi, half-moon dumplings filled with potato and cheese, meat, or blueberries, appear at every celebration, alongside bigos hunter's stew and pączki doughnuts before Lent. Most Poles are Catholic, and Christmas Eve supper of twelve meatless dishes, eaten when the first star appears, is the year's biggest meal. Chopin's piano music and the poetry of Nobel winners Wisława Szymborska and Czesław Miłosz are national treasures, and the astronomer Copernicus was born in Toruń. Soccer, volleyball, and ski jumping fill stadiums, and speedway motorcycle racing draws bigger crowds here than almost anywhere else.
content.history: Slavic tribes united under Mieszko I, who accepted Christianity in 966 and founded the Polish state. Joined with Lithuania in 1386, Poland became one of Europe's largest realms, with an elected king and a famously stubborn parliament. Neighboring powers carved it up in the late 1700s, and Poland vanished from the map for 123 years before returning in 1918. Nazi Germany invaded on September 1, 1939, beginning World War II, and the Soviet Union invaded weeks later. The occupation killed about six million Polish citizens, around half of them Jews murdered in the Holocaust at camps including Auschwitz, built on Polish soil. Soviet-backed communist rule followed until the Solidarity trade union helped force free elections in 1989.
funFacts: Warsaw's old town was rebuilt so faithfully after the war that UNESCO lists the reconstruction itself as world heritage.
The Wieliczka salt mine near Kraków holds an underground chapel with chandeliers, altars, and statues carved entirely from rock salt.
Marie Curie, born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, named the element polonium after her homeland.
European bison, once extinct in the wild, were bred back from zoo animals and now roam Białowieża Forest again.
The Crooked Forest near Gryfino has about 400 pine trees that all bend sharply at the base, and nobody is certain why.

content.tagline: The northern half of a divided peninsula
content.overview:
North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia, bordering China and Russia in the north and South Korea across a heavily fortified line in the south. It covers about 120,000 km², a little larger than Virginia, and mountains cover roughly four-fifths of it.

About 26 million people live in North Korea, all speaking Korean. Pyongyang, the capital, stands on the Taedong River and holds the country's grandest monuments, wide avenues and a subway decorated like a palace.
