Officially the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, it is a socialist state led since 1948 by three generations of one family: Kim Il Sung, Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un.

North Korea is one of the most closed and tightly controlled countries in the world. Travel inside the country, contact with foreigners, and access to outside news and the internet are strictly limited, and the state directs the economy and the media. It has developed nuclear weapons, which has led to international sanctions.
content.landAndNature: Steep forested mountains fill the north and east. Mount Paektu, an active volcano of 2,744 meters on the Chinese border, is the highest point on the peninsula and holds a deep crater lake called Heaven Lake in its summit. The Yalu and Tumen rivers mark the frontier with China. Narrow plains along the west coast, facing the Yellow Sea, grow most of the country's rice and corn; floods and droughts here have repeatedly caused food shortages. Winters are long and bitterly cold, with summer monsoon rains. The Demilitarized Zone dividing the two Koreas has been almost empty of people since 1953, and wildlife including rare cranes, black bears and possibly leopards has thrived in that four-kilometer-wide strip.
content.peopleAndCulture: Koreans on both sides of the border share a language, an alphabet called hangul, and a long culinary tradition of rice, kimchi, soups and grilled meat; naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles, is a specialty of Pyongyang. North Korean life is organized around the state: schoolchildren learn the history of the ruling family, mass gymnastics displays fill stadiums with thousands of performers moving in unison, and giant statues and murals honor past leaders. Soccer is the most popular sport, and the women's national team has done well internationally. Taekwondo, which developed in Korea, is widely practiced. Most people live in apartment blocks in cities or in farming cooperatives, and private phones and computers are far less common than in neighboring countries.
content.history: Korea was a single country for more than a thousand years, ruled by the Goryeo and then Joseon dynasties, before Japan annexed it in 1910 and governed harshly until 1945. At the end of World War II the peninsula was divided along the 38th parallel: Soviet forces occupied the north, American forces the south. Two rival governments formed in 1948. In 1950 North Korea invaded the south, starting the Korean War; China entered on the north's side and a United Nations force led by the United States on the south's. Millions died and cities on both sides were flattened. The fighting stopped with an armistice in 1953, not a peace treaty, so the war has technically never ended. Kim Il Sung built a state around his own leadership, and his family has ruled since.
funFacts: North and South Korea have never signed a peace treaty, so the Korean War has formally paused rather than ended since 1953.
North Korea uses its own calendar in which year 1 is 1912, the birth year of Kim Il Sung.
The Demilitarized Zone between the Koreas is one of the most heavily guarded borders on Earth and an accidental wildlife refuge.
Pyongyang's metro stations sit more than 100 meters underground, among the deepest in the world.
North Korea and South Korea have marched together under one flag at some Olympic opening ceremonies.

content.tagline: Atlantic edge of Europe
content.overview:
Portugal occupies the western rim of the Iberian Peninsula, the last mainland in Europe before the open Atlantic. It shares a border with only one country, Spain, and covers about as much ground as Indiana. Two Atlantic island groups, the volcanic Azores and subtropical Madeira, belong to Portugal as well.

About 10 million people live here and speak Portuguese, a language sailors and settlers carried around the globe; more than 250 million people now speak it, in Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, and beyond. Lisbon, the capital, climbs steep hills above the Tagus River, with yellow trams grinding up the slopes past building fronts covered in painted tiles called azulejos. Porto in the north gave its name both to port wine and to the country. Portugal is a republic with an elected president and parliament, and it joined the European Union in 1986.

Fishing, cork, wine, and visitors drawn by sunshine and surf shape much of the economy.
content.landAndNature: The Tagus River cuts Portugal in two. North of it the country is green, hilly, and rainy, rising to the Serra da Estrela, where snow falls and the mainland's highest point reaches 1,993 meters. South of the river the Alentejo spreads into wide, dry plains of wheat, olives, and cork oaks, whose bark is stripped by hand every nine years without harming the tree; Portugal produces about half the world's cork. The Algarve coast in the south is lined with golden cliffs and sea caves. Atlantic storms drive enormous waves onto the beach at Nazaré, among the biggest ever surfed, and offshore the Azores and Madeira rise as volcanic peaks where whales gather.
content.peopleAndCulture: Fado, meaning fate, is Portugal's own music: a singer and a pear-shaped Portuguese guitar performing songs about saudade, a word for longing after something you may never get back. The food centers on the sea, from sardines grilled on street corners at June festivals to bacalhau, salted cod, which Portuguese cooks say has a different recipe for every day of the year. Pastéis de nata, custard tarts in crackly pastry, were first baked by monks in Lisbon. Most Portuguese are Catholic, and summer nights fill with paper lanterns and pots of basil. Soccer is the national passion, and Cristiano Ronaldo, born in Madeira, became one of the most famous athletes alive.
content.history: Celtic peoples, Romans, and then Muslim rulers from North Africa each shaped this coast. The kingdom of Portugal emerged in 1139 and reached today's borders by 1249, giving it some of the oldest fixed frontiers in Europe. In the 1400s Portuguese captains pushed farther and farther down Africa: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in Brazil in 1500. The empire that followed brought spices and gold, and Portugal became a leading trafficker in the transatlantic slave trade, shipping millions of enslaved Africans to Brazil. An earthquake destroyed Lisbon in 1755. A dictatorship ruled from 1933 until the peaceful Carnation Revolution of 1974, after which Portugal's African colonies became independent.
funFacts: Portugal and Spain agreed in 1494 to split newly encountered lands along a line drawn across the Atlantic, which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese.
Lisbon's Tram 28 still uses wooden carriages from the 1930s to climb streets too narrow and steep for modern trams.
Surfers at Nazaré ride some of the largest waves ever recorded, raised by a deep underwater canyon just offshore.
Bertrand in Lisbon, open since 1732, is recognized as the oldest bookshop in the world still selling books.
Cork oaks are stripped of their bark by hand and then left alone for nine years while a fresh layer grows back.

content.tagline: Heart of South America, two languages strong
content.overview:
Paraguay lies landlocked in the middle of South America, sharing borders with Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia. The Paraguay River splits the country in two: a green, populated east of hills, farms and forest, and a vast, thorny, thinly settled west called the Chaco. The whole country is about the size of California.

About 7 million people live here, and Paraguay is unusual in that most of them speak two languages every day. Guaraní, an Indigenous language, is official alongside Spanish, and people switch between them mid-sentence. Asunción, the capital, sits on the riverbank and is one of the oldest cities in South America.

Paraguay is a presidential republic. Soybeans, beef and hydroelectric power drive its economy; the Itaipú dam it shares with Brazil is among the largest power stations in the world, and Paraguay produces far more electricity than it uses.
content.landAndNature: Eastern Paraguay is rolling, red-soiled and warm, with remnants of the Atlantic Forest and the Paraná River thundering along the Brazilian border. West of the river spreads the Gran Chaco, a flat expanse of thorn scrub, palm savanna and seasonal marsh that floods in the wet season and bakes hard in the dry; summer temperatures there can top 45°C, among the hottest in South America. The Pantanal's southern fringe reaches the northeast. Wildlife includes jaguars, giant anteaters, maned wolves with stilt-like legs, capybaras and the Chacoan peccary, a pig-like animal known only from fossils until living ones were found in 1975. Flocks of parrots and the enormous jabiru stork are common sights.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Paraguayans are mestizo, of mixed Guaraní and Spanish descent, and Guaraní words color the way Spanish is spoken here. Tereré, cold yerba mate infused with herbs and drunk through a metal straw from a shared cup, is sipped all day in the heat and is a social ritual as much as a drink. Chipa, a chewy cheese bread made with cassava starch, is sold at bus windows, and sopa paraguaya, confusingly, is a dense corn-and-cheese cake rather than a soup. Ñandutí lace, named for the Guaraní word for spiderweb, is embroidered in fine radiating circles. The Paraguayan harp, with 36 strings and a bright, rippling sound, is the national instrument, and soccer is the national sport.
content.history: Guaraní peoples farmed and fished along the rivers long before Spaniards founded Asunción in 1537. Jesuit missionaries built self-governing Guaraní towns, the reducciones, in the 1600s and 1700s, whose stone ruins still stand, until Spain expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay declared independence in 1811. The War of the Triple Alliance against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay from 1864 to 1870 was catastrophic: Paraguay lost territory and, by many estimates, more than half its population, including most of its adult men. The Chaco War with Bolivia in the 1930s won it more territory at great cost. General Alfredo Stroessner ruled as dictator for 35 years, from 1954 to 1989, jailing and exiling opponents, until he was overthrown and democracy returned.
funFacts: Paraguay is one of very few countries where an Indigenous language, Guaraní, is spoken by most of the population, including non-Indigenous people.
The Itaipú dam on the Paraná River supplies almost all of Paraguay's electricity and a large share of Brazil's.
Paraguayans drink tereré, ice-cold mate, from a shared cup, and offering it to someone is a mark of friendship.
The Chacoan peccary was known only from fossils until scientists found living herds in the Paraguayan Chaco in 1975.
Paraguay's flag is one of the few in the world with a different emblem on each side.

content.tagline: A desert peninsula built on gas
content.overview:
Qatar is a small peninsula jutting north into the Persian Gulf from the Arabian mainland, with a single land border, shared with Saudi Arabia. At about 11,600 km² it is roughly the size of Jamaica, and almost all of it is flat desert and salt flat, with no permanent rivers.

Around 3 million people live in Qatar, but only a small fraction are Qatari citizens; most are workers from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, the Philippines and elsewhere. Arabic is the official language and English is used everywhere in business. Doha, the capital, has grown in a generation from a pearling town into a skyline of curved towers, museums and stadiums on the Gulf shore.

Qatar is a monarchy ruled by an emir. It sits above one of the largest natural gas fields on Earth, which has made it one of the richest countries per person, and it hosted the 2022 soccer World Cup, the first in the Arab world.
content.landAndNature: Qatar is low and dry, the highest ground barely 100 meters above sea level. Summers are ferociously hot, often above 45°C, with humid Gulf air, and rain falls only a few days a year. In the southeast, dunes of the Khor Al Adaid roll right down to a sea inlet, the rare place where large desert dunes meet the sea. Inland lie gravel plains and sabkha, crusted salt flats that shimmer in the heat. Despite the harshness, Arabian oryx, the national animal saved from extinction by captive breeding, roam reserves, and ghaf and acacia trees survive on deep roots. Gulf waters hold dugongs, whale sharks that gather in summer, and the oyster beds that once made the country famous for pearls.
content.peopleAndCulture: Qatari traditions come from the desert and the sea: falconry, camel racing, dhow sailing and pearl diving. Camel races are now run with lightweight robot jockeys controlled from cars alongside the track. Majlis gatherings, where men sit and talk over cardamom coffee and dates, remain a social anchor. Machboos, spiced rice with meat and dried lime, is the everyday feast dish. Modern Qatar is a place of striking architecture: the Museum of Islamic Art rises from its own island, and the National Museum is shaped like interlocking desert rose crystals. Soccer is the top sport; Qatar won the Asian Cup in 2019 and 2023 and built air-conditioned stadiums for the World Cup, a tournament for which its treatment of migrant construction workers drew international criticism.
content.history: People have lived along this coast for thousands of years, fishing and trading. Qatar became known for pearl diving, dangerous work in which divers went down on a rope with a nose clip and a basket, and by the 1800s pearls were the backbone of its economy. The Al Thani family emerged as rulers in the 1800s. Qatar came under Ottoman, then British protection, signing a treaty in 1916. The invention of cultured pearls in Japan in the 1920s wrecked the pearl trade and brought hard times. Oil was found in 1939 and exports began after World War II. Qatar became fully independent on September 3, 1971. Gas production from the offshore North Field, starting in the 1990s, transformed the country, and in 1996 it launched the Al Jazeera news network.
funFacts: Qatar has no rivers or lakes, so nearly all its drinking water comes from desalination plants that remove salt from seawater.
Camel races in Qatar use small robot jockeys that owners operate by remote control from cars racing alongside.
The 2022 World Cup was moved to November and December because Qatari summers are too hot for outdoor sport.
Before oil, Qatar's wealth came from pearls gathered by divers who held their breath for two minutes at a time.
Qatar's Khor Al Adaid is called the Inland Sea, a place where large sand dunes run straight down into salt water.

content.tagline: Carpathian forests and Danube marshes
content.overview:
Romania curls around the Carpathian Mountains in southeastern Europe, with the Danube River along its southern edge and the Black Sea to the east. It is the largest country in the region, about the size of Oregon, bordering Ukraine, Moldova, Bulgaria, Serbia, and Hungary.

About 19 million people live in Romania. Romanian is a Romance language descended from Latin, like French and Italian, which makes it unusual among Slavic and Hungarian-speaking neighbors. Bucharest, the capital, mixes grand nineteenth-century boulevards with vast concrete projects from the communist era, among them the Palace of the Parliament. Romania is a republic with an elected president and parliament, and it joined the European Union in 2007.

Transylvania, in the center, is a region of forested hills, fortified Saxon churches, and hilltop castles, one of which, Bran Castle, is linked in tourist legend to Dracula. Beyond the mountains lie wide farming plains where horse carts still share the roads with trucks.
content.landAndNature: The Carpathians sweep through Romania in a great arc, carpeted in beech and spruce and rising above 2,500 meters in the Făgăraș range. These forests hold the largest brown bear population in Europe outside Russia, thousands of animals, along with wolves, lynx, and wild boar, and shepherds still walk flocks up to summer pastures. Outside the mountains the land opens into the plains of Wallachia and Moldavia, thick with wheat and sunflowers. In the east the Danube finishes a journey of about 2,850 kilometers in a huge delta of reeds and shifting channels, where pelicans, egrets, and roughly 300 bird species nest and sturgeon still swim upstream. Mud volcanoes bubble in the hills near Buzău.
content.peopleAndCulture: Romanians share the country with Hungarian, Roma, and German-speaking communities, and many villages keep their own costumes and dances, some circling hand in hand, others in fast lines with stamping feet. Most people belong to the Romanian Orthodox Church. Food is filling: sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with pork and rice, mămăligă, a cornmeal porridge much like polenta, and sour soups called ciorbă. The painted monasteries of Bucovina are covered on the outside with bright biblical scenes from the 1500s. Romania gave the world the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși, the composer George Enescu, and the gymnast Nadia Comăneci, and soccer and handball fill its stadiums.
content.history: The Dacians lived here until Rome conquered them in 106 AD, and Roman settlers left behind the country's language and its name. Waves of migrating peoples followed, and the medieval principalities of Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania took shape. Vlad the Impaler, a fifteenth-century Wallachian prince, later lent his family name, Dracula, to a British novel. Ottoman, Habsburg, and Russian power all pressed on these lands. Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859, independence was recognized in 1878, and Transylvania joined in 1918. After World War II Romania became a communist state; Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled from 1965 with harsh controls and huge demolition projects until a revolution in December 1989 removed him. Democratic elections have been held since.
funFacts: The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is the heaviest building in the world, with more than a thousand rooms.
Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect ten in Olympic gymnastics in 1976; the scoreboard could only display 1.00.
The Danube Delta grows a little larger every year as the river drops its silt into the Black Sea.
An old salt mine at Turda has been turned into an underground park with a Ferris wheel and rowing boats on a lake.
Timișoara was the first European city to light its streets with electric lamps, in 1884.

content.tagline: The largest country on Earth
content.overview:
Russia is by far the largest country on Earth, covering about an eighth of the world's land and stretching across eleven time zones from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. It is nearly twice the size of the United States and shares borders with fourteen countries. The Ural Mountains divide it into European Russia in the west, where most people live, and Siberia in the east.

About 145 million people live in Russia and speak Russian, written in the Cyrillic alphabet, while more than a hundred other languages are spoken by peoples across the country. Moscow, the capital, has the Kremlin fortress and Red Square at its heart and a subway system whose older stations look like marble palaces. Saint Petersburg, built on marshy islands, is a city of canals and imperial palaces.

Russia is a federal republic with a powerful presidency, and it is a leading producer of oil, natural gas, wheat, and metals.
content.landAndNature: Siberia is a world of its own: taiga, the largest forest on the planet, runs for thousands of kilometers in larch and pine before giving way to treeless tundra, frozen underground as permafrost. Winters in Yakutia fall below minus 50 degrees Celsius, among the coldest anywhere people live. Lake Baikal, a crack in the Earth's crust filled 1,642 meters deep, holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water and its own species of freshwater seal. The Volga, Europe's longest river, waters the west, while the Kamchatka Peninsula in the far east bristles with active volcanoes and geysers. Siberian tigers, brown bears, reindeer, and sables live in the forests.
content.peopleAndCulture: Russia is home to many peoples besides Russians, among them Tatars, Chechens, Bashkirs, Buryats, and reindeer-herding Nenets in the Arctic. Orthodox Christianity and Islam are the largest faiths. Meals often open with soup, whether beet borscht or fish solyanka, followed by pelmeni dumplings, blini pancakes, and dark rye bread. Russian writers such as Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Chekhov are read everywhere, and the Bolshoi and Mariinsky theaters made Russian ballet world-famous. Chess is taught in schools, while ice hockey and figure skating draw huge audiences. New Year, with a decorated tree and Grandfather Frost, is the biggest holiday, and the banya, a hot steam bath, is a weekly ritual.
content.history: Slavic peoples settled the plains, and the state of Kievan Rus took shape around Kyiv in the 800s, adopting Orthodox Christianity in 988. Mongol armies overran it in the 1200s. Moscow later grew into the center of power, and in 1547 Ivan IV was crowned tsar; Peter the Great and Catherine the Great pushed the empire across Siberia to the Pacific. Revolution in 1917 overthrew the last tsar and brought the communists to power, creating the Soviet Union. Under Stalin, industry grew quickly while millions died in famines and political purges. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people defeating Nazi Germany in World War II, then rivaled the United States through the Cold War. It broke into fifteen countries in 1991. Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the war has continued since.
funFacts: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs about 9,300 kilometers from Moscow to Vladivostok, a trip of roughly seven days.
Lake Baikal holds around a fifth of all the liquid fresh water on Earth and freezes clear enough to see down into it.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite, in 1957, and Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space in 1961.
Russia is so wide that when the day begins in Kamchatka, clocks in Moscow are still nine hours behind.
Matryoshka nesting dolls, now a symbol of Russia, were first carved only in the 1890s.

content.tagline: Land of a thousand hills
content.overview:
Rwanda is a small, green, steeply folded country in the heart of East Africa, landlocked between Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. About the size of Maryland, it is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa, with roughly 14 million people farming terraced slopes that earn it the nickname land of a thousand hills.

Kinyarwanda is spoken by nearly everyone, and English and French are official languages too. Kigali, the capital, spreads across several ridges and is known around the continent for its clean, orderly streets; plastic bags are banned nationwide, and on the last Saturday of each month neighbors turn out for umuganda, a morning of shared community work.

Rwanda is a republic with an elected president. Coffee, tea, and visitors who come to track mountain gorillas are its main earners, and the country has rebuilt determinedly since the genocide of 1994.
content.landAndNature: Rwanda sits high, mostly between 1,000 and 4,500 meters, so even on the edge of the equator the air stays mild and evenings turn cool. Volcanoes rise along the northern border as part of the Virunga chain, where Karisimbi reaches 4,507 meters and bamboo forest shelters roughly a third of the world's remaining mountain gorillas. Nyungwe Forest in the southwest is one of Africa's oldest rainforests, full of chimpanzees, colobus monkeys, and orchids, with a walkway slung across the treetops. Akagera National Park in the east holds swamps and savanna where lions and rhinos have been returned after years away. Lake Kivu fills a deep valley on the Congolese border.
content.peopleAndCulture: Rwandans share a single language and many traditions across the groups known as Hutu, Tutsi, and Twa; since 1994 the government has emphasized one common Rwandan identity. Most people are Christian. Meals are built on beans, plantains, cassava, sweet potatoes, and isombe, a stew of pounded cassava leaves. Imigongo art covers wooden boards with bold black, white, and red geometric patterns. The intore dance, once performed for kings, has men in long grass headdresses leaping to the beat of drums. Tightly woven baskets with peaked lids, called agaseke, are given as wedding gifts. Cycling is the national sporting passion, and the Tour du Rwanda climbs those endless hills.
content.history: Twa hunter-gatherers, then farmers and cattle herders, settled these hills, and by the 1700s a strong kingdom ruled from the center under a mwami, or king. Germany claimed Rwanda in the 1890s, and Belgium took over after World War I, hardening the divide between Hutu and Tutsi with identity cards. Independence came on July 1, 1962, followed by decades of ethnic violence and waves of refugees. In 1994, over about a hundred days, extremist forces and militias killed around 800,000 people, most of them Tutsi along with moderate Hutu, in a genocide that the outside world watched without intervening. A rebel army ended the killing that July. Rwanda has since concentrated on justice, reconciliation, and rebuilding.
funFacts: Rwanda banned plastic bags in 2008, and airport officials still take them from arriving travelers' luggage.
Rwanda's parliament has one of the highest shares of women in the world, with more than half its lower house.
Drones launched from Rwandan bases deliver blood to remote hospitals by parachute, a service started in 2016.
Mountain gorilla numbers have climbed back above a thousand, and every new gorilla baby is named at a public ceremony.
Kigali sits just south of the equator but rarely gets hot, because the whole city stands about 1,500 meters above sea level.

content.tagline: Deserts, oil, and Islam's holiest cities
content.overview:
Saudi Arabia fills most of the Arabian Peninsula, the large wedge of land between Africa and Asia, with the Red Sea on one side and the Persian Gulf on the other. At about 2.15 million km² it is the largest country in the Middle East, roughly a quarter the size of the United States, and most of it is desert.

About 36 million people live in Saudi Arabia, including millions of foreign workers. Arabic is the official language. Riyadh, the capital, is a modern city in the center of the country, while Jeddah is the Red Sea port and Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, lie inland from it.

Saudi Arabia is a monarchy ruled by the Al Saud family. It holds some of the world's largest oil reserves, and the government has been investing oil money in new cities, tourism, entertainment and sport as it tries to build an economy less dependent on petroleum.
content.landAndNature: The Rub al Khali, the Empty Quarter, covers the south: about 650,000 km² of sand, the largest continuous sand desert on the planet, with dunes up to 250 meters tall. The Nafud desert in the north has red-tinted sand. Mountains run down the western edge along the Red Sea, rising above 3,000 meters near the Yemeni border, where the Asir highlands catch enough monsoon rain for terraced farms, juniper forests and even fog. Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers at all; water comes from underground aquifers and desalination plants. Arabian oryx, sand cats, hyenas and the Arabian leopard, now extremely rare, survive in the wild, while the Red Sea's reefs are among the healthiest and least damaged anywhere.
content.peopleAndCulture: Islam shapes daily life: prayers five times a day, fasting during the month of Ramadan, and the feasts of Eid. Every year millions of Muslims from around the world travel to Mecca for the hajj pilgrimage, walking seven times around the Kaaba, a duty for every Muslim who is able. Kabsa, spiced rice with lamb or chicken, is served on large shared platters, and Arabic coffee with dates greets guests. Men often wear a white thobe and a checked headscarf; women commonly wear an abaya. Camel racing, falconry and the ardah sword dance are old traditions, while soccer fills stadiums and Saudi clubs have signed some of the world's most famous players.
content.history: Trading caravans carrying frankincense and spices crossed Arabia thousands of years ago, and the Nabataeans carved tombs into cliffs at Hegra, now the country's first World Heritage site. The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 and the religion of Islam began here, spreading across three continents within a century. For centuries the region was divided among tribes and ruled in part from Ottoman Istanbul. In the 1700s the Al Saud family allied with the religious reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and after long campaigns Abdulaziz ibn Saud united most of the peninsula, founding the modern kingdom in 1932. Oil was discovered in 1938, transforming a poor desert country into a wealthy one within a generation. Since 2017 the kingdom has lifted rules such as its ban on women driving.
funFacts: Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers or lakes, and is one of the world's largest producers of desalinated seawater.
The Empty Quarter is so vast that some of its dunes have never been crossed on foot or by vehicle.
Mecca's Grand Mosque can hold more than a million worshippers at once during the hajj pilgrimage.
Al-Ahsa in the east is one of the largest oasis systems in the world, with more than two million date palms.
Saudi Arabia uses the Islamic lunar calendar for religious life, so Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year.

content.tagline: Pyramids, deserts and two great Niles
content.overview:
Sudan lies in northeastern Africa, where the Blue Nile flowing from Ethiopia joins the White Nile coming up from the south. The two meet at Khartoum, the capital, and continue north as a single river toward Egypt. Sudan is the third largest country in Africa, about a quarter the size of the United States, with a Red Sea coast in the northeast and borders with seven countries.

Roughly 48 million people live in Sudan. Arabic and English are the official languages, and dozens more, including Beja, Fur and the Nuba languages, are spoken across the regions; most Sudanese are Muslim. Sudan is a republic, though the military has governed for much of its history. Farming along the Nile and on the rain-fed plains produces sorghum, peanuts and most of the world's gum arabic, a tree sap used in soft drinks and candy. Since April 2023 a war between rival armed forces has driven millions of people from their homes.
content.landAndNature: Desert covers the north, where the Sahara meets the Nile and dunes press against the riverbanks; the Nubian Desert is among the driest places on Earth. Farther south the land becomes dry grassland and thorny savanna that turns green during the summer rains. The Red Sea coast is edged with coral reefs famous among divers. In the far west the Marra Mountains of Darfur reach about 3,000 meters, a volcanic massif cool enough for orchards. Acacia trees yield gum arabic, and the Dinder wetlands hold elephants, lions and huge flocks of birds. Dust storms called haboobs can roll over Khartoum as a wall hundreds of meters high.
content.peopleAndCulture: Sudanese hospitality is a point of pride: guests are served coffee roasted with ginger and poured through a straw filter from a clay jebena pot. Bread and kisra, a thin sorghum pancake, are eaten with stews of okra, beans or lamb, and mashed fava beans called ful are the standard breakfast. Nubian communities along the northern Nile keep their own languages and brightly painted houses. Wrestling is a traditional sport among the Nuba, and soccer is followed everywhere. Sudanese poetry and music, often played on the oud, are admired across the Arab world, and a wedding can fill a whole street for days.
content.history: The kingdom of Kush ruled the middle Nile for more than a thousand years from cities such as Kerma, Napata and Meroë, and around 750 BC its kings conquered Egypt and ruled there as pharaohs. Sudan's builders left more pyramids than Egypt, smaller and steeper than the famous ones. Christian kingdoms held the region for centuries before Islam spread from the 1300s. Egypt conquered Sudan in the 1820s, a revolt led by the Mahdi drove out foreign rule in 1885, and Britain and Egypt took over in 1898. Sudan became independent on January 1, 1956. Long civil wars followed, South Sudan separated in 2011, conflict in Darfur from 2003 displaced huge numbers, and fighting resumed in 2023.
funFacts: Sudan has around 200 ancient pyramids, more than twice as many as Egypt, most of them clustered at Meroë.
Where the Blue and White Niles meet in Khartoum, the two differently colored waters run side by side for a stretch.
Most of the world's gum arabic, an ingredient in soft drinks and candy, comes from acacia trees growing in Sudan.
Kings from Kush ruled Egypt as pharaohs for about a century, known to historians as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty.
Sudan was Africa's largest country until South Sudan separated in 2011; it is now the third largest.

content.tagline: West Africa's Atlantic gateway
content.overview:
Senegal holds the westernmost point of mainland Africa, where the continent pushes out into the Atlantic on the Cape Verde Peninsula. About the size of South Dakota, it wraps almost entirely around the narrow country of The Gambia, which follows its own river inland. Mauritania lies to the north, Mali to the east, and Guinea and Guinea-Bissau to the south.

Around 18 million people live in Senegal. French is the official language, but Wolof is the language of streets and markets, with Pulaar, Serer, and Diola widely spoken too. Dakar, the capital, is a busy port and cultural capital on the peninsula, famous for its music and for the island of Gorée just offshore. Senegal is a republic with an elected president.

The country is known across Africa for teranga, a Wolof word meaning hospitality and generosity toward guests, and for a long record of peaceful transfers of power between elected leaders.
content.landAndNature: Senegal is mostly flat and dry, a land of savanna and sandy plains that turns green during a rainy season from about June to October. The Senegal River marks the northern border, while the Saloum and Casamance rivers spread into mangrove deltas in the south, where the Casamance region is wetter and greener, thick with palms and rice fields. Djoudj National Park near the river mouth is one of the world's great bird sanctuaries, where millions of pelicans, flamingos, and ducks arrive from Europe each winter. Baobab trees, the national symbol, stand alone in the fields with thick trunks and stubby branches, and Lake Retba turns pink when salt-loving microbes bloom.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Senegalese are Muslim, many belonging to Sufi brotherhoods such as the Mouride order, whose holy city of Touba fills with pilgrims once a year; Christian and older traditional practices are part of the mix as well. Thieboudienne, rice cooked with fish, tomato, and vegetables, is the national dish and is often eaten from one big shared platter. Music is a national strength: griot families have carried history in song for centuries, and mbalax, with its fast sabar drumming, made Youssou N'Dour famous worldwide. Senegalese wrestling, called laamb, draws crowds larger than soccer matches, and the national team won the Africa Cup of Nations in 2022.
content.history: The empires of Ghana, Mali, and Jolof ruled or traded across this region, and Islam spread here from about the eleventh century. From the 1400s European ships arrived for gold, gum arabic, and enslaved people; the island of Gorée off Dakar became a trading post and now stands as a memorial to the transatlantic slave trade. France took control through the 1800s, made Saint-Louis the capital of French West Africa, and built a railway inland to carry peanuts. Senegal became independent on April 4, 1960, with the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor as its first president; he governed for twenty years and then stepped down voluntarily, a rare act at the time. Governments have changed through elections since.
funFacts: Pointe des Almadies, on the edge of Dakar, is the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
The Dakar Rally took its name from Senegal's capital, where the desert race finished until it moved to South America in 2009.
Senegal's first president, Léopold Sédar Senghor, was a celebrated poet and the first African elected to the French Academy.
Senegal's giant baobabs can store thousands of liters of water in their trunks and live for over a thousand years.
The African Renaissance Monument outside Dakar is a bronze statue taller than the Statue of Liberty.

content.tagline: A city, an island, and a country
content.overview:
Singapore is a city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, one main island plus about 60 small ones, sitting almost on the equator. At roughly 710 km² it is smaller than New York City, and it has grown by about a quarter since independence by reclaiming land from the sea. Causeways and a bridge link it to Malaysia; Indonesia lies just across the strait.

About 6 million people live in Singapore, one of the most densely populated countries on Earth. Four languages are official: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil. English is the language of school and business, and Malay provides the national anthem.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic and has been governed by the same party since 1959. Its harbor is one of the busiest ports in the world, and in about sixty years the country went from a struggling trading post to one of the wealthiest places on the planet.
content.landAndNature: The island is low and flat; Bukit Timah Hill, at 164 meters, is the highest natural point, and its surrounding reserve holds a patch of original rainforest with long-tailed macaques, pangolins and flying lemurs. Being just north of the equator, Singapore is hot and humid all year, around 31°C most days, with sudden heavy downpours and thunder more than 150 days a year. The city calls itself a City in a Garden: trees line the expressways, and the Gardens by the Bay built vertical steel Supertrees planted with ferns and orchids. The Sungei Buloh wetlands attract migrating shorebirds, otters swim in the reservoirs and canals right through downtown, and the national flower is a hybrid orchid.
content.peopleAndCulture: Singapore's people are mainly of Chinese, Malay and Indian descent, and public holidays include Chinese New Year, Hari Raya Puasa, Deepavali and Christmas. Many people speak Singlish, a quick-fire English sprinkled with Malay and Chinese words and ending tags like lah. Food is a national obsession, eaten in hawker centers where dozens of stalls sell chicken rice, laksa, chili crab, char kway teow and roti prata for a few dollars; the hawker culture is on UNESCO's heritage list. About four in five people live in well-planned public housing blocks. Rules are strict and famously enforced: chewing gum cannot be sold, and littering brings heavy fines, which is part of why the city is so clean.
content.history: A port called Temasek stood here in the 1300s, and the name Singapura, Lion City, comes from a legend of a prince who saw a strange beast. Sir Stamford Raffles established a British trading post in 1819, and the free port drew merchants and workers from China, India and the Malay world, becoming one of Asia's busiest harbors. Japan captured Singapore in February 1942 in a shattering defeat for Britain and occupied it for three and a half years. After the war Singapore moved toward self-rule, joined Malaysia in 1963, and was expelled two years later, becoming an unwilling independent country on August 9, 1965. Under Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew it built housing, schools, industry and clean government, and living standards rose dramatically within a single generation.
funFacts: Singapore is one of only three surviving city-states in the world, along with Monaco and Vatican City.
The country has grown about 25 percent larger since the 1960s by filling in land along its coasts.
Selling chewing gum is banned, though gum prescribed by a dentist or pharmacist is allowed.
Changi Airport has a 40-meter indoor waterfall, and its terminals include gardens, slides and a cinema.
Singapore collects rainwater across two-thirds of the island and recycles wastewater into drinking water called NEWater.

content.tagline: Rainforest islands of the western Pacific
content.overview:
Solomon Islands is a scattered nation of roughly 1,000 islands in Melanesia, southeast of Papua New Guinea and northeast of Australia. Six main islands, including Guadalcanal, Malaita and Santa Isabel, hold most of the land, which totals about 28,900 km², a little smaller than Belgium, spread across a great expanse of ocean.

About 800,000 people live here. English is the official language, but almost everyone speaks Solomon Islands Pijin as a common tongue, and more than 60 local languages are spoken at home. Honiara, on Guadalcanal, is the capital.

Solomon Islands is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Most families live in villages, growing sweet potato, taro and cassava and fishing the lagoons; logging, fish and palm oil are the main exports. The islands are known for rainforest, spectacular diving over World War II wrecks, and shell money still used in traditional exchanges.
content.landAndNature: The islands are mostly volcanic, with steep forested interiors, rivers and narrow coastal flats; Mount Popomanaseu on Guadalcanal reaches about 2,335 meters. Kavachi, an underwater volcano in the west, erupts often and has sharks living inside its crater. Marovo Lagoon is one of the largest saltwater lagoons in the world, enclosed by a double barrier reef. The forests hold cuscus, a slow-moving marsupial, huge monitor lizards, and hornbills, while the reefs are part of the Coral Triangle, with hundreds of coral species. The Solomons is home to the world's largest extinct-volcano atoll, and its beaches host leatherback turtles. Cyclones and earthquakes strike regularly; a tsunami in 2007 destroyed coastal villages.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Solomon Islanders are Melanesian, with Polynesian communities on some outer islands and Micronesian settlers on others. Wealth and ceremony can still involve shell money: strings of tiny shell discs, cut, drilled and polished mainly on Malaita, are used for bride-price and compensation. Panpipe orchestras from Malaita play interlocking bamboo melodies, and bamboo bands beat lengths of pipe with rubber sandals to make deep booming notes. Food is cooked in stone ovens, and fish with taro or cassava pudding is common. Canoes carved from a single log, some with inlaid shell decoration, remain important for travel and fishing. Soccer and futsal are popular, and the national futsal team has done well in Oceania.
content.history: People settled these islands at least 30,000 years ago, and Austronesian voyagers arrived later, bringing pottery and new crops. Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña reached them in 1568 and named them after the biblical King Solomon, hoping for gold that was never found. In the 1800s blackbirding ships carried thousands of islanders, sometimes by force or trickery, to work on plantations in Queensland and Fiji. Britain declared a protectorate in 1893. During World War II the Battle of Guadalcanal, from August 1942 to February 1943, was a turning point in the Pacific, and the seabed off Honiara, nicknamed Iron Bottom Sound, holds dozens of sunken ships. Independence came on July 7, 1978. Ethnic conflict between 1998 and 2003 was ended with the help of a regional peacekeeping mission.
funFacts: Around one in ten Solomon Islanders has naturally blond hair with dark skin, caused by a gene found almost nowhere else.
Strings of polished shell discs are still used as money for bride-price and settling disputes.
The waters off Honiara are called Iron Bottom Sound because so many warships sank there during World War II.
Sharks have been filmed living inside the crater of Kavachi, an active undersea volcano, between eruptions.
A young John F. Kennedy was rescued here in 1943 after islanders carried his message carved on a coconut shell.

content.tagline: Lion mountains above an Atlantic harbor
content.overview:
Sierra Leone curves along the Atlantic coast of West Africa, a country about the size of South Carolina wedged between Guinea and Liberia. Its name comes from Portuguese sailors who in the 1400s called the hills above the shore Serra Leoa, the lion mountains, perhaps for the thunder that rolls off them in storms. The capital, Freetown, sits on one of the world's largest natural harbors, its houses climbing steep green slopes above the water.

About 8 million people live in Sierra Leone. English is the official language, used in schools and government, while nearly everyone talks in Krio, a language built from English and African languages that lets the country's many ethnic groups understand one another. Sierra Leone is a republic with an elected president. Farming, fishing and mining drive the economy, and the country's diamonds are famous around the world. South of the capital, beaches of white sand run for miles below forested hills.
content.landAndNature: Mangrove swamps and sandbars line the coast, giving way inland to rolling forest and savanna and rising in the northeast to Mount Bintumani, about 1,945 meters high. The rainy season from May to October is drenching, and Freetown is among the wettest capital cities in Africa. Tiwai Island, a research reserve in the Moa River, has one of the densest populations of primates on Earth, including the rare pygmy hippopotamus, which is roughly the size of a large pig and hides in rainforest streams. Chimpanzees, forest elephants and hundreds of bird species live in the remaining woodland, and sea turtles nest on the beaches.
content.peopleAndCulture: The Mende in the south and the Temne in the north are the largest of about sixteen ethnic groups, and Muslims and Christians live side by side, often within the same family. Rice is the heart of every meal, served with cassava leaf stew, groundnut soup or fried plantain, and pepper is used generously. Palm wine is tapped straight from the trees. Masked dancers, drummers and storytellers perform at harvests and ceremonies, and gumbe and bubu music keep villages moving. Soccer is the national passion, played barefoot on the beaches at low tide, and Krio proverbs season everyday conversation.
content.history: Farming peoples settled these forests thousands of years ago. Portuguese traders arrived in the 1400s, and for centuries the coast became a departure point for the transatlantic slave trade. In 1787 British campaigners against slavery founded a settlement for freed people that grew into Freetown, later home to thousands rescued from slave ships by the Royal Navy; their descendants became the Krio. Britain ruled the country as a colony until independence on April 27, 1961. From 1991 to 2002 a brutal civil war tore the country apart, funded partly by diamonds and marked by attacks on civilians and the use of child soldiers. Peacekeepers helped end it, an Ebola epidemic struck in 2014, and Sierra Leone has rebuilt in peace since.
funFacts: Freetown's harbor is one of the largest natural deep-water harbors in the world, big enough to shelter whole fleets of ships.
The Star of Sierra Leone, dug up in 1972, weighed about 969 carats and is among the largest diamonds ever found.
A giant cotton tree stood for centuries in the middle of Freetown as a national symbol until a storm brought it down in 2023.
Pygmy hippos weigh about a tenth as much as common hippos and live alone in the forest rather than in herds.
Krio, spoken by almost everyone in Sierra Leone, grew out of English mixed with West African languages and is understood far beyond the country.

content.tagline: Land of volcanoes and pupusas
content.overview:
El Salvador is the smallest country in Central America and the only one without a Caribbean coast; all of its shoreline faces the Pacific Ocean. It borders Guatemala and Honduras and covers about 21,000 km², about the size of the US state of New Jersey. Roughly 6 million people live there, making it the most densely populated country on the mainland of the Americas.

Salvadorans call their home the Land of Volcanoes, and more than 20 cones rise above its coffee farms and towns. The capital, San Salvador, sits in a valley beneath one of them. Spanish is the language, and nearly everyone shares a love of pupusas, thick corn cakes stuffed with cheese, beans or pork.

El Salvador is a republic with an elected president. After a long civil war ended in 1992, the country struggled with poverty and gang violence, and many Salvadorans moved to the United States; money they send home is a major part of the economy. Surfing beaches, coffee and factory exports are important, and it has used the US dollar as its money since 2001.
content.landAndNature:
A volcanic mountain chain runs the length of El Salvador parallel to the coast, with a narrow, hot coastal plain to the south and cooler highlands to the north along the Honduran border. Santa Ana, the highest volcano at about 2,380 meters, holds a glowing turquoise crater lake, and Izalco erupted so constantly from 1770 to 1958 that sailors called it the Lighthouse of the Pacific. Lake Ilopango and Lake Coatepeque fill ancient volcanic craters.

Earthquakes are frequent because the land sits where ocean and continental plates collide. The climate is tropical, with a rainy season from May to October. Much of the original forest was cleared for coffee and farms, but El Imposible National Park protects pumas, ocelots and hundreds of bird species. The turquoise-browed motmot, called the torogoz, is the national bird.
content.peopleAndCulture:
Most Salvadorans are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous Pipil and Spanish descent, and Spanish is spoken everywhere, sprinkled with local slang like "cipote" for kid. Family and Catholic or evangelical faith are central to life. Pupusas are the national dish, eaten with curtido, a tangy cabbage slaw, and the second Sunday of November is National Pupusa Day.

Soccer is the favorite sport, and the Pacific coast has become a world surfing destination; the beach town of El Tunco hosts international championships. Music ranges from cumbia to folk songs played on the marimba. During Holy Week, towns cover their streets with colorful sawdust carpets, and August's Fiestas Agostinas in San Salvador honor the country's patron, the Divine Savior of the World, with parades and fairs.
content.history:
The Pipil people, relatives of the Aztecs, ruled a kingdom called Cuzcatlán when Spanish soldiers under Pedro de Alvarado invaded in 1524. Long before that, around the year 600, a volcanic eruption buried the Maya farming village of Joya de Cerén in ash, preserving houses, gardens and food so perfectly it is called the Pompeii of the Americas.

El Salvador broke from Spain in 1821 and became a separate republic in 1841. Coffee made a few families rich while most people stayed poor; a peasant uprising in 1932 was crushed with the killing of thousands. From 1980 to 1992 a civil war between the military government and leftist rebels killed about 75,000 people, including Archbishop Óscar Romero, who was later declared a saint. Peace accords in 1992 brought democracy, but gangs and emigration have shaped the decades since.
funFacts: Joya de Cerén is the only place where an ordinary Maya village, not a temple or palace, was preserved by volcanic ash.
El Salvador is nicknamed the land of volcanoes and has more than 20 of them in a country the size of New Jersey.
In 2021 El Salvador became the first country to make bitcoin an official currency, an experiment it later scaled back.
The name El Salvador means "The Savior" in Spanish.
The 1969 Football War with Honduras began after tensions flared during World Cup qualifying matches and lasted about 100 hours.
Izalco volcano erupted almost nonstop for nearly 200 years, then suddenly went quiet in 1958.

SMR.name: San Marino
SMR.officialName: Most Serene Republic of San Marino

content.tagline: The world's oldest surviving republic
content.overview:
San Marino is a tiny country entirely surrounded by Italy, tucked into the hills about 10 kilometers inland from the Adriatic coast at Rimini. Its 61 square kilometers would fit inside many single cities, yet it is a fully independent state with its own government, stamps, and license plates, and it claims to be the oldest surviving republic in the world, founded by tradition in the year 301.

About 34,000 people live here and speak Italian. The capital, the City of San Marino, clings to the slopes of Monte Titano beneath three stone towers that appear on the flag and the coat of arms. San Marino is a republic led by two captains regent who hold office together for six months at a time, a system in place for more than 700 years.

Tourism, banking, ceramics, and collectible coins and stamps support the economy. San Marino uses the euro but is not a member of the European Union.
content.landAndNature: The whole country tilts across the eastern flank of the Apennine foothills, climbing from farmland at about 55 meters to the limestone crest of Monte Titano at 739 meters. From the top on a clear day the Adriatic Sea glitters to the east and Italian mountains stand to the west. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and mild, damp winters, and snow occasionally dusts the towers. There are no lakes and no large rivers, only small streams such as the Ausa and the Marano cutting shallow valleys. Vineyards, olive groves, and woods of oak and chestnut cover the slopes, where foxes, badgers, and hovering kestrels are common.
content.peopleAndCulture: Daily life closely resembles life in the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna that surrounds the country. Kitchens turn out handmade pasta such as tagliatelle and passatelli, piadina flatbread folded around cheese and ham, and torta tre monti, a layered wafer cake named for the three peaks. Catholicism is the main faith, and September 3, the feast of Saint Marinus, brings crossbow contests, medieval costumes, and flag-throwing displays. San Marino enters its own national teams in international sport; its soccer players are mostly part-timers with day jobs, so a single goal becomes national news. Motorcycle racing is followed closely, and Alessandra Perilli won the country's first Olympic medals in shooting in 2021.
content.history: By tradition a stonecutter named Marinus, fleeing persecution, climbed Monte Titano in the year 301 and founded a Christian community there. Mountains and stubbornness kept the little settlement free while popes, emperors, and Italian city-states fought over the land all around it. A written constitution from 1600 is still partly in force, among the oldest anywhere. San Marino sheltered Giuseppe Garibaldi in 1849 during Italy's wars of unification, and the new Italian state later agreed to respect its independence. It stayed neutral in both world wars, taking in more than 100,000 refugees during the second, though it was bombed in 1944. San Marino joined the United Nations in 1992.
funFacts: San Marino elects two heads of state at once, and they serve together for only six months before handing over.
Three medieval towers stand along the ridge of Monte Titano, linked by a cliffside path called the Witches' Passage.
San Marino's soccer team, made up largely of part-time players, won its first competitive match in 2024 after decades of defeats.
The country has no airport and no railway, though an electric train climbed up from Rimini until 1944.
Collectible stamps and coins, printed and minted for collectors abroad, have been a source of national income for generations.

content.tagline: Africa's longest coastline, poets and camels
content.overview:
Somalia occupies the Horn of Africa, the pointed cape that juts into the Indian Ocean beside the mouth of the Red Sea. It has the longest coastline of any country on mainland Africa, roughly 3,300 kilometers, and covers an area a little smaller than Texas. Mogadishu, the capital, is an ancient Indian Ocean trading port of white buildings and long beaches, slowly rebuilt after years of fighting.

About 18 million people live in Somalia, and they share one language, Somali, alongside Arabic; almost everyone is Muslim, which makes the country unusually united in language and faith. Somalia is a federal republic. Many families are nomadic or semi-nomadic, moving herds of camels, goats and sheep between wells and pastures, and Somalia keeps more camels than any other country on Earth. Decades of conflict have made life hard, yet livestock trade, money sent home by Somalis living abroad, and a fast mobile-phone industry keep the economy moving.
content.landAndNature: Most of Somalia is hot, dry plain and thorny scrub. In the north the Golis and Cal Madow ranges rise above the Gulf of Aden to about 2,400 meters, catching enough sea mist to support pockets of juniper forest. Only two permanent rivers, the Jubba and the Shabelle, flow down from the Ethiopian highlands and water the farmland of the south. Rains arrive in two seasons, gu and deyr, and when they fail, drought follows quickly. Frankincense and myrrh trees, whose fragrant resin has been traded for thousands of years, grow on the northern cliffs. Wildlife includes the Somali wild ass, the long-necked gerenuk antelope, and many birds found nowhere else.
content.peopleAndCulture: Somalis call their country a nation of poets. Poems are composed aloud, memorized and recited at gatherings, and a well-made verse can settle an argument or make a reputation. Family lineages are recited too, tracing ancestors back many generations. Camel milk, rice with goat, and anjero, a spongy sourdough pancake, are everyday foods, and bananas are often eaten alongside rice. Tea is spiced with cardamom and cinnamon. Somali has been written in the Latin alphabet only since 1972. Soccer and basketball are popular, music with the oud and drums accompanies weddings, and intricate henna patterns are painted on hands for celebrations.
content.history: Somali lands traded with Egypt, Arabia, Persia and China for thousands of years, and coastal cities such as Mogadishu and Zeila grew rich on incense, cloth and gold. Islam arrived early, carried across the Red Sea. In the 1800s Britain and Italy divided the region into colonies, and the two parts joined at independence on July 1, 1960. A military government under Siad Barre took power in 1969 and collapsed in 1991, leaving no working national government and beginning decades of civil war, famine and piracy at sea. In 1991 the northwest declared itself the Republic of Somaliland; it governs itself but is not widely recognized by other countries. A federal government was re-established in 2012, and rebuilding continues.
funFacts: Somalia keeps more camels than any other country, roughly seven million, and camel milk is an ordinary everyday drink.
Somali was given an official written alphabet only in 1972, after which a nationwide campaign taught people to read it.
Frankincense, burned in temples since ancient Egypt, still comes largely from trees growing on Somalia's northern hillsides.
The caves of Laas Geel hold vivid rock paintings of long-horned cattle made as much as 5,000 years ago.
Somalia's coastline, about 3,300 kilometers long, is the longest of any country on the African mainland.

content.tagline: Where the Danube meets the Balkans
content.overview:
Serbia sits at the center of the Balkan Peninsula, a landlocked country about the size of South Carolina, with mountains in the south and the flat, fertile plains of Vojvodina in the north. The Danube crosses it from west to east, meets the Sava River at Belgrade, and then squeezes through the Iron Gates gorge on the Romanian border.

About 6.6 million people live in Serbia and speak Serbian, which is unusual for being written in two alphabets, Cyrillic and Latin. Belgrade, the capital, is one of the oldest cities in Europe, watched over by a fortress on the ridge above the meeting of the rivers. Serbia is a parliamentary republic and has applied to join the European Union.

Kosovo, formerly a province in southern Serbia, declared independence in 2008. Serbia does not recognize it, many countries do, and talks between the two sides have continued for years.
content.landAndNature: Northern Serbia belongs to the Pannonian Plain, a checkerboard of wheat, corn, and sunflower fields so level that the horizon seems to run on forever. South of the Danube the land climbs into hills and then mountains, reaching 2,169 meters at Midžor on the Bulgarian border, with the Dinaric ranges to the west. The Iron Gates, known in Serbian as Đerdap, form one of the longest and deepest river gorges in Europe, where the Danube narrows between cliffs. Oak and beech forests shelter wolves, bears, deer, and imperial eagles, while the Uvac canyon has become a stronghold for the griffon vulture, a bird whose wings can span nearly three meters.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Serbs belong to the Serbian Orthodox Church, and each family honors a patron saint on a day called slava, when the house fills with guests, round bread, and boiled wheat. Hungarian, Bosniak, Roma, and other communities add their own traditions, especially in Vojvodina. Meals are generous: grilled ćevapi and pljeskavica, sarma cabbage rolls, ajvar pepper relish, and flaky burek for breakfast. Brass bands take over the town of Guča each summer for a trumpet festival where the music runs all night. Serbia produces outstanding athletes for its size, particularly in basketball, water polo, volleyball, and tennis, where Novak Djokovic became one of the greatest players in the sport's history.
content.history: Several Roman emperors, including Constantine the Great, were born in this region. Slavs settled in the 600s, and a medieval Serbian kingdom reached its height in the 1300s before Ottoman armies won the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and eventually absorbed the land. Uprisings beginning in 1804 rebuilt Serbian self-rule, and full independence was recognized in 1878. The killing of an Austrian archduke in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered World War I, in which Serbia suffered enormous losses. Afterward it became the largest part of Yugoslavia. When Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s, wars in Croatia, Bosnia, and later Kosovo killed more than 100,000 people across the region, and NATO bombed Serbia in 1999. Montenegro left their union in 2006.
funFacts: Belgrade's fortress stands on a ridge that armies have fought over for roughly 2,000 years, and the city has been rebuilt dozens of times.
Nikola Tesla, whose ideas made alternating-current electricity practical, was an ethnic Serb; Belgrade's airport and a museum carry his name.
The Guča trumpet festival draws hundreds of thousands of visitors to a small Serbian town every summer.
Serbia is one of the world's leading raspberry growers, supplying a large share of the frozen raspberries sold worldwide.
Vinča, near Belgrade, was a farming settlement about 7,000 years ago that left behind clay figures with striking masked faces.

content.tagline: The world's youngest nation
content.overview:
South Sudan became the world's newest country in 2011, when it separated from Sudan after decades of war. It is landlocked in east-central Africa, bordered by Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic, and covers about 620,000 km², roughly the size of France. The capital is Juba, a river port on the White Nile.

Around 11 million people live in South Sudan, belonging to more than sixty ethnic groups; the Dinka and Nuer are the largest. English is the official language, while a simplified form called Juba Arabic serves as a common tongue in markets, and Dinka, Nuer and Zande are spoken at home. Most people are Christian or follow traditional beliefs. Cattle stand at the center of life, wealth and ceremony across much of the country. South Sudan is a republic with plentiful oil but few paved roads outside the capital, and it remains one of the world's least developed countries.
content.landAndNature: The White Nile flows north through the heart of the country and spreads into the Sudd, one of the largest wetlands on Earth, a maze of papyrus, reeds and floating islands that can double in size during the rains and once blocked boats from sailing upriver. Around it stretch grassy plains and woodland, and the Imatong Mountains rise near the Ugandan border to about 3,187 meters at Mount Kinyeti. South Sudan hosts one of the greatest animal migrations left on the planet: well over a million white-eared kob, tiang and gazelle sweep across the Boma and Badingilo plains in long columns, followed by lions and hyenas. Elephants, giraffes and shoebill storks live here too.
content.peopleAndCulture: Cattle shape daily life for Dinka, Nuer and Mundari herders, who name favorite bulls, compose songs about them and dust them with ash to keep off flies. Young people know their cattle camp the way others know a hometown. Sorghum and millet are ground into porridge and eaten with stews of okra, beans, peanuts or fish from the Nile. Communities gather for wrestling matches, a serious sport with drums, chanting and champions known across whole regions. Dances mark weddings and harvests. South Sudanese are famously tall, and several have become star basketball players abroad; the national team reached the Olympics in 2024.
content.history: Nilotic peoples, including the Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk, have herded cattle in these grasslands for many centuries. Egyptian and Ottoman expeditions pushed up the Nile in the 1800s, raiding for slaves and ivory, and Britain later governed the south separately from the Arabic-speaking north within Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. When Sudan became independent in 1956, southerners feared domination, and two long civil wars followed, from 1955 to 1972 and from 1983 to 2005, killing millions and forcing many more from their homes. A peace deal in 2005 promised a vote, and in 2011 almost 99 percent of southerners chose separation. Independence came on July 9, 2011, but a power struggle brought civil war from 2013 to 2018, and recovery has been slow.
funFacts: South Sudan is the world's newest widely recognized country, independent since July 9, 2011.
The Sudd wetland is so vast that its papyrus mazes once made the upper Nile nearly impossible to navigate.
More than a million antelope migrate across South Sudan's plains, a spectacle that rivals the Serengeti's wildebeest.
Mundari herders sleep beside their cattle and rub themselves with ash, which dries white and keeps insects away.
South Sudan's basketball team qualified for the Olympics in 2024, only thirteen years after the country was founded.

STP.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
STP.officialName: Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe

content.tagline: Chocolate islands on the equator
content.overview:
São Tomé and Príncipe is a country of two main volcanic islands and a scattering of rocky islets in the Gulf of Guinea, about 250 kilometers off the coast of Central Africa. It is the second-smallest country in Africa, covering less ground than New York City, and the equator crosses an islet just south of São Tomé island.

About 230,000 people live here, nearly all of them on São Tomé, the larger island; Príncipe, to the northeast, holds only a few thousand. Portuguese is the official language, and most people also speak a creole such as Forro. The capital, São Tomé, is a small port of pastel-colored colonial buildings, and the country is a republic with an elected president and parliament.

Nobody lived on these islands before Portuguese ships arrived in the 1470s. Cocoa plantations later made them one of the world's great chocolate suppliers, and cocoa still ripens in the shade of the rainforest.
content.landAndNature: Both islands are the tops of volcanoes rising from the deep Atlantic floor, and rainforest covers most of their steep interiors. Pico de São Tomé reaches 2,024 meters, and towers of hardened lava, including the needle-shaped Pico Cão Grande, stand above the trees. Rain falls heavily in the southwest and much more lightly in the drier north. Because the islands were never joined to the mainland, the plants and animals that arrived by wind, wave, or wing evolved on their own: the giant São Tomé begonia, the world's smallest ibis, and several birds found nowhere else. Sea turtles nest on the beaches, whales pass offshore, and no large predators live on land.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most islanders descend from Africans brought here by force, along with Portuguese settlers and later contract workers from Angola, Mozambique, and Cape Verde. Portuguese is used in school and government, while Forro, Angolar, and Principense creoles are spoken at home. Meals combine Atlantic fish with tropical crops: calulu, a stew of smoked fish with leafy greens and palm oil, breadfruit, and fried or boiled bananas. The tchiloli, a centuries-old masked play performed to drums and flutes, retells a medieval European legend in island style. Village festivals fill with ússua and socopé dancing, soccer is played on every flat patch of ground, and islanders describe their pace of life as leve-leve, gently gently.
content.history: Portuguese navigators reached these uninhabited islands around 1470 and began settling them within a few years. Sugar plantations were built with the labor of enslaved Africans, making São Tomé one of the first plantation slave colonies in the world and a model later copied across the Americas. Enslaved people revolted repeatedly, and some escaped into the mountains to form free communities. After sugar declined, coffee and then cocoa took over in the 1800s, worked under conditions so harsh that British chocolate makers boycotted the islands around 1909. Forced labor continued until a massacre of workers in 1953 hardened the independence movement. The country became independent from Portugal on July 12, 1975, and has held multiparty elections since 1991.
funFacts: The equator runs through Ilhéu das Rolas, where a stone marker lets visitors stand with one foot in each hemisphere.
São Tomé and Príncipe was the world's leading cocoa producer in the early 1900s, and cocoa still grows in its forests.
Pico Cão Grande is a needle of solidified lava rising roughly 300 meters straight out of the rainforest.
Príncipe island is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, almost entirely forested and home to fewer than 10,000 people.
No one lived on these islands before the 1470s, so every family here arrived by ship within the last 550 years.

content.tagline: Rainforest nation of many languages
content.overview:
Suriname is the smallest country in South America, tucked on the northeast shoulder of the continent between Guyana and French Guiana, with Brazil to the south and the Atlantic Ocean to the north. It covers about 164,000 km², similar to Florida, and rainforest blankets more than 90 percent of it, one of the highest proportions of any country.

Only about 620,000 people live here, nearly all of them on the narrow coastal plain. Dutch is the official language, a reminder of colonial rule, while Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is the everyday shared tongue, and Hindi, Javanese, Chinese and Indigenous languages are also spoken. Paramaribo, the capital, has a historic center of white wooden Dutch buildings beside the Suriname River.

Suriname is a presidential republic. Gold, oil and bauxite drive its economy, and offshore oil discoveries could change it considerably.
content.landAndNature: Behind the muddy coastal strip and its mangroves rise savannas and then a huge, almost roadless interior of tropical forest, cut by black-water rivers and rapids. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve protects an area larger than some countries, including the Voltzberg, a bare granite dome that pushes above the canopy. The Brokopondo reservoir, made by damming the Suriname River in the 1960s, flooded a vast area and left drowned trees standing in the water. Jaguars, giant river otters, tapirs, harpy eagles and eight kinds of monkey live in the forest, and the Guiana cock-of-the-rock, a flame-orange bird, displays on rocky slopes. Leatherback turtles, the largest turtles on Earth, nest on the beaches at Galibi.
content.peopleAndCulture: Suriname is one of the most diverse countries anywhere: descendants of Indian and Javanese indentured workers, Africans brought in slavery, Chinese and Dutch settlers, Lebanese traders, and Indigenous Kalina and Lokono peoples live side by side. Mosques stand beside synagogues and Hindu temples in Paramaribo. Maroon communities, descended from Africans who escaped plantations and built free societies in the forest, keep distinct languages, drumming and wood carving, and still govern their own villages. Food reflects everything at once: Indian roti, Javanese bami and saoto soup, Chinese noodles, and pom, a baked dish of grated root vegetable and chicken served at every celebration. Soccer is the leading sport, and many Dutch stars have Surinamese roots.
content.history: Indigenous peoples lived along the rivers long before Europeans arrived. The English settled here briefly, then in 1667 traded the colony to the Dutch in exchange for New Amsterdam, which became New York. The Dutch built sugar, coffee and cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans under brutal conditions; many escaped into the interior and formed Maroon communities that fought the colonists and won treaties recognizing their freedom in the 1760s. Slavery was abolished in 1863, and planters then recruited indentured laborers from India and Java, which is why the country is so mixed today. Suriname became independent from the Netherlands on November 25, 1975, and about a third of the population moved to the Netherlands around that time. Military rule in the 1980s gave way to elected government.
funFacts: The Dutch swapped New York for Suriname in 1667, trading Manhattan to England for a sugar colony.
More than 90 percent of Suriname is covered in forest, making it one of the greenest countries on Earth.
Paramaribo's main square has a mosque and a synagogue standing peacefully next door to each other.
Maroon peoples in the interior descend from Africans who escaped plantations and won their freedom by treaty in the 1700s.
Suriname is the only country in the Americas where Dutch is the official language.

content.tagline: Castles, caves and Carpathian peaks
content.overview:
Slovakia is a small, mountainous country in the heart of Europe, landlocked between Poland, Ukraine, Hungary, Austria and the Czech Republic. It covers about 49,000 km², a little larger than Denmark, and roughly 5.4 million people live there. The Danube River forms part of the southern border and flows through the capital, Bratislava, which sits so close to its neighbors that a cyclist can reach two other countries in an afternoon.

Slovak is the national language, so close to Czech that most Slovaks understand it without ever studying it. Slovakia is a parliamentary republic, a member of the European Union, and it uses the euro. Car factories are its biggest industry; Slovakia builds more cars for each person living there than any other country. Beyond the factory towns the landscape is one of forested hills, ruined castles perched on rocky crags, spa towns, and wooden churches built without a single iron nail.
content.landAndNature: The Carpathian Mountains sweep across northern Slovakia, and their highest range, the High Tatras, throws up bare granite peaks; Gerlachovský štít reaches 2,655 meters. Below them lie glacial lakes called tarns and deep valleys where brown bears, wolves, lynx and chamois still live, giving Slovakia one of Europe's largest bear populations. Limestone underlies much of the country, dissolved by water into more than 7,000 known caves, several open to visitors. The Dobšiná Ice Cave keeps its ice all year round. Rivers such as the Váh and Hron run south into the fertile Danube lowland, where white storks build enormous nests on chimneys and poles each summer.
content.peopleAndCulture: Slovak folk traditions are living habits rather than museum pieces: embroidered costumes, painted village houses like those at Čičmany, and the fujara, a shepherd's flute nearly two meters long that is played standing up and is protected by UNESCO. Hearty food suits cold winters, and the national dish is bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese and bacon. Ice hockey empties the streets when the national team plays; Slovakia won the world championship in 2002. Hiking and skiing fill weekends in the Tatras. At Easter, boys in some villages still sprinkle girls with water for good health, and Christmas brings carp, sauerkraut soup and wafers with honey.
content.history: Slavic peoples settled the region in the 500s, and in the 800s the empire of Great Moravia spread Christianity here using a new Slavic alphabet brought by the monks Cyril and Methodius. For roughly a thousand years the land belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary, and Bratislava, then called Pressburg, served as the Hungarian capital and coronation city. After World War I, Slovaks joined Czechs in the new state of Czechoslovakia. It was broken apart during World War II, then governed by a communist party from 1948 until the peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989. On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia divided calmly in two, and Slovakia became an independent country without a shot being fired.
funFacts: Slovakia builds more cars per person than any other country, with giant factories turning out around a million vehicles a year.
Bratislava is the only national capital in the world that borders two other countries, Austria and Hungary.
Eleven Hungarian kings and several queens were crowned in Bratislava's St. Martin's Cathedral between 1563 and 1830.
Slovakia's embassies have long swapped misdelivered mail with Slovenia's, because letters are so often sent to the wrong country.
Slovakia has more than 180 castles and hundreds of smaller manor houses, one of the highest numbers per person anywhere.

content.tagline: Alps, caves and a green heart
content.overview:
Slovenia packs an astonishing variety into an area smaller than New Jersey. In one day a traveler can ski in the Julian Alps, walk through a cave the size of a cathedral, and swim in the Adriatic Sea, because the country's 47 kilometers of coastline lie only a couple of hours from its northern peaks. Slovenia borders Italy, Austria, Hungary and Croatia, and about 2.1 million people live there.

The capital, Ljubljana, is a small city of pastel houses along a willow-lined river, with a hilltop castle above and a car-free center. Slovene, a Slavic language with a rare grammatical form used for exactly two of something, is the national language. Slovenia is a parliamentary republic and joined the European Union in 2004. More than half the country is covered in forest, one of the highest shares in Europe, and Slovenes are known for their beekeeping, their mountain huts, and cyclists who rank among the best in the world.
content.landAndNature: The Julian Alps fill the northwest, crowned by Mount Triglav at 2,864 meters, a three-headed peak that appears on the national flag; Slovenes joke that nobody is truly Slovene until they have climbed it.
