Beneath the southwest lies the Karst, a limestone plateau so famous that geographers everywhere borrow its name for landscapes of sinkholes, underground rivers and caves. Postojna Cave runs more than 24 kilometers and shelters the olm, a pale blind salamander that can live a century. Lake Bled reflects the Alps around a tiny island church. Brown bears, lynx and ibex still roam the forests and high slopes.
content.peopleAndCulture: Slovenes head for the mountains on weekends, and hiking is close to a national habit, with wardens serving soup in huts along the ridges. Bees matter here more than almost anywhere: Slovenia is known for painted beehive panels and persuaded the United Nations to declare World Bee Day on May 20, the birthday of the beekeeper Anton Janša. Food mixes Alpine, Italian and Balkan flavors, and potica, a rolled nut cake, is the festive favorite. Skiing and ski jumping fill winter television, and Slovenian riders have won the Tour de France. Culture Day on February 8 honors the poet France Prešeren, whose verses became the national anthem.
content.history: Celts and then Romans built towns here, including Emona, which lies beneath modern Ljubljana. Slavic ancestors of the Slovenes arrived in the 500s and formed the early duchy of Carantania. For more than 600 years the region was ruled by the Habsburgs from Vienna, which is why Austrian styles mark its churches and coffee houses. After World War I, Slovenia joined the kingdom that became Yugoslavia; it was occupied and divided during World War II, then returned to a communist-led Yugoslavia. In 1991 Slovenia declared independence, and the fighting that followed lasted only ten days, the briefest of the Yugoslav wars. Slovenia joined the European Union and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2007.
funFacts: The olm, a blind cave salamander found in Slovenia, can survive more than ten years without eating anything.
A small railway has carried visitors through Postojna Cave since 1872, one of the earliest underground train lines anywhere.
Ljubljana's symbol is a dragon, and four bronze dragons guard the corners of one bridge over the river.
About 60 percent of Slovenia is forest, making it one of the most densely wooded countries in Europe.
Roughly one in every 200 Slovenes keeps bees, and the country's campaign created the United Nations World Bee Day.

content.tagline: Forests, lakes and the midnight sun
content.overview:
Sweden stretches nearly 1,600 kilometers from the Baltic Sea in the south to well above the Arctic Circle in the north, making it the largest country in northern Europe and about the size of California. Forest covers roughly two-thirds of the land, and there are close to 100,000 lakes. Stockholm, the capital, is built across fourteen islands where a great lake meets the sea, stitched together by bridges and ferries.

About 10.5 million people live in Sweden, most of them in the milder south. Swedish is the national language, and the Sami people of the north speak Sami languages. Sweden is a constitutional monarchy: a king serves as ceremonial head of state while an elected parliament called the Riksdag governs. The country is known for a strong welfare system, long parental leave, and design that favors simple, useful things. Swedish inventions, from the safety match to the three-point seatbelt, have traveled far beyond its borders.
content.landAndNature: The Scandinavian Mountains run along the Norwegian border, rising to Kebnekaise at about 2,100 meters and dotted with small glaciers. Below them lie the tundra and marshes of Lapland, then vast spruce and pine forests, and finally farmland and beech woods in the far south. Sweden's coast is fringed with archipelagos; the Stockholm archipelago alone counts some 30,000 islands and rocky skerries. North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set for weeks in summer and barely rises in winter, when the northern lights ripple green overhead. Moose, lynx, wolverines and brown bears live in the forests, and reindeer herds are tended by Sami herders.
content.peopleAndCulture: Swedes take a daily coffee break called fika, pausing with a cinnamon bun and company rather than rushing. Food runs from meatballs with lingonberry jam to pickled herring, crispbread and, in the north, the famously pungent fermented fish surströmming. Midsummer in late June is the biggest celebration, with flower crowns, a leafy maypole and dancing outdoors until the sky barely darkens. Saint Lucia's Day in December brings children in white robes carrying candles and singing at dawn. A legal right of public access lets anyone walk and camp in the countryside. Ice hockey and soccer are the main sports, and Swedish songwriters shape pop music worldwide.
content.history: Sweden's Viking Age seafarers sailed east down Russian rivers to Constantinople and traded as far as Baghdad. Christianity arrived around the year 1000, and by the 1300s Sweden had joined Denmark and Norway in the Kalmar Union, breaking away under Gustav Vasa in 1523. In the 1600s Sweden became a great military power around the Baltic before losing most of those lands, and Finland passed to Russia in 1809. Still a poor farming country in the 1800s, it sent more than a million emigrants to America. Sweden stayed out of both world wars and used the peace to build industry and a generous welfare state. It joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024.
funFacts: Sweden has about 100,000 lakes, and a right of public access lets anyone walk, swim or camp on most land.
Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist who invented dynamite, left his fortune to create the Nobel Prizes.
The three-point seatbelt was invented at Volvo in 1959, and the patent was given away free to save lives.
Sweden burns much of its household waste for heat and electricity, and imports rubbish from other countries as fuel.
Swedes celebrate a cinnamon bun day every October 4, honoring the country's most beloved pastry.

content.tagline: Africa's last absolute monarchy
content.overview:
Eswatini, known until 2018 as Swaziland, is a small landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, tucked between South Africa and Mozambique. It is smaller than New Jersey but rises from hot lowland bush in the east to cool green mountains in the west. The country has two capitals: Mbabane, where the government offices are, and Lobamba, the royal and traditional capital, home to the parliament and the residence of the Queen Mother.

About 1.2 million people live in Eswatini, almost all of them Swazi. Swazi, also called siSwati, and English are the official languages. Eswatini is the last absolute monarchy in Africa: the king, Mswati III, appoints the prime minister and can overrule parliament, and political parties are not allowed to contest elections. Many Swazis are proud of their traditions and royal ceremonies, while others have protested for democracy. People farm sugarcane, corn, and cattle, work in forestry and textiles, or commute to jobs in South Africa. Wildlife reserves and craft markets draw visitors.
content.landAndNature: Eswatini is small but varied. The western Highveld is a land of misty mountains, waterfalls, and pine plantations, with Emlembe peak reaching 1,862 meters; the Malolotja reserve there has one of the oldest known rocks on Earth and ancient iron and ochre mines at Ngwenya. The central Middleveld is rolling farmland where most people live. The eastern Lowveld is hot, dry savanna of thorn trees and sugarcane fields, sheltered by the Lubombo Mountains along the Mozambican border. Rivers such as the Komati and Great Usutu cut across the country. Hlane Royal National Park protects lions, elephants, and white rhinos, and Mkhaya reserve shelters rare black rhinos, while Mlilwane is famous for zebras and blue cranes.
content.peopleAndCulture: Swazi culture centers on the monarchy, clans, and cattle, which are still a measure of wealth. Every year tens of thousands of young men gather for Incwala, the sacred first-fruits ceremony, and unmarried girls in beaded skirts and tassels dance for the Queen Mother at Umhlanga, the Reed Dance, one of Africa's largest cultural events. Traditional dress of bright cloth wraps and animal-skin skirts is worn on special occasions. Corn is the staple, eaten as a stiff porridge with beans, pumpkin, sour milk, or meat stew. Most Swazis are Christian, often blending church with ancestor traditions. Soccer is the top sport, and Swazi crafts such as glassblowing, batik cloth, and woven sisal baskets are sold worldwide.
content.history: Stone Age hunters and later Bantu-speaking farmers lived here for thousands of years. In the 1700s and 1800s the Dlamini clan under kings Sobhuza I and Mswati II united smaller chiefdoms into the Swazi nation, defending it from Zulu raids; the country is named after Mswati II. Boer and British settlers took much of the land in the late 1800s, and Britain made Swaziland a protectorate in 1903. King Sobhuza II ruled for 82 years, the longest reign of any monarch in recorded history, guiding the country to independence on September 6, 1968 and then suspending the constitution in 1973 to rule directly. His son Mswati III became king in 1986. In 2018 the king renamed the country Eswatini, meaning land of the Swazis. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were put down by force.
funFacts: King Sobhuza II reigned for 82 years, from 1899 to 1982, the longest verified reign of any monarch in history.
The Ngwenya mine in Eswatini was dug by humans about 43,000 years ago, making it one of the oldest mines in the world.
The country changed its name from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018 partly because people kept confusing it with Switzerland.
Eswatini has two capital cities: Mbabane for the government and Lobamba for the king and parliament.
The Umhlanga Reed Dance draws tens of thousands of girls and young women who present reeds to the Queen Mother.

content.tagline: Granite islands in the Indian Ocean
content.overview:
Seychelles is an archipelago of about 115 islands scattered across the Indian Ocean roughly 1,500 kilometers east of the African mainland. It is the smallest country in Africa by both land and population: all the islands together cover about 450 square kilometers, and only around 100,000 people live on them.

Most Seychellois live on Mahé, where the capital, Victoria, sits beneath forested peaks; Praslin and La Digue are the next largest islands. Three languages are official: Seychellois Creole, which nearly everyone speaks at home, plus English and French. Seychelles is a republic with an elected president.

The inner islands are unusual because they are made of granite, the remains of an ancient continent that split apart, rather than coral or volcanic rock like most ocean islands. Their boulder-strewn beaches, clear water, and rare wildlife draw visitors from around the world, and tourism and tuna fishing are the country's main industries.
content.landAndNature: The granite inner islands rise steeply from the sea, reaching 905 meters on Mahé, with huge weathered boulders piled along the shore. Farther out lie flat coral islands and atolls, including Aldabra, one of the largest coral atolls on Earth and home to roughly 100,000 giant tortoises, more than anywhere else in the world. The climate is warm and humid all year, with a rainy northwest monsoon and a drier, breezier southeast season. The Vallée de Mai on Praslin is a palm forest holding the coco de mer, whose nut is the heaviest seed of any plant. Black parrots, fairy terns, and hawksbill turtles live here among fringing coral reefs.
content.peopleAndCulture: Seychellois people descend from French settlers, enslaved Africans, and later Indian, Chinese, and British arrivals, and Creole culture blends all of it. Seychellois Creole grew out of French and has its own spelling system. Meals come from the sea and the garden: grilled fish with chili and lime, octopus curry in coconut milk, breadfruit, and mangoes. The moutya, a slow drum dance once performed by enslaved people at night and long discouraged by authorities, is now recognized by UNESCO, while the faster sega is danced at parties. Most Seychellois are Catholic. Fishing, sailing, and soccer fill free time, and the Creole Festival each October celebrates language, food, and music.
content.history: Seychelles had no permanent inhabitants until modern times, though Arab and other sailors probably passed by and Portuguese ships charted the islands in the 1500s. France claimed them in 1756 and brought settlers and enslaved Africans to grow spices, cotton, and coconuts. Britain took over in 1814 and abolished slavery in the 1830s; Africans freed from intercepted slave ships were landed here, adding to the population. Seychelles became independent on June 29, 1976. A coup the following year brought one-party rule that lasted until multiparty elections returned in 1993. The country is now known for protecting its environment, setting aside nearly half its land and a vast stretch of ocean as reserves.
funFacts: The coco de mer palm produces the heaviest seed in the world, weighing up to about 18 kilograms.
Aldabra atoll is home to far more giant tortoises than the whole country has people, roughly 100,000 of them.
Seychelles has no native land mammals except bats; nearly every other animal on land arrived by ship.
Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise hatched around 1832 and now living on Saint Helena, is the oldest known land animal.
The inner islands are granite, a rock usually found on continents, left stranded when India drifted away millions of years ago.

content.tagline: Ancient crossroads of the Middle East
content.overview:
Syria sits at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea, bordering Turkey, Iraq, Jordan, Israel and Lebanon. It covers about 185,000 km², roughly the size of Washington state, with a green coastal strip, mountains, a wide steppe and desert reaching toward the Euphrates River.

Before 2011 about 21 million people lived in Syria; since then war has displaced more than half the population, and millions live as refugees in neighboring countries and beyond. Arabic is the official language, with Kurdish, Armenian, Syriac and other languages spoken by minority communities. Damascus, the capital, is one of the oldest cities in the world that has been lived in without a break.

Syria is a republic. It has been the site of a civil war since 2011, which has destroyed cities, damaged ancient sites and caused one of the largest humanitarian crises of modern times. The country is now working to recover and rebuild.
content.landAndNature: A narrow, fertile coastal plain runs along the Mediterranean, backed by the Coastal Mountain Range and, further inland, the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, where Mount Hermon's snow feeds springs. East of the mountains the land dries into steppe and then the Syrian Desert of stone and scrub, crossed by the Euphrates, the country's only major river, which is dammed at Lake Assad. Winters are mild and wet on the coast and cold inland, summers hot and dry. Pistachio, olive and citrus groves cover the west, and wheat and cotton grow along the river. Desert wildlife includes gazelles, striped hyenas and the northern bald ibis, a strange-looking bird whose last wild eastern colony was found near Palmyra.
content.peopleAndCulture: Syrian food is famous across the Middle East: hummus, tabbouleh, kibbeh, and grilled meats, followed by pastries dripping with syrup and pistachios. Aleppo was known for its soap made from olive and laurel oil and for its enormous covered market, much of it damaged in the fighting. Most Syrians are Arab and Muslim, with Kurdish, Armenian and Assyrian communities and long-established Christian churches where some villagers still speak Aramaic, the language of Jesus. Family gatherings, poetry, backgammon in cafés and strong sweet tea are part of daily life. Syrian craftspeople are known for inlaid woodwork, brocade weaving and glassblowing, skills passed down for centuries in the old cities.
content.history: Some of the world's first farming villages, writing and alphabets appeared in this region; Ebla and Ugarit kept clay-tablet libraries more than 3,000 years ago. Syria was ruled in turn by Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, who built the desert caravan city of Palmyra, and Byzantines. After Arab armies arrived in the 630s, Damascus became the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, ruling from Spain to India. Crusaders, Mongols and Ottomans followed; Ottoman rule lasted 400 years. France governed Syria after World War I, and independence came in 1946. Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970 and his son Bashar succeeded him in 2000. Peaceful protests in 2011 were met with force and grew into a civil war involving many armed groups and foreign powers; the Assad government fell in December 2024.
funFacts: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, with people living there for around 4,000 years or more.
The world's oldest known complete alphabet was found at Ugarit on Syria's coast, written in wedge-shaped signs.
Krak des Chevaliers is one of the best-preserved crusader castles anywhere, with walls up to 30 meters thick in places.
In the village of Maaloula, some people still speak Aramaic, a language spoken in the region 2,000 years ago.
Aleppo soap, made from olive oil and laurel oil and aged for months, has been produced by the same method for centuries.

content.tagline: Sahara giant with a shrinking lake
content.overview:
Chad is a huge landlocked country in north-central Africa, about three times the size of California, stretching from the empty Sahara in the north to wet savanna in the south. It is named after Lake Chad on its western border, a lake that was once one of Africa's largest but has shrunk dramatically over the past 60 years. The capital, N'Djamena, lies on the Chari River across from Cameroon. Neighbors include Libya, Sudan, the Central African Republic, Cameroon, Nigeria, and Niger.

About 18 million people live in Chad, most in the greener south and center. Arabic and French are the official languages, and more than 120 other languages are spoken by groups such as the Sara, Kanembu, Toubou, and Zaghawa. Herding camels, cattle, and goats is a way of life in the north, while farmers in the south grow cotton, sorghum, and peanuts. Oil has been pumped since 2003. Chad is a republic that has experienced many coups and rebellions, and it hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees from Sudan and other neighbors.
content.landAndNature: Northern Chad is deep Sahara, where the Tibesti Mountains rise to 3,415 meters at Emi Koussi, a volcano and the highest point in the desert. The Ennedi Plateau nearby is a wonderland of sandstone arches, towers, and canyons with ancient rock paintings and a permanent pool, the Guelta d'Archei, where camels drink beside a tiny surviving population of Nile crocodiles. The Lakes of Ounianga sparkle blue and green amid the dunes, fed by underground water. Moving south, the land turns to Sahel scrub, then savanna with baobabs, then woodland near the Central African border. Zakouma National Park protects elephants, giraffes, lions, and vast flocks of birds. Lake Chad, though shrunken, is still a lifeline for fishers and farmers.
content.peopleAndCulture: Chad's people are roughly half Muslim, mostly in the north and center, and nearly half Christian, mostly in the south, with some following traditional beliefs. The Sara are the largest group. Millet and sorghum are made into a firm porridge called boule, eaten with sauces of okra, dried fish, or meat, and grilled fish from the Chari River is a N'Djamena favorite. Tea is brewed strong and sweet in three rounds. Nomadic Toubou and Arab herders move with their camels across the north, and the Gerewol festival of the Wodaabe Fulani features young men in makeup competing in beauty and dance. Wrestling is a traditional sport, soccer the most popular modern one, and archaeologists prize the region for fossils of some of the earliest human ancestors.
content.history: Around Lake Chad, the Sao people built walled towns more than a thousand years ago, and from about 700 the Kanem Empire, later Kanem-Bornu, grew rich on trade routes across the Sahara, lasting nearly a thousand years. The kingdoms of Baguirmi and Wadai rose later. France conquered the area in the early 1900s and ruled it as part of French Equatorial Africa, with little investment outside the cotton-growing south. Chad became independent on August 11, 1960. A civil war between north and south began in 1965 and merged into a long conflict with Libya, which tried to seize northern Chad in the 1980s. Idriss Déby took power in 1990 and ruled for 30 years until he was killed fighting rebels in 2021, when his son took over.
funFacts: Lake Chad has lost about 90 percent of its water area since the 1960s, shrinking from a great inland sea to marshes and pools.
A skull nicknamed Toumaï, found in Chad in 2001, belongs to a human ancestor that lived about seven million years ago.
The Guelta d'Archei in the Ennedi desert is one of the last places where crocodiles survive in the Sahara.
Emi Koussi, at 3,415 meters, is the highest mountain in the entire Sahara Desert.
Chad's flag is nearly identical to Romania's, differing only in a slightly darker shade of blue.

content.tagline: A slender strip from sea to savanna
content.overview:
Togo is a ribbon of a country in West Africa, only about 110 kilometers wide at its broadest but stretching some 550 kilometers inland from a short Atlantic coast. Squeezed between Ghana and Benin, with Burkina Faso to the north, it is roughly the size of West Virginia. The capital, Lomé, sits right on the beach in the southwestern corner, so close to Ghana that the border runs along the edge of the city, and its port serves landlocked countries far inland.

About 9 million people live in Togo, in some 40 ethnic groups; the Ewe are the largest in the south and the Kabye in the north. French is the official language, while Ewe and Kabye are widely spoken at home and in markets. Togo is a republic. Most families farm, growing maize, yams, cassava and cocoa, and phosphate rock for fertilizer is the main mineral export. Togo is also one of the homelands of the Vodun religion.
content.landAndNature: Sandy beaches and coconut palms line the coast, backed by lagoons and shallow Lake Togo. Inland the ground rises into the Togo Mountains, a green chain of forested hills where Mount Agou reaches 986 meters, the country's highest point, and waterfalls drop through the trees near Kpalimé. Farther north the land flattens into savanna of tall grass and baobab trees, hotter and drier, where the harmattan wind carries Saharan dust each winter. Fazao-Malfakassa and Kéran parks protect elephants, antelope, monkeys and hippos. Butterflies are so numerous in the hills around Kpalimé that collectors and naturalists travel there just to see them.
content.peopleAndCulture: Togolese meals center on pounded yam or a maize dough called akoumé, eaten with sauces of okra, tomato or peanut, and plenty of fish along the coast. Street stalls sell fried plantain and spicy beans. Music ranges from ceremonial drumming and dance to Afrobeat and reggae in Lomé's bars. Vodun, a religion of spirits and ancestors that began in this region, is practiced alongside Christianity and Islam. In the northeast, the Tamberma build fortified mud houses with rounded towers, protected as a World Heritage site. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Togo reached the World Cup finals in 2006.
content.history: Ewe, Kabye and other peoples settled this land over many centuries, some moving here to escape wars elsewhere. For roughly 200 years the shore was part of what Europeans called the Slave Coast, a place where captured people were shipped across the Atlantic; the old town of Aného still carries that history. Germany claimed the territory as Togoland in 1884 and built railways and plantations. After World War I it was divided between Britain and France, and the British part later joined Ghana. French Togoland became independent on April 27, 1960. Gnassingbé Eyadéma ruled from 1967 until his death in 2005, one of Africa's longest-serving leaders, and his son took over after him.
funFacts: Togo is one of Africa's narrowest countries, in places only about 50 kilometers from its western to its eastern border.
Lomé is one of the very few capital cities built directly against an international border, in this case with Ghana.
Lomé's Grand Marché was long run by powerful women traders nicknamed the Nana Benz for the cars they drove.
The Tamberma build two-story mud houses with towers and flat roofs that look like small castles in the savanna.
Phosphate rock mined near Togo's coast is shipped worldwide to make fertilizer, and is the country's leading export mineral.

content.tagline: Land of smiles, temples, and street food
content.overview:
Thailand sits at the center of mainland Southeast Asia, bordering Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia, with a long tail of land running down the Malay Peninsula between the Andaman Sea and the Gulf of Thailand. At about 513,000 km² it is roughly the size of Spain.

About 70 million people live in Thailand and nearly all speak Thai, a tonal language written in a looping alphabet with no spaces between words. Bangkok, the capital, is a vast, hot, energetic city of canals, temples, markets and elevated trains; its full ceremonial name is the longest place name in the world.

Thailand is a constitutional monarchy, and the king is deeply respected. The country is the only one in Southeast Asia never colonized by a European power, a fact Thais take pride in. Rice farming, factories and tourism support the economy, and Thai food has become one of the world's favorite cuisines.
content.landAndNature: Forested mountains rise in the north around Chiang Mai, where Doi Inthanon reaches 2,565 meters and winter nights are cool. The center is a flat, wet plain of rice paddies watered by the Chao Phraya River, one of the world's great rice-growing regions. The northeast, called Isan, is a drier plateau. In the south, limestone karst towers erupt from turquoise water at Phang Nga and Krabi, hiding caves and hidden lagoons, and coral reefs ring islands like Phuket and Koh Tao. The monsoon brings heavy rain from May to October. Wild elephants, gibbons, hornbills and the occasional tiger live in national parks, and the Mekong giant catfish, which can weigh 300 kilograms, swims the northern river.
content.peopleAndCulture: Thai greetings use the wai, palms pressed together with a small bow, and heads are considered the highest part of a person while feet are the lowest, so pointing feet at someone is rude. Most Thais are Buddhist, and many young men spend time as monks; temples with gilded roofs and spirit houses outside buildings are everywhere. Food balances sweet, sour, salty and spicy: pad thai noodles, green curry, som tam papaya salad pounded in a mortar, and mango with sticky rice. Muay Thai, boxing that uses fists, elbows, knees and shins, is the national sport, opened with a slow dance of respect. Songkran in April is a nationwide water fight marking the traditional new year, and Loy Krathong floats candlelit baskets on rivers.
content.history: People have farmed and made bronze in this region for thousands of years; Ban Chiang's pottery is more than 4,000 years old. Thai-speaking peoples moved south and founded the kingdom of Sukhothai in the 1200s, where the Thai alphabet was created. Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, grew into one of the largest and richest cities in the world, trading with China, Japan, Persia and Europe, until Burmese armies destroyed it in 1767. A new capital was built at Bangkok in 1782 under the Chakri dynasty, which still reigns. Kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernized the country and used careful diplomacy to stay independent while Britain and France colonized their neighbors. Absolute monarchy ended in a 1932 revolution, and the name changed from Siam to Thailand in 1939. Politics since has included many military coups.
funFacts: Bangkok's full ceremonial name has 168 letters in Thai and is recognized as the longest place name in the world.
Thailand was never colonized by a European power, unlike every one of its neighbors.
During Songkran in April, whole cities turn into a three-day water fight with buckets, hoses and water guns.
The Thai alphabet has 44 consonants and no spaces between words, so readers work out where each word ends.
Thailand is one of the world's biggest exporters of rice, and Thai has a word meaning 'to eat rice' that simply means to eat.

content.tagline: Roof of the world in Central Asia
content.overview:
Tajikistan is a landlocked country in Central Asia, bordered by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China and Afghanistan. Mountains cover about 93 percent of it, and half the country lies more than 3,000 meters above sea level. Its area of about 143,000 km² is a little smaller than Wisconsin, but folded upward into some of the highest terrain on Earth.

About 10 million people live in Tajikistan. Tajik, a language closely related to Persian, is the state language, and Russian is widely used in government and business. Dushanbe, the capital, takes its name from the Tajik word for Monday, after the weekly market once held there.

Tajikistan is a presidential republic and one of the poorer countries in the region; many Tajiks work abroad, especially in Russia, and send money home. Aluminum, cotton and hydroelectric power from towering dams on mountain rivers are its main industries.
content.landAndNature: The Pamir Mountains in the east are nicknamed the Roof of the World. Ismoil Somoni Peak reaches 7,495 meters, the highest point in the former Soviet Union, and the Fedchenko Glacier is about 77 kilometers long, one of the longest outside the polar regions. The Pamir Highway climbs over passes above 4,600 meters through a cold, treeless high desert where yaks graze. Deep valleys in the west grow apricots, mulberries and cotton, and the Fann Mountains hold lakes of extraordinary blue and green. In 1911 an earthquake dammed a river and created Lake Sarez, which now holds an enormous volume of water behind a natural landslide barrier. Snow leopards, Marco Polo sheep with huge spiral horns, and ibex live in the high country.
content.peopleAndCulture: Tajiks are a Persian-speaking people, and their poetry, music and New Year traditions link them to Iran and Afghanistan. Navruz, the spring new year on about March 21, is the biggest festival, with families cooking sumalak, a sweet paste stirred from sprouted wheat for a whole night. Osh, or plov, rice cooked with carrots, meat and onions in a wide pot, is the dish of celebration, eaten with round flatbread that is never placed upside down out of respect. Pamiri houses have a five-pillared room and a skylight of four square frames representing earth, water, air and fire. Guests are given the best of everything. Soccer and the wrestling style gushtigiri are popular, and the national instrument, the long-necked setor, accompanies singers.
content.history: The Sogdians and Bactrians who lived here were traders and merchants along the Silk Road, sending goods between China and the Mediterranean. Alexander the Great's armies passed through in the 320s BC. Arab conquest brought Islam in the 700s, and the Samanid empire of the 800s and 900s, ruled from Bukhara, is celebrated by modern Tajiks as their golden age of Persian poetry and learning. Mongols, Timurids and the emirate of Bukhara followed. Russia took control in the late 1800s, and after the 1917 revolution the region became a Soviet republic in 1929, with borders drawn so that the old Persian-speaking cities of Samarkand and Bukhara ended up in Uzbekistan. Independence came in 1991, followed by a five-year civil war that killed tens of thousands before a peace deal in 1997.
funFacts: Dushanbe means Monday in Tajik, named after the Monday bazaar that once stood on the site.
The Pamir Highway is one of the highest roads in the world, crossing passes over 4,600 meters.
Lake Sarez was created by an earthquake in 1911 that dropped a mountainside across a river valley.
Tajikistan's flag flew from one of the tallest free-standing flagpoles ever built, in central Dushanbe.
The Fedchenko Glacier is so large that it holds more ice than many entire mountain ranges.

content.tagline: Marble capital beside a burning crater
content.overview:
Turkmenistan lies in Central Asia on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea, bordering Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Iran. The Karakum, a sandy desert, covers around 70 percent of the country's 488,000 km², an area a little larger than Sweden.

About 6 million people live here, mostly in oases along the desert edges. Turkmen is the state language and Russian is also widely spoken. Ashgabat, the capital, was rebuilt after a catastrophic earthquake and is now a city of white marble buildings, gold domes and enormous monuments; it holds a world record for the highest density of white marble-clad buildings.

Turkmenistan is a presidential republic and one of the most closed countries in the world, with tightly controlled media and few visitors. It holds some of the largest natural gas reserves on Earth, which fund government spending and, for many years, provided households with free gas, water and electricity.
content.landAndNature: The Karakum, meaning black sand, spreads across most of the country in long dune ridges and gravel plains where summer temperatures can exceed 45°C. At Darvaza a gas crater has been burning since it was set alight decades ago, a fiery pit in the desert that locals call the Door to Hell. The Kopet Dag mountains rise along the Iranian border, and the Amu Darya river waters the east. The Karakum Canal, one of the longest irrigation canals in the world, carries river water hundreds of kilometers to cotton fields, and that diversion of water is one reason the Aral Sea to the north has shrunk drastically. Akhal-Teke horses, famous for their metallic golden sheen and endurance, are a national treasure, and goitered gazelles and wild ass roam reserves.
content.peopleAndCulture: Turkmen identity rests on tribes, horses and carpets. Hand-knotted Turkmen rugs in deep red with repeating octagon motifs called guls are so central that the guls appear on the national flag, and there is a public holiday devoted to carpets. The Akhal-Teke horse, bred here for thousands of years, has its own festival too. Traditional dress includes bright embroidered dresses and tall sheepskin hats. Bread baked in a clay tandyr oven is treated with great respect, and plov, green tea and fermented camel milk called chal are everyday foods. The dutar, a two-stringed lute, accompanies bagshy singers who recite long epic poems. Most Turkmen are Muslim, and family celebrations are large and formal.
content.history: The oasis city of Merv on the Silk Road was, by some estimates, the largest city in the world around 1150, a center of learning with great libraries, until Mongol armies destroyed it in 1221 and killed much of its population. Nisa, near Ashgabat, was a capital of the Parthian empire 2,000 years ago. Turkmen tribes herded and traded across the deserts for centuries. The Russian empire conquered the region in the 1880s after heavy fighting at Geok Tepe. Under Soviet rule from the 1920s, nomads were forced to settle, cotton growing was expanded with massive irrigation, and religion was suppressed. An earthquake destroyed Ashgabat in 1948, killing tens of thousands. Turkmenistan became independent in 1991, and its first president, Saparmurat Niyazov, ruled with a strong personality cult until his death in 2006.
funFacts: The Darvaza gas crater in the Karakum desert has burned continuously for decades and glows orange at night.
Ashgabat holds a Guinness record for the world's highest concentration of white marble-covered buildings.
Turkmenistan's flag is the most detailed national flag in the world, showing five carpet designs down one side.
The Akhal-Teke horse has a coat that can shine like polished metal, and one appears on the country's coat of arms.
Ancient Merv was possibly the largest city on Earth in the 1100s, before the Mongols destroyed it.

content.tagline: Asia's youngest nation, coffee and coral
content.overview:
Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor, at the far southeastern end of the Indonesian archipelago and about 650 kilometers northwest of Australia. It also includes the enclave of Oecusse on the island's northern coast, surrounded by Indonesia, and two small islands. The whole country covers about 14,900 km², similar in size to Connecticut.

About 1.4 million people live here. Tetum and Portuguese are the official languages, and Indonesian and English are working languages, while more than fifteen local tongues are spoken in the mountains. Dili, the capital, lies on the northern coast beneath steep hills.

Timor-Leste is a parliamentary republic and one of the youngest countries in the world, fully independent since May 20, 2002. Offshore oil and gas have provided most government income, and the country is working to build farming, coffee exports and tourism as those reserves decline.
content.landAndNature: A rugged mountain spine runs the length of the country, rising to Tatamailau at 2,986 meters, so steep that road journeys of 100 kilometers can take many hours. The north coast is dry and hot with a short rainy season, while the south gets rain for much of the year. Coffee grows in the cool highlands under shade trees, much of it organic by default because farmers cannot afford chemicals. Eucalyptus and sandalwood, once the island's great export, cling to the slopes. The sea is the real treasure: the Ombai Strait off Atauro island has some of the highest reef fish diversity ever recorded, and blue whales, sperm whales and dolphins pass through the deep channel between the islands.
content.peopleAndCulture: Timorese society is built around clans and the uma lulik, a sacred house with a high thatched roof that holds a family's heirlooms and history. Weavings called tais, made on backstrap looms in patterns specific to each district, are given at weddings, funerals and welcomes. Most people are Catholic, a faith that became a symbol of identity during occupation, and village festivals mix church rituals with older ceremonies involving animal offerings and ancestor respect. Corn, rice, cassava and fish are everyday food, and coffee is drunk strong. Soccer is popular, along with a martial art dance called bidu. Tetum borrows many Portuguese words, so speakers slip between languages naturally.
content.history: Timor was famous for sandalwood, which drew Chinese and Malay traders centuries ago. Portugal claimed the east and the Dutch the west, dividing the island by treaty in 1859. Japan occupied Timor in World War II, and tens of thousands of Timorese died, many while helping Australian soldiers. Portugal withdrew in 1975, and days after Timor-Leste declared independence, Indonesia invaded. During 24 years of occupation an estimated 100,000 to 180,000 Timorese died from fighting, hunger and illness. In a United Nations referendum in 1999, nearly 80 percent voted for independence; violence followed, and much of the country was burned before international peacekeepers arrived. After a period of UN administration, Timor-Leste became fully independent on May 20, 2002. Two of its independence leaders, Bishop Belo and José Ramos-Horta, shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996.
funFacts: Timor-Leste is called Timor Timur in Indonesian and Timór Lorosa'e in Tetum; both mean roughly 'east east'.
The country uses the US dollar as its currency but mints its own centavo coins.
Atauro island's reefs were found to have the highest average number of reef fish species of any surveyed site on Earth.
Nearly all Timorese coffee is grown without chemicals, mostly by smallholder families in shaded mountain gardens.
The giant statue of Cristo Rei above Dili stands atop a hill reached by climbing nearly 600 steps.

content.tagline: The Pacific kingdom that stayed a kingdom
content.overview:
Tonga is a Polynesian country of about 170 islands in the South Pacific, of which around 36 are inhabited. They are scattered in a long north-south chain east of Fiji, and their combined land area is only about 747 km², smaller than New York City, though they are spread across a huge stretch of ocean.

About 105,000 people live in Tonga, speaking Tongan and English. Nuku'alofa, the capital, is on Tongatapu, the largest and flattest island, where most of the population lives.

Tonga is a constitutional monarchy, and it is the only Pacific island nation that was never fully colonized by a foreign power, keeping its royal line unbroken for around a thousand years. Farming, fishing, tourism and money sent home by Tongans living in New Zealand, Australia and the United States support the economy. Rugby is close to a national religion, and Tongan players appear on teams worldwide.
content.landAndNature: Tonga's islands come in two kinds: low coral islands in the east, including flat Tongatapu ringed by reef, and steep volcanic islands to the west, some still active. The country sits beside the Tonga Trench, one of the deepest places in any ocean at over 10,800 meters. In January 2022 the undersea volcano Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai exploded in one of the most powerful eruptions ever recorded, sending a plume into space, triggering tsunami waves and being heard as far away as Alaska. Humpback whales come from Antarctica each winter to give birth in the warm, sheltered water, and Tonga is one of the few places where people may swim with them. Flying foxes, large fruit bats, hang in protected trees at Kolovai.
content.peopleAndCulture: Tongan life places family, church and respect for rank at the center. Sunday is quiet by law: shops close, and most people attend church, where hymn singing in rich harmony fills the buildings. The ta'ovala, a woven pandanus mat worn wrapped around the waist over clothes, is formal dress for school, work and ceremonies. Ngatu, or tapa cloth, is beaten from mulberry bark by groups of women and painted with brown patterns, then given in enormous lengths at weddings and funerals. Feasts are laid on long low tables with roast pig, root crops and coconut cream dishes cooked in an umu oven. Rugby union is the favorite sport, and the national team performs the sipi tau challenge before matches.
content.history: Lapita voyagers settled Tonga around 2,800 years ago, and from about 950 the Tu'i Tonga line of kings built an empire whose influence reached Fiji, Samoa and beyond; huge stone tombs and the coral trilithon Ha'amonga 'a Maui date from that era. Dutch sailors arrived in the 1600s and James Cook in the 1770s, calling the islands the Friendly Islands. Missionaries brought Christianity in the 1800s, and King George Tupou I united the islands, freed commoners from serfdom and gave Tonga a constitution in 1875. Tonga accepted British protection in 1900 while keeping its own monarchy and government, and full control of foreign affairs returned in 1970. Reform movements led to a more democratic parliament in 2010, with most seats now elected by the people.
funFacts: Tonga is one of the first places on Earth to see each new day, thanks to its position near the date line.
The 2022 eruption of Hunga Tonga sent a plume higher than any volcanic cloud ever measured, reaching the edge of space.
Tonga's constitution makes Sunday a day of rest, and even most shops and flights pause.
Tonga has never been ruled by a foreign power and keeps a royal line stretching back around a thousand years.
Tongan tapa cloth is sometimes made in single pieces tens of meters long for weddings and royal occasions.

content.tagline: Birthplace of steel pan and calypso
content.overview:
Trinidad and Tobago is a two-island country at the southern end of the Caribbean, so close to South America that Trinidad lies only about 11 kilometers off the coast of Venezuela. Trinidad is the larger, busier island; Tobago, to the northeast, is smaller, greener and quieter. Together they cover about 5,130 km², roughly the size of Delaware.

About 1.4 million people live here, speaking English along with a lively Trinidadian creole. Port of Spain, on Trinidad's northwest coast, is the capital.

The country is a republic with an elected parliament and a president as head of state. Unlike most Caribbean nations it does not depend on tourism: oil, natural gas and petrochemicals make it one of the wealthiest countries in the region. It is best known for Carnival, for inventing the steel pan, and for giving the world calypso and soca music.
content.landAndNature: Trinidad broke away from South America long ago, so its wildlife is continental rather than island-style: it has ocelots, red howler monkeys, capybaras and around 480 bird species, including scarlet ibis that fly in flocks to roost in the Caroni swamp, turning the mangroves red at sunset. Three mountain ranges cross Trinidad, the tallest reaching about 940 meters. Pitch Lake in the southwest is the world's largest natural deposit of asphalt, a slow-moving pool of tar that visitors can walk on. Tobago is ringed by coral reefs and has a rainforest reserve protected since 1776, thought to be the oldest legally protected forest in the Western Hemisphere. Leatherback turtles nest in large numbers on both islands, and the islands lie mostly south of the main hurricane track.
content.peopleAndCulture: The population is split roughly evenly between people of Indian and of African descent, with Chinese, European, Syrian-Lebanese and Indigenous roots as well, and holidays include Diwali, Eid, Christmas and Carnival. Carnival, in the days before Lent, is the biggest event: months of preparation lead to costume bands of thousands, calypso and soca competitions, and J'ouvert, a dawn street party in mud and paint. The steel pan, made by hammering oil drums into tuned playing surfaces, was invented here in the 1930s and 1940s and is the national instrument. Food shows the mix: doubles, curried chickpeas in fried bread, is the classic street breakfast, alongside roti, callaloo and pelau. Cricket is the main sport, and Brian Lara scored the highest individual score in Test cricket.
content.history: Indigenous Arawak and Carib peoples lived on both islands when Columbus arrived in 1498. Spain held Trinidad for nearly 300 years with little development, then invited French planters in the 1780s, which is why many places have French names. Britain took Trinidad in 1797 and had already fought over Tobago, which changed hands among European powers more than twenty times. Enslaved Africans worked sugar and cocoa estates until abolition in 1834; afterward, over 140,000 indentured laborers came from India between 1845 and 1917, reshaping the islands. Oil drilling began early, in 1857. The two islands were joined administratively in 1889. Trinidad and Tobago became independent on August 31, 1962 and a republic in 1976. Its economy has risen and fallen with world energy prices ever since.
funFacts: The steel pan, invented in Trinidad from discarded oil drums, is the only widely played acoustic instrument created in the 20th century.
Pitch Lake holds roughly 10 million tonnes of natural asphalt and has been mined for over a century without running out.
Tobago's Main Ridge Forest Reserve, protected since 1776, is likely the oldest forest reserve in the Western Hemisphere.
The scarlet ibis, one of the country's two national birds, gets its brilliant red color from the crabs it eats.
Trinidad's Carnival costumes can take a year to design and build, and some headpieces stand taller than a person.

content.tagline: Where the Sahara meets the Mediterranean
content.overview:
Tunisia is the northernmost country in Africa, a wedge of land on the Mediterranean between Algeria and Libya. It is about the size of Wisconsin, the smallest country in North Africa, yet it packs in beaches, olive groves, Roman ruins and Sahara dunes. Sicily lies only about 150 kilometers across the water, and for thousands of years that short crossing has made Tunisia a meeting point of Africa and Europe. The capital, Tunis, spreads around a lagoon beside the ruins of ancient Carthage.

About 12 million people live in Tunisia. Arabic is the official language, spoken in a distinctive Tunisian dialect, and French is widely used in business and schools; Amazigh, or Berber, survives in a few southern villages. Tunisia is a republic. Olive oil, dates, phosphates and tourism support the economy, and nearly all Tunisian children, girls and boys alike, attend school, one of the highest rates in the region.
content.landAndNature: Northern Tunisia is green and hilly, with cork oak forests in the Kroumirie range and wheat fields watered by winter rains. The Dorsal, the tail end of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country to Jebel ech Chambi, its highest point at about 1,544 meters. South of it lie the chotts, vast salt flats that shimmer white and turn into shallow lakes after rain; Chott el Jerid is the largest in the Sahara. Beyond them stretch sand dunes and palm-filled oases at the desert's edge. Flamingos winter in the coastal lagoons, and the island of Djerba is carpeted with olive and date trees.
content.peopleAndCulture: Couscous, steamed semolina served with vegetables and lamb or fish, is the national dish, often shared from one large platter on Fridays. Harissa, a fiery chili paste, goes on almost everything, and brik, a crisp pastry folded around an egg, is a street favorite. Mint tea with pine nuts follows a meal. Medinas, walled old towns of narrow alleys and shaded courtyards, form the heart of Tunis, Sousse and Kairouan. Music blends Arab malouf with Mediterranean rhythms, and the Carthage festival fills a Roman theater each summer. Soccer is the national sport, and Tunisia has qualified for several World Cups.
content.history: Phoenician traders founded Carthage near modern Tunis around 814 BC, and it grew into a sea empire that fought Rome in three long wars; the general Hannibal marched war elephants over the Alps before Carthage was destroyed in 146 BC. Rome rebuilt the region as a grain basket, leaving the huge amphitheater at El Jem. Arab armies arrived in the 600s, bringing Islam and founding the city of Kairouan. Ottoman rule followed, and France took control as a protectorate in 1881. Independence came on March 20, 1956, under Habib Bourguiba, who expanded schooling and women's rights. In 2011 mass protests removed the long-serving president and helped set off uprisings across the Arab world.
funFacts: The Roman amphitheater at El Jem could seat around 35,000 people, nearly as many as the Colosseum in Rome.
Scenes from Star Wars were filmed in southern Tunisia, and some of the desert sets still stand near Tozeur.
Tunisia is among the world's leading olive oil producers, with roughly 80 million olive trees.
In Matmata, families built homes by digging deep pits into the ground, staying cool in the Saharan heat.
Carthage was once Rome's greatest rival, and its ruins now sit in a seaside suburb of Tunis.

content.tagline: Where Europe and Asia meet
content.overview:
Türkiye, also written Turkey in English, straddles two continents: a small European corner called Thrace and the much larger Asian peninsula of Anatolia, divided by narrow straits and the Sea of Marmara. It borders eight countries, from Greece and Bulgaria in the west to Georgia, Armenia, Iran, Iraq and Syria in the east, and has coasts on the Black, Aegean and Mediterranean seas. At about 784,000 km² it is roughly twice the size of Germany.

About 85 million people live here, speaking Turkish, with Kurdish spoken by a large minority in the southeast. Ankara, in the center of Anatolia, is the capital, while Istanbul, on the Bosphorus strait, is the largest city and the only major city in the world standing on two continents.

Türkiye is a presidential republic. It is known for its food, its carpets, its ancient ruins and its landscapes of cotton-white terraces and fairy-chimney rocks.
content.landAndNature: Most of Türkiye is a high plateau ringed by mountains, rising in the east to Mount Ararat, a snow-capped volcanic cone of 5,137 meters. The Tigris and Euphrates rivers both begin here. In Cappadocia, soft volcanic rock has eroded into tall cones and pillars that people hollowed into houses, churches and whole underground cities; hot-air balloons drift over them at dawn. At Pamukkale, mineral-rich hot springs have built a hillside of dazzling white limestone terraces filled with warm water. Coastlines range from pine-backed Mediterranean coves to the humid, tea-growing Black Sea hills. The country sits on major fault lines and suffers severe earthquakes, including a devastating one in 2023. Brown bears, wolves, wild goats and loggerhead turtles all live here.
content.peopleAndCulture: Turkish food is one of the world's great cuisines: kebabs and meze, stuffed vine leaves, pide flatbreads, baklava layered with pistachios, and thick coffee whose grounds are sometimes read for fortunes. Tea, served in tulip-shaped glasses, is drunk all day. Hospitality is a point of honor; a guest is offered food before anything else. Most Turks are Muslim, and the country's government is officially secular. Oil wrestling, in which competitors coated in olive oil grapple at Kırkpınar, has been held for over 650 years, and soccer draws enormous crowds. Turkish carpets, ceramics from İznik, and shadow puppet plays are old arts, and the whirling dervishes of Konya spin in a meditative ceremony descended from the poet Rumi.
content.history: Anatolia holds some of humanity's oldest settlements: Göbekli Tepe's carved stone circles are about 11,500 years old, older than farming. Hittites, Greeks, Persians and Romans ruled in turn, and Constantinople, founded in 330, became the capital of the Byzantine empire for over a thousand years. Turkic peoples moved in from Central Asia, and in 1453 the Ottomans took Constantinople, building an empire that stretched across the Middle East, North Africa and southeastern Europe. During World War I the Ottoman government carried out mass killings and deportations of its Armenian population beginning in 1915, in which around a million or more people died; most historians and many countries recognize this as genocide, while Türkiye's government disputes that term. The empire collapsed after the war, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded a republic in 1923, changing the alphabet, calendar and laws.
funFacts: Istanbul is the only major city in the world built on two continents, linked by bridges across the Bosphorus.
Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Türkiye has carved stone pillars about 11,500 years old, built before pottery or farming.
Beneath Cappadocia lie underground cities, one with at least eight levels that sheltered thousands of people.
Türkiye grows about 70 percent of the world's hazelnuts, mostly on the steep Black Sea coast.
Oil wrestling at Kırkpınar has been contested every year since 1346, making it one of the oldest sporting events anywhere.

content.tagline: Nine low islands facing a rising sea
content.overview:
Tuvalu is a nation of nine tiny coral islands and atolls strung across the central Pacific, between Australia and Hawaii. Its total land area is only about 26 km², the fourth-smallest of any country, and no point rises much more than four or five meters above the ocean.

About 11,000 people live in Tuvalu, making it one of the least populated countries in the world. Tuvaluan and English are the official languages. Funafuti, the capital atoll, holds roughly half the population on a ribbon of land so narrow that in places you can see the lagoon on one side and the open ocean on the other.

Tuvalu is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Fishing licenses sold to foreign fleets, money sent home by Tuvaluan sailors, and the country's internet domain name are its main sources of income. Rising seas are a serious and immediate threat to its future.
content.landAndNature: Each island is a ring or strip of coral built on the rim of a sunken volcano, with sandy soil too poor for most crops; families grow pulaka, a swamp taro, in pits dug down to the freshwater layer. Coconut palms, pandanus and breadfruit provide food and materials. Funafuti's lagoon is a conservation area where turtles, reef sharks and hundreds of fish species live, and seabirds nest on uninhabited islets. There are no rivers or streams, so people collect rainwater from roofs in tanks; droughts force emergency water shipments. Because the land is so low, king tides now push seawater up through the porous coral ground, flooding gardens and roads even on clear days, and storm surges reach across whole islets.
content.peopleAndCulture: Tuvaluans are Polynesian, and life centers on the extended family, the church and the maneapa, an open community hall where island decisions are made, feasts held and visitors welcomed. Fatele is the great communal performance: rows of singers chant while others drum on a wooden box and dancers move faster and faster as the song builds. Fish, coconut, breadfruit and rice are everyday food, cooked in earth ovens for celebrations. Women weave fans, mats and dance skirts from pandanus leaves. Te ano, a game played with two hard balls kept in the air by teams, is a national sport, along with kilikiti, an island version of cricket. Funafuti's airstrip doubles as the town's main playing field between the few flights.
content.history: Polynesian voyagers settled these atolls around 3,000 years ago, sailing from Samoa and Tonga, and each island kept its own chiefs and traditions. European ships passed from the 1500s onward. In the 1860s Peruvian slave raiders took hundreds of islanders, devastating some communities. Britain declared a protectorate over the Ellice Islands in 1892 and later governed them with the Gilbert Islands as a single colony. American forces built an airstrip on Funafuti in World War II. In 1974 Ellice Islanders voted to separate from the Gilberts, and Tuvalu became independent on October 1, 1978. In 2000 the country leased its .tv internet address, which brought in significant income. Tuvalu has since become a leading voice at international climate talks, arguing that rising seas threaten its existence.
funFacts: Tuvalu earns millions of dollars a year by leasing its internet domain, .tv, to video and streaming websites.
Funafuti's airport runway becomes a public space between flights, used for soccer, volleyball and evening strolls.
Tuvalu is the least visited country in the world, with only a few thousand tourists arriving in a typical year.
The highest natural point in Tuvalu is only about 4.6 meters above sea level.
Tuvalu has begun creating a digital record of its land, culture and archives in case its islands become uninhabitable.

content.tagline: Kilimanjaro, Serengeti and Zanzibar spice
content.overview:
Tanzania occupies a great slab of East Africa between the Indian Ocean and three of Africa's largest lakes. It is about twice the size of California and holds both the continent's highest point, Mount Kilimanjaro, and a share of Lake Tanganyika, the second deepest lake on Earth. The spice island of Zanzibar lies off the coast, Dar es Salaam is the biggest city and main port, and Dodoma, inland at the country's center, is the official capital.

About 65 million people live in Tanzania, in more than 120 ethnic groups. Swahili is the national language, spoken by nearly everyone and taught in primary schools, with English used in government and universities; that shared language has helped keep the country unusually united. Tanzania is a republic. Most people farm, growing maize, cassava, coffee and cloves, while visitors come for national parks and reserves that cover roughly a third of the land, among the largest protected areas anywhere.
content.landAndNature: Mount Kilimanjaro rises alone out of the plains to 5,895 meters, the highest mountain in Africa and the tallest freestanding mountain on Earth, carrying glaciers almost on the equator. The Serengeti's grasslands carry the largest land migration in the world, roughly two million wildebeest, zebra and gazelle circling year after year in search of rain. Ngorongoro Crater, a collapsed volcano 20 kilometers across, holds a whole ecosystem inside its walls. The Great Rift Valley splits the country and cradles Lake Tanganyika, alive with hundreds of fish species found nowhere else. Coral reefs and mangroves line the coast, and chimpanzees live in the forests at Gombe.
content.peopleAndCulture: Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with beans, greens or grilled fish, while the coast and Zanzibar add coconut, cloves, cardamom and cinnamon to rice and seafood; Zanzibar's night market grills skewers by lamplight. Taarab music blends Swahili poetry with Arab and Indian instruments, and bongo flava is the pop sound of the cities. The Maasai herd cattle across the northern plains in red cloaks, and the Hadza near Lake Eyasi are among the last hunter-gatherer communities in Africa. Soccer is followed passionately. Greetings are long and unhurried, a matter of good manners, and Swahili proverbs season everyday speech.
content.history: Some of the oldest known human footprints, made about 3.6 million years ago, were preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli, and nearby Olduvai Gorge has yielded famous fossils of early humans. Swahili city-states such as Kilwa grew wealthy on Indian Ocean trade from the 900s. Portugal and later the sultans of Oman controlled Zanzibar, which became a center of the clove and slave trades. Germany colonized the mainland in the 1880s, and Britain took over after World War I. Tanganyika became independent in 1961 under Julius Nyerere and united with Zanzibar in 1964 to form Tanzania. Nyerere promoted Swahili and a village socialism called ujamaa; multiparty elections returned in 1995.
funFacts: Kilimanjaro is the tallest freestanding mountain in the world, and climbers pass through five climate zones on the way up.
Tanzanite, a blue-violet gemstone, is found in only one place on Earth, a few square kilometers near Kilimanjaro.
Footprints preserved in volcanic ash at Laetoli show human ancestors walking upright about 3.6 million years ago.
Tanzania sets aside roughly a third of its territory as parks and reserves, one of the largest shares of any country.
Zanzibar's clove trees once supplied much of the world, and the scent of drying spices still hangs over its villages.

content.tagline: Source of the Nile, home of gorillas
content.overview:
Uganda is a landlocked country on the equator in East Africa, sharing Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa, with Kenya and Tanzania. It is about the size of Oregon, and the White Nile begins here, flowing out of the lake at Jinja and heading north on a long journey to Egypt. Kampala, the capital, sprawls across green hills near the lakeshore.

About 48 million people live in Uganda, and the population is among the youngest in the world, with more than half under 18. English and Swahili are the official languages, Luganda is the common tongue around Kampala, and dozens of other languages are spoken across the regions. Uganda is a republic, and several traditional kingdoms, including Buganda, survive as cultural institutions. Farming employs most people, and coffee is the largest export. Winston Churchill called Uganda the pearl of Africa for its greenness, and the nickname has stuck ever since.
content.landAndNature: Uganda sits high on a plateau, so even on the equator the air stays mild. Lake Victoria fills the southeast, while the Rwenzori Mountains on the western border, known as the Mountains of the Moon, rise to 5,109 meters with glaciers and giant lobelia plants that tower over hikers. Volcanoes stand in the southwest, and the Great Rift Valley cradles Lakes Albert and Edward. At Murchison Falls the Nile is squeezed through a gap only about seven meters wide and explodes downward. Bwindi Impenetrable Forest shelters roughly half the world's remaining mountain gorillas, and Uganda counts over 1,000 bird species, including the towering shoebill stork.
content.peopleAndCulture: Matoke, steamed green bananas mashed into a soft dish, is the staple across much of the country, served with groundnut sauce, beans or chicken; the rolex, a chapati rolled around fried egg, is the favorite street snack. Most Ugandans speak three or four languages. Drumming and dance differ by region, from the fast kiganda drums of the Baganda to the Acholi bwola. Soccer fills every open field, and Ugandan runners have won Olympic gold on the track. Boda-boda motorcycle taxis weave through Kampala traffic. Families are close, and a proper greeting asks after each relative before any business begins.
content.history: Powerful kingdoms grew here from the 1300s, notably Buganda on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, alongside Bunyoro, Toro and Ankole. Arab and European traders arrived in the 1800s, and explorers searching for the Nile's source reached the lake in 1862. Britain made Uganda a protectorate in 1894, ruling partly through the kingdoms and bringing laborers from India to build a railway. Independence came on October 9, 1962. Idi Amin seized power in 1971 and ran a violent dictatorship for eight years, expelling the country's Asian community and killing many Ugandans, until he was overthrown in 1979. Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986, and a long insurgency troubled northern Uganda for years afterward.
funFacts: About half of the world's mountain gorillas, fewer than 1,100 in all, live in Uganda's mountain forests.
The White Nile begins its journey to the Mediterranean at Jinja, where it flows out of Lake Victoria.
Uganda has one of the youngest populations on Earth, with more than half its people under 18 years old.
At Murchison Falls the entire Nile is forced through a gap about seven meters wide before plunging 43 meters.
Uganda's national bird, the grey crowned crane, wears a spray of stiff golden feathers and appears on the flag.

content.tagline: Black soil, golden domes, wide steppe
content.overview:
Ukraine is the largest country lying entirely within Europe, roughly the size of Texas, stretching from the Carpathian Mountains in the west to the Russian border in the east and south to the Black Sea. Its land is famous for chernozem, a deep black soil so fertile that Ukraine has long been called a breadbasket, sending wheat, corn, barley and sunflower oil to many countries.

Before 2022 about 41 million people lived in Ukraine; millions have since left the country or moved within it. Ukrainian is the state language, a Slavic language written in the Cyrillic alphabet, and many people also speak Russian. Ukraine is a republic with an elected president and parliament. Kyiv, the capital, stands on the Dnipro River and is one of the oldest cities in eastern Europe, known for gold-domed churches and a very deep metro. Russia began a full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the war continues.
content.landAndNature: Most of Ukraine is flat or gently rolling steppe and farmland, a plain of wheat and enormous fields of sunflowers that turn to follow the sun. The Carpathian Mountains in the west are wooded and green, rising to Hoverla at 2,061 meters and holding some of Europe's largest surviving beech forests, where brown bears, wolves and lynx live. The Dnipro River runs the length of the country to the Black Sea, whose northern shore has sandy spits, salt lakes and the marshy Danube delta where pelicans breed. Around the abandoned Chornobyl nuclear plant, empty of people since 1986, wolves, boar and wild horses now roam freely.
content.peopleAndCulture: Borscht, a beet soup served with sour cream and garlic bread, is the best-known Ukrainian dish and is listed by UNESCO as cultural heritage; varenyky dumplings follow close behind. Embroidered shirts called vyshyvanky carry patterns that differ from region to region and are worn with pride on holidays. Pysanky, eggs decorated with wax and dye in fine geometric designs, are made at Easter. Layered folk singing and the many-stringed bandura belong to old traditions, while Kyiv has a lively modern music scene. Soccer, boxing and chess are popular, and Ukrainian boxers have held world heavyweight titles.
content.history: Kyiv grew into the center of Kyivan Rus, a powerful medieval state that adopted Christianity in 988. Mongol armies destroyed it in 1240, and the lands were later ruled by Poland-Lithuania, by Cossack hosts, and by the Russian Empire. In 1932 and 1933 a famine known as the Holodomor, caused by Soviet grain seizures, killed millions of Ukrainians. Ukraine suffered enormously in World War II, and the Chornobyl reactor exploded in 1986. Independence came when the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and fighting began in the eastern regions; in February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion, and the war has continued since.
funFacts: Ukraine's black soil, called chernozem, covers much of the country and is among the most fertile farmland on Earth.
Ukraine grows more sunflowers than almost any other country and is a leading supplier of sunflower oil.
Kyiv's Arsenalna station is one of the deepest metro stations in the world, about 105 meters underground.
The world's largest cargo aircraft, the Antonov An-225 Mriya, was built in Ukraine and destroyed in 2022.
The bandura, Ukraine's national instrument, has more than 60 strings and is held upright against the player's chest.

content.tagline: Europe's youngest country, and its youngest people
content.overview:
Kosovo is a small landlocked territory in the central Balkans, about the size of Delaware and Rhode Island together, ringed by mountains and bordered by Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, and Serbia. The capital, Pristina, is a lively city of cafés, new glass buildings, and a huge library covered in domes and metal netting. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, but its status is disputed: more than 100 countries, including the United States and most of the European Union, recognize it as a country, while Serbia, Russia, China, and others do not, and it is not a member of the United Nations.

About 1.6 million people live in Kosovo, and it has the youngest population in Europe, with roughly half under 30. Most are Albanian and Muslim; Serbs, mostly Orthodox Christian, form the largest minority, living mainly in the north and in scattered enclaves. Albanian and Serbian are the official languages. Kosovo is a parliamentary republic and uses the euro. Many families depend on money sent home by relatives working in Germany and Switzerland, and young Kosovars have become known for pop music and soccer talent.
content.landAndNature: Kosovo is a high basin, mostly between 400 and 700 meters above sea level, split by low hills into two plains: the Kosovo plain in the east and the Dukagjin plain in the west. Mountains rise on all sides. The Šar Mountains in the south and the Accursed Mountains in the west top 2,600 meters, with Gjeravica at 2,656 meters the highest peak, and their slopes hold ski runs at Brezovica, alpine lakes, and old beech forests. The Rugova Canyon near Peja is a deep gorge with waterfalls and caves. The Mirusha waterfalls cascade through 13 lakes. Rivers such as the Sitnica and White Drin flow to three different seas. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, and chamois live in the mountains. Winters are cold and snowy, summers warm.
content.peopleAndCulture: Kosovo Albanians share language and customs with Albania, including the besa code of honor and hospitality, and Serbian culture centers on the medieval Orthodox monasteries of Dečani and Gračanica, which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Meals begin with flija, a layered pancake baked slowly under a metal dome, or with flaky pite pastries, and include grilled meats, peppers stuffed with cheese, and ajvar, a red pepper spread. Coffee culture fills Pristina's streets with cafés. Weddings are lavish, and the traditional plis, a white felt cap, is worn by older men. Music ranges from folk songs with the çifteli lute to pop stars Dua Lipa and Rita Ora, both of Kosovar heritage. Soccer, judo, and basketball are the top sports; Majlinda Kelmendi won Kosovo's first Olympic gold in judo in 2016.
content.history: Illyrians and later Romans lived here, and Slavs arrived in the 600s. In the Middle Ages Kosovo was the center of the Serbian kingdom, which built its great monasteries there. The Battle of Kosovo in 1389 against the Ottomans became a founding legend of Serbian history, and the Ottoman Empire ruled for more than 500 years, during which most of the population became Albanian-speaking and Muslim. Serbia took Kosovo in 1912, and it became a province of Yugoslavia with self-rule under Tito. Serbia stripped that autonomy in 1989, and tensions grew into war in 1998 and 1999, in which thousands died and hundreds of thousands of Albanians were driven from their homes before NATO bombing forced Serbian forces out. The United Nations administered Kosovo until it declared independence on February 17, 2008.
funFacts: Kosovo has the youngest population in Europe, with an average age of about 30.
Pristina has a statue of Bill Clinton and a street named after him, thanking the United States for its role in 1999.
The National Library in Pristina, covered in 99 domes and metal mesh, is often listed among the world's strangest buildings.
Kosovo joined the Olympics in 2016 and won gold at its very first Games, in women's judo.
Pop stars Dua Lipa and Rita Ora both have Kosovar Albanian parents and are celebrated as heroes in Pristina.

content.tagline: Green plains, long beaches, soccer pioneers
content.overview:
Uruguay is a small country on the Atlantic coast of South America, wedged between Brazil to the north and Argentina across the wide Río de la Plata to the west. At about 181,000 km² it is the second-smallest country in South America after Suriname, roughly the size of Washington state, and almost all of it is gently rolling grassland.

About 3.4 million people live in Uruguay, speaking Spanish. Nearly half of them live in or around Montevideo, the capital, a city of tree-lined avenues, a long waterfront promenade called the rambla, and an old port market smoky with grills.

Uruguay is a presidential republic with a long democratic tradition and one of the highest living standards in Latin America. Cattle outnumber people several times over, beef and soybeans are leading exports, and almost all its electricity comes from wind, water and other renewable sources. Soccer is close to a national identity.
content.landAndNature: Uruguay has no mountains to speak of; its highest hill, Cerro Catedral, reaches only about 514 meters. Instead the country is a wide expanse of pampas grassland grazed by cattle and sheep, crossed by slow rivers and dotted with palm groves. The Atlantic coast runs for hundreds of kilometers in long sandy beaches, lagoons and dunes, with sea lions and fur seals crowding rocky islands near Cabo Polonio and southern right whales passing offshore from July to November. Inland wetlands attract flamingos, black-necked swans and storks, and capybaras, the world's largest rodents, wallow in the marshes. The climate is temperate with four clear seasons and no extremes, and thunderstorms roll in off the plains in summer.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Uruguayans descend from Spanish and Italian immigrants, with Afro-Uruguayan communities whose candombe drumming, played on three sizes of barrel drum in street parades, is a national art form. Carnival here lasts about forty days, the longest in the world, with murga groups performing satirical songs in painted makeup. Mate, a bitter herbal tea, is drunk constantly from a gourd through a metal straw; Uruguayans carry a thermos under one arm everywhere they go. Asado, beef grilled slowly over wood coals, is the weekend ritual, and chivito, a loaded steak sandwich, is the favorite snack. Uruguay hosted and won the first soccer World Cup in 1930 and won again in 1950, and the national team still plays far above the country's size.
content.history: The Charrúa people hunted and fished on these plains for thousands of years; most were killed or displaced during the 1800s. Spain and Portugal both wanted the land, and Portugal founded Colonia del Sacramento in 1680 to challenge Spanish Buenos Aires across the river. José Gervasio Artigas led a struggle for independence and self-rule, and after a war involving Argentina and Brazil, Uruguay became an independent buffer state in 1828. Waves of European immigrants arrived, and in the early 1900s President José Batlle y Ordóñez built one of the world's first welfare states, with free schooling, an eight-hour workday and the separation of church and state. A military dictatorship from 1973 to 1985 jailed and exiled thousands, after which democracy returned and has held firmly since.
funFacts: Uruguay won the very first soccer World Cup in 1930, playing at home in a stadium built for the tournament.
There are roughly three or four cattle for every person in Uruguay, and every cow is electronically tagged and traceable.
Uruguay's Carnival runs about forty days, the longest celebration of its kind in the world.
Almost all of Uruguay's electricity comes from renewable sources, chiefly wind and hydropower.
Uruguayans drink more mate per person than any other nation, often carrying a thermos of hot water everywhere.

content.tagline: Fifty states from ocean to ocean
content.overview:
The United States stretches across the middle of North America from the Atlantic to the Pacific, plus Alaska in the far northwest and the Hawaiian islands in the Pacific. Covering about 9.4 million km², it is among the largest countries in the world, bordering Canada and Mexico and spanning six main time zones.

About 335 million people live in the United States, the third most of any country. English is the main language, though Spanish is spoken by tens of millions and hundreds of other languages are heard in its cities. Washington, D.C. is the capital; New York, Los Angeles and Chicago are the biggest cities.

The country is a federal republic of fifty states, each with its own laws and government, under an elected president and Congress. Its films, music, universities, technology companies and sports have influence far beyond its borders, and it has long been shaped by people arriving from everywhere.
content.landAndNature: Almost every landscape on Earth appears somewhere in the United States. The Appalachian Mountains roll down the east; the flat interior grows corn and wheat across the Great Plains; the Rocky Mountains rise in the west, followed by deserts and the Sierra Nevada. The Mississippi River drains a basin covering much of the country. The Grand Canyon cuts 1,800 meters into Arizona rock, Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano and holds half the world's geysers, and California's giant sequoias are the largest trees alive. Alaska has grizzly bears and glaciers; Hawaii has active volcanoes and reefs. Tornado Alley in the center sees more tornadoes than anywhere else on the planet, and hurricanes strike the Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
content.peopleAndCulture: American culture is a mixture built from Indigenous nations, European settlers, Africans brought in slavery, and waves of immigrants from Asia, Latin America and beyond.
