That mix gave the world jazz, blues, country, rock and roll and hip-hop, all rooted in African American musical traditions. Hollywood films and American television travel everywhere. Baseball, basketball, American football and ice hockey fill enormous stadiums, and basketball was invented here in 1891. Thanksgiving in November brings families together over turkey; July 4 marks independence with fireworks. Food ranges from Texas barbecue and New Orleans gumbo to New York bagels and Californian tacos. The National Park System, begun with Yellowstone in 1872, was among the world's first efforts to protect wild land for everyone.
content.history: Hundreds of Indigenous nations lived across the continent for thousands of years, from the Haudenosaunee in the east to the Lakota on the plains and the Navajo in the southwest. English colonies grew along the Atlantic from 1607, and thirteen declared independence in 1776. As the country expanded west, Indigenous peoples were pushed off their lands by treaty and force; the Cherokee and other southeastern nations were driven west in the 1830s on the Trail of Tears, where thousands died. Millions of enslaved Africans worked southern plantations until the Civil War of 1861–1865 ended slavery. Segregation laws followed, and the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s, led by figures such as Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks, overturned them. The country emerged from World War II as a superpower and landed astronauts on the Moon in 1969.
funFacts: Alaska is so wide that it holds both the westernmost and easternmost points of the country, crossing the date line.
Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park and sits above a supervolcano.
The Library of Congress holds well over 170 million items, making it the largest library in the world.
Hawaii's Big Island keeps growing as lava from Kilauea flows into the sea and hardens into new land.
The United States has no official national language at the federal level, though English is used in government.
A bristlecone pine in California's White Mountains has been alive for more than 4,800 years, older than the pyramids of Giza.

content.tagline: Silk Road cities of blue tile
content.overview:
Uzbekistan lies in the heart of Central Asia, bordered by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan. It is one of only two countries in the world that is double landlocked, meaning every neighbor is landlocked too. Its 447,000 km², about the size of California, run from desert to the foothills of high mountains.

About 36 million people live in Uzbekistan, the most populous country in Central Asia. Uzbek is the state language and Russian is widely spoken. Tashkent, the capital, is the region's largest city, rebuilt after a 1966 earthquake and known for a subway whose stations are decorated like palaces.

Uzbekistan is a presidential republic. Cotton, gold, gas and fruit are its main products. Its greatest fame comes from the Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, where turquoise-tiled domes, minarets and madrasas have stood for centuries.
content.landAndNature: Most of Uzbekistan is flat and dry: the Kyzylkum, or red sand desert, fills the center, and steppe covers much of the rest. Mountains rise in the east toward Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, feeding the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, whose water was diverted on a huge scale in the Soviet era to irrigate cotton. As a result the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake in the world, has shrunk to a fraction of its size, leaving rusting fishing boats stranded on salty sand and a dust problem that harms local health. The Fergana Valley in the east is fertile and densely farmed, famous for melons, apricots and mulberries. Wildlife includes saiga antelope, goitered gazelles and, in the mountains, snow leopards.
content.peopleAndCulture: Uzbek hospitality centers on plov, rice cooked with lamb, carrots, onions and sometimes quince in a huge cast-iron kazan, prepared by men for guests and weddings. Round non bread is stamped with patterns and never set down upside down. Suzani embroidery, worked in bright silk on cotton, is made for brides, and ikat silk is dyed before weaving so its patterns blur like flames. Navruz in March brings the spring new year with music and communal cooking. Most Uzbeks are Muslim. Kurash, a traditional jacketed wrestling style, is a national sport alongside soccer, and Uzbek boxers and judoka win Olympic medals. Tea is poured, returned to the pot and poured again three times before serving, a gesture of care.
content.history: Cities here were stops on the Silk Road for 2,000 years, where caravans traded Chinese silk for glass, horses and ideas. Alexander the Great conquered Sogdiana in the 320s BC; Arab armies brought Islam in the 700s, and Bukhara and Samarkand became centers of science and poetry, home to the mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word algorithm, and the physician Ibn Sina. Genghis Khan's Mongols destroyed the cities in the 1220s. Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, rebuilt Samarkand as his capital in the late 1300s, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory that measured the year to within a minute. Russia conquered the region in the 1800s, and Soviet rule from the 1920s expanded cotton farming with the irrigation that drained the Aral Sea. Uzbekistan became independent in 1991.
funFacts: Uzbekistan is one of only two double-landlocked countries on Earth; the other is Liechtenstein.
The Registan in Samarkand is a square framed by three tiled schools, once a center of astronomy and mathematics.
The Aral Sea has shrunk so far that ships now sit rusting in desert sand kilometers from any water.
The word algorithm comes from al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician from the region who worked in the 800s.
Ulugh Beg's 1400s observatory in Samarkand measured the length of a year accurate to within about a minute.

content.tagline: The world's smallest country
content.overview:
Vatican City is the smallest country in the world, covering about 0.44 km² and sitting entirely inside Rome, Italy. Its walls enclose St. Peter's Basilica, the wide oval of St. Peter's Square, the Vatican Museums, the Sistine Chapel and a large stretch of gardens. A person can walk from one side of the country to the other in roughly fifteen minutes.

Vatican City is the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church and the home of the pope, who leads the Church and is also head of state. Fewer than a thousand people live there, among them cardinals, priests, staff and the Swiss Guard, the soldiers in striped uniforms who protect the pope. Italian is used day to day, and Latin remains the official language of Church documents. Millions of visitors and pilgrims arrive each year, and for so small a place the Vatican keeps a great deal of its own: a post office, a newspaper, a radio station and a railway station.
content.landAndNature: There is almost no wild landscape in a country this small, but slightly more than half of the Vatican is garden. Behind the basilica lie about 23 hectares of lawns, clipped hedges, fountains, orange and olive trees, and stands of palm, oak and cedar planted over the centuries, along with a replica of the grotto at Lourdes. These gardens have been cultivated since the 1200s. Ring-necked parakeets, gulls and peregrine falcons nest on the rooftops and domes. The country sits on the Vatican Hill, a low rise on the west bank of the Tiber River, and has no rivers, coastline or farmland of its own.
content.peopleAndCulture: Life inside the Vatican follows the Church calendar. On many Sundays the pope appears at a window above St. Peter's Square to speak to the crowd below, and at Christmas and Easter the square fills with hundreds of thousands of people. The Sistine Chapel, painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512, is used for the conclave, the sealed meeting at which cardinals elect a new pope; black smoke from a chimney means no decision has been reached, white smoke means a pope has been chosen. The Vatican Museums hold one of the world's great art collections, and the Swiss Guard has protected popes since 1506.
content.history: Tradition holds that the apostle Peter was buried on this hill in Roman times, and a church was raised over the site in the 300s; the present St. Peter's Basilica was built between 1506 and 1626, with Michelangelo among its designers. For more than a thousand years popes governed the Papal States, a broad band of territory across central Italy. When Italy was unified in 1870 it absorbed those lands, and popes refused to leave the Vatican for nearly sixty years afterward. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 settled the dispute by recognizing Vatican City as an independent state. It has remained neutral in conflicts since and keeps diplomatic relations with most countries in the world.
funFacts: The whole of Vatican City would fit inside New York's Central Park nearly eight times over.
Vatican City has the shortest national railway in the world, a track about 300 meters long with one station.
The Swiss Guard, founded in 1506, is among the oldest military units still in continuous service anywhere.
Michelangelo spent four years painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling, working on scaffolding high above the floor.
Nobody is born a Vatican citizen; citizenship is granted for as long as a person works there and then ends.
The Vatican Library holds manuscripts more than a thousand years old on about 80 kilometers of shelving.

content.tagline: One volcano and a string of islets
content.overview:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is a Caribbean country made of one main mountainous island, Saint Vincent, and a chain of about 30 smaller islands and cays called the Grenadines trailing southwest toward Grenada. The total land area is only about 389 km², but the islands are spread over a long stretch of clear blue sea.

About 110,000 people live here, nearly all on Saint Vincent itself. English is the official language, and a Vincentian creole is spoken every day. Kingstown, the capital, is a working port town of arched stone shopfronts beneath steep green hills.

The country is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Bananas and arrowroot were long the main crops, and tourism, especially sailing among the Grenadines, has grown. The active volcano La Soufrière looms over the north of the main island and erupted as recently as 2021.
content.landAndNature: Saint Vincent is steep, volcanic and wet, with a forested ridge running its length and La Soufrière, 1,234 meters high, at the northern end. Its 2021 eruption sent ash across the Caribbean and forced about 20,000 people from their homes. Black sand beaches line the windward side, and the Vermont Nature Trail in the rainforest is the place to look for the Saint Vincent parrot, a bronze, blue and gold bird found nowhere else and shown on the coat of arms. The Grenadines are lower and drier, fringed with white sand and coral: the Tobago Cays sit inside a horseshoe reef where green turtles graze on sea grass, and Mustique and Bequia are known for sailing and boatbuilding.
content.peopleAndCulture: Most Vincentians descend from enslaved Africans, with Indigenous Kalinago and Garifuna, Indian and Portuguese heritage also in the mix. Roasted breadfruit with fried jackfish is the national dish, and callaloo soup and rotis are everyday food. Vincy Mas, the carnival that peaks in early July, fills Kingstown with steel pan, soca, calypso competitions and masquerade bands. Bequia has a long whaling and boatbuilding tradition and is famous for model boats built by hand. Cricket is the leading sport, and Vincentians play for the West Indies team. Nine Mornings, a Christmas custom found nowhere else, has people rising before dawn for nine days of street dancing, swimming and concerts before sunrise.
content.history: Kalinago people held Saint Vincent longer than almost any other Caribbean island, resisting European settlement into the 1700s. Shipwrecked and escaped Africans joined them, forming the Garifuna, or Black Caribs. Britain gained the island in 1763, and after two wars the Garifuna were defeated in 1796 and about 5,000 were deported to an island off Honduras, from where their descendants spread along the Central American coast. Sugar estates worked by enslaved Africans dominated until slavery ended in 1834. In 1902 La Soufrière erupted catastrophically, killing about 1,600 people on the same day as the Mont Pelée disaster on Martinique. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became fully independent on October 27, 1979, just months after another eruption of the volcano.
funFacts: Parts of the first Pirates of the Caribbean film were shot on Saint Vincent, and some set pieces remain at Wallilabou Bay.
During Nine Mornings, Vincentians get up before dawn for nine days in December to dance, swim and watch concerts.
The Tobago Cays are a group of uninhabited islands inside a horseshoe reef, where sea turtles feed in shallow water.
The world's oldest botanical garden in the Western Hemisphere, founded in Kingstown in 1765, still grows a breadfruit tree descended from Captain Bligh's plants.
La Soufrière's 2021 eruption blanketed the island in ash and forced about a fifth of the population to evacuate.

content.tagline: Andes, oil, and the world's tallest waterfall
content.overview:
Venezuela occupies the northern edge of South America, with a long Caribbean coastline and borders with Colombia, Brazil and Guyana. At about 916,000 km² it is roughly twice the size of California, and it contains snow-capped Andean peaks, tropical grasslands, the Orinoco River delta and a corner of the Amazon rainforest.

About 28 million people live in Venezuela, speaking Spanish along with more than thirty Indigenous languages. Caracas, the capital, sits in a narrow valley just inland from the Caribbean, hemmed in by a steep green mountain called Ávila.

Venezuela is a presidential republic. It holds the largest proven oil reserves of any country, which once made it among the richest in Latin America. Since around 2014 it has experienced a severe economic and political crisis: extreme inflation, shortages of food and medicine, disputed elections, and the departure of more than seven million people, one of the largest movements of people in the world.
content.landAndNature: The Andes reach into western Venezuela, topping out at Pico Bolívar at about 4,978 meters. North of the Orinoco spread the llanos, vast seasonal grasslands that flood in the wet season and dry to hard earth in the dry, home to capybaras, anacondas, caimans and the scarlet ibis. South and east lies the Guiana Shield, where flat-topped mountains called tepuis rise sheer from the forest, their summits isolated for millions of years so that unique plants grow there. From one of them, Auyán-tepui, Angel Falls drops 979 meters, the tallest uninterrupted waterfall on Earth. Over Lake Maracaibo, lightning flashes hundreds of nights a year in a phenomenon called the Catatumbo lightning, among the most frequent anywhere.
content.peopleAndCulture: Venezuelan food centers on corn: arepas, split and stuffed with cheese, beans or shredded beef, are eaten at any meal, and hallacas, corn dough parcels steamed in banana leaves, are made by families together at Christmas. Baseball is the leading sport, and Venezuela has sent many players to the major leagues; soccer has grown fast. Joropo, a swift music of harp, four-stringed cuatro and maracas, comes from the llanos. El Sistema, a program founded in 1975, has given free classical music training to hundreds of thousands of children and produced the conductor Gustavo Dudamel. Beauty pageants are followed with unusual enthusiasm, and Venezuela has won Miss Universe many times.
content.history: Indigenous peoples including the Carib, Arawak and Timoto-Cuica lived here when Columbus reached the coast in 1498; a later explorer called the stilt villages on Lake Maracaibo 'little Venice', which gave the country its name. Spanish rule lasted three centuries. Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas, led the fight that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain, and Venezuela became fully independent in 1830 after the union he founded broke apart. Civil wars and strongmen filled the 1800s. Oil discovered around Lake Maracaibo in the 1920s transformed the country, which became a stable democracy from 1958. Hugo Chávez was elected president in 1998 and used oil money for social programs; after his death in 2013 and a collapse in oil prices, the country entered a deep crisis under Nicolás Maduro.
funFacts: Angel Falls plunges 979 meters, so far that much of the water turns to mist before reaching the bottom.
The Catatumbo lightning over Lake Maracaibo flashes on more nights per year than almost anywhere else on Earth.
Venezuela's tepuis are flat-topped mountains that inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The Lost World.
El Sistema has taught free classical music to hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan children since 1975.
Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves of any country, much of it heavy crude near the Orinoco River.

content.tagline: Dragon-shaped coast of rice and limestone
content.overview:
Vietnam curves down the eastern edge of mainland Southeast Asia in a long S, with more than 3,200 kilometers of coastline on the South China Sea and borders with China, Laos and Cambodia. At about 331,000 km² it is a little larger than New Mexico, and Vietnamese often describe its shape as a bamboo pole carrying two rice baskets: the Red River delta in the north and the Mekong delta in the south.

About 100 million people live in Vietnam, speaking Vietnamese, a tonal language written in a Latin alphabet with added marks. Hanoi in the north is the capital; Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, in the south is the largest city and its business hub.

Vietnam is a socialist republic led by the Communist Party. Since economic reforms in 1986 it has grown rapidly, making clothing, phones and electronics, and it is one of the world's largest exporters of rice and coffee.
content.landAndNature: Mountains and hills cover about three-quarters of Vietnam, rising to Fansipan at 3,147 meters in the northwest, where terraced rice fields wrap the slopes in green and gold steps. Ha Long Bay in the north holds nearly 2,000 limestone islands and pillars standing in emerald water, and beneath the mountains of Phong Nha lies Son Doong, the largest known cave passage in the world, big enough to hold a skyscraper and containing its own jungle and clouds. The Mekong delta in the south is a maze of channels, floating markets and paddies. Monsoon rains and typhoons hit the coast. Rare wildlife includes the saola, a forest antelope-like animal unknown to science until 1992, plus langurs, gibbons and Asian elephants.
content.peopleAndCulture: Vietnamese food is fresh and herb-heavy: pho, a beef or chicken noodle soup, banh mi sandwiches in crisp baguettes, spring rolls, and coffee thick with condensed milk, dripped slowly through a metal filter. Motorbikes flow through city streets in enormous numbers. Tet, the lunar new year, is the biggest holiday, when people return home, clean their houses, settle debts and give lucky money in red envelopes. Water puppetry, invented by delta farmers centuries ago, has carved puppets dancing on a flooded stage while musicians play. The ao dai, a long silk tunic over trousers, is worn at ceremonies. Soccer draws huge crowds, and the martial art vovinam started here. Fifty-four recognized ethnic groups give northern highlands their own dress, languages and festivals.
content.history: Bronze drums from the Dong Son culture date back more than 2,000 years. China ruled the north for about a thousand years, leaving deep influence, until Vietnamese forces won independence in 938. Dynasties then held off repeated invasions, including Mongol fleets defeated by stakes hidden in a riverbed. France colonized Vietnam in the 1800s, joining it to French Indochina. After Japanese occupation in World War II, Ho Chi Minh declared independence in 1945 and the Viet Minh defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The country was divided at the 17th parallel, and the Vietnam War followed between the communist north and the American-backed south; millions died before the north won and reunified the country in 1975. Reforms from 1986, called Doi Moi, opened the economy and living standards rose quickly.
funFacts: Son Doong cave in Vietnam is the largest known cave passage on Earth, with its own jungle, river and clouds.
Vietnam is the world's second-largest coffee exporter, and most of it is robusta grown in the central highlands.
Water puppets perform waist-deep in a pond, controlled by puppeteers hidden behind a bamboo screen.
The Cu Chi tunnels near Ho Chi Minh City run for over 200 kilometers, with kitchens and hospitals underground.
Vietnamese uses a Latin alphabet with accent marks for six tones, unlike most of its neighbors' writing systems.

content.tagline: Volcano islands where land diving began
content.overview:
Vanuatu is a Y-shaped chain of about 80 islands in the South Pacific, roughly 1,750 kilometers east of Australia and north of New Caledonia. Around 65 islands are inhabited, and the total land area is about 12,200 km², a little smaller than Connecticut, scattered over a long stretch of ocean.

About 320,000 people live here. Vanuatu has three official languages: Bislama, an expressive creole built largely from English words, plus English and French, and more than 100 local languages, giving it one of the highest numbers of languages per person on Earth. Port Vila, on Efate island, is the capital.

Vanuatu is a parliamentary republic. Most families grow yams, taro and kava and fish the reefs, while tourism and copra are the main exports. The country sits on the Ring of Fire, with active volcanoes, frequent earthquakes and some of the most damaging cyclones in the Pacific.
content.landAndNature: The islands are volcanic and steep, wrapped in rainforest and fringed with reef. Mount Yasur on Tanna is one of the world's most accessible active volcanoes: visitors can stand on the crater rim at night and watch it throw glowing rock into the air, as it has done almost continuously for centuries. Ambrym holds lava lakes, and underwater volcanoes rumble offshore. Cyclones can be severe; Cyclone Pam devastated the country in 2015. Coral reefs support turtles, dugongs and clouds of fish, and the coconut crab, the largest land arthropod in the world, can crack coconuts with its claws. Millipedes, flying foxes and the incubator bird, which buries its eggs in warm volcanic soil to hatch, live in the forests.
content.peopleAndCulture: Ni-Vanuatu society is organized by custom, called kastom, which governs land, ceremony and rank. On Pentecost island, men build tall wooden towers and dive head-first with only vines tied to their ankles, a yam-harvest ritual called naghol that inspired modern bungee jumping. Sand drawing, in which artists trace continuous patterns in sand to tell stories, is recognized by UNESCO. Kava, a drink made from a pepper plant root, is shared at dusk in quiet nakamal meeting places. Pigs with curved tusks are traditional wealth, and one appears on the flag. Laplap, grated root vegetable baked in leaves with coconut cream, is the national dish. Soccer and cricket are popular, and string bands play at village celebrations.
content.history: Lapita voyagers reached these islands about 3,000 years ago, and pottery and a burial site on Efate record their arrival. European contact began with Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós in 1606, followed by James Cook, who named the group the New Hebrides in 1774. In the 1800s blackbirding ships took thousands of islanders to work on plantations in Australia and Fiji, often by force, and introduced diseases killed a large share of the population. From 1906 Britain and France governed the islands jointly in an unusual arrangement called a condominium, with two of nearly everything, including two police forces and two school systems. Independence came on July 30, 1980, and the country took the name Vanuatu, meaning roughly 'our land forever'.
funFacts: Bungee jumping was inspired by naghol, the Pentecost island ritual where men dive from towers with vines tied to their ankles.
Vanuatu has more languages per person than any other country, over 100 for about 320,000 people.
Mount Yasur has been erupting almost continuously for hundreds of years and can be visited on foot.
The coconut crab, found here, can grow a leg span of about a meter and climbs trees to cut down coconuts.
In Bislama, a helicopter is 'mixmaster blong Jesus' and a piano 'bigfala bokis we i gat waet tut mo blak tut'.

content.tagline: Cradle of Polynesian voyaging traditions
content.overview:
Samoa lies in the middle of the South Pacific, roughly halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii. Two large volcanic islands, Savai'i and Upolu, hold almost everyone, with several small islands nearby. The land totals about 2,840 km², a little smaller than Luxembourg, and it is green, steep and edged with reef.

About 220,000 people live in Samoa, speaking Samoan and English. Apia, on the north coast of Upolu, is the capital and only real town, a line of shops, churches and a busy market along a curved harbor.

Samoa is a parliamentary republic whose system blends elected government with the authority of matai, the chiefs who head extended families. Nearly all land is held by families rather than sold, and village life, church and family duty shape daily routines. Samoa was the first Pacific island nation to gain independence in the modern era, in 1962.
content.landAndNature: Both main islands are built from volcanoes, and Savai'i's Mount Silisili reaches about 1,860 meters. Savai'i's last big eruption, between 1905 and 1911, poured lava across villages, and the lava field with a church buried to its windows is still there. Rainforest covers the highlands, waterfalls spill into pools, and blowholes at Alofaaga shoot seawater high into the air through lava tubes. The To Sua ocean trench on Upolu is a deep garden sinkhole filled with clear seawater, reached by a long ladder. Coral reefs ring the coasts, and the tooth-billed pigeon, or manumea, Samoa's national bird and the closest living relative of the extinct dodo, is now critically endangered.
content.peopleAndCulture: Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, guides life: respect for elders, service to family, and ceremony. Villages are built around a malae, an open green where meetings and cricket are played, with open-sided fale houses shaded by thatch or tin. Tatau, the traditional tattoo applied by hand with combs of bone and wood, covers a man from waist to knee and takes days of painful work; women wear the finer malu. Feasts are cooked in an umu, an above-ground oven of hot stones, with taro, breadfruit, palusami, coconut cream baked in taro leaves, and fish. Rugby is a passion, and Samoans play for national and overseas teams in numbers far beyond the country's size. The siva is a graceful dance of hands and story.
content.history: Polynesians settled Samoa about 3,000 years ago, and the islands became a center from which voyagers sailed to Tonga, Fiji and beyond. Powerful chiefly titles and long rivalries shaped its politics for centuries. European missionaries arrived in the 1830s and Christianity spread quickly. Germany, Britain and the United States competed for the islands, and in 1899 they were split: the west went to Germany, the east became American Samoa. New Zealand took the German part in 1914 and administered it for decades. In 1918 a ship from New Zealand brought influenza that killed about a fifth of the population. The nonviolent Mau movement pressed for self-rule, and Samoa became independent on January 1, 1962. In 2011 the country skipped December 30 entirely to move west across the international date line.
funFacts: Samoa jumped from December 29 to December 31 in 2011, deleting a whole day to be on the same side of the date line as Australia and New Zealand.
Traditional Samoan tattooing is done by hand with bone combs and takes many painful days to complete.
Author Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years in Samoa and is buried on a hilltop above Apia.
Samoa switched from driving on the right to driving on the left in 2009, one of very few countries ever to change sides.
Samoan cricket, kilikiti, uses a three-sided bat and can involve entire villages on the field at once.

content.tagline: Tower houses on ancient Arabian hills
content.overview:
Yemen occupies the southwestern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, where the Red Sea meets the Arabian Sea, bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman and facing Africa across a narrow strait. It covers about 528,000 km², roughly the size of France, with mountains, desert and the island of Socotra far out in the Arabian Sea.

About 34 million people live in Yemen, speaking Arabic. Sana'a, the capital, sits on a high plateau at about 2,250 meters, and its old city is famous for tall tower houses of brown brick trimmed with white gypsum patterns around the windows.

Yemen is a republic, but since 2014 it has been divided by civil war between rival authorities, with several foreign countries involved. The fighting has wrecked the economy and caused one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, leaving millions short of food, clean water and medical care. Yemen is also among the oldest centers of civilization in Arabia.
content.landAndNature: A spine of mountains runs down the west, catching monsoon rain and allowing terraced farms to climb the slopes in narrow stone steps built over centuries; Jabal an-Nabi Shu'ayb, at about 3,666 meters, is the highest peak in Arabia. East of the mountains the land falls away into the sands of the Rub al Khali, and the Hadhramaut is a deep desert valley with mud-brick towns. Socotra island, about 350 kilometers offshore, is one of the strangest places on Earth: a third of its plants grow nowhere else, including the dragon's blood tree, an umbrella-shaped tree whose red sap was once traded as a dye and medicine. Arabian leopards, ibex and hundreds of migrating bird species pass through.
content.peopleAndCulture: Yemeni architecture is distinctive: mud-brick skyscrapers in Shibam rise up to eight stories and are centuries old, and Sana'a's decorated houses have stained-glass fanlights that glow at dusk. Saltah, a bubbling stew topped with fenugreek froth and eaten with flatbread, is the national dish, and Yemeni honey and coffee are prized worldwide; the port of Mocha gave its name to a kind of coffee. Many men wear a curved dagger called a jambiya in a wide belt. Afternoons often involve chewing qat leaves in gatherings, a widespread social custom that uses a great deal of the country's scarce water. Yemeni poetry contests and the dances of different regions are strong traditions.
content.history: Southern Arabia grew rich on frankincense and myrrh, and the kingdom of Saba, linked to the biblical Queen of Sheba, built the Marib dam around 2,700 years ago, an engineering feat that watered a large oasis for over a thousand years. Later kingdoms traded with Rome and India. Islam arrived in the 600s. Yemen was long divided: the Ottoman empire and local imams contested the north, while Britain ruled the port of Aden from 1839 as a coaling station for ships to India. North Yemen became a republic after a 1962 civil war; South Yemen became independent in 1967 and took a socialist path. The two united in 1990. Conflict returned, and since 2014 the country has been split by war between the Houthi movement and the internationally recognized government and its allies.
funFacts: Shibam's mud-brick tower houses, up to eight stories high and 500 years old, are nicknamed the Manhattan of the desert.
The dragon's blood tree of Socotra looks like an upturned umbrella and bleeds red sap when cut.
The coffee drink called mocha is named after Yemen's Red Sea port of Mocha, once the world's main coffee harbor.
The Marib dam, built about 2,700 years ago, watered farmland for more than a thousand years before it finally broke.
About a third of Socotra's plant species exist nowhere else on Earth, earning it the name Galapagos of the Indian Ocean.

content.tagline: Rainbow nation at Africa's southern tip
content.overview:
South Africa fills the southern end of the continent, where the cold Atlantic and warm Indian oceans meet around the Cape of Good Hope. It is about twice the size of Texas and wraps completely around the small mountain kingdom of Lesotho. Unusually, it has three capitals: Pretoria is the administrative capital, parliament sits in Cape Town, and the highest court of appeal is in Bloemfontein. Johannesburg, built on the world's richest goldfields, is the largest city.

About 60 million people live here. The country recognizes twelve official languages: eleven spoken ones, among them Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and English, plus South African Sign Language, added in 2023. Many people switch between three or four languages in a single day. South Africa is a parliamentary republic, and its 1996 constitution is admired worldwide for its bill of rights. Mining, farming and tourism drive the economy. South Africans call their country the rainbow nation, though wide gaps between rich and poor remain from the apartheid era.
content.landAndNature: A high inland plateau called the highveld drops to the coast down a steep rim of mountains, the Great Escarpment, whose grandest stretch is the Drakensberg, rising above 3,400 meters. Red Kalahari sands cover the northwest, and the Karoo, a dry scrubland of flat-topped hills, fills the interior. Table Mountain stands flat above Cape Town, often draped in a cloud that locals call the tablecloth. The Cape floral kingdom is the smallest and richest of the world's plant kingdoms, with roughly 9,000 species of fynbos, most growing nowhere else. Kruger National Park, about the size of Wales, protects lions, elephants, rhinos, leopards and buffalo, and southern right whales calve along the coast each winter.
content.peopleAndCulture: South Africa's peoples include Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, Tswana, Venda and Tsonga communities, descendants of Dutch and British settlers, and families of Indian, Malay and mixed heritage. A braai, or barbecue over wood coals, is a national ritual, served with boerewors sausage and pap, a maize porridge; Cape Malay curries and Durban's bunny chow, a curry served in a hollowed loaf, show the country's mixed kitchens. Soccer is the most popular sport, and South Africa hosted the 2010 World Cup; the Springboks have won the rugby World Cup four times. Gumboot dancing began in the mines, and kwaito and amapiano music came out of the townships.
content.history: Southern Africa holds some of the oldest human fossils, and San hunter-gatherers painted its rock shelters for thousands of years. Bantu-speaking farmers moved south about 1,800 years ago. Dutch settlers founded a supply station at the Cape in 1652, followed by British rule, wars against the Zulu kingdom and the Boer republics, and a gold and diamond rush that built Johannesburg. In 1948 the government imposed apartheid, a system of laws that separated people by race and stripped the Black majority of their rights. Protests, strikes and international pressure grew for decades, and leaders such as Nelson Mandela were imprisoned for years. Apartheid was dismantled in the early 1990s, and in 1994 all South Africans voted together for the first time, electing Mandela president.
funFacts: South Africa is the only country with three capital cities, splitting its government between Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
The world's first successful human heart transplant was carried out in Cape Town by Christiaan Barnard in 1967.
Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison and became president four years after his release in 1990.
South Africa gave up its nuclear weapons in the early 1990s, the only country ever to dismantle an arsenal it had built.
The Cape Peninsula alone contains more plant species than the whole of Britain, and most grow nowhere else on Earth.
Table Mountain is far older than the Himalayas or the Alps, formed hundreds of millions of years ago.

content.tagline: Thundering water and copper hills
content.overview:
Zambia is a landlocked country in south-central Africa, shaped a little like a butterfly and about the size of Texas. It borders eight countries, one of the highest totals on the continent, and shares Victoria Falls with Zimbabwe on the Zambezi River, the river that gives the country its name. Lusaka, the capital, stands on a high plateau in the south-center.

About 20 million people live in Zambia, in more than 70 ethnic groups. English is the official language, used in schools and government, while Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga and Lozi are the main languages spoken at home. Zambia is a republic. Copper has shaped the country for a century: the Copperbelt in the north is one of the world's major mining regions, and the metal still earns most of Zambia's export income. Farming, especially maize, feeds most families, and vast national parks draw visitors who explore them on foot.
content.landAndNature: Zambia is mostly high savanna plateau, between roughly 1,000 and 1,400 meters up, which takes the edge off the tropical heat. The Zambezi crosses the west and south and drops 108 meters over Victoria Falls in a curtain more than 1.7 kilometers wide; the spray rises hundreds of meters, and the local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means the smoke that thunders. Lake Kariba, formed by damming the Zambezi, is one of the largest reservoirs on Earth. The Bangweulu swamps hold shoebill storks and the water-loving black lechwe antelope. South Luangwa National Park is known for leopards, elephants and guided walking safaris.
content.peopleAndCulture: Nshima, a thick maize porridge, is eaten by hand with relish dishes of greens, beans, fish or chicken at nearly every meal. Kapenta, tiny dried fish netted from Lake Tanganyika and Lake Kariba, is a common source of protein. Ceremonies mark the year across the regions, and the most spectacular is the Kuomboka, when the Lozi king travels by decorated barge from the flooding Zambezi plain to higher ground, escorted by drummers and dozens of paddlers. Soccer is the national sport, and Zambia's women's team has played at the Olympics and the World Cup. Kalindula music and rumba play in buses and markets.
content.history: People have lived here a very long time; the Broken Hill skull, found at Kabwe in 1921, belonged to an early human species and is roughly 300,000 years old. Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers settled the plateau, and kingdoms such as the Lozi and the Bemba took shape. In the late 1800s the British South Africa Company, led by Cecil Rhodes, claimed the territory, which became the colony of Northern Rhodesia, and copper mining boomed from the 1920s. Independence came on October 24, 1964, under Kenneth Kaunda, who governed for 27 years. Zambia sheltered liberation movements from neighboring countries, returned to multiparty elections in 1991, and has changed governments peacefully since.
funFacts: Victoria Falls is neither the tallest nor the widest waterfall, but together its height and width make the largest sheet of falling water on Earth.
When the river is low, swimmers sit in the Devil's Pool, a rock basin right at the lip of Victoria Falls.
Zambia borders eight countries, one of the highest numbers anywhere in Africa.
The Kuomboka ceremony moves the Lozi king by decorated barge whenever the Zambezi floods his palace grounds.
The shoebill of Zambia's Bangweulu swamps stands over a meter tall and has a bill shaped like a wooden clog.

content.tagline: Stone ruins, big skies, great falls
content.overview:
Zimbabwe is a landlocked country in southern Africa, a little larger than Montana, spread across a high plateau between the Zambezi River in the north and the Limpopo in the south. The Zambezi plunges over Victoria Falls on the border with Zambia, and Lake Kariba, one of the world's largest reservoirs, stretches along the same frontier. Harare, the capital, sits on cool high ground in the northeast.

About 16 million people live in Zimbabwe. English is an official language used in schools and government, alongside Shona and Ndebele, which most people speak at home; the constitution recognizes sixteen languages in all, including sign language. Zimbabwe is a republic. The country takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, a medieval city whose name means houses of stone, and its national emblem is a soapstone bird carved there centuries ago. Mining, tobacco farming and tourism are the main industries.
content.landAndNature: Most of Zimbabwe lies on the highveld, a broad plateau above 1,200 meters where the air stays pleasant most of the year. The Eastern Highlands along the Mozambique border are cooler and often misty, with pine forests, tea estates and Mount Nyangani, the highest point at 2,592 meters. Hotter, lower country spreads to the south. Balancing rocks, huge granite boulders left stacked by erosion, stand across the country and appear on the banknotes. Hwange National Park holds one of Africa's largest elephant populations, along with lions, giraffes and painted wild dogs. Baobab trees, some over a thousand years old, store water in their swollen trunks.
content.peopleAndCulture: Sadza, a stiff maize porridge, is the daily food, eaten with relish of vegetables, beans or stewed beef. Zimbabwean sculptors have made the country famous: Shona stone carvers shape serpentine and springstone into smooth human and animal forms shown in galleries worldwide. Music centers on the mbira, a thumb piano of metal keys played inside a gourd, whose rippling patterns accompany ceremonies honoring ancestors; chimurenga music grew out of those rhythms. Soccer is the biggest sport, and Zimbabwe's cricket team plays international matches. The swimmer Kirsty Coventry won seven Olympic medals, more than any other African swimmer.
content.history: Farming and cattle-keeping peoples built Great Zimbabwe between roughly 1100 and 1450, a city of mortarless stone walls that traded gold and ivory with the Indian Ocean coast; perhaps 10,000 people lived there at its height. Shona and later Ndebele states ruled the plateau afterward. In the 1890s Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company seized the land, which became the colony of Southern Rhodesia, and white settlers took the best farmland. A white minority government declared independence in 1965, and a liberation war followed until majority rule and recognized independence came on April 18, 1980, with Robert Mugabe leading. He governed for 37 years, during which land seizures and hyperinflation wrecked the economy, and he was removed in 2017.
funFacts: Zimbabwe printed a 100-trillion-dollar banknote during hyperinflation in 2008; it is now sold mainly as a souvenir.
The walls of Great Zimbabwe were built without any mortar, the stones fitted so tightly they have stood for 700 years.
The Zimbabwe bird, carved from soapstone at Great Zimbabwe long ago, appears on the national flag and coins.
Hwange National Park shelters tens of thousands of elephants, one of the largest concentrations anywhere in Africa.
Spray from Victoria Falls can be seen from 50 kilometers away, which is why the falls are called the smoke that thunders.
